statement.text:
QUESTION T3 [10 pts]. Chasing the absolute zero

A refrigeration cycle must be carried out by a system with characteristics appropriate for the temperatures to be achieved. One hundred years ago, in 1926, the chemist William Giauque and, independently, the physicist Peter Debye proposed paramagnetic salts as ideal systems for lowering temperatures far below $1\,\mathrm{K}$. Indeed, beginning in the following decade, temperatures as low as $0.0044\,\mathrm{K}$ were achieved (Wander de Haas and Gerrit Wiersma, 1935, Leiden Cryogenic Laboratories). In this question, the paramagnetic Carnot refrigeration cycle is studied.

Consider a torus with mean radius $R$ and inner radius $r$ made of a homogeneous, isotropic paramagnetic material, around which an insulated conducting wire is wound, with its ends connected to an external voltage source (emf), as shown in figure 3a. The resistance of the wire is so low that energy losses due to the heating of the wire can be neglected. The winding is dense, with $N$ turns in total, and it is assumed that $r\ll R$, so that the fields $\vec{H}$ and $\vec{B}$ and the magnetization $\vec{M}$ have approximately constant magnitudes throughout the torus. Let $V$ and $A$ be the volume and the cross-section area of the torus. Hereinafter, the abbreviation Pm-T is used to refer to the paramagnetic torus.

In paramagnetic materials, $\vec{M}$ is parallel to $\vec{H}$ and the following relation holds:

$$\vec{B}=\mu_0\vec{H}+\mu_0\vec{M}.$$

Energy transfer sign convention: in this problem, Work ($W$) and Heat ($Q$) are considered positive when they flow into the system, and negative when they flow out.

T3-A [1.0 pts]. Work in the Pm-T

Hint: in magnetic materials, $\oint_C\vec{H}\cdot d\vec{\ell}=I_C$, where $I_C$ is the net free current passing through the area bounded by the closed curve $C$.

T3-A1 [0.2 pts]. Let $H$ be the magnitude of $\vec{H}$ in the torus. Write $H$ in terms of $N$, $A$, $V$ and the instantaneous electric current $I$ in the wire.

T3-A2 [0.6 pts]. Let $dW_{emf}$ be the work that the external voltage source performs to change the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ by $dB$. Write $dW_{emf}$ in terms of $V$, $H$, and $dB$.

T3-A3 [0.2 pts]. The total work done by the voltage source, $dW_{emf}$, can be divided in two parts: the work that would be performed to change the magnetic field if the toroid had a vacuum core, $dW_{vac}$, and the work done on the paramagnetic material itself, $dW$. Write $dW$ in terms of $\mu_0$, $H$, $V$ and $dM$.

T3-B [3.0 pts]. Heat and temperature in the Pm-T

The following table compares two thermodynamic systems: the ideal gas and the Pm-T. Use this information and your answer to question T3-A3 to solve the following questions. This information will also be used in part C. If you did not find an answer for $dW$ in question T3-A3, you may use $dW=\alpha V\mu_0H\,dM$ where $\alpha$ is a number. The volume $V$ of the paramagnetic torus is constant, so that there is no work due to pressure. Below, $T$ is the temperature in all instances.

In order to continuously lower the temperature of a body with constant heat capacity $C_c$, Carnot cycles are allowed to occur over time in such a way that the power $P$ transferred to the refrigerator remains constant. It is then assumed that the temperature $T_h$ of the hot reservoir remains constant and that in each operating cycle the temperature $T_c$ of the cooled body decreases by $dT_c$, satisfying the relation $dQ_c/dQ_h=T_c/T_h$. If at $t=0$ we have $T_c=T_0$, determine the time $t$ that the Carnot refrigerator must operate for the cooled body to reach a temperature $T<T_0$. solution.text:
SOLUTION T3 [10 pts]. Chashing abolute zero

T3-A [1.0 points]

T1-A1 [0.2 pts]. Field $\vec{H}$ inside the torus is almost entirely confined to its core, forming concentric circumferential circles. Therefore, from magnetic circuital law $\oint_C\vec{H}\cdot d\vec{\ell}=I_C$ we have $H\cdot2\pi R=NI$. Dividing and multiplying by $A=\pi r^2$ yields to

$$H=\frac{NI}{2\pi R}\frac{A}{\pi r^2}=\frac{NIA}{V}.$$

T3-A2 [0.6 pts]. When $I$ is changed, there is induced an emf $\mathcal{E}_{ind}$. Thus, since

$$\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{E}_{ind}=\mathrm{resistance}\times I\approx0,$$

from Faraday's law of induction, the work done by the external emf is given by

$$dW_{emf}=\mathcal{E}\,dq=-\mathcal{E}_{ind}I\,dt=\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}I\,dt=I\,d\Phi_B,$$

where $dq$ is the quantity of electric charge flowing during the time interval $dt$ and $\Phi_B=NAB$ is the flux of the field $\vec{B}$ inside the torus. Therefore,

$$dW_{emf}=NIA\,dB=VH\,dB.$$

T3-A3 [0.2 pts]. Since $\vec{B}$, $\vec{H}$ and $\vec{M}$ are paralell vectors, from $\vec{B}=\mu_0\vec{H}+\mu_0\vec{M}$ we get

$$dB=\mu_0\,dH+\mu_0\,dM,$$

from which, after substitution in the answer of question T3-A2, yields to

$$dW_{emf}=\mu_0VH\,dH+\mu_0VH\,dM.$$

Hence,

$$dW=\mu_0VH\,dM.$$

T3-B [3.0 pts]

T3-B1 [1.5 pts]. The first law of thermodynamics for the torus is $dU=dW+dQ=\mu_0VH\,dM+C\,dT$. At constant $M$, we have $dU=C_M\,dT=n\lambda\,dT/T^2$, i. e., $U$ depends only on $T$. Hence, for isothermal processes, $dQ=-dW=-\mu_0VH\,dM$. Furthermore, from the equation of state we have for isothermal processes that $TV\,dM=nK\,dH$ and then

$$dQ=-\mu_0VH\left(\frac{nK}{TV}\,dH\right)=-\mu_0\frac{nK}{T}H\,dH.$$

Integration from $H_i$ to $H_f$ gives

$$Q=-\mu_0\frac{nK}{T}\frac{H_f^2-H_i^2}{2}.$$

Note: This is proportional to the volume because it has the number of moles.

T3-B2 [1.5 pts]. For adiabatic processes, the first law yields to $dU=dW$ and then

$$\frac{n\lambda}{T^2}\,dT=\mu_0VH\,dM=\mu_0V\frac{TMV}{nK}\,dM,$$

where we have used the equation of state to substitute $H$. Separating variables we have

$$\frac{n\lambda}{T^3}\,dT=\mu_0\frac{V^2}{nK}M\,dM,$$

and hence, after integration from $(T_i,M_i)$ to $(T_f,M_f)$,

$$\frac{n\lambda}{2}\left(\frac{1}{T_i^2}-\frac{1}{T_f^2}\right)=\mu_0\frac{V^2}{nK}\frac{M_f^2-M_i^2}{2}.$$

Since $M=nKH/TV$, this equation simplifies to

$$\frac{\lambda}{T_i^2}-\frac{\lambda}{T_f^2}=\mu_0K\left(\frac{H_f^2}{T_f^2}-\frac{H_i^2}{T_i^2}\right),$$

from which

$$\frac{T_f^2}{T_i^2}=\frac{\lambda+\mu_0KH_f^2}{\lambda+\mu_0KH_i^2}.$$

Hence

$$\Delta T=T_f-T_i=T_i\left(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda+\mu_0KH_f^2}{\lambda+\mu_0KH_i^2}}-1\right).$$

T3-C [6.0 pts]

T3-C1 [0.2 pts].

T3-C2 [1.5 pts]. In the Carnot cycle

$$\frac{Q_c}{Q_h}=\frac{T_c}{T_h}.$$

Particularly, for the Carnot cycle of paramagnetic refrigeration, we have $Q_c=|Q_{2\to3}|=Q_{2\to3}$ and $Q_h=|Q_{4\to1}|=-Q_{4\to1}$. From the answer to question T3-B1,

$$Q_c=-\mu_0\frac{nK}{T_c}\frac{H_3^2-H_2^2}{2}=\mu_0\frac{nK}{T_c}\frac{H_2^2-H_3^2}{2},$$

$$Q_h=-\left(-\mu_0\frac{nK}{T_h}\frac{H_1^2-H_4^2}{2}\right)=\mu_0\frac{nK}{T_h}\frac{H_1^2-H_4^2}{2},$$

where $T_c=T_2=T_3$ and $T_h=T_4=T_1$ are the respective temperatures of the isothermal processes $2\to3$ and $4\to1$. Therefore, after substitution and simplification in the Carnot identity, we have

$$\frac{T_h}{T_c}\frac{H_2^2-H_3^2}{H_1^2-H_4^2}=\frac{T_c}{T_h},\qquad\frac{H_2^2-H_3^2}{T_c^2}=\frac{H_1^2-H_4^2}{T_h^2}.$$

Since, by the equation of state, $M=nKH/TV$, we get

$$M_2^2-M_3^2=M_1^2-M_4^2,\qquad M_1=\sqrt{M_2^2-M_3^2+M_4^2}.$$

T3-C3 [0.8 pts]. By substituting the given numerical values

$$Q_c=\mu_0\frac{nK}{T_c}\frac{H_2^2-H_3^2}{2}=1.29\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{J}.$$

Hence

$$\begin{aligned}|\Delta T|_{\mathrm{helium}}&=\frac{1.29\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{J}}{130\,\mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m}^{-3}\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^3\times10^2\,\mathrm{J}\cdot\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{K}^{-1}}\\&=\frac{1.29}{1.30}\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{K}=9.92\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K}.\end{aligned}$$

Hence

$$T_f=T_i-|\Delta T|=1.00\,\mathrm{K}-0.00992\,\mathrm{K}=0.99008\,\mathrm{K}.$$

T3-C4 [2.0 pts]. From the Carnot cycle identity $dQ_c/dQ_h=T_c/T_h$ and the first law in differential form $dQ_h=dW+dQ_c$, we have

$$\frac{dW+dQ_c}{dQ_c}=\frac{dW}{dQ_c}+1=-\frac{P\,dt}{C_c\,dT_c}+1=\frac{T_h}{T_c},$$

where $dW=P\,dt$ and $dQ_c=-C_c\,dT_c$ have been used. Hence, after separation of variables,

$$dt=-\frac{C_cT_h}{P}\left(\frac{dT_c}{T_c}-\frac{dT_c}{T_h}\right).$$

Integrating from $t=0$ ($T_c=T_0$) to $t$ ($T_c=T$) we get

$$t=\frac{C_cT_h}{P}\left(\ln\frac{T_0}{T}-\frac{T_0-T}{T_h}\right).$$

T3-C5 [1.5 pts]. Since $W=Pt$ and $Q_c=C_c(T_0-T)$,

$$W=Pt=C_cT_h\ln\frac{T_0}{T}-Q_c.$$

Therefore

$$\mathrm{COP}=\frac{Q_c}{W}=\left(\frac{T_h}{T_0-T}\ln\frac{T_0}{T}-1\right)^{-1}.$$

children.text: QUESTION T2 [10 pts]. Cooking with sunlight?

The redistribution of luminous flux into regions of high and low intensity due to reflection or refraction can lead to the formation of caustics: curves formed by the intersection of infinitesimally close light rays. As an example, Figure 2a shows the caustic formed by rays incident paraxially on a half-cylindrical mirror. Figure 2b shows a photograph of the caustic formed by the reflection of light on the bottom part of a coffee cup. The brightest and central point of the caustic is called the cusp, at this point, the light intensity is maximal.

children.alt: Parallel incident rays reflected by a semicircular mirror form a curved caustic and a central cusp.
Photograph of a coffee cup showing a bright caustic on its bottom surface.

children.text: Caustics have a variety of applications in science, ranging from high-precision optics and quantum optics to astrophysics. In this question, you will study the caustic formation by light reflection on a half-cylinder mirror of radius $R$, as shown in figure 2c. You will also investigate other aspects of this mirror, such as its application in solar cookers.

Throughout the problem, assume that the incident rays come from a distant external light source and are parallel to the mirror's optical axis. By symmetry, it is sufficient to study reflection in one plane. Figure 2d shows such a plane, the mirror, and the coordinate system used throughout the problem.

children.alt: Perspective view of the half-cylinder mirror with diameter 2R and an incident ray reflecting inside the curved surface.
Mirror cross-section with x and y axes, endpoints at minus R and R, and an upward incident ray at horizontal distance x.
Step graph of the reflection count N against incident coordinate x, with open and closed endpoints at plus and minus x1, x2 and x3.

children.text: Figure 2e shows the relationship between the $x$-coordinate of an incident ray and the number $N$ of reflections it undergoes, up to $N=3$. As $x$ varies over the interval $(-R,R)$, the variable $N$ varies over all natural numbers greater than or equal to 1. The maximum distance from the optical axis that allows an incident ray to be reflected by the mirror at most $N$ times is denoted $x_N$.

T2-A1 [1.5 pts]. Find the general expression for $x_N$ in the infinite sequence $x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots$ that limits the coordinates of the rays with at most $N$ reflections. Express your answer in terms of $R$ and $N$.

children.alt: Solar cooker with a half-cylinder mirror of diameter 2R and an absorbing cylinder of radius a whose centre is R over 2 from the mirror.

The mirror radius is $R$. The container radius $a$. The axes of the mirror and the container are parallel. QUESTION T2 [10 pts]. Cooking with sunlight?

The redistribution of luminous flux into regions of high and low intensity due to reflection or refraction can lead to the formation of caustics: curves formed by the intersection of infinitesimally close light rays. As an example, Figure 2a shows the caustic formed by rays incident paraxially on a half-cylindrical mirror. Figure 2b shows a photograph of the caustic formed by the reflection of light on the bottom part of a coffee cup. The brightest and central point of the caustic is called the cusp, at this point, the light intensity is maximal.

Caustics have a variety of applications in science, ranging from high-precision optics and quantum optics to astrophysics. In this question, you will study the caustic formation by light reflection on a half-cylinder mirror of radius $R$, as shown in figure 2c. You will also investigate other aspects of this mirror, such as its application in solar cookers.

Throughout the problem, assume that the incident rays come from a distant external light source and are parallel to the mirror's optical axis. By symmetry, it is sufficient to study reflection in one plane. Figure 2d shows such a plane, the mirror, and the coordinate system used throughout the problem.

T2-A [1.5 pts]. Multiple reflections

Figure 2e shows the relationship between the $x$-coordinate of an incident ray and the number $N$ of reflections it undergoes, up to $N=3$. As $x$ varies over the interval $(-R,R)$, the variable $N$ varies over all natural numbers greater than or equal to 1. The maximum distance from the optical axis that allows an incident ray to be reflected by the mirror at most $N$ times is denoted $x_N$.

T2-A1 [1.5 pts]. Find the general expression for $x_N$ in the infinite sequence $x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots$ that limits the coordinates of the rays with at most $N$ reflections. Express your answer in terms of $R$ and $N$.

solution.text:
SOLUTION T2 [10 pts]. Cooking with sunlight?

PART A [1.5 pts]. Multiple reflections

T2-A1 [1.5 pts]. For $n=1$, finding $x_1$ corresponds to considering the limiting case of the ray, shown in blue in the figure below.



In this case, the incident ray passes through point $A$, and the reflected ray, shown in red in the figure, passes exactly through point $B$ on the edge of the mirror.

Let $\theta_1$ be the angle formed by the radius passing through the reflection point $C_1$ with the vertical axis (the $y$ axis). Let $O$ be the center of the mirror.

Since the incident ray is parallel to the $y$ axis, the angle of incidence is

$$\angle OC_1A=\theta_1.$$

By the law of reflection,

$$\angle OC_1A=\angle OC_1B=\theta_1.$$

Additionally, note that the triangle $C_1BO$ is isosceles, so

$$\angle C_1BO=\theta_1.$$

Finally, summing the internal angles of the triangle $C_1BA$, we have

$$3\theta_1+\frac{\pi}{2}=\pi,$$

$$\theta_1=\frac{\pi}{6}.$$

Correspondingly, from the triangle $OC_1A$, we obtain

$$x_1=R\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{R}{2}.$$

For $n=2$, the limiting case for two reflections is shown in the figure below.



In analogy with the case $n=1$, we let $\theta_2$ be the angle between the radius passing through the reflection point $C_2$ and the mirror axis. We see that the trajectory of the reflected ray determines two isosceles triangles with a common side and a base angle of $\theta_2$. Also note that the ray's trajectory forms half of a regular pentagon. Summing over the internal angles of the two isosceles triangles and the rectangular triangle, we obtain

$$5\theta_2+\frac{\pi}{2}+\pi=3\pi,$$

which simplifies to

$$\theta_2=\frac{3\pi}{10}.$$

Correspondingly,

$$x_2=R\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}R\approx0.8R.$$

Case n=3: For completeness, we present the limiting case for 3 reflections in the figure below.



Letting $\theta_3$ be the incidence angle, we observe that the trajectory of the reflected ray determines three isosceles triangles with common sides and a base angle of $\theta_3$. Also notice that the ray's trajectory now forms half of a regular heptagon. Summing over the internal angles of the three isosceles triangles and the rectangular triangle, we obtain

$$7\theta_3+\frac{\pi}{2}+\pi=4\pi,$$

which simplifies to

$$\theta_3=\frac{5\pi}{14}$$

Correspondingly

$$x_3=R\sin\frac{5\pi}{14}\approx0.9R.$$

Generalizing the result, the limiting case for $n$ reflections corresponds to the ray with incidence angle $\theta_N$.

The trajectory of the reflected ray determines $n$ isosceles triangles with common sides and a base angle of $\theta_N$.

Also note that the ray's trajectory now forms half of a regular $2n+1$-gon. Summing over the internal angles of the $n$ isosceles triangles and the rectangular triangle determined by the incident ray, we obtain

$$(2n\theta_N+\pi)+\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta_N\right)=(n+1)\pi,$$

$$(2n+1)\theta_N+\frac{3\pi}{2}=(n+1)\pi,$$

which simplifies to

$$\theta_N=\frac{2n-1}{4n+2}\pi$$

Correspondingly

$$x_n=R\sin\frac{2N-1}{4N+2}\pi=R\cos\frac{\pi}{2N+1}$$

T2-B [4.0 pts]. Solar Cooker

T2-B1 [2.0 pts].

The limiting case is shown in the figure below.



$O_c$ is the center of the container.

$A$ is the incidence point on the $x$-axis

$B$ is the reflection point

The reflected ray is tangential to the container at the point $C$

The reflected ray crosses the $y$-axis at $D$.

As the triangle $ODB$ is isosceles,

$$\angle ODB=\pi-2\theta_{\max},$$

$$\cos\theta_{\max}=\frac{R}{2\overline{OD}}.$$

$$\overline{OD}=\frac{R}{2\cos\theta_{\max}}.$$

The triangle $O_cDC$ is rectangle

$$\begin{aligned}a&=\overline{O_cD}\sin(\pi-2\theta_{\max})\\&=\left(\overline{OD}-\frac{R}{2}\right)\sin(2\theta_{\max})\\&=\left(\frac{R}{2\cos\theta_{\max}}-\frac{R}{2}\right)\sin(2\theta_{\max})\\&=R\sin\theta_{\max}-\frac{R}{2}\sin(2\theta_{\max})\end{aligned}$$

The coefficients read

$$\alpha=R$$

$$\beta=-\frac{R}{2}$$

T2-B2 [1.5 pts]. Without the mirror:

$$P_0=2Ial,$$

where $I$ is the sunlight intensity and $l$ is the length of the cylinder.

With the mirror:

$$\begin{aligned}P&=2I\overline{OA}l\\&=2IRl\sin\theta_{\max}\end{aligned}$$

Thus

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{P}{P_0}&=\frac{2IRl\sin\theta_{\max}}{2Ial}\\&=\frac{R\sin\theta_{\max}}{R\sin\theta_{\max}(1-\cos\theta_{\max})}\end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{P}{P_0}=\frac{1}{1-\cos\theta_{\max}}.$$

Alternative answer in terms of $\alpha$ and $\beta$:

Without the mirror:

$$P_0=2Ial=2I(\alpha\sin\theta_{\max}+\beta\sin(2\theta_{\max}))l$$

where $I$ is the sunlight intensity and $l$ is the length of the cylinder.

With the mirror:

$$\begin{aligned}P&=2I\overline{OA}l\\&=2IRl\sin\theta_{\max}\end{aligned}$$

Thus

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{P}{P_0}&=\frac{2IRl\sin\theta_{\max}}{2Ial}\\&=\frac{R\sin\theta_{\max}}{\alpha\sin\theta_{\max}+\beta\sin(2\theta_{\max})}\end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{P}{P_0}=\frac{R}{\alpha+2\beta\cos\theta_{\max}}.$$

T2-B3 [0.5 pts]. If $P=5P_0$

$$5=\frac{1}{1-\cos\theta_{\max}},$$

$$\cos\theta_{\max}=\frac{4}{5},$$

$$\sin\theta_{\max}=\frac{3}{5}.$$

Finally

$$a=(1\mathrm{m})\frac{3}{5}\left(1-\frac{4}{5}\right).$$

$$a=12\,\mathrm{cm}.$$

Alternative solution parametrized in terms of $\alpha$ and $\beta$

$$a=-\frac{R\sqrt{100\beta^2-(R-5\alpha)^2}}{50\beta}$$

T2-C [4.5 pts]. Caustics and Cusp

T2-C1 [0.5 pts].



The reflected ray forms an angle $2\theta$ with the vertical axis. Therefore, the slope of the line is

$$m_A=\cot(2\theta).$$

The reflected ray intersects the $y$-axis at $C$, $\overline{OC}=b_A$, forming the isosceles triangle $OBC$. from the intersection

$$\cos\theta=\frac{R}{2b_A}.$$

$$b_A=\frac{R}{2\cos\theta}.$$

Equivalent expressions:

$$\begin{aligned}m_A&=\cot(2\theta)=\frac{1}{\tan(2\theta)}=\frac{\cot(\theta)}{2}-\frac{\tan(\theta)}{2}\\b_A&=\frac{R}{2\cos\theta}=\frac{R}{2}\sec\theta\end{aligned}$$

T2-C2 [2.0 pts].



The slope is

$$\begin{aligned}m_B&=\cot(2\theta+2\Delta\theta)\\&=\frac{\cot(2\theta)\cot(2\Delta\theta)-1}{\cot(2\theta)+\cot(2\Delta\theta)}\\&=\frac{\cot(2\theta)-\tan(2\Delta\theta)}{\cot(2\theta)\tan(2\Delta\theta)+1}\\&=(\cot(2\theta)-2\Delta\theta)(1-2\Delta\theta\cot(2\theta))+\ldots\\&=\cot(2\theta)-2\Delta\theta(1+\cot^2(2\theta))+\ldots\end{aligned}$$

Then, the first-order expansion of $m_B$ reads

$$m_B=\cot(2\theta)-2\csc^2(2\theta)\Delta\theta.$$

On the other hand, the intercept is

$$\begin{aligned}b_B&=\frac{R}{2}\sec(\theta+\Delta\theta)\\&=\frac{R}{2}\frac{\sec(\theta)\sec(\Delta\theta)}{1-\tan(\theta)\tan(\Delta\theta)}\\&=\frac{R}{2}(\sec(\theta)(1+\tan(\theta)\Delta\theta))+\ldots\end{aligned}$$

and the first-order expansion reads

$$b_B=\frac{R}{2}\sec(\theta)(1+\tan(\theta)\Delta\theta)$$

Equivalent expressions:

$$\begin{aligned}m_B&=\cot(2\theta)-2\csc^2(2\theta)\Delta\theta\\&=\frac{1}{2}\csc^2(2\theta)(\sin(4\theta)-4\Delta\theta)\\&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\cot(\theta)-\tan(\theta)-\csc^2(\theta)\sec^2(\theta)\Delta\theta\right)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}b_B&=\frac{R}{2}\sec(\theta)(1+\tan(\theta)\Delta\theta)\\&=\frac{R}{2\cos(\theta)}(1+\tan(\theta)\Delta\theta)\end{aligned}$$

T2-C3 [1.0 pts].

The coordinates of the intersection point, $(X_C,Y_C)$, fulfill the following equations:

$$\begin{aligned}Y_C&=m_AX_C+b_A\\Y_C&=m_BX_C+b_B,\end{aligned}$$

Solving:

$$(X_C,Y_C)=\left(-\frac{b_A-b_B}{m_A-m_B},\frac{m_Ab_B-b_Am_B}{m_A-m_B}\right)$$

Replacing $m_B$ and $b_B$, we find:

$$(X_C,Y_C)=\left(R\sin^3(\theta),\frac{R}{2}\cos(\theta)(2-\cos(2\theta))\right)$$

Physics review note. The intermediate slope expansion in T2-C2 is corrected to $\cot(2\theta)-2[1+\cot^2(2\theta)]\Delta\theta$. The source prints $1-\tan^2(2\Delta\theta)$ in that line. Differentiating $\cot(2\theta)$ gives $-2\csc^2(2\theta)$, which agrees with the final first-order formula, caustic coordinates and cusp exponent.

$$X_C=R\sin^3(\theta)$$

$$Y_C=\frac{R}{2}\cos(\theta)(2-\cos(2\theta))$$

Equivalent expressions:

$$\begin{aligned}Y_C&=\frac{R}{2}\cos(\theta)(2-\cos(2\theta))\\&=\frac{R}{4}(3\cos(\theta)-\cos(3\theta))\\&=\frac{R}{4}(3\cos(\theta)-\cos^3(\theta)+3\sin^2(\theta)\cos(\theta))\end{aligned}$$

T2-C4 [1.0 pts]. For $\theta\ll1$, we use the approximations

$$\sin\theta\approx\theta,$$

$$\cos\theta\approx1-\frac{\theta^2}{2}.$$

Thus, near the cusp, the caustic is approximated as

$$(X_C,Y_C)\approx\left(R\theta^3,\frac{R}{4}(2+3\theta^2)\right)$$

$$(X_C,Y_C)\approx\left(R\theta^3,\frac{R}{2}+\frac{3R}{4}\theta^2\right)$$

Solving for $\theta$, we get

$$\theta=\left(\frac{X_C}{R}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}},$$

and substitute in $Y_C$

$$Y_C=\frac{R}{2}+\frac{3R}{4}\left(\frac{X_C}{R}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}$$

Comparing with

$$Y_C=v|X_C|^{p/q}+u,$$

we find

$$v=\frac{3}{4}R^{\frac{1}{3}}$$

$$u=\frac{R}{2},$$

$$p=2$$

$$q=3$$

This shows that the shape of the cusp is universal and that its tip is located at $y=\frac{R}{2}$.

QUESTION T1 [10 pts]. Three problems

This question consists of three independent problems.

T1-A [3.0 pts]. Hydrostatic gate

Two water reservoirs are separated by a vertical wall MN, as shown in the figure 1a. The left reservoir can receive water from a source. It must be ensured that the maximum possible difference between the water levels is $\Delta h = 1.41\ \mathrm{m}$. To achieve this, a slot of vertical size $a\sqrt{2}/2$ is cut in MN and sealed with a solid cubic block of side length $a$. The block has density $3\rho_0$, with $\rho_0$ the density of water. The block is fully submerged, fixed to the wall at $O$ and can rotate without friction about the axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure that passes through point $O$.

T1-A1 [3.0 pts.]

Calculate the value of $a$ that ensures the maximum permissible difference in water levels is not exceeded.

T1-B [3.5 pts]. Electron-positron pair

At a certain instant of time, a positron $e^+$ is located at a distance of $100a_0$ from an electron $e^-$. The particles are moving in such a way that their velocities are antiparallel at that instant, perpendicular to their separation, as shown in figure 1b. It is known that each particle has an angular momentum of magnitude $\mu\hbar$ with respect to the system's center of mass, where $\mu$ is a dimensionless numerical factor. Assume that the only interaction between $e^+$ and $e^-$ is electrostatic (both particles have the same mass $m$ and equal magnitude of the charge but of opposite sign). Furthermore, assume that this system remains isolated and that its dynamics are classical and non-relativistic.

The Bohr radius $a_0$ is given by $a_0=4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar^2/(me^2)$.

T1-B1 [1.0 pts.]

If $\mu=4$, the system is bound, meaning that the particles move in a closed orbit around the system's center of mass. Find the maximum separation distance between $e^+$ and $e^-$ in terms of $a_0$.

T1-B2 [2.5 pts].

If $\mu=\frac{15}{2}$, the system is unbound, meaing that the particles are no longer in closed orbit around the system's center of mass. Let $\vec{u}_\infty$ be the velocity of $e^+$ relative to $e^-$ as the separation distance between them tends to infinity. Calculate the angle between $\vec{u}_\infty$ and the initial line of motion of $e^+$. Give your answer in degrees.

Hint 1: The eccentricty $\varepsilon$ of a conic trajectory for the present case is given by

$$\varepsilon=\sqrt{1+\frac{4L^2E}{k^2e^4m}}$$

where E and L are the total energy and the magnitude of the total angular momentum, respectively. k is Coulombs constant $k=1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)$.

Hint 2: The equation of a conic in polar coordinates is

$$r=\frac{a}{1-\varepsilon\cos(\theta)}$$

T1-C [3.5 pts]. Photodissociation of ozone

A photon with angular frequency $\omega$ strikes an ozone molecule O₃ at rest, dissociating it (breaking it apart) into an oxygen molecule O₂ and an oxygen atom O, as shown in figure 1c. The photon is absorbed in this process. Let $U_i$ and $U_f$ be the ground state energies of the ozone and oxygen molecules, respectively. Assume that this system remains isolated and that its dynamics is classical (potential energies do not contribute to mass and the motion of the Oxygen atoms are non-relativistic). Use the relation $p=E/c$ for the linear momentum of the photon, where $E$ is its energy.

T1-C1 [2.5 pts].

If the angle that the momentum of the outgoing O₂ with respect to the incident photon is $\theta$, determine the minimum angular frequency $\omega_{\min}$ required for this dissociation to occur at this angle. Write your answer in terms of $\hbar$, $c$, $\theta$, $\Delta U=U_f-U_i$, and the mass $m$ of an oxygen atom.

T1-C2 [1.0 pts].

If $\theta=\pi/6$, calculate the value of $\hbar\omega_{\min}-\Delta U$. Give your answer in electronvolts (eV). Take $\Delta U=1.10\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $m=16.0\ \mathrm{amu}$.

Hint:

$$(1+x)^r=1+rx+\frac{r(r-1)}{2!}x^2+\frac{r(r-1)(r-2)}{3!}x^3+\cdots$$

solution.text:
SOLUTION T1 [10 pts]. Three problems

T1-A [3.0 pts]. Hydrostatic gate

T1-A1 [3.0 pts].

Since the dam is perfectly sealed, the area of the opening is $a\cdot(a/\sqrt{2})$:

The horizontal force exerted by the water on either side is equal to the pressure at the centroid of the cube sections on the corresponding side times the effective area, as calculated previously:

$$\Delta F=\frac{a^2}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_0g\Delta h$$

With an effective application point at the centroid of the left region of the block. The other relevant forces are the block's weight $\rho\times g\times\mathrm{vol}$, the vertical component of the force exerted by the fluid (buoyant force) $\rho_0\times g\times\mathrm{vol}$, and the force that the hinge applies to the block (which exerts no torque).

At the critical $\Delta h$, the bottom edge of the opening applies zero force to the block. For the net torque to be 0,

$$\frac{a^2}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_0g\Delta h\left(\frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)=(\rho-\rho_0)a^3g\left(\frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$$

Note: Arms are $a/(2\sqrt{2})$ from O either in the horizontal or vertical direction for pressure difference and effective weight respectively.

$$a=\frac{\rho_0}{\sqrt{2}(\rho-\rho_0)}\Delta h$$

For $\rho=3\rho_0$,

$$a=\frac{\Delta h}{2\sqrt{2}}=0.50\mathrm{m}$$

T1-B [2.5 pts]. Electron-positron pair

From the definition of angular momentum,

$$mv_0(50a_0)=\mu\hbar$$

$$v_0=\frac{\mu\hbar}{50ma_0}$$

The total energy of the system is

$$2\left(\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2\right)-\frac{ke^2}{100a_0}=\frac{ke^2}{a_0}\left(\frac{\mu^2}{50^2}-\frac{1}{100}\right)$$

T1-B1 [1.0 pts].

For $\mu=4$,

$$E=-\frac{9ke^2}{2500a_0}$$

SOLUTION 1:

At the critical separation distances, $\vec{v}\perp\vec{r}$ and $L=mvr$. The energy at $r_{\max}$ and $r_{\min}$ can be written as

$$E=2\frac{L^2}{2mr^2}-\frac{ke^2}{r}$$

Using $L=2\mu\hbar=8\hbar$ and the conservation of energy,

$$-\frac{9ke^2}{2500a_0}=\frac{64\hbar^2}{mr^2}-\frac{ke^2}{r}$$

$$\frac{ke^2}{a_0}\left(\frac{9}{2500}r^2-a_0r+64a_0^2\right)=0$$

$$r=\frac{a_0\pm\sqrt{a_0^2-\frac{576}{625}a_0^2}}{9/1250}$$

$$r=\frac{1250}{9}a_0\left(1\pm\frac{7}{25}\right)$$

The maximum separation corresponds to the solution with the plus sign,

$$r_{\max}=\frac{1600}{9}a_0$$

SOLUTION 2:

Since the energy is negative and the electrostatic force is central and proportional to $r^{-2}$, the trajectory of the particles will be elliptical with respect to the CM. The energy can be written in terms of the semi-major axis $x$ as

$$E=-\frac{ke^2}{2x}$$

$$x=\frac{1250}{9}a_0$$

Since $\vec{v}_0$ is perpendicular to the vector that connects the two particles, the initial position must correspond to either $r_{\max}$ or $r_{\min}$. The other critical distance, $r_2$ is given by the definition of $x$:

$$2x=r_0+r_2$$

$$r_2=\left(\frac{2500}{9}-100\right)a_0=\frac{1600}{9}a_0$$

Which is greater than $r_0$ and corresponds to $r_{\max}$

SOLUTION 3:

The general equation for the trajectory in polar coordinates is

$$r(\theta)=\frac{\ell}{1+\varepsilon\cos(\theta-\theta_0)}$$

with $\ell=\frac{2L^2}{mke^2}$ the semi-latus rectum and $\varepsilon$ the eccentricity, as given by the hint in question T1-B2. The maximum separation distance is reached when $\cos(\theta-\theta_0)=-1$:

$$r_{\max}=\frac{\ell}{1-\varepsilon}$$

Calculating the values of $\ell$ and $\varepsilon$,

$$\ell=\frac{2(8\hbar)^2}{mke^2}=128a_0$$

$$\varepsilon=\sqrt{1-\frac{36ke^2(8\hbar)^2}{2500a_0m(ke^2)^2}}$$

$$\varepsilon=\sqrt{1-\frac{2304}{2500}}=\frac{7}{25}$$

Replacing these values in the expression for $r_{\max}$,

$$r_{\max}=\frac{128}{1-(7/25)}a_0=\frac{1600}{9}a_0$$

T1-B2 [2.5 pts].

For $\mu=15/2$,

$$E=+\frac{ke^2}{80a_0}$$

The distance between particles follows

$$r(\theta)=\frac{\ell}{1+\varepsilon\cos(\theta-\theta_0)}$$

Since the initial position corresponds to the closest approach, it is convenient to measure the angle $\theta$ with respect to the $y$ axis so that $\cos\theta_0=1$, $\theta_0=0$.

For $r\to\infty$,

$$1+\varepsilon\cos\theta'\to0$$

$$\theta'=\arccos(-1/\varepsilon)$$

Calculating the eccentricity,

$$\varepsilon=\sqrt{1+\frac{4ke^2(15\hbar)^2}{80a_0m(ke^2)^2}}$$

$$\varepsilon=\sqrt{1+\frac{45}{4}}=\frac{7}{2}$$

Replacing this value in the expression for $\theta$,

$$\theta'=\arccos(-2/7)=106.60^\circ$$

Since this is the angle with respect to the y-axis but the initial $e^+$ velocity is directed towards the positive x-axis, heading downward

$$\theta=90^\circ-\theta'=-16.60^\circ$$

T1-C [3.5 pts]. Photodissociation of ozone

T1-C1 [2.5 pts].

SOLUTION 1: pure algebra

The momentum conservation is

$$\hbar\frac{\omega}{c}\hat{k}=\vec{p}+\vec{q},$$

where $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$ are the momentum of the O₂ and the O, respectively. Solving for $q^2$,

$$q^2=\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{c}-p\cos(\theta)\right)^2+p^2\sin^2(\theta).$$

The energy conservation reads

$$\hbar\omega=\Delta U+\frac{p^2}{4m}+\frac{q^2}{2m}$$

where $\Delta U=U_f-U_i$.

For a given $\theta$, $p$ can be written in terms of $\omega$. Replacing $q^2$ on energy balance and simplifying, we get

$$p^2-\frac{4\hbar\omega\cos(\theta)}{3c}p+\frac{2\hbar^2\omega^2}{3c^2}+\frac{4}{3}m(\Delta U-\hbar\omega)=0.$$

This gives a quadratic equation on $p$. For $p$ to be real, the discriminant must be positive.

$$\frac{16\hbar^2\omega^2\cos^2(\theta)}{9c^2}-4\left(\frac{2\hbar^2\omega^2}{3c^2}+\frac{4}{3}m(\Delta U-\hbar\omega)\right)\geq0$$

The previous bound determines $\omega_{\min}$ as the minimal root of the quadratic equation on $\omega$

$$(\cos(2\theta)-2)\hbar^2\omega^2+6mc^2\hbar\omega-6\Delta U\,mc^2=0$$

$$\omega_\pm=\frac{-6mc^2\hbar\pm\sqrt{D}}{2(\cos(2\theta)-2)\hbar^2}$$

$$D=36\hbar^2m^2c^4+24\Delta U\,mc^2\hbar^2(\cos(2\theta)-2)$$

For $0\le\theta<\pi/2$, the smaller root $\omega_+$ has nonnegative outgoing O₂ momentum. Thus, simplifying, one gets

$$\omega_{\min}=\frac{3mc^2-\sqrt{3mc^2(3mc^2+2\Delta U(\cos(2\theta)-2))}}{\hbar(2-\cos(2\theta))}$$

SOLUTION 2: Center of mass approach

Part I: Conservation laws

First, find the velocity of the center of mass. We get

$$(3mv_{\mathrm{CM}})=p_\gamma=\hbar\omega/c$$

We will use $p_\gamma$ for calculations

$$v_{\mathrm{CM}}=p_\gamma/(3m)$$

We want to relate the relative velocities in CM. We have by magnitude

$$2mv_1=mv_2$$

And $v_2$ is the single oxygen atom (the one we don't want). The energy conservation equation is

$$\begin{aligned}E_\gamma=p_\gamma c&=\frac{1}{2}(3m)v_{\mathrm{CM}}^2+\Delta U+\frac{1}{2}mv_2^2+\frac{1}{2}(2m)v_1^2\\&=\Delta U+\frac{p_\gamma^2}{6m}+\frac{1}{2}\times6m(v_1)^2\end{aligned}$$

We can now find $v_1$ in terms of $p_\gamma$.

Part 2: geometry and critical condition

We see that the set of possible velocities $\vec{v}_1$ form a circle (they have constant $v_1$). We need to consider that $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{CM}}$ and $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\vec{v}_1$ (this is the full velocity of particle 1).

If the circle of radius $v_1$ is too small there is no solution (the straight line at the angle will not intersect the circle). If the radius $v_1$ is big enough, there will always be two solutions intersecting the circle. The critical case (crossover from no solution to two) is when the circle is tangent to the straight line. This is the case we need.

In that case the triangle formed by $0$, $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{CM}}$, $\vec{v}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\vec{v}_1$ is a right triangle.

Warning: This can only happen if $\theta\leq90^\circ$. The other case will be dealt with separately.

This way

$$v_1=v_{\mathrm{CM}}\sin(\theta)$$

Replace above to find that in conservation of energy

$$p_\gamma c=\Delta U+\frac{p_\gamma^2}{6m}+\frac{p_\gamma^2\sin^2(\theta)}{3m}$$

now we can solve the quadratic equation for $p_\gamma$. We get (we need to choose the correct solution of the quadratic equation)

$$p_\gamma=\frac{3cm-\sqrt{3}\sqrt{m}\sqrt{3c^2m+2\Delta U\cos(2\theta)-4\Delta U}}{2\sin^2(\theta)+1}$$

Note: Any of the following expressions are the same:

$$2\sin^2(\theta)+1=3-2\cos^2(\theta)=2-\cos(2\theta)$$

Rewrite as the angular frequency

$$\omega_{\min}=3mc^2\left[\frac{1-\sqrt{1-\frac{2\Delta U}{3mc^2}(2\sin^2(\theta)+1)}}{(2\sin^2(\theta)+1)\hbar}\right]$$

Special case: $\theta\geq90^\circ$, this is essentially impossible to see in a brute force algebraic solution, but it is an important feature of the problem. Needs a small amount of points in this solution

For angle greater than $90^\circ$, as soon as the circle reaches the answer for $90^\circ$ it becomes big enough to allow all angles. Formula is the same with $\theta=90^\circ$.

T1-C2 [1.0 pts].

Up to second order in $\Delta U$

$$\omega_{\min}=\frac{\Delta U}{\hbar}-\frac{(\cos(2\theta)-2)\Delta U^2}{6\hbar mc^2}$$

$$\hbar\omega_{\min}-\Delta U=\frac{(2-\cos(2\theta))}{6mc^2}(\Delta U)^2$$

$$\hbar\omega_{\min}-\Delta U=2.03\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{eV}$$

Physics review notes. In T1-B2 the eccentricity calculation uses $(15\hbar)^2$, not the source's $15\hbar^2$. The angle between the two velocity directions is the nonnegative $16.60^\circ$. The displayed $-16.60^\circ$ is the signed clockwise deflection in the source drawing.

In the alternate ozone derivation, the relative kinetic energy is $3mv_1^2=p_\gamma^2\sin^2\theta/(3m)$. The source drops a factor of two in that substitution and in the final square-root argument. Both are corrected here. Put $A=3-2\cos^2\theta$ for $0\le\theta<\pi/2$. A stable equivalent expression is $$\omega_{\min}=\frac{2\Delta U}{\hbar\left[1+\sqrt{1-2A\Delta U/(3mc^2)}\right]}.$$ It tends to $\Delta U/\hbar$ in the small-recoil limit and gives the stated $2.03\times10^{-11}$ eV correction at $\theta=\pi/6$.

For $\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi$, minimizing over the nonnegative O₂ momentum puts the minimum at zero momentum. Its direction is then undefined. Use $A=3$ in the preceding expression for the infimum frequency. Every specified nonzero outgoing momentum at these angles requires a frequency strictly above that infimum. A discriminant test alone does not enforce the nonnegative-momentum condition. The original PDF remains unchanged.

\[\ddot z=\frac{2\varphi_0z}{z_0^2}\ln(r/r_0)e^{-(z/z_0)^2}.\] Since the logarithm is negative, the linear force restores z to zero and \[\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{2\varphi_0}{z_0^2}\ln(r_0/r)}.\]

Use \(a=v^2/r\). At v=160 km/s and r=5 kpc, \(a\simeq1.66\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), decreasing farther out.

children.text: In 1765, British clockmaker James Cox invented a clock whose only source of energy is the fluctuations in atmospheric pressure. Use uniform gravity \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), incompressible liquids, no surface tension, constant ambient temperature and isothermal transformations. Atmospheric pressure is uniform with height. Part A uses a thin-walled vertical cylinder, open at the bottom and closed at the top, length H=1 m, area \(S=10\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), mass m=0.5 kg, in a semi-infinite bath whose surface is z=0. The top has altitude h and internal liquid surface altitude zl. Initially h=zl=0 and no gas is trapped. Lift it slowly until its bottom reaches the bath level. Outside pressure is \(P_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

A finite cistern and two-part tube hang from cables attached to opposite sides of a mass M sliding horizontally with friction magnitude Fs and stops at x=plus or minus X. Initially x=0 and P1=0 balance. The cistern has area Sc=210 square centimetres, height 30 cm, and the total mercury volume is 5 L. Keep the tube dimensions above. Assume its bottom stays submerged and its liquid level stays inside the bulb. Let \(\xi=(S_b+S_c-S_t)F_s/(S_bS_cA)\), with St negligible compared with Sb,Sc. statement.text:
Cox's Timepiece
In 1765, British clockmaker James Cox invented a clock whose only source of energy is the fluctuations in atmospheric pressure. Use uniform gravity \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), incompressible liquids, no surface tension, constant ambient temperature and isothermal transformations. Atmospheric pressure is uniform with height. Part A uses a thin-walled vertical cylinder, open at the bottom and closed at the top, length H=1 m, area \(S=10\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), mass m=0.5 kg, in a semi-infinite bath whose surface is z=0. The top has altitude h and internal liquid surface altitude zl. Initially h=zl=0 and no gas is trapped. Lift it slowly until its bottom reaches the bath level. Outside pressure is \(P_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
A.1. Submerged-tube force

Before vapour appears, find water pressure at the top and upward force F holding the tube.
A.2. Three water temperatures

For water at 20,80,99 degrees Celsius use respectively densities 1000,970,960 kg/m cubed and saturated vapour pressures 2340,47400,99800 Pa. Determine whether F rises throughout lifting, or levels off at a height hstar. Find maximal force and any accessible hstar.
A.3. Mercury vapour correction
Replace water by mercury at 20 degrees Celsius, density 13500 kg/m cubed and Psat=0.163 Pa. Find relative error in maximal force if Psat is ignored.
B.1. Added mercury mass

Now neglect mercury vapour. A two-part tube has lower area St and height Ht=80 cm, and top bulb area Sb greater than St and height Hb=20 cm. Let ht be junction altitude. Its holding force is \((m_{tb}+m_{add})g\). Identify the mercury volume responsible for madd.
B.2. Added mass versus lift
At fixed P0 lift from fully immersed to ht=Ht. Sketch madd versus ht, including slopes and breakpoints.
B.3. Pressure-driven mass amplitude

Fix ht so the liquid is midway up the bulb at mean P0. Pressure perturbation P1 is a triangular wave of amplitude A=500 Pa and period one week. Use St=5 square centimetres and Sb=200 square centimetres. Find mass-variation amplitude while the surface stays inside the bulb.
C.1. Motion threshold

Use the original pulley diagram. A finite cistern and two-part tube hang from cables attached to opposite sides of a mass M sliding horizontally with friction magnitude Fs and stops at x=plus or minus X. Initially x=0 and P1=0 balance. The cistern has area Sc=210 square centimetres, height 30 cm, and the total mercury volume is 5 L. Keep the tube dimensions above. Assume its bottom stays submerged and its liquid level stays inside the bulb. Let \(\xi=(S_b+S_c-S_t)F_s/(S_bS_cA)\), with St negligible compared with Sb,Sc. Find the threshold above which the mass always remains at rest.
C.2. Tension at the stop
Temporarily block M at x=X and set P1=0. Find the resultant cable tension along x.
C.3. Operating regimes
For xi below threshold define \(\lambda=2(S_b-S_t)\rho gX/(S_bA)\simeq2\rho gX/A\). Classify the two regimes and sketch x(t)/X over three weeks against the triangular pressure wave. Neglect switching time compared with one week.
C.4. Optimal recovered energy
In the switching steady regime, W is the frictional work per pressure period. With Sb approximately Sc and negligible St, optimize Fs and X and find Wstar numerically.
C.5. Atmospheric work and efficiency
Find the atmospheric pressure work in the optimal cycle and the ratio of recovered work to it. A P-V plot may help.

children.text: Hydrostatic balance gives \(P_w=P_0-\rho gh\). The top cap experiences downward pressure difference \((P_0-P_w)S\). Thus \(F=mg+\rho gSh\), upward along z.

Vapour appears when \(P_w=P_{sat}\), so \(h_*= (P_0-P_{sat})/(\rho g)\). If this exceeds H, force rises to \((m+\rho SH)g\). At 20 C, hstar=9.97 m, inaccessible, Fmax=14.7 N. At 80 C, hstar=5.53 m, inaccessible, Fmax=14.4 N. At 99 C, hstar=0.0213 m, accessible, and Fmax=mg+S(P0-Psat)=5.10 N. The first two follow behaviour A, the third behaviour B.
The true maximum is \(mg+S(P_0-P_{sat})\). Neglecting vapour increases it by \(SP_{sat}\), giving \[\epsilon=\frac{SP_{sat}}{mg+S(P_0-P_{sat})}\simeq1.55\times10^{-6}.\]

It is the mercury inside the tube above the outside bath surface. Shade that region up to the internal liquid level. The empty tube weight is already included in mtb. Mercury below the bath surface does not contribute added load in the thin-wall model.

Let \(z_*=P_0/(\rho g)=0.756\,\mathrm m\). The four segments are \[m_{add}=\begin{cases}\rho S_b(h_t+H_b),&-H_b\le h_t\le0,\\\rho(S_bH_b+S_th_t),&0\le h_t\le z_*-H_b,\\\rho[S_th_t+S_b(z_*-h_t)],&z_*-H_b\le h_t\le z_*,\\\rho S_tz_*,&z_*\le h_t\le H_t.\end{cases}\] Slopes are \(\rho S_b,\rho S_t,-\rho(S_b-S_t),0\). They join continuously at 0, zstar-Hb, zstar.
The internal level changes by \(P_1/(\rho g)\), so added mass changes by \(S_bP_1/g\). Its amplitude is \(S_bA/g=1.020\,\mathrm{kg}\).

At fixed x, pressure P1 transfers apparent load between containers. Hydrostatic balance and volume conservation give the net tension \[T_P=\frac{2S_bS_c}{S_b+S_c-S_t}P_1.\] Its maximum magnitude is this coefficient times A. Static friction can hold throughout if xi is greater than 2. Thus \(\xi_*=2\). Equality is the marginal threshold.

The container displacements are opposite because of the cables. Solve equal liquid-level shift and mercury-volume conservation to find the cistern apparent-mass change \(-2\rho S_c(S_b-S_t)X/(S_b+S_c-S_t)\). Its opposite is the tube load change, hence \[T=\frac{4S_c(S_b-S_t)}{S_b+S_c-S_t}\rho gX\simeq\frac{4S_bS_c}{S_b+S_c}\rho gX.\] It is positive, towards the same stop, not a restoring force.

General tension is \(T=C_P[P_1+2\rho g(S_b-S_t)x/S_b]\), with \(C_P=2S_bS_c/(S_b+S_c-S_t)\). Initially motion starts when P1/A exceeds xi/2 and rapidly reaches +X. If \(\xi+2\lambda>2\), even the most negative pressure cannot release it from that stop, so it stays there. If \(\xi+2\lambda<2\), it repeatedly switches between the stops. Draw an initial 0 plateau, then +1. In the switching regime it settles to a rectangular wave between +1 and -1 with the forcing period and equal dwell times. The equality is a marginal switching limit. No inertial trajectory is specified by this slow-switching approximation.

The total distance per cycle is 4X, so \(W=4F_sX\). The switching boundary is \(F_s/(S_cA)+2\rho gX/A\le1\). The optimum is approached at \[X_*=A/(4\rho g),\quad F_{s,*}=AS_c/2,\quad W_*=A^2S_c/(2\rho g).\] With the stated values, Xstar=0.945 mm, Fsstar=5.25 N, and Wstar=19.84 mJ. In an exactly quasistatic model the boundary is marginal, so this is the limiting maximum approached from the switching side.

In the equal-area approximation the exposed system volume change is \(V_1=-S_c[x+P_1/(2\rho g)]\). Over the cycle \(W_{pr}=-\oint P_1dV_1\). At optimum switches occur at pressure extrema. The P1-V1 parallelogram has height 2A and horizontal width \(2S_cX_*\), giving \[W_{pr,*}=4AS_cX_*=S_cA^2/(\rho g)=39.68\,\mathrm{mJ},\quad W_*/W_{pr,*}=1/2.\]

Static friction can hold throughout if xi is greater than 2. Thus \(\xi_*=2\). Equality is the marginal threshold.
C.2. Tension at the stop
The container displacements are opposite because of the cables. Solve equal liquid-level shift and mercury-volume conservation to find the cistern apparent-mass change \(-2\rho S_c(S_b-S_t)X/(S_b+S_c-S_t)\). Its opposite is the tube load change, hence \[T=\frac{4S_c(S_b-S_t)}{S_b+S_c-S_t}\rho gX\simeq\frac{4S_bS_c}{S_b+S_c}\rho gX.\] It is positive, towards the same stop, not a restoring force.
C.3. Operating regimes
General tension is \(T=C_P[P_1+2\rho g(S_b-S_t)x/S_b]\), with \(C_P=2S_bS_c/(S_b+S_c-S_t)\). Initially motion starts when P1/A exceeds xi/2 and rapidly reaches +X. If \(\xi+2\lambda>2\), even the most negative pressure cannot release it from that stop, so it stays there. If \(\xi+2\lambda<2\), it repeatedly switches between the stops. Draw an initial 0 plateau, then +1. In the switching regime it settles to a rectangular wave between +1 and -1 with the forcing period and equal dwell times. The equality is a marginal switching limit. No inertial trajectory is specified by this slow-switching approximation.
C.4. Optimal recovered energy
The total distance per cycle is 4X, so \(W=4F_sX\). The switching boundary is \(F_s/(S_cA)+2\rho gX/A\le1\). The optimum is approached at \[X_*=A/(4\rho g),\quad F_{s,*}=AS_c/2,\quad W_*=A^2S_c/(2\rho g).\] With the stated values, Xstar=0.945 mm, Fsstar=5.25 N, and Wstar=19.84 mJ. In an exactly quasistatic model the boundary is marginal, so this is the limiting maximum approached from the switching side.
C.5. Atmospheric work and efficiency
In the equal-area approximation the exposed system volume change is \(V_1=-S_c[x+P_1/(2\rho g)]\). Over the cycle \(W_{pr}=-\oint P_1dV_1\). At optimum switches occur at pressure extrema. The P1-V1 parallelogram has height 2A and horizontal width \(2S_cX_*\), giving \[W_{pr,*}=4AS_cX_*=S_cA^2/(\rho g)=39.68\,\mathrm{mJ},\quad W_*/W_{pr,*}=1/2.\]

children.text: For one liquid-gas interface the Laplace pressure jump is \[P_b=P_0+2\sigma/a.\]
Growth requires \(c_\ell>k_H(P_0+2\sigma/a)\). Thus \[a_c=\frac{2\sigma c_0}{P_0(c_\ell-c_0)}.\] At cl=4c0, ac=2sigma/(3P0)=0.313 micrometres.

The ideal-gas moles are \(n_c=4\pi a^3P_0/(3RT_0)\). Since \(\dot n_c=4\pi a^2j\), \(\dot a=jRT_0/P_0\). Consequently \[a^2=a_0^2+2DRT_0(c_\ell-c_0)t/P_0\] in model 1, and \[a=a_0+KRT_0(c_\ell-c_0)t/P_0\] in model 2. The measured radius grows linearly at about \(q_a=0.24\,\mathrm{mm/s}\), selecting model 2. For cl=4c0, \(K=q_a/(3k_HRT_0)\simeq1.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m/s}\). The source marking range omits its power-of-ten factor in one line.

Buoyancy is \(4\pi a^3\rho_\ell g_0/3\), downward weight is \(4\pi a^3\rho_g g_0/3\), and viscous drag is downward. Since gas density is small, \[v\simeq2\rho_\ell g_0a^2/(9\eta).\] Neighbour spacing divided by \(1/f_b\) estimates speed at a measured radius. Representative graph measurements a about 0.20 mm and v about 4.5 cm/s give \(\eta\sim2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}\). Pair the measured radius and spacing consistently.

Use \(dz/da=v/q_a=2\rho_\ell g_0a^2/(9\eta q_a)\). Integrating gives \[H_\ell=2\rho_\ell g_0(a_H^3-a_0^3)/(27\eta q_a).\] Neglecting a0, \(a_H=[27\eta q_aH_\ell/(2\rho_\ell g_0)]^{1/3}\simeq0.40\,\mathrm{mm}\) for viscosity 0.002 Pa s.

The bubble gas-volume outflow is \((4\pi/3)a_H^3N_bf_b\). Using A.5 this is \(18\pi\eta q_aH_\ell N_bf_b/(\rho_\ell g_0)\). Convert volume to moles by P0/(RT0) and use \(q_a=KRT_0(c_\ell-c_0)/P_0\): \[\frac{dc_\ell}{dt}=-\frac{18\pi N_bf_b\eta KH_\ell}{\rho_\ell g_0V_\ell}(c_\ell-c_0),\quad\tau=\frac{\rho_\ell g_0V_\ell}{18\pi N_bf_b\eta KH_\ell}.\] It is the excess concentration above c0 that decays exponentially.
An area increase dA removes surface energy \(2\sigma dA\). Half, \(\sigma dA\), becomes kinetic energy \(\rho_\ell h\,dA\,v_f^2/2\). Thus \[v_f=\sqrt{2\sigma/(\rho_\ell h)}.\]
Adiabatic pressure is \(P=P_0[V_0/(V_0+Sz)]^\gamma\simeq P_0(1-\gamma Sz/V_0)\). Thus \(m_p\ddot z=-\gamma P_0S^2z/V_0\), giving \[f_0=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P_0S^2}{m_pV_0}}.\]

Substitute \(S=\pi r_c^2\) into B.2 and eliminate rc. This gives \[a=\frac{3\sqrt3\gamma P_0}{64\pi\rho_gf_{max}^2}\sqrt{\frac{\rho_\ell g_0}{\sigma}}\simeq0.53\,\mathrm{mm}.\] Then rc is about 0.15 mm and \(v_f=r_c/t_b\simeq5\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Finally \(h=2\sigma/(\rho_\ell v_f^2)\simeq3.7\,\mu\mathrm m\).

Conservation with Henry law gives \(n_T=k_HP_iV_L+P_iV_G/(RT_0)\), hence \[P_i=\frac{n_T}{k_HV_L+V_G/(RT_0)}.\] The pressures are about 4.81 bar at 6 C and 7.76 bar at 20 C. These are distinct from the pressures explicitly supplied for the following questions.

Adiabatic expansion gives \(T_f=T_0(P_0/P_i)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). This gives approximately 195 K from 6 C, and 184 K from 20 C. The CO2 sublimation temperature at one bar from the supplied law is approximately 194.4 K. Thus the 6 C case stays just above sublimation and produces the stated grey-white water fog. The 20 C case crosses below sublimation and produces blue CO2-crystal fog. In the multiple-choice wording, statements 1 and 4 are true. Once crystallization occurs, latent heat modifies the no-transition temperature estimate.

Initial balance gives \(\alpha\simeq(P_i-P_0)d/(4\ell_0)\). During extraction at height z, friction is \(\alpha\pi d(\ell_0-z)\), with work \(W_f=-(P_i-P_0)\pi d^2\ell_0/8\). Put \(\Delta V=\pi d^2\ell_0/4\). Adiabatic gas work is \[W_g=\frac{P_iV_G}{\gamma-1}\left[1-\left(\frac{V_G}{V_G+\Delta V}\right)^{\gamma-1}\right].\] Atmospheric work is \(-P_0\Delta V\). The exit kinetic energy is approximately \(W_g+W_f-P_0\Delta V\), about 0.76 J, ignoring small gravitational work during extraction as in the source. Free-flight rise is this divided by mg0, approximately 7.7 m. Including the cork weight in initial friction balance and extraction changes the result slightly, rather than changing the dominant gas-energy calculation.

children.text: Conserve solar luminosity over a sphere of radius d: \(S_0=\sigma T_S^4(R_S/d)^2=1.35\times10^3\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).
The absorbing disc has one quarter the radiating surface area. Thus \(T_E=[S_0/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}=T_S\sqrt{R_S/(2d)}=278\,\mathrm K\).

Differentiating u with respect to λ gives \(f(x)=5(1-e^{-x})-x=0\). Any nonzero multiple yields the same root. Any nonzero constant multiple defines the same equation, so the derivation and equation use self-review rather than a unique expression key.
Iterate x=5(1−e⁻ˣ) starting near 5. The physical root is xm=4.965≈4.97. Hence \(b=hc/(x_mk_B)\simeq2.90\times10^6\,\mathrm{nm\,K}\). The supplied rounded constants allow 2.89 to 2.90 million nm K.
Use b/T, giving approximately 502 nm for the Sun and \(1.04\times10^{4}\) nm for Earth.
At the maximum, x has the same value for both temperatures, and the peak exitance scales as T⁵. Thus \(\gamma=(d/R_S)^2(T_E/T_S)^5\simeq1.20\times10^{-2}\).

Let F=(1−rA)S0/4. Surface balance is F+σTA⁴=σTE⁴ and atmospheric balance is σTE⁴=2σTA⁴. Thus \(T_A=(F/\sigma)^{1/4}=258\,\mathrm K\) and \(T_E=(2F/\sigma)^{1/4}=307\,\mathrm K\). The factor two counts upward and downward emission.
The direct reflected fraction is rA. The once-surface-reflected escaped fraction is (1−rA)²rE, with successive ratio rArE. Therefore \[\alpha=r_A+\frac{(1-r_A)^2r_E}{1-r_Ar_E}=0.313.\]
For ε>0 atmospheric balance gives TE⁴=2TA⁴. Surface balance is (1−α)S0/4+εσTA⁴=σTE⁴. Hence \[T_E=\left[\frac{(1-\alpha)S_0}{2\sigma(2-\epsilon)}\right]^{1/4}.\]
At fixed S0 and α, \(dT_E/d\epsilon=T_E/[4(2-\epsilon)]\). A relative increase means Δε=0.01ε, not 0.01. At TE=288 K and ε≈0.809, ΔTE≈0.489 K.

Put F=(1−α)S0/4. The balances are \(F+\epsilon\sigma T_A^4=\sigma T_E^4+k(T_E-T_A)\) and \(\epsilon\sigma T_E^4+k(T_E-T_A)=2\epsilon\sigma T_A^4\). Thus \[\epsilon=\frac{\sigma T_E^4-F}{\sigma(T_E^4-T_A^4)},\qquad k=\frac{\epsilon\sigma(2T_A^4-T_E^4)}{T_E-T_A}.\] Numerically ε≈0.850 and k≈0.361 W m⁻² K⁻¹.

Differentiating the surface and atmospheric balances directly gives \[(4\sigma T_E^3+k)X-(4\epsilon\sigma T_A^3+k)Y=\sigma T_A^4,\] \[(4\epsilon\sigma T_E^3+k)X-(8\epsilon\sigma T_A^3+k)Y=\sigma(2T_A^4-T_E^4).\] These are algebraically equivalent to the logarithmic-derivative equations in the official solution.
Solve the two linear equations at the B5 equilibrium and multiply X by 0.01ε. The result is approximately 0.524 K, with the source rounding range 0.521 to 0.528 K.

solution.text:
The greenhouse effect
a-1. Solar constant
Conserve solar luminosity over a sphere of radius d: \(S_0=\sigma T_S^4(R_S/d)^2=1.35\times10^3\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).
a-2. Airless blackbody Earth
The absorbing disc has one quarter the radiating surface area. Thus \(T_E=[S_0/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}=T_S\sqrt{R_S/(2d)}=278\,\mathrm K\).
a-3. Wien equation
Differentiating u with respect to λ gives \(f(x)=5(1-e^{-x})-x=0\). Any nonzero multiple yields the same root. Any nonzero constant multiple defines the same equation, so the derivation and equation use self-review rather than a unique expression key.
a-4. Wien constant
Iterate x=5(1−e⁻ˣ) starting near 5. The physical root is xm=4.965≈4.97. Hence \(b=hc/(x_mk_B)\simeq2.90\times10^6\,\mathrm{nm\,K}\). The supplied rounded constants allow 2.89 to 2.90 million nm K.
a-5. Solar and terrestrial peaks
Use b/T, giving approximately 502 nm for the Sun and \(1.04\times10^{4}\) nm for Earth.
a-6. Equal-height rescaling
At the maximum, x has the same value for both temperatures, and the peak exitance scales as T⁵. Thus \(\gamma=(d/R_S)^2(T_E/T_S)^5\simeq1.20\times10^{-2}\).
b-1. Opaque infrared atmosphere
Let F=(1−rA)S0/4. Surface balance is F+σTA⁴=σTE⁴ and atmospheric balance is σTE⁴=2σTA⁴. Thus \(T_A=(F/\sigma)^{1/4}=258\,\mathrm K\) and \(T_E=(2F/\sigma)^{1/4}=307\,\mathrm K\). The factor two counts upward and downward emission.
b-2. Multiple-reflection albedo
The direct reflected fraction is rA. The once-surface-reflected escaped fraction is (1−rA)²rE, with successive ratio rArE. Therefore \[\alpha=r_A+\frac{(1-r_A)^2r_E}{1-r_Ar_E}=0.313.\]
b-3a. Partially absorbing atmosphere
For ε>0 atmospheric balance gives TE⁴=2TA⁴. Surface balance is (1−α)S0/4+εσTA⁴=σTE⁴. Hence \[T_E=\left[\frac{(1-\alpha)S_0}{2\sigma(2-\epsilon)}\right]^{1/4}.\]
b-3b. Present-temperature emissivity
Rearrange B3a: \(\epsilon=2-(1-\alpha)S_0/(2\sigma T_E^4)\simeq0.809\).
b-4. Radiative temperature sensitivity
At fixed S0 and α, \(dT_E/d\epsilon=T_E/[4(2-\epsilon)]\). A relative increase means Δε=0.01ε, not 0.01. At TE=288 K and ε≈0.809, ΔTE≈0.489 K.
b-5. Non-radiative transfer
Put F=(1−α)S0/4. The balances are \(F+\epsilon\sigma T_A^4=\sigma T_E^4+k(T_E-T_A)\) and \(\epsilon\sigma T_E^4+k(T_E-T_A)=2\epsilon\sigma T_A^4\). Thus \[\epsilon=\frac{\sigma T_E^4-F}{\sigma(T_E^4-T_A^4)},\qquad k=\frac{\epsilon\sigma(2T_A^4-T_E^4)}{T_E-T_A}.\] Numerically ε≈0.850 and k≈0.361 W m⁻² K⁻¹.
b-6a. Coupled sensitivity equations
Differentiating the surface and atmospheric balances directly gives \[(4\sigma T_E^3+k)X-(4\epsilon\sigma T_A^3+k)Y=\sigma T_A^4,\] \[(4\epsilon\sigma T_E^3+k)X-(8\epsilon\sigma T_A^3+k)Y=\sigma(2T_A^4-T_E^4).\] These are algebraically equivalent to the logarithmic-derivative equations in the official solution.
b-6b. Sensitivity with heat transfer

For dynamic trapping take λ=λ0+u cosΩt. In B, a trapped atom has transition energy ℏωA, excited lifetime τ and line half-width Γ estimated by energy-time uncertainty. Work to first order in v/c and assume m≫ℏωA/c² and sL≪αωL. An absorbed photon is re-emitted with nearly the same atom-frame frequency, with equal probability in either x direction. children.text: On axis the ring charge 2πRλ gives \(E_z=\lambda Rz/[2\epsilon_0(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}]\simeq\lambda z/(2\epsilon_0R^2)\). Symmetry and ∇·E=0 then give \[\mathbf E=\frac\lambda{4\epsilon_0R^2}(-x,-y,2z).\]
For Qλ>0, x and y are restoring while z is unstable. Thus \(\omega_x=\omega_y=\sqrt{Q\lambda/(4\epsilon_0R^2m)}\). The static ring cannot confine all directions.
Compare coefficients with QEz/m: \(k=\sqrt{Q\lambda_0/(2\epsilon_0R^2m)}\), \(a=Qu/(2\epsilon_0R^2m\Omega^2)\). The field checks a.
On a fast cycle freeze p, neglect its acceleration and the small q in the driving force. Then \(\ddot q=pa\Omega^2\cos\Omega t\).
Integration gives \(q=-pa\cos\Omega t+c_1t+c_2\). Bounded micromotion requires c1=0 and zero mean requires c2=0, so \(q=-pa\cos\Omega t\).
Substitute q and average, using ⟨cosΩt⟩=0 and ⟨cos²Ωt⟩=1/2. This gives \(\ddot p=(k^2-a^2\Omega^2/2)p\).
The coefficient must be negative: \(a^2\Omega^2/2>k^2\), or Ω>√2 k/|a|. For a>0 this is Ω>√2 k/a. Equality is marginal, not a restoring oscillation.

\(k=\sqrt{e\lambda_0/(2\epsilon_0R^2\,100m_H)}\simeq2.08\times10^5\,\mathrm{rad/s}\). Thus Ωmin≈\(7.35\times10^{6}\) rad/s, rounded in the source to \(7\times10^{6}\) rad/s. This is angular frequency, corresponding to about 1.17 MHz.
Use ΔE τ≈ℏ and ΔE=ℏΓ, giving Γ≈1/τ in the source width convention. Factors associated with precise linewidth definitions are outside this estimate.

The frequencies are \(\omega_\pm=\omega_L(1\pm v/c)\), so \(s_\pm=s_L\pm\alpha\omega_Lv/c\). With k±=ω±/c, \(\pi_+=-\hbar k_+s_+\) and \(\pi_-=+\hbar k_-s_-\). Re-emission has zero mean momentum in this frame.

Adding momentum rates and retaining first-order terms gives \(-2\hbar k_L^2\alpha v[1+s_L/(\alpha\omega_L)]\). Neglect the bracket correction. To this order the lab force is \(F=-2\alpha\hbar k_L^2v\).

For incoming momentum +ℏkL, the final momentum is 0 or 2ℏkL with equal probability. The mean kinetic gain is ℏ²kL²/m. Thus \(P_{in}=\hbar^2k_L^2/(m\tau)\). The opposite incident direction gives the same energy.

\(P_{cool}=Fv=-2\alpha\hbar k_L^2v^2\). Balance the mean against recoil heating to obtain \(\langle v^2\rangle=\hbar/(2\alpha m\tau)\). One-dimensional equipartition gives \(T=\hbar/(2\alpha k_B\tau)=\hbar\Gamma/(2\alpha k_B)\). The field checks T.
Substitution gives T≈\(1.91\times10^{-4}\) K, about 0.2 mK. Mass and laser frequency cancel in this simplified balance.

children.text: A circular binary contains point masses M1 and M2 separated by a. Its centre of mass is the origin of co-rotating xy coordinates, with M1 on negative x and M2 on positive x. The effective potential per test mass includes gravity and centrifugal potential. Mass transfer from M2 to M1 has small rate β>0, so orbits remain nearly circular. Assume conservative transfer and conserved total orbital angular momentum in A4. In A5 use a steady thin blackbody accretion disc close to M1, ignore M2's pull and gas heat capacity, and balance the local loss of circular orbital energy with radiation from both faces. For PSR J2215+5135 use MNS=2.27M☉, MS=0.33M☉, P=4.14 h, M☉=\(1.98\times10^{30}\) kg, β=\(9\times10^{-10}\) M☉/yr, G=\(6.67\times10^{-11}\) SI and σ=\(5.67\times10^{-8}\) SI. In B, a spherical isolated star obeys p=Kργ. Central values are pc and ρc, and outward acceleration is positive.
Only here let M2=M1/3. Find x0/a to two significant figures for gas overflow from M2 towards M1.
Find da/dt and dP/dt under slow conservative mass transfer.
Find temperature at disc radius r.
Calculate T at r=a/10 for the specified binary.
An explosion leaves mass M1′ and relative speed v′ at separation a. Find the limiting v′ for a bound binary and the limiting M1′ if the explosion is isotropic.
Find g(r) close to the centre.
Construct r0=Gℓpcmρcn with length dimensions and no numerical prefactor.
Put x=r/r0 and u=ρ/ρc. Find A1 and A2 in d[A1 du/dx]/dx+A2u=0.

children.text: Set M=M1+M2, a1=M2a/M and a2=M1a/M, with Ω²=GM/a³. Then \[\varphi=-\frac{GM_1}{\sqrt{(x+a_1)^2+y^2}}-\frac{GM_2}{\sqrt{(x-a_2)^2+y^2}}-\frac{GM}{2a^3}(x^2+y^2).\] The centrifugal potential has a negative sign.

Draw downward divergences on both sides of x=−a1 and x=a2, and φ→−∞ as x→±∞ because of centrifugal potential. There is one local maximum in each of the three intervals separated by the two masses, at the three collinear Lagrange points. The central maximum is closer to the smaller mass.
The masses lie at −a/4 and 3a/4. With ξ=x/a, solve \(\frac{3}{4(\xi+1/4)^2}-\frac{1}{4(3/4-\xi)^2}-\xi=0\) between them. The inner stationary point is ξ≈0.3607, hence 0.36.

Conserved angular momentum is \(J=M_1M_2\sqrt{Ga/(M_1+M_2)}\). Using Ṁ1=β=−Ṁ2 gives \[\dot a=-2\beta a(1/M_1-1/M_2),\qquad\dot P=-3\beta P(1/M_1-1/M_2),\] where \(P=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/[G(M_1+M_2)]}\). For M1>M2 the separation and period grow.

The circular specific orbital energy is −GM1/(2r). An annulus releases GM1βdr/(2r²). Its two radiating faces have area 4πrdr. Thus \[T(r)=\left(\frac{GM_1\beta}{8\pi\sigma r^3}\right)^{1/4}.\] This uses the local energy model requested here, without the angular-momentum-transport correction of a detailed viscous-disc theory.
Kepler gives \(a=[GP^2(M_{NS}+M_S)/(4\pi^2)]^{1/3}\). Convert β to kg/s and P to seconds, giving \(T=[500\pi M_{NS}\beta/(\sigma P^2(M_{NS}+M_S))]^{1/4}\simeq9.0\times10^3\,\mathrm K\).

The new orbital energy is negative only for \(v^{\prime}<\sqrt{2G(M_1^{\prime}+M_2)/a}\). Isotropic rapid ejection produces no kick, so v′²=G(M1+M2)/a. The condition is \(M_1^{\prime}>(M_1-M_2)/2\). Equality in either condition is a parabolic, marginally unbound orbit.
Enclosed mass is approximately 4πρcr³/3, hence \(g=-4\pi G\rho_cr/3\).

Combine dp/dr=−GM(r)ρ/r² with M′=4πr²ρ and p=Kργ. Eliminate M to obtain \[\frac d{dr}\left(r^2\rho^{\gamma-2}\frac{d\rho}{dr}\right)+\frac{4\pi Gr^2}{K\gamma}\rho=0.\] Thus h1=r²ργ−2 and h2=4πGr²/(Kγ).
Matching mass, length and time exponents gives ℓ=−1/2, m=1/2, n=−1. Thus \(r_0=\sqrt{p_c/G}/\rho_c\).
Using pc=Kρcγ and the B3 scale, \[\frac d{dx}\left(x^2u^{\gamma-2}\frac{du}{dx}\right)+\frac{4\pi x^2}{\gamma}u=0.\] Thus A1=x²uγ−2 and A2=4πx²/γ.
The equation reduces to f″+2πf=0. Regularity gives f(0)=0 and u(0)=f′(0)=1. Hence \(f=\sin(\sqrt{2\pi}x)/\sqrt{2\pi}\).

Regularity imposes u′(0)=0. Expanding the dimensionless equation near zero gives \(3u^{\prime\prime}(0)+4\pi/\gamma=0\). The plotted initial slope of u′ is approximately −2.51, giving γ≈1.67. The official graphical acceptance interval is 1.64 to 1.70.
Mass conservation for a homologously expanded shell gives \(\tilde\rho=\rho(1+\epsilon)^{-3}\simeq\rho(1-3\epsilon)\). Fixed enclosed mass gives \(\tilde g=g(1+\epsilon)^{-2}\simeq g(1-2\epsilon)\).

Gravity plus pressure force per mass gives \[\ddot{\tilde r}=\tilde g-\frac1{\tilde\rho}\frac{\partial\tilde p}{\partial\tilde r}=\tilde g-K\gamma\tilde\rho^{\gamma-2}\frac{\partial\tilde\rho}{\partial\tilde r}.\]

The pressure acceleration scales as (1+ε)²−3γ, while gravity scales as (1+ε)⁻². Cancel equilibrium forces to find \[\ddot\epsilon=\frac gr(3\gamma-4)\epsilon=-\frac{4\pi G\rho_c}{3}(3\gamma-4)\epsilon.\] Stable restoring motion requires γ>4/3, and \(\omega=\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_c(3\gamma-4)/3}\). solution.text:
Black widow pulsar
a-1. Rotating potential
Set M=M1+M2, a1=M2a/M and a2=M1a/M, with Ω²=GM/a³. Then \[\varphi=-\frac{GM_1}{\sqrt{(x+a_1)^2+y^2}}-\frac{GM_2}{\sqrt{(x-a_2)^2+y^2}}-\frac{GM}{2a^3}(x^2+y^2).\] The centrifugal potential has a negative sign.
a-2. Axial potential sketch
Draw downward divergences on both sides of x=−a1 and x=a2, and φ→−∞ as x→±∞ because of centrifugal potential. There is one local maximum in each of the three intervals separated by the two masses, at the three collinear Lagrange points. The central maximum is closer to the smaller mass.
a-3. Overflow point
The masses lie at −a/4 and 3a/4. With ξ=x/a, solve \(\frac{3}{4(\xi+1/4)^2}-\frac{1}{4(3/4-\xi)^2}-\xi=0\) between them. The inner stationary point is ξ≈0.3607, hence 0.36.
a-4. Secular binary evolution
Conserved angular momentum is \(J=M_1M_2\sqrt{Ga/(M_1+M_2)}\). Using Ṁ1=β=−Ṁ2 gives \[\dot a=-2\beta a(1/M_1-1/M_2),\qquad\dot P=-3\beta P(1/M_1-1/M_2),\] where \(P=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/[G(M_1+M_2)]}\). For M1>M2 the separation and period grow.
a-5. Disc temperature law
The circular specific orbital energy is −GM1/(2r). An annulus releases GM1βdr/(2r²). Its two radiating faces have area 4πrdr. Thus \[T(r)=\left(\frac{GM_1\beta}{8\pi\sigma r^3}\right)^{1/4}.\] This uses the local energy model requested here, without the angular-momentum-transport correction of a detailed viscous-disc theory.
a-6. Observed-system estimate
Kepler gives \(a=[GP^2(M_{NS}+M_S)/(4\pi^2)]^{1/3}\). Convert β to kg/s and P to seconds, giving \(T=[500\pi M_{NS}\beta/(\sigma P^2(M_{NS}+M_S))]^{1/4}\simeq9.0\times10^3\,\mathrm K\).
a-7. Sudden mass loss
The new orbital energy is negative only for \(v^{\prime}<\sqrt{2G(M_1^{\prime}+M_2)/a}\). Isotropic rapid ejection produces no kick, so v′²=G(M1+M2)/a. The condition is \(M_1^{\prime}>(M_1-M_2)/2\). Equality in either condition is a parabolic, marginally unbound orbit.
b-1. Central gravitational acceleration
Enclosed mass is approximately 4πρcr³/3, hence \(g=-4\pi G\rho_cr/3\).
b-2. Density equilibrium equation
Combine dp/dr=−GM(r)ρ/r² with M′=4πr²ρ and p=Kργ. Eliminate M to obtain \[\frac d{dr}\left(r^2\rho^{\gamma-2}\frac{d\rho}{dr}\right)+\frac{4\pi Gr^2}{K\gamma}\rho=0.\] Thus h1=r²ργ−2 and h2=4πGr²/(Kγ).
b-3. Central length scale
Matching mass, length and time exponents gives ℓ=−1/2, m=1/2, n=−1. Thus \(r_0=\sqrt{p_c/G}/\rho_c\).
b-4. Dimensionless equation
Using pc=Kρcγ and the B3 scale, \[\frac d{dx}\left(x^2u^{\gamma-2}\frac{du}{dx}\right)+\frac{4\pi x^2}{\gamma}u=0.\] Thus A1=x²uγ−2 and A2=4πx²/γ.
b-5. Analytic density for γ=2
The equation reduces to f″+2πf=0. Regularity gives f(0)=0 and u(0)=f′(0)=1. Hence \(f=\sin(\sqrt{2\pi}x)/\sqrt{2\pi}\).
b-6. Infer equation-of-state exponent
Regularity imposes u′(0)=0. Expanding the dimensionless equation near zero gives \(3u^{\prime\prime}(0)+4\pi/\gamma=0\). The plotted initial slope of u′ is approximately −2.51, giving γ≈1.67. The official graphical acceptance interval is 1.64 to 1.70.
b-7. Small homologous perturbation
Mass conservation for a homologously expanded shell gives \(\tilde\rho=\rho(1+\epsilon)^{-3}\simeq\rho(1-3\epsilon)\). Fixed enclosed mass gives \(\tilde g=g(1+\epsilon)^{-2}\simeq g(1-2\epsilon)\).
b-8. Perturbed shell acceleration
Gravity plus pressure force per mass gives \[\ddot{\tilde r}=\tilde g-\frac1{\tilde\rho}\frac{\partial\tilde p}{\partial\tilde r}=\tilde g-K\gamma\tilde\rho^{\gamma-2}\frac{\partial\tilde\rho}{\partial\tilde r}.\]
b-9. Radial stability criterion
The pressure acceleration scales as (1+ε)²−3γ, while gravity scales as (1+ε)⁻². Cancel equilibrium forces to find \[\ddot\epsilon=\frac gr(3\gamma-4)\epsilon=-\frac{4\pi G\rho_c}{3}(3\gamma-4)\epsilon.\] Stable restoring motion requires γ>4/3, and \(\omega=\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_c(3\gamma-4)/3}\). At γ=4/3 this linear model is marginal.

Characterization of soil colloids

a.1. Single impulse
A collision at t0 supplies impulse I0 to a resting particle. Determine v0 and τ in \(v(t)=v_0e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}\).
a.2. Successive collisions
Impulses Ii occur at ti after t=0. Find v(t) and specify which collision times contribute.
b.1. Displacement moments
At t=Nδ find the mean displacement and its mean square in terms of C, δ and t.
b.2. Continuum scaling
For a finite nonzero Brownian mean square as δ tends to zero, find α and β in C∝δα and MSD∝tβ.
c.1. Right-going crossing rate

Half the particles have speed +v and half −v. Linearize n(x) about x0. Find N+(x0), the right-going number crossing per area per time, using n0=n(x0) and s=dn/dx at x0.
c.2. Diffusion coefficient
Use the analogous N− and ⟨v²⟩=C to find JD, D and the MSD.
c.3. Osmotic balance
For the stationary concentration under E, balance osmotic forces on a slice of width Δx. Find dn/dx in terms of n, Q, E, k and T.
c.4. Drift velocity
With Fext=QE, zero mean initial velocity and ⟨F⟩=0, find ⟨v(t)⟩ and terminal velocity u.
c.5. Einstein relation
Use JD+JQ=0 to express D in terms of k, T and γ.
d.1. Experimental Avogadro estimate

Using the histogram of displacements sampled at Δt=60 s, estimate NA to two significant digits. Do not use a known value of k or NA.
d.2. Drift crossover
Replace each vn by u+vn. Find the MSD, its small- and large-time power laws, the crossover t*, and sketch a log-log plot.
d.3. Swimming microbes

A microbe swims at randomly selected velocity ±u0 for independent intervals δ0, in addition to Brownian motion. The supplied MSD plot has three regimes. Express each power law using D, u0, δ0 and t.
e.1. Coagulation threshold
Two colloidal particles interact through \(U(d)=-A/d+B\epsilon(kT)^2e^{-d/\lambda}/q^2\), with A,B>0, dielectric constant ε, ion charges ±q, and \(\lambda=\sqrt{\epsilon kT/(2N_Aq^2c)}\). Neglect thermal fluctuations and assume instantaneous terminal motion. Find the lowest salt concentration c that guarantees coagulation.

children.text: Integrate through the collision to obtain Mv0=I0. Afterwards Mdv/dt=−γv. Thus \(v_0=I_0/M\) and \(\tau=M/\gamma\). The field checks τ.
Linearity permits superposition: \[v(t)=\sum_{0<t_i<t}\frac{I_i}{M}e^{-(t-t_i)/\tau}.\] At an impulse include the instantaneous velocity jump Ii/M if using a right-continuous convention.

Write Δx=δΣvn. Each mean vanishes and every cross correlation vanishes. Therefore \(\langle\Delta x\rangle=0\) and \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=N C\delta^2=C\delta t\). The field checks the mean square.
The product Cδ must remain finite. Hence α=−1 and β=1.
Only particles between x0−vδ and x0 cross. Thus \(N_+=\frac1{2\delta}\int_{x_0-v\delta}^{x_0}[n_0+s(x-x_0)]dx=n_0v/2-sv^2\delta/4\).
\(N_-=n_0v/2+sv^2\delta/4\), giving \(J_D=-sC\delta/2\). Therefore \(D=C\delta/2\) and \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=2Dt\). The field checks D.
Force balance is Π(x)A+nAΔxQE=Π(x+Δx)A. Since Π=nkT, \(dn/dx=nQE/(kT)\).
The mean obeys \(M d\langle v\rangle/dt=-\gamma\langle v\rangle+QE\). Thus \(\langle v\rangle=(QE/\gamma)(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) and \(u=QE/\gamma\). The field checks u.
Substitute C3 and u=QE/γ into −Ddn/dx+nu=0. Cancelling nQE gives \(D=kT/\gamma\).

Take the frequency-weighted mean square of the histogram, approximately 6.34 μm². Since \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=RT\Delta t/(3\pi a\eta N_A)\), obtain \(N_A\simeq5.6\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). This is the estimate from these data, not the modern defined constant.

The nonzero mean adds a squared drift term: \(\langle\Delta x^2\rangle=u^2t^2+2Dt\). The terms match at \(t_*=2D/u^2\). The log-log slope rises from 1 at t≪t* to 2 at t≫t*. Draw continuous asymptotes meeting near t*.

If 2D/u0²≪δ0, the successive laws are \(2Dt\) for t≪2D/u0², \(u_0^2t^2\) for 2D/u0²≪t≪δ0, and \(u_0^2\delta_0t\) for t≫δ0. More exactly the last coefficient is u0²δ0+2D. The assumed intermediate regime makes its Brownian contribution negligible. The source solution labels this item D.1 in its prose, but its answer box and question identify D.3.

Under overdamped deterministic motion every repulsive-force interval must disappear. The threshold satisfies U′=U″=0, giving d=2λ and \(\lambda=e^2Aq^2/[4B\epsilon(kT)^2]\), where e is Euler's number. Hence \[c=\frac{8B^2\epsilon^3(kT)^5}{e^4N_AA^2q^6}.\] Setting only the potential barrier height to zero would not eliminate the force barrier and does not meet the stated deterministic criterion. The value above is the critical concentration, an infimum for finite-time coagulation from initially separated particles. At equality the force has a double zero at \(d=2\lambda\), approached only asymptotically in this overdamped model. Finite-time passage requires \(c>c_{\rm crit}\).

Here \(B/A=a_V-a_SA^{-1/3}-a_CA^{2/3}/4\). Set the derivative to zero to get \(A=2a_S/a_C\simeq50\).

A.3. Equal-fission threshold
Volume and symmetry terms cancel. Surface cost competes with Coulomb release, giving \[C_{fission}=\frac{2^{1/3}-1}{1-2^{-2/3}}=0.70.\] This is an energy criterion and does not remove a fission barrier.
B.1. Gravitational binding threshold
\[a_{grav}=\frac{3Gm_N^2}{5R_0}=6.4\times10^{-37}\,\mathrm{MeV}\simeq6\times10^{-37}\,\mathrm{MeV}.\] Positive binding requires \((a_V-a_{sym})A+a_{grav}A^{5/3}>0\), so \[A_c=[(a_{sym}-a_V)/a_{grav}]^{3/2}=4.4\times10^{55}\simeq4\times10^{55}.\] This is the source's positive-total-binding criterion, an estimate rather than a complete neutron-star stability calculation.

The lower clock runs more slowly. To first order, \[\Delta\tau_{II}=(1-\Delta\phi/c^2)\Delta\tau_I.\] The given local falling-frame argument uses \(\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\simeq1-v^2/(2c^2)\). C.2. Shapiro time delay
Expand reciprocal speed and integrate \(\phi=-GM_{WD}/\sqrt{x^2+d^2}\): \[\Delta t=\frac{2GM_{WD}}{c^3}\int_{x_N}^{x_E}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+d^2}}\simeq\frac{2GM_{WD}}{c^3}\ln\frac{4|x_N|x_E}{d^2}.\]

At the maximum, \(d\simeq L\varepsilon\), giving \(\Delta t_{max}=(2GM_{WD}/c^3)\ln[4x_E/(L\varepsilon^2)]\). At the minimum N is in front of W, so the same integral has positive lower limit and gives \(\Delta t_{min}=(2GM_{WD}/c^3)\ln(x_E/L)\). The graph range is about \(50\,\mathrm{\mu s}\), and \(\varepsilon^2\simeq2(1-\cos\varepsilon)=0.00022\). Thus \(M_{WD}/M_\odot=50/[10\ln(4/0.00022)]\simeq0.5\).

children.text: The new radius is \(2^{1/3}a\), mass \(8\pi\rho a^3/3\), and released surface energy \(4\pi\gamma a^2(2-2^{2/3})\). Hence \[v=\sqrt{\frac{3k\gamma(2-2^{2/3})}{\rho a}}=0.23\,\mathrm{m/s}.\]
Hydrostatic equilibrium gives \(P=P_0-\rho gz\), including negative gauge pressure above the far surface.
B.2. Pressure force on a surface block
Integrate the gauge pressure on the two faces: \[f_x=\frac12\rho g(z_2^2-z_1^2).\] In the illustrated hydrophilic case this is negative, towards the board.
Surface tension on the block has component \(\gamma(\cos\theta_2-\cos\theta_1)\). Force balance gives \[f_x=\gamma(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2).\]

Combine B2 and B3: \(\rho gz^2/2+\gamma\cos\theta\) is constant, equal to \(\gamma\) far away. Therefore \(a=2\) and \(\ell=\sqrt{\gamma/(\rho g)}\). Gravity is required in \(\ell\), although it is omitted from one parameter list in the source.

Use \(\cos\theta\simeq1-(z^{\prime})^2/2\) to get \(z^2/\ell^2-(z^{\prime})^2=0\). Differentiate to obtain \(z^{\prime\prime}=z/\ell^2\). The decaying solution is \[z(x)=-\ell\tan\theta_0e^{-x/\ell}.\]

Pressure integration gives \(\rho g(z_b^2-z_a^2)/2\), and surface tension gives \(\gamma(\cos\theta_b-\cos\theta_a)\). Therefore \[F_x=\frac{\rho g}{2}(z_b^2-z_a^2)+\gamma(\cos\theta_b-\cos\theta_a).\]

children.text: Each moment is \(m=J\pi d^2h/4=0.75\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\). Differentiate the axial dipole interaction energy to obtain \(F=3\mu_0m^2/(2\pi L^4)=2.11\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N\).
Bound surface current density is J, so the total circulating current across cylinder height is \(I=Jh\simeq2.39\times10^3\,\mathrm A\).

Locally the side currents are parallel wires separated by L. Integrate the force per length μ0I²/(2πL) around circumference πd: \(F\simeq\mu_0I^2d/(2L)\simeq14\,\mathrm N\). This neglects curvature and finite height.

For one sphere m=Jπδ³/6 and mass M=ρπδ³/6. The top sphere supports the lower chain through \(F=3\mu_0m^2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-4}/(2\pi\delta^4)=\mu_0m^2\pi^3/(60\delta^4)\). Equate to NMg, giving roughly 1320 spheres and length 6.6 m. This is an ideal straight-chain estimate ignoring mechanical instability.
a.5. Field near a long chain end

The moments per unit length m/δ form a thin solenoid. Away from its remote end the near endpoint acts as a magnetic pole of strength m/δ. Thus \[B=\frac{\mu_0m}{4\pi\delta r^2}=\frac{\mu_0J\delta^2}{24r^2},\] independent of θ. Field is radial from O, outward for a north endpoint and inward for a south endpoint. The conditions permit a continuum approximation and neglect of the far endpoint.
b.1. Field lines at a permeable plate

Normal B and tangential H are continuous. If α and β are the angles to the surface normal inside and outside the plate, \(\tan\alpha=(\mu/\mu_0)\tan\beta\). For μ≫μ0 the external line meets the surface almost normally. Each magnetic line must close. Lines entering the plate return through it and emerge elsewhere, possibly very far away. They must not terminate in the plate or leave through its distant lower face in the depicted thick-plate approximation. The source statement refers to three points on a separate answer sheet, not retained with its PDF. Here those path families are stated explicitly, and the source worked sketch is supplied in the solution.

children.text: An image magnet mirrored in the plane has parallel normal moment, with centre separation δ. Either polarity normal to the plate is a stable orientation. The attractive force is \(F=3\mu_0m^2/(2\pi\delta^4)\simeq5.9\,\mathrm N\).

Flux conservation gives B1d²=B2(D²−d²), so B1=3B2. Ampère circulation with side current Jh gives B1+B2=μ0J. Hence B1=3μ0J/4=1.125 T and opposite return field has magnitude B2=μ0J/4=0.375 T. Maxwell pressure integrated over the inner disc and outer annulus gives \[F=\frac\pi{8\mu_0}[d^2B_1^2+(D^2-d^2)B_2^2]=\frac{3\pi\mu_0J^2d^2}{32}\simeq210\,\mathrm N.\] Field energy alone at fixed permanent magnetization misses the magnet's interaction energy and can give a wrong force sign.

One stable pattern has parallel moments along each horizontal row and opposite moments in adjacent rows. The nearest-neighbour field at a sphere is \(B=3\mu_0m/(2\pi\delta^3)\), aligned with its moment. Removing the sphere breaks its interactions and costs \(W=mB=3\mu_0m^2/(2\pi\delta^3)\simeq29\,\mathrm{mJ}\). Do not divide this single-removal energy by two. The source also accepts an appropriate vortex-like stable pattern, so the sketch is self-reviewed.

A stable arrangement has all moments parallel to one lattice direction. Sum the six dipole fields, whose transverse components cancel, to get \(B=3\mu_0m/(4\pi\delta^3)\). The removal energy is \(W=3\mu_0m^2/(4\pi\delta^3)\simeq15\,\mathrm{mJ}\).
