children.text: The small angular size is \(d_o/D\). Thus \(d_i=fd_o/D=26.2\,\mu\mathrm m\).

Use an equal-area circular aperture \(D_m=2\sqrt{A_m/\pi}=5.64\,\mathrm m\). The Airy diameter is \(d_d=2.44\lambda f/D_m=45.0\,\mu\mathrm m\). This is the equal-area circular-aperture Airy estimate. The simpler diameter \(2\lambda f/D_m\) is 36.9 micrometres. The actual segmented aperture has a different diffraction pattern. State the aperture and diameter convention, then compare the estimate in self-review.

The collected power is \(P=A_m\sigma T_*^4(d_o/(2D))^2\). If it is uniformly deposited over spot diameter d, balance \(P=\sigma T_i^4\pi d^2/4\): \[T_i=T_*\left(\frac{A_md_o^2}{\pi D^2d^2}\right)^{1/4}.\] With geometrical d=di this is about 530 K. Taking the source approximate broadened diameter d=di+dd gives about 320 K. A diffraction-only area gives about 410 K. State the spot model. A real point-spread function has nonuniform intensity, so these are effective spot temperatures.

The graph slope of log base 10 current against 1/T is approximately -100 K. Hence \(|\Delta E_g|/(6k_B)\simeq100\ln10=230\,\mathrm K\), and the characteristic photon thermal-energy scale is \(|\Delta E_g|/k_B\simeq1380\,\mathrm K\), of order \(10^3\,\mathrm K\). A thermal spectrum has no sharp cutoff, so the intended answer is a scale.

Read id approximately 5 electrons/s from the graph. Put P=p tau. Solve \(P^2=100(14^2+5\times10^4+P)\), obtaining P approximately 2291 and \(p=0.229\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Graph-reading uncertainty gives roughly 0.206 to 0.250 per second.
The threshold photon energy is about \(1380k_B=1.91\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm J\). Thus \(I=p\Delta E_g/A_m\simeq1.75\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).

Let \(q_i=\epsilon\sigma A_sT_i^4\), \(f_i=\alpha(q_i-q_{i+1})\), and \(r=1+\beta/\alpha\). The source recurrence is \(f_{i-1}=rf_i\), with \(f_4=q_5\). Summing differences gives \(q_1=Kq_5\), \[K=1+(1+r+r^2+r^3)/\alpha.\] Sheet-one balance is \(\epsilon A_sI_0=q_1+rf_1=(K+r^4)q_5\). Hence \[T_5=\left[\frac{I_0}{\sigma(K+r^4)}\right]^{1/4},\quad T_1=\left[\frac{I_0K}{\sigma(K+r^4)}\right]^{1/4}.\] This explicitly follows the stipulated difference-flux recurrence. A physical view-factor model for gap radiation instead depends on a sum of surface emissions. The official discussion acknowledges that distinction, so do not combine the two models silently.

The gap area is \(A_g=4h\sqrt{A_s}=14.14\,\mathrm{m^2}\). Repeated diffuse reflection weights the two sheet absorbing areas epsilon As and the open gap. Therefore \(\alpha\simeq\epsilon A_s/(2\epsilon A_s+A_g)=0.293\), while the escape probability is \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}\simeq A_g/(2\epsilon A_s+A_g)=0.414\). This is a probability for total radiation, not automatically the beta multiplying a temperature difference. Using beta approximately beta prime is the elementary problem approximation. A conversion requires temperature ratios and gives a somewhat larger effective beta.

Using the explicit C.1 recurrence with alpha=0.293 and beta=0.414 gives r=2.414, K=80.60 and \(T_1\simeq360\,\mathrm K,T_5\simeq120\,\mathrm K\). Different self-consistent gap approximations change the estimates. The retained official solution tabulates roughly 380 K and 102 K for rounded alpha=0.3,beta=0.4, but this does not follow the displayed recurrence used here. Formula and convention consistency matter, so this is self-review.

Pressure decreases, entropy increases through irreversibility, and equal-area mass continuity with higher downstream speed implies molar volume increases. Thus P1>P2, S1<S2, V1<V2. For an unspecified real gas the signs of T2-T1 and U2-U1 are not determined by these facts alone. The official key asserts U1<U2 from viscous dissipation, but this neglects the competing pressure-work terms. From conserved enthalpy, U2-U1=P1V1-P2V2, whose sign needs an equation of state.

Upstream gas does work P1V1 on a mole entering the plug, while that mole does P2V2 on downstream gas. No heat is exchanged and kinetic energy changes are negligible, so \(U_2-U_1=P_1V_1-P_2V_2\). Thus \(H=U+PV\) is constant. More precisely steady flow conserves specific enthalpy plus bulk kinetic energy per mass.

At the specified point draw the local isentrope tangent. Since \((\partial U/\partial V)_S=-P\), its intercept at V=0 is U+PV. Bracket with nearby tangents and interpolate: approximately \(40.7\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}\). The additional official answer-sheet graph and full solution are supplied because the archive retained solution ends before Part D.

From the enthalpy intercept draw candidate tangents to isentropes. Their contact points trace states of the same enthalpy. The largest isotherm touched is approximately 11 K. Above that inlet temperature no state on the required enthalpy locus reaches the specified outlet.
Pressure is minus the isentrope tangent slope. With the constructed inlet point, the graph gives approximately \(1.8\,\mathrm{MPa}\), with rough graphical estimates around 1.6 to 2.4 MPa.

children.text: Use scaling arguments to establish the physical dependence in each independent part. A final numerical answer needs a justification of the relevant length, force or time scales.

A straw of spaghetti is balanced horizontally at its midpoint. At diameter \(d=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), it breaks under its own weight at length \(l=50\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the breaking length for \(d'=1\,\mathrm{cm}\), assuming the same material.

Coarse sand grains have ten times the mean volume of fine grains. Both sands have optimal water content and form cylinders of identical shape and size. Coarse sand breaks under a compressive force of 10 N. Find the force for fine sand, ignoring gravity.

A spacecraft maintains constant proper-acceleration magnitude \(g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). Passengers must return to Earth within 50 years of onboard elapsed time. Let \(d\) be maximum distance reached. Find \(d'/d\) for \(g'=15\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). Start and finish at rest at Earth. Use \(c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and 365.25 days per year. Hyperbolic functions are defined by \(\cosh x=(e^x+e^{-x})/2\), \(\sinh x=(e^x-e^{-x})/2\).

A wooden sphere of radius \(r_0\) floats in water. Its frictionless small-oscillation frequency would be \(\omega_0\), but viscous damping lowers it to \(0.99\omega_0\). Find the smallest radius permitting oscillations. Drag is proportional to velocity and fluid viscosity \(\eta\), whose units are \(\mathrm{kg/(m\,s)}\).

statement.text:
Scaling laws
Use scaling arguments to establish the physical dependence in each independent part. A final numerical answer needs a justification of the relevant length, force or time scales.
A.1. Spaghetto strength
A straw of spaghetti is balanced horizontally at its midpoint. At diameter \(d=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), it breaks under its own weight at length \(l=50\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the breaking length for \(d'=1\,\mathrm{cm}\), assuming the same material.
B.1. Wet sand strength
Coarse sand grains have ten times the mean volume of fine grains. Both sands have optimal water content and form cylinders of identical shape and size. Coarse sand breaks under a compressive force of 10 N. Find the force for fine sand, ignoring gravity.
C.1. Relativistic expedition range
A spacecraft maintains constant proper-acceleration magnitude \(g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). Passengers must return to Earth within 50 years of onboard elapsed time. Let \(d\) be maximum distance reached. Find \(d'/d\) for \(g'=15\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). Start and finish at rest at Earth. Use \(c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and 365.25 days per year. Hyperbolic functions are defined by \(\cosh x=(e^x+e^{-x})/2\), \(\sinh x=(e^x-e^{-x})/2\).
D.1. Threshold floating-ball radius
A wooden sphere of radius \(r_0\) floats in water. Its frictionless small-oscillation frequency would be \(\omega_0\), but viscous damping lowers it to \(0.99\omega_0\). Find the smallest radius permitting oscillations. Drag is proportional to velocity and fluid viscosity \(\eta\), whose units are \(\mathrm{kg/(m\,s)}\).

children.text: The bending moment scales as weight times length, \(\rho gd^2l^2\). The maximum tensile stress scales as moment divided by section modulus \(\sim d^3\), hence as \(\rho gl^2/d\). Equal breaking stress implies \(l\propto\sqrt d\). Thus \(l'=50\sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{cm}=1.58\,\mathrm m\).

For grain size \(r\), capillary force per bridge scales as \(\gamma r\). The number of bridges across a fixed area scales as \(r^{-2}\). Strength therefore scales as \(r^{-1}\). The size ratio is \(10^{1/3}\), giving \(F_f=10\times10^{1/3}=21.5\,\mathrm N\).

The optimal rest-to-rest outward and inward trip has four equal proper-time acceleration legs of \(T/4\). Rapidity obeys \(dw/d\tau=g/c\). Integrating \(dx/d\tau=c\sinh(g\tau/c)\) gives \[d(g)=\frac{2c^2}{g}[\cosh(gT/(4c))-1].\] Hence \[\frac{d'}d=\frac g{g^{\prime}}\frac{\cosh(g^{\prime}T/(4c))-1}{\cosh(gT/(4c))-1}\simeq480.\] The source uses rounded dimensionless arguments. Small differences from year conventions are accepted.

Added water mass as well as sphere mass scales as \(r^3\). Buoyancy stiffness scales as \(r^2\), so \(\omega_0^2\propto r^{-1}\). Dimensional analysis gives viscous drag \(F_d\propto\eta rv\), hence damping rate \(b\propto r^{-2}\). Thus \(b^2/\omega_0^2\propto r^{-3}\). At \(r_0\), this ratio is \(1-0.99^2\). Critical damping requires it to reach one: \[r_{min}=r_0(1-0.99^2)^{1/3}=0.271r_0.\] Strictly oscillatory motion requires \(r>r_{min}\).

a.3. Asymptotic crust thickness
Far from the ridge the temperature varies linearly across the crust from T0 to T1. Use hydrostatic mantle and water pressures to find D.
a.4. Horizontal force on the crust
Find the leading-order horizontal force on the right half of the crust in terms of ρ0,ρ1,h,L,k,g. Treat the mantle pressure as hydrostatic and use the source's leading-order thin-crust model.
a.5. Thermal relaxation time
If the crust is thermally isolated from the rest of Earth, estimate the timescale for its upper and lower temperatures to approach one another. Assume independence from the two initial temperatures.
b.1. Returning seismic ray

A line source at x=z=0 emits a ray at angle 0<θ0<π/2 from the downward vertical into a medium of speed v(z)=v0(1+z/z0). Its path is a circle arc. Find its next surface coordinate x1=A cot(bθ0), determining A,b.
b.2. Absorbed seismic energy density
The source releases energy E per unit length uniformly into the downward half-plane. Waves are absorbed on their first return to the surface. Find and sketch ε(x), energy per surface area.
b.3. Furthest shadow zone
Now reflect waves perfectly at the surface. Emit only the small angular interval θ0±δθ0/2, with δθ0≪θ0 and ≪1. To leading order find the furthest surface distance that is not reached by this signal.

children.text: a.1. Oil force on a plate

Bottom pressure matching gives oil column height \(h_o=\rho_0h/\rho_{oil}\). Integrating triangular pressure distributions on both sides yields \[F_x=\frac{\rho_0gh^2w}{2}\left(\frac{\rho_0}{\rho_{oil}}-1\right)>0.\]
Each dimension changes by the same factor, so \[\rho(T)=\rho_1[1-k_l(T_1-T)/(T_1-T_0)]^{-3}\simeq\rho_1[1+3k_l(T_1-T)/(T_1-T_0)].\] Thus k=3kl.
The same mantle depth has equal pressure on the ridge axis and at infinity: \(\rho_1(h+D)=\rho_0h+\rho_1D(1+k/2)\). Therefore \[D=\frac{2h}{k}(1-\rho_0/\rho_1).\]
a.4. Horizontal force on the crust

Integrating the pressure tractions on the sloping upper and lower surfaces gives the difference of their projected vertical integrals. With common pressure pO at z=0, \[F=L\int_0^{h+D}(p_O+\rho_1gz)dz-L\int_0^h(p_O+\rho_0gz)dz.\] Thus \(F=Lp_OD+L\rho_1g(h+D)^2/2-L\rho_0gh^2/2\). Since D∝1/k and pO and h are fixed, the leading term is \[F\simeq\frac{2gLh^2(\rho_1-\rho_0)^2}{k^2\rho_1},\] directed away from the ridge. This is the force from the exterior fluids on the specified crust region.

The heat per area to redistribute is of order ρ1cDΔT, and conductive flux is of order κΔT/D. Their ratio gives \(\tau\sim\rho_1cD^2/\kappa\). Dimensional analysis determines the same scaling, with an undetermined order-one prefactor. The temperature difference cancels.

Snell's law gives \(\sin\theta/(1+z/z_0)=\sin\theta_0\). The circle radius is \(R=z_0/\sin\theta_0\), with centre at depth −z0. Its surface chord is \(x_1=2R\cos\theta_0=2z_0\cot\theta_0\). Thus A=2z0,b=1.

An angular interval dθ carries E dθ/π. Since \(|dx/d\theta|=2z_0\csc^2\theta\), \[\epsilon(x)=\frac{2Ez_0}{\pi(4z_0^2+x^2)}.\] The plot is even, peaks at E/(2πz0) at the origin, decays as 1/x², and integrates to E over the entire surface.

The nth return illuminates an interval centred at n x1 with width n|x1′|δθ0. Adjacent intervals first overlap when \(n\sim x_1/(|x_1^{\prime}|\delta\theta_0)\). Thus the last gap lies near \[x_{max}\simeq\frac{x_1^2}{|x_1^{\prime}|\delta\theta_0}=\frac{2z_0\cos^2\theta_0}{\delta\theta_0}.\] This is a leading narrow-beam estimate, with discrete-reflection corrections.

statement.text:
Electrostatic lens
A metallic ring of radius R carries uniform charge q. Its circular toroidal cross-section has radius a≪R, neglected except in part D. Its plane is xy and its axis is z. Potential is zero at infinity. An electron has mass m and charge −e, e>0, and does not perturb the ring charge distribution. Near the origin use \((1+x)^s\simeq1+sx+s(s-1)x^2/2\). In lens operation the electron speed v along z is approximately constant, with kinetic energy E=mv²/2. The ring is activated only while the electron packet crosses \(|z|<d/2\), where d≪R. Work in the paraxial limit r≪R, with focal distances much greater than d, ignoring magnetic fields and propagation delay. Parts D and E replace instantaneous charging by a capacitance C and contact resistance R0. For focusing choose the appropriate signed supply V0.

a.1. Axial potential
Find Φ(z) on the axis.
a.2. Near-centre axial expansion
Expand through the first position-dependent nonzero term for |z|≪R.
a.3. Axial electron force
Find the leading signed axial force and the sign of q needed for oscillations.
a.4. Axial oscillation frequency
For the stable sign of q find ω.
b.1. Radial potential coefficient
In the ring plane let Φ(r)≈q(α+βr²). Derive β.
b.2. Radial electron force
Find the leading radial force and the sign of q for radial harmonic confinement.
c.1. Pulsed lens focal length

With instantaneous switching, find f in terms of β and the given quantities. Initially the electron packet is parallel to z.
c.2. Finite-source image
A point source is on the axis distance b>f from the ring and emits at small angles. Find image distance c.
c.3. Thin-lens relation
Calculate 1/b+1/c and determine whether the optical thin-lens relation holds.
d.1. Thin torus capacitance
Retain cross-section radius a≪R and calculate C to leading thin-ring accuracy.
d.2. Charging waveform

At entry connect the ring through R0 to V0, and at exit connect it through R0 to ground. Time t=0 is passage through the ring plane. Find and sketch q(t), and give its maximum signed charge q0.
e.1. Focal length with finite charging
Assume f/v≫R0C and d/v is comparable to R0C. Find f, including the discharge tail after the electron exits the nominal active region.
e.2. Effective charge
Express qeff such that the result has the instantaneous-lens form with q replaced by qeff.

children.text: Every ring element is the same distance \(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\) away, so \[\Phi(z)=\frac q{4\pi\epsilon_0\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}.\]
Because electron potential energy is −eΦ, \(F_z=e\partial_z\Phi=-eqz/(4\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). It restores toward the centre for q>0.
Compare \(m\ddot z=-m\omega^2z\) with A3: \(\omega=\sqrt{eq/(4\pi\epsilon_0mR^3)}\), with q>0.

Expand \((R^2+r^2-2Rr\cos\phi)^{-1/2}\) and average cosφ and cos²φ around the ring. The result is \(\Phi(r)=q[1+r^2/(4R^2)]/(4\pi\epsilon_0R)\). Thus \(\beta=1/(16\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). This also follows from the charge-free Laplace equation and the axial expansion.
\(F_r=e\partial_r\Phi=2eq\beta r=eqr/(8\pi\epsilon_0R^3)\). Radial restoration requires q<0, opposite to axial restoration. The ring cannot provide simultaneous static confinement in all directions.
The active time is d/v. Radial impulse gives \(\Delta v_r=2eq\beta rd/(mv)\), negative for q<0. The subsequent crossing time is −r/Δvr. Thus \[f=-\frac{mv^2}{2eq\beta d}=-\frac E{eq\beta d}.\]

At the ring the initial radial velocity is vr/b. Add the impulse from C1, then propagate to the axis: \[c=-\left(\frac1b+\frac{eq\beta d}{E}\right)^{-1}.\] With b>f and q<0 the denominator is negative and c>0.
C2 gives \(1/b+1/c=-eq\beta d/E=1/f\). Thus the same thin-lens equation holds in the stated impulse approximation.

Split the ring at a small angular cutoff η with a/R≪η≪1. The nearby piece is approximately a straight line and contributes \(q\ln(2\eta R/a)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The remainder contributes \(q\ln(4/\eta)/(4\pi^2\epsilon_0R)\). The arbitrary cutoff cancels, giving \[C=\frac{4\pi^2\epsilon_0R}{\ln(8R/a)}.\]

Write τ=R0C and t0=d/v. The continuous waveform is \[q(t)=\begin{cases}0&t<-t_0/2,\\CV_0[1-e^{-(t+t_0/2)/\tau}]&-t_0/2\le t\le t_0/2,\\CV_0(1-e^{-t_0/\tau})e^{-(t-t_0/2)/\tau}&t>t_0/2.\end{cases}\] The largest magnitude occurs at exit, with \(q_0=CV_0(1-e^{-d/(vR_0C)})\). For focusing V0<0, so the curve dips below zero and returns exponentially to it.
e.1. Focal length with finite charging

During the impulse r changes negligibly and the electron remains near the ring because vR0C is of order d≪R. Integrating \(R_0\dot q+q/C=V(t)\) over the full charging and discharge history gives \(\int qdt=CV_0d/v\), independent of R0. Therefore \(\Delta v_r=(2e\beta r/m)CV_0d/v\) and \[f=-\frac E{e\beta CV_0d}.\] Omitting the discharge tail would give a different and incomplete impulse.
The complete charge-time integral matches a rectangular pulse of height \(q_{eff}=CV_0\) and duration d/v. It is not the peak charge q0.

children.text: The longest standing-wave wavelength is 2L, giving p=h/(2L) and \(E_{min}=h^2/(8mL^2)\).
Fit n half-wavelengths into L: λn=2L/n. Thus \(E_n=h^2n^2/(8mL^2)\).

Two opposite-spin electrons fit each spatial level, filling n=1 to 5. The smallest allowed excitation is 5→6, giving \[\lambda=\frac{8m_ec(10.5\ell)^2}{11h}=\frac{882m_ec\ell^2}{11h}\simeq647\,\mathrm{nm}.\]

Cy3 fills four levels and absorbs in the 4→5 transition. With L=8.5ℓ, \(\lambda_{Cy3}=8m_ec(8.5\ell)^2/(9h)\simeq518\,\mathrm{nm}\). The absorption edge shifts about 129 nm towards blue. The electron count must change along with box length.

The dimensions force \(K\propto\epsilon_0^{-1}h^{-1}\lambda^{-3}d^2\). Thus \[K=\frac{16\pi^3d^2}{3\epsilon_0h\lambda^3}.\] As a positive decay rate, K satisfies dN/dt=−KN. The source's unsigned definition omits that minus sign.
Use the Cy5 emission/absorption-edge wavelength in the rate expression. \(\tau=3\epsilon_0h\lambda^3/[16\pi^3(2.4e\ell)^2]\simeq3.3\,\mathrm{ns}\).
The volume per atom gives ℓ=n^(−1/3). Equating wavelengths gives \(T_c=h^2n^{2/3}/(3mk_B)\). This is the problem's estimate, not the exact ideal-Bose-gas transition coefficient.

\(n_c=(3mk_BT_c)^{3/2}/h^3\simeq1.59\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The ideal gas law gives \(n_0=p_0/(k_BT_0)\simeq2.41\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The ordinary gas is about \(1.5\times10^{7}\) times denser.

Use 〈cos a cos b〉=cos(a−b)/2. Then \[V=-\alpha E_0^2[3/2+\cos(\mathbf b_1\cdot\mathbf r)+\cos(\mathbf b_2\cdot\mathbf r)+\cos(\mathbf b_3\cdot\mathbf r)],\] with b1=k2−k3=k(0,√3), b2=k3−k1=k(−3/2,−√3/2), b3=k1−k2=k(3/2,−√3/2).
A 60° rotation permutes the set of six reciprocal vectors ±b1,±b2,±b3. Since cosine is even, changing a vector to its negative does not alter its term. The sum and hence V are invariant.

\[V_X=-\alpha E_0^2[5/2+2\cos(3kx/2)],\quad V_Y=-\alpha E_0^2[3/2+\cos2\phi+2\cos\phi],\quad\phi=\sqrt3ky/2.\] VX has minima at x=0 and maxima at x=2π/(3k), modulo 4π/(3k). For VY, solve sin2φ+sinφ=0. In 0≤φ<2π, minima occur at φ=0 (deep) and π (shallow), maxima at 2π/3 and 4π/3. The φ=π minimum is only a one-dimensional minimum.

The point x=0, φ=π is a minimum along y but a maximum along x, so is a saddle. The nearest true minima are \((a,0),(a/2,\sqrt3a/2),(-a/2,\sqrt3a/2),(-a,0),(-a/2,-\sqrt3a/2),(a/2,-\sqrt3a/2)\). Here \(a=4\pi/(3k)=2\lambda_{las}/3\).
Equate Coulomb and centripetal forces and impose merv=nħ. Then \(r=4\pi\epsilon_0n^2\hbar^2/(m_ee^2)\), so \[n=\frac e\hbar\sqrt{\frac{m_e\lambda_{las}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}}\simeq85.\]

solution.text:
Particles and Waves
a.1. Ground-state energy
The longest standing-wave wavelength is 2L, giving p=h/(2L) and \(E_{min}=h^2/(8mL^2)\).
a.2. All box levels
Fit n half-wavelengths into L: λn=2L/n. Thus \(E_n=h^2n^2/(8mL^2)\).
a.3. First emission wavelength
The photon energy is \(3h^2/(8mL^2)\). Therefore \(\lambda_{21}=hc/(E_2-E_1)=8mcL^2/(3h)\).
b.1. Cy5 absorption edge
Two opposite-spin electrons fit each spatial level, filling n=1 to 5. The smallest allowed excitation is 5→6, giving \[\lambda=\frac{8m_ec(10.5\ell)^2}{11h}=\frac{882m_ec\ell^2}{11h}\simeq647\,\mathrm{nm}.\]
b.2. Cy3 spectral shift
Cy3 fills four levels and absorbs in the 4→5 transition. With L=8.5ℓ, \(\lambda_{Cy3}=8m_ec(8.5\ell)^2/(9h)\simeq518\,\mathrm{nm}\). The absorption edge shifts about 129 nm towards blue. The electron count must change along with box length.
b.3. Spontaneous emission rate
The dimensions force \(K\propto\epsilon_0^{-1}h^{-1}\lambda^{-3}d^2\). Thus \[K=\frac{16\pi^3d^2}{3\epsilon_0h\lambda^3}.\] As a positive decay rate, K satisfies dN/dt=−KN. The source's unsigned definition omits that minus sign.
b.4. Cy5 lifetime
Use the Cy5 emission/absorption-edge wavelength in the rate expression. \(\tau=3\epsilon_0h\lambda^3/[16\pi^3(2.4e\ell)^2]\simeq3.3\,\mathrm{ns}\).
c.1. Thermal momentum and wavelength
Equipartition gives p²/(2m)=3kBT/2. Hence \(p=\sqrt{3mk_BT}\), \(\lambda_{dB}=h/\sqrt{3mk_BT}\).
c.2. Condensation estimate
The volume per atom gives ℓ=n^(−1/3). Equating wavelengths gives \(T_c=h^2n^{2/3}/(3mk_B)\). This is the problem's estimate, not the exact ideal-Bose-gas transition coefficient.
c.3. Critical density and comparison
\(n_c=(3mk_BT_c)^{3/2}/h^3\simeq1.59\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The ideal gas law gives \(n_0=p_0/(k_BT_0)\simeq2.41\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The ordinary gas is about \(1.5\times10^{7}\) times denser.
d.1. Three-beam lattice potential
Use 〈cos a cos b〉=cos(a−b)/2. Then \[V=-\alpha E_0^2[3/2+\cos(\mathbf b_1\cdot\mathbf r)+\cos(\mathbf b_2\cdot\mathbf r)+\cos(\mathbf b_3\cdot\mathbf r)],\] with b1=k2−k3=k(0,√3), b2=k3−k1=k(−3/2,−√3/2), b3=k1−k2=k(3/2,−√3/2).
d.2. Sixfold symmetry
A 60° rotation permutes the set of six reciprocal vectors ±b1,±b2,±b3. Since cosine is even, changing a vector to its negative does not alter its term. The sum and hence V are invariant.
d.3. Axis profiles and extrema
\[V_X=-\alpha E_0^2[5/2+2\cos(3kx/2)],\quad V_Y=-\alpha E_0^2[3/2+\cos2\phi+2\cos\phi],\quad\phi=\sqrt3ky/2.\] VX has minima at x=0 and maxima at x=2π/(3k), modulo 4π/(3k). For VY, solve sin2φ+sinφ=0. In 0≤φ<2π, minima occur at φ=0 (deep) and π (shallow), maxima at 2π/3 and 4π/3. The φ=π minimum is only a one-dimensional minimum.
d.4. True lattice minima
The point x=0, φ=π is a minimum along y but a maximum along x, so is a saddle. The nearest true minima are \((a,0),(a/2,\sqrt3a/2),(-a/2,\sqrt3a/2),(-a,0),(-a/2,-\sqrt3a/2),(a/2,-\sqrt3a/2)\). Here \(a=4\pi/(3k)=2\lambda_{las}/3\).
d.5. Rydberg quantum number
Equate Coulomb and centripetal forces and impose merv=nħ. Then \(r=4\pi\epsilon_0n^2\hbar^2/(m_ee^2)\), so \[n=\frac e\hbar\sqrt{\frac{m_e\lambda_{las}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}}\simeq85.\]

children.text: A homogeneous zero-effective-length spring has mass \(M\), minimum and unstretched length \(L_0\), and tension \(F=kL\) when stretched to \(L>L_0\). It stays at \(L_0\) for smaller tensile forces. Define \(\alpha=kL_0/(Mg)<1\). Label material points by their unstretched distance \(0\le\ell\le L_0\) from the bottom. After release from hanging equilibrium, the spring contracts from the top. Its moving part forms a rigid chunk that collects stationary turns. Each lower point stays at rest until reached. Once the spring has collapsed to length \(L_0\), it falls as a rigid body without tumbling. Use this model, neglect air resistance, and retain finite \(L_0\).

children.text: A segment of unstretched length \(\Delta\ell\) is pulled by force \(F\) in weightlessness. Find its length \(\Delta y\).
Find work to extend that segment from \(\Delta\ell\) to \(\Delta y\ge\Delta\ell\).
Find the time \(t_c\) until the spring reaches length \(L_0\).
While a stretched stationary section exists, its mass is \(M\ell/L_0\). Show that the rigid moving section has speed \(v_I(\ell)=\sqrt{A\ell+B}\), and determine \(A,B\).
Find minimum speed before ground impact, using \(A,B,L_0,\alpha\).

statement.text:
Zero-length springs and slinky coils
A homogeneous zero-effective-length spring has mass \(M\), minimum and unstretched length \(L_0\), and tension \(F=kL\) when stretched to \(L>L_0\). It stays at \(L_0\) for smaller tensile forces. Define \(\alpha=kL_0/(Mg)<1\). Label material points by their unstretched distance \(0\le\ell\le L_0\) from the bottom. After release from hanging equilibrium, the spring contracts from the top. Its moving part forms a rigid chunk that collects stationary turns. Each lower point stays at rest until reached. Once the spring has collapsed to length \(L_0\), it falls as a rigid body without tumbling. Use this model, neglect air resistance, and retain finite \(L_0\).

A.1. Segment extension
A segment of unstretched length \(\Delta\ell\) is pulled by force \(F\) in weightlessness. Find its length \(\Delta y\).
A.2. Stretching work
Find work to extend that segment from \(\Delta\ell\) to \(\Delta y\ge\Delta\ell\).
A.3. Hanging length
Find the equilibrium total length \(H\).
B.1.formula. Collapse time
Find the time \(t_c\) until the spring reaches length \(L_0\).
B.1.value. Collapse time value
Evaluate for \(k=1.02\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(L_0=0.055\,\mathrm m\), \(M=0.201\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(g=9.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\).
B.2. Moving-front velocity
While a stretched stationary section exists, its mass is \(M\ell/L_0\). Show that the rigid moving section has speed \(v_I(\ell)=\sqrt{A\ell+B}\), and determine \(A,B\).
B.3. Minimum moving speed
Find minimum speed before ground impact, using \(A,B,L_0,\alpha\).
C.1. Mechanical energy lost
Find the heat generated from release until just before ground impact.

children.text: Homogeneity gives an effective segment constant \(k_*=kL_0/\Delta\ell\). Thus \[\Delta y=\Delta\ell\max\left(1,\frac F{kL_0}\right).\]
Integrate the force \(k_*y\) from the minimum length: \[\Delta W=\frac{kL_0}{2\Delta\ell}(\Delta y^2-\Delta\ell^2).\]

Tension at material coordinate \(\ell\) is \(Mg\ell/L_0\). Turns remain touching up to \(\ell_0=\alpha L_0\). Above that, \(dy/d\ell=\ell/(\alpha L_0)\). Integrating both regions gives \[H=\frac{L_0}{2}(\alpha+1/\alpha).\]

The initial centre-of-mass height above the bottom is \(y_{cm}=L_0[1/(6\alpha)-\alpha^2/6+\alpha/2]\). At collapse it is \(L_0/2\), since the bottom has stayed at rest. The CM falls freely, so \(gt_c^2/2=y_{cm}-L_0/2=L_0(1-\alpha)^3/(6\alpha)\). Hence \[t_c=\sqrt{\frac{L_0(1-\alpha)^3}{3g\alpha}}.\]

Total downward momentum is \(Mgt\). The moving mass is \(M(1-\ell/L_0)\), so \((1-\ell/L_0)v_I=gt\). The boundary height is \(y(\ell)=\ell^2/(2\alpha L_0)+\alpha L_0/2\), and the moving chunk has length \(L_0-\ell\). Its top height therefore has derivative \(\ell/(\alpha L_0)-1\) with respect to \(\ell\). Combining the kinematic front speed with momentum gives \[v_I^2=\frac{2g}{3\alpha}\ell+gL_0\left(\frac1{3\alpha}-1\right).\] Thus \(A=2g/(3\alpha)\), \(B=gL_0[1/(3\alpha)-1]\). These apply for \(\alpha L_0<\ell<L_0\). The singular instantaneous start is a feature of the ideal collection model, not an initially nonzero speed of a finite mass.

The moving chunk slows until reaching the touching bottom section at \(\ell=\alpha L_0\). It then inelastically collects the bottom mass \(\alpha M\). Momentum conservation gives \[v_{min}=(1-\alpha)\sqrt{A\alpha L_0+B}.\] Subsequently the full spring accelerates downwards. This also equals \(gt_c\).

The CM gravitational energy decrease becomes its translational kinetic energy. All initial elastic energy is therefore lost to heat and other internal dissipation. Integrate the segment energy over the stretched part: \[Q=\int_{\alpha L_0}^{L_0}\frac{kL_0}{2}\left[\frac{\ell^2}{\alpha^2L_0^2}-1\right]d\ell=\frac{MgL_0(1-\alpha)^2(2\alpha+1)}{6\alpha}.\]

children.text: The Physics of a Microwave Oven

A model magnetron has a central cathode of radius a and a positive cylindrical anode of radius b, with eight LC resonator cavities. Adjacent cavities carry opposite oscillating charge. Their frequency is f=2.45 GHz. Static magnetic field B0 points out of the cross-section. The alternating electric-field amplitude is roughly one third of the static field, and electrons transfer about 80% of their acquired static-field energy to the oscillations. The resonator figure supplies its dimensions. Treat its slot as a parallel-plate capacitor and its cylindrical cavity as an inductor whose magnetic field is 0.6 times that of an infinite solenoid. Use ε0=\(8.85\times10^{-12}\) F/m, μ0=\(4\pi\times10^{-7}\) H/m, electron m=\(9.1\times10^{-31}\) kg, charge −e with e=\(1.6\times10^{-19}\) C, and c=\(3.0\times10^{8}\) m/s. For the operating magnetron use b−a=15 mm, B0=0.30 T and maximum kinetic energy 800 eV.

statement.text:

a.1. Cavity resonance estimate

a.2. Crossed-field trajectories
In free space let E=−E0 yhat and B=B0 zhat. Find the drift velocity and sketch two cyclotron periods for initial u=(3E0/B0)xhat and u=−(3E0/B0)xhat.

a.4. Radial drift directions

a.5. Angular focusing

a.6. Electron spokes

children.text: The Physics of a Microwave Oven

If cavity radius is R, height h, slot length ℓ and width d, \(L=0.6\pi\mu_0R^2/h\), \(C=\epsilon_0\ell h/d\). Therefore \[f_{est}=\frac{c}{2\pi R}\sqrt{\frac d{0.6\pi\ell}}\simeq2.0\,\mathrm{GHz}.\] Height cancels. This approximate geometry need not reproduce 2.45 GHz exactly.

\(\mathbf u_D=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/B^2=-(E_0/B_0)\hat x\). Set ωc=eB0/m. If initial relative x velocity is vprime, then \[x(t)=-E_0t/B_0+(v^{\prime}/\omega_c)\sin\omega_ct,\quad y(t)=(v^{\prime}/\omega_c)(1-\cos\omega_ct).\] The two values are vprime=4E0/B0 and −2E0/B0, so radii are 4mE0/(eB0²) and 2mE0/(eB0²). Plot for 0<t<4π/ωc. Both have the same negative-x drift, with differently oriented loops.

The relative circular speed is at most the laboratory maximum speed. Hence \(r\lesssim\sqrt{2mK_{max}}/(eB_0)=0.318\,\mathrm{mm}\). It is much smaller than the 15 mm gap, supporting the pure-drift approximation.

Use \(\mathbf u_D=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/B^2\). Only the azimuthal electric field gives radial drift. A and B drift towards the cathode. C,D,E drift towards the anode. None of these five points is in the perpendicular-only category. The radial static field contributes only azimuthal drift.

At equal radius the common static drift cancels from relative angular velocities. The radial alternating field focuses A,B,C and defocuses D,E,F. Thus AB,AC,BC decrease in angular separation, while DE,DF,EF increase.

There are four spokes separated by π/2. They rotate counterclockwise. In one half-period the field flips and a spoke advances to the adjacent cavity, by π/4. Thus \(\omega_s=(\pi/4)/(1/2f)=\pi f/2=3.85\times10^9\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).
At r=(a+b)/2 the drift speed V0/[B0(b−a)] equals rωs. Hence \[V_0=\frac{\pi fB_0}{4}(b^2-a^2).\] This is a model estimate of the minimum operating voltage.

The restoring signed torque is \(\tau_z=-p_0E(t)\sin\theta\), so its magnitude is \(|p_0E\sin\theta|\). Power is \(H_i=\tau_z\dot\theta=-p_0E\sin\theta\dot\theta=E\,d(p_0\cos\theta)/dt\). Torque magnitude alone must not be used for signed work.
Power density is \(H=E\dot P\). Averaging the product of sine and phase-shifted cosine gives \[\langle H\rangle=\tfrac12\beta\epsilon_0\omega E_0^2\sin\delta.\]

Total mean energy density is εrε0E0(z)²/2, so \(I=\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\epsilon_0cE_0(z)^2/2\). Energy balance gives \(dI/dz=-\langle H\rangle=-\beta\omega\sin\delta\,I/(c\sqrt{\epsilon_r})\). Thus \[I(z)=I(0)\exp[-\beta\omega z\sin\delta/(c\sqrt{\epsilon_r})].\]
Squaring the field gives intensity attenuation exponent \(-\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\omega z\tan\delta/c\). Match this with B3 to obtain β=εr in the stated approximation.

At 20°C read εr≈78 and εloss≈10. Then \[z_{1/2}=\frac{c\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\ln2}{\omega\epsilon_{loss}}\simeq12\,\mathrm{mm}.\] In pure water εloss decreases strongly on warming, so penetration increases. In dilute salt solution εloss increases while εr decreases, so penetration decreases. These are trends at the fixed specified frequency, not all frequencies.

Total mean energy density is εrε0E0(z)²/2, so \(I=\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\epsilon_0cE_0(z)^2/2\). Energy balance gives \(dI/dz=-\langle H\rangle=-\beta\omega\sin\delta\,I/(c\sqrt{\epsilon_r})\). Thus \[I(z)=I(0)\exp[-\beta\omega z\sin\delta/(c\sqrt{\epsilon_r})].\]
b.4. Polarization coefficient
Squaring the field gives intensity attenuation exponent \(-\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\omega z\tan\delta/c\). Match this with B3 to obtain β=εr in the stated approximation.
b.5. Penetration depth and temperature
At 20°C read εr≈78 and εloss≈10. Then \[z_{1/2}=\frac{c\sqrt{\epsilon_r}\ln2}{\omega\epsilon_{loss}}\simeq12\,\mathrm{mm}.\] In pure water εloss decreases strongly on warming, so penetration increases. In dilute salt solution εloss increases while εr decreases, so penetration decreases. These are trends at the fixed specified frequency, not all frequencies.

statement.text:
Thermoacoustic Engine
An ideal gas fills a sealed insulating tube of length \(L\) and cross-section \(S\), along x. Equilibrium pressure, temperature and density are \(p_0,T_0,\rho_0\). Ignore viscosity and transverse variation. A small standing-wave displacement is \(u(x,t)=a\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)\), with \(a\ll L\) and \(k=2\pi/\lambda\). Use the longest allowed wavelength throughout. A narrow parcel has \(V_0=S\Delta x\). Write \(V=V_0+V_1(x)\cos\omega t\), \(p=p_0-p_1(x)\cos\omega t\), and \(T=T_0-T_1(x)\cos\omega t\). Changes are small, and compression is adiabatic with index \(\gamma\) unless thermal contact is specified.
A.1. Longest wavelength
Find the longest allowed wavelength.
A.2. Volume amplitude
Find the signed volume-oscillation coefficient.
A.3. Pressure amplitude
Use forces on a parcel to find the pressure coefficient.
A.4. Sound speed
Find sound speed using the adiabatic relation.
A.5. Temperature amplitude
Find the temperature coefficient.
A.6. Thermal effect on the tube
For this task only, allow weak thermal interaction with the tube while keeping the wave approximately unchanged. State long-time temperature changes at the left end A, centre B and right end C.
B.1. Stack temperature amplitude

A short stack of plates parallel to x is centred at \(x_0=L/4\), length \(\ell\ll L\), filling cross-section \(S\). Its left and right edges are held at \(T_H=T_0+\tau/2\) and \(T_C=T_0-\tau/2\). The plate temperature is \(T_0-(x-x_0)\tau/\ell\). For a parcel at \(x_0\), write its local environment temperature as \(T_0-T_{st}\cos\omega t\) and find \(T_{st}\).
B.2. Critical thermal gradient
Find the critical \(\tau_{cr}\) above which gas transports heat from hot to cold. Assume \(\tau\ll T_0\), nearly uniform pressure and displacement over the stack, no edge effects, and negligible axial conduction. Only gas-stack conduction and convective transport matter.
B.3. Linearized heat-flow law
Find \(dQ/dt\) in terms of \(\dot V,\dot p,p_0,V_0,\gamma\). You may use \(c_v=R/(\gamma-1)\).
B.4. Volume phase coefficients
The heat input is \(\dot Q=-\beta V_0(T_{st}-T_1)\cos\omega t\), with \(\beta>0\). Its temperature perturbation is negligible at operating frequency. Write \(p=p_0+p_a\sin\omega t-p_b\cos\omega t\), \(V=V_0+V_a\sin\omega t+V_b\cos\omega t\). Given \(p_a,p_b\), find \(V_a,V_b\).
B.5. Acoustic work

B.6. Heat transported per cycle
Find heat carried from left to right across \(x=x_0\) per cycle. You may use convective current \(j=Q\,du/dt\).

children.text: Displacement vanishes at both sealed ends, so the fundamental has \(kL=\pi\) and \(\lambda_{max}=2L\).
The length change is \(\Delta x\,\partial u/\partial x\). Thus \(V_1=akV_0\cos kx\).
Linearized Newton's law is \(\rho_0\ddot u=-\partial p/\partial x\). Integrate in x to obtain \[p_1=\frac{a\omega^2\rho_0}{k}\cos kx.\]
Linearize the ideal-gas relation: \(T_1/T_0=p_1/p_0-V_1/V_0\). Thus \(T_1=ak(\gamma-1)T_0\cos kx\).
A.6. Thermal effect on the tube

Displacement and temperature are correlated so parcels carry heat away from the centre towards both ends. A and C warm, while B cools. The effect is thermal pumping by the acoustic motion, not viscous heating.
Heat follows hot to cold when \(T_{st}>T_1(x_0)\). Equating amplitudes gives \[\tau_{cr}=k\ell(\gamma-1)T_0.\]
From \(E=pV/(\gamma-1)\) and \(\dot Q=\dot E+p\dot V\), keep first-order changes: \[\dot Q=\frac{V_0\dot p+\gamma p_0\dot V}{\gamma-1}.\]

Match cosine and sine in B3, using \(T_{st}-T_1=a(\tau-\tau_{cr})/(\ell\sqrt2)\): \[V_b=\frac{V_0p_b}{\gamma p_0},\quad V_a=-\frac{V_0}{\gamma p_0}\left[p_a+\frac{(\gamma-1)\beta a(\tau-\tau_{cr})}{\omega\ell\sqrt2}\right].\] The source has an intermediate sign typo in its heat-input substitution. These final coefficients follow the question's negative heat-input convention.
Integrate \(\oint p\,dV=-\pi(p_aV_b+p_bV_a)\). Thus \(w=-\pi(p_aV_b+p_bV_a)/V_0\). With leading \(p_b=ak\gamma p_0/\sqrt2\), \[W_{tot}=wS\ell=\frac\pi{2\omega}(\gamma-1)\beta(\tau-\tau_{cr})ka^2S.\]

Integration by parts of the convected heat gives \(Q_{tot}=-(1/\Delta x)\oint\dot Q\,u\,dt\). Substitute the heat-input and displacement cosines: \[Q_{tot}=\frac\pi{2\omega}\frac{\beta(\tau-\tau_{cr})a^2S}{\ell}.\]

Dividing B5 by B6 gives \(\eta=(\gamma-1)k\ell=\tau_{cr}/T_0\). Since \(\eta_c\simeq\tau/T_0\) for \(\tau\ll T_0\), \[\eta\simeq\frac{\tau_{cr}}\tau\eta_c.\] This is the leading weak-gradient result on the engine branch \(\tau>\tau_{cr}\).

solution.text:
Thermoacoustic Engine
A.1. Longest wavelength
Displacement vanishes at both sealed ends, so the fundamental has \(kL=\pi\) and \(\lambda_{max}=2L\).
A.2. Volume amplitude
The length change is \(\Delta x\,\partial u/\partial x\). Thus \(V_1=akV_0\cos kx\).
A.3. Pressure amplitude
Linearized Newton's law is \(\rho_0\ddot u=-\partial p/\partial x\). Integrate in x to obtain \[p_1=\frac{a\omega^2\rho_0}{k}\cos kx.\]
A.4. Sound speed
Linearizing \(pV^\gamma=\mathrm{constant}\) gives \(p_1/p_0=\gamma V_1/V_0\). Therefore \(c=\omega/k=\sqrt{\gamma p_0/\rho_0}\).
A.5. Temperature amplitude
Linearize the ideal-gas relation: \(T_1/T_0=p_1/p_0-V_1/V_0\). Thus \(T_1=ak(\gamma-1)T_0\cos kx\).
A.6. Thermal effect on the tube
Displacement and temperature are correlated so parcels carry heat away from the centre towards both ends. A and C warm, while B cools. The effect is thermal pumping by the acoustic motion, not viscous heating.
B.1. Stack temperature amplitude
Substitute parcel displacement \(u(x_0,t)=a\cos\omega t/\sqrt2\). Then \(T_{st}=a\tau/(\ell\sqrt2)\).
B.2. Critical thermal gradient
Heat follows hot to cold when \(T_{st}>T_1(x_0)\). Equating amplitudes gives \[\tau_{cr}=k\ell(\gamma-1)T_0.\]
B.3. Linearized heat-flow law
From \(E=pV/(\gamma-1)\) and \(\dot Q=\dot E+p\dot V\), keep first-order changes: \[\dot Q=\frac{V_0\dot p+\gamma p_0\dot V}{\gamma-1}.\]
B.4. Volume phase coefficients
Match cosine and sine in B3, using \(T_{st}-T_1=a(\tau-\tau_{cr})/(\ell\sqrt2)\): \[V_b=\frac{V_0p_b}{\gamma p_0},\quad V_a=-\frac{V_0}{\gamma p_0}\left[p_a+\frac{(\gamma-1)\beta a(\tau-\tau_{cr})}{\omega\ell\sqrt2}\right].\] The source has an intermediate sign typo in its heat-input substitution. These final coefficients follow the question's negative heat-input convention.
B.5. Acoustic work
Integrate \(\oint p\,dV=-\pi(p_aV_b+p_bV_a)\). Thus \(w=-\pi(p_aV_b+p_bV_a)/V_0\). With leading \(p_b=ak\gamma p_0/\sqrt2\), \[W_{tot}=wS\ell=\frac\pi{2\omega}(\gamma-1)\beta(\tau-\tau_{cr})ka^2S.\]
B.6. Heat transported per cycle
Integration by parts of the convected heat gives \(Q_{tot}=-(1/\Delta x)\oint\dot Q\,u\,dt\). Substitute the heat-input and displacement cosines: \[Q_{tot}=\frac\pi{2\omega}\frac{\beta(\tau-\tau_{cr})a^2S}{\ell}.\]
B.7. Engine efficiency
Dividing B5 by B6 gives \(\eta=(\gamma-1)k\ell=\tau_{cr}/T_0\). Since \(\eta_c\simeq\tau/T_0\) for \(\tau\ll T_0\), \[\eta\simeq\frac{\tau_{cr}}\tau\eta_c.\] This is the leading weak-gradient result on the engine branch \(\tau>\tau_{cr}\).

a.1. Newtonian acceleration
Write \(\ddot{\mathbf r}_1=-\alpha\mathbf r_1/r_1^n\). Find n and α.
a.2. Binary kinetic energy
In \(E=A(\mu,\Omega,L)-GM\mu/L\), find A.
a.3. Circular energy coefficient
Write the energy as \(E=\beta GM\mu/L\). Find β.
b.1. Time-dependent quadrupole
Choose mass 1 at \(r_1(\cos\Omega t,\sin\Omega t)\). Write \(Q_{ii}=\mu L^2(a_i+b_i\cos kt)/2\), \(Q_{ij}=\mu L^2c_{ij}\sin kt/2\) for i≠j. Find k and all coefficients.
b.2. Radiated power coefficient
Find ξ in \(\mathcal P=\xi G\mu^2L^4\Omega^6/c^5\).
b.3. Chirp mass
Use \(\dot E=-\mathcal P\) to obtain \((\dot\Omega)^3=(3\xi)^3\Omega^{11}(GM_c)^5/c^{15}\). Find Mc in terms of M and μ.
b.4. Chirp integration
Relate Ω to fGW and integrate to show \(f_{GW}^{-8/3}=8\pi^{8/3}\xi(GM_c/c^3)^{2/3+p}(t_0-t)^{2-p}\). Determine p.
b.5. Mass from the measured chirp

In the strain graph A,B,C,D occur at t=0.000, 0.009, 0.034, 0.040 s. Estimate fGW at midpoint tAB and tCD, then estimate Mc and total M in solar masses assuming equal component masses.
b.6. Compactness and orbital speed

children.text: \(\mathbf r_2=-(M_1/M_2)\mathbf r_1\), so separation is \((M_1+M_2)r_1/M_2\). Newton's law then gives \(n=3\), \(\alpha=GM_2^3/(M_1+M_2)^2\).
The centre-of-mass identity \(M_1r_1^2+M_2r_2^2=\mu L^2\) gives \(A=\mu L^2\Omega^2/2\).
Force balance gives \(\Omega^2=GM/L^3\). Substitution gives \(E=-GM\mu/(2L)\), so β=−1/2.

The matrix is \[Q=\frac{\mu L^2}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1/3+\cos2\Omega t&\sin2\Omega t&0\\\sin2\Omega t&1/3-\cos2\Omega t&0\\0&0&-2/3\end{pmatrix}.\] Hence k=2Ω, a=(1/3,1/3,−2/3), b=(1,−1,0), c12=c21=1 and all remaining off-diagonal coefficients vanish.
Third derivatives have amplitude \(4\mu L^2\Omega^3\). Summing both diagonal and both off-diagonal contributions gives twice its square. Thus \(\xi=32/5\).
Differentiate \(E=-GM\mu/(2L)\) and \(L^3\Omega^2=GM\) to eliminate L and its derivative. This gives \(\dot\Omega=3\xi G^{5/3}\mu M^{2/3}\Omega^{11/3}/c^5\), hence \(M_c=(\mu^3M^2)^{1/5}\).

b.5. Mass from the measured chirp

The indicated intervals are half-periods: fAB=1/(2×0.009)=55.6 Hz and fCD=1/(2×0.006)=83.3 Hz, at 0.0045 s and 0.037 s. \(\Omega=\pi f_{CD}\simeq262\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(L=(GM/\Omega^2)^{1/3}\simeq500\,\mathrm{km}\). Non-overlap implies Rmax≈L/2≈250 km, so Rsun/Rmax≈3000. Each equal mass moves at \(v=\Omega L/2\simeq7\times10^4\,\mathrm{km/s}\simeq0.2c\). These large speeds also expose the limits of the nonrelativistic model.

b.3. Reconstructed top masses

b.4. Select the likely candidate

b.5. Distance before decay

For v≈c, \(a=ecB/(\gamma m)\) and E=γmc². Substitution yields \(P=e^4E^2B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\). Thus ξ=1/(6π), k=4, n=5.
Integrating \(\dot E=-\alpha E^2\) gives the stated law with \(\alpha=e^4B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\).

Its curvature radius is about 167 m, so flight time is R/c. Loss \(E_0-E(R/c)\simeq\alpha E_0^2R/c\simeq56\,\mathrm{MeV}\). The signed energy change is −56 MeV, while the requested lost energy is positive.

For each root add the three final energies \(E_t=c(p_\mu+p_\nu+p_j)\) and vectors \(\mathbf p_t=\mathbf p_\mu+\mathbf p_\nu+\mathbf p_j\). Then \(m_t=c^{-2}\sqrt{E_t^2-c^2p_t^2}\). The exact-root candidates are about 169.3 and 311.2 GeV/c² respectively. Rounded fallback roots give nearby but different values.

The dashed signal curve is about 0.1 near 169.3 GeV/c² and below 0.01 near 311.2 GeV/c², favouring the positive-pz candidate. The plotted normalized bin weight is roughly 0.1. It is not a posterior probability between the two candidates without an additional likelihood model.
Its energy is about 272.6 GeV. Time dilation gives \(d=v\gamma\tau_0=(p_t/m_t)\tau_0=c\tau_0\sqrt{[E_t/(m_tc^2)]^2-1}\simeq2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm m\).

solution.text:
Where is the neutrino?
a.1. Classical cyclotron radius
From \(evB=mv^2/r\) and \(K=mv^2/2\), \(r=\sqrt{2mK}/(eB)\).
a.2. Escape momentum
The track's largest radial distance is twice its curvature radius, so r=R/2=0.55 m. The relativistic relation p=eBr gives p≈330 MeV/c.
a.3. Ultrarelativistic radiation
For v≈c, \(a=ecB/(\gamma m)\) and E=γmc². Substitution yields \(P=e^4E^2B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\). Thus ξ=1/(6π), k=4, n=5.
a.4. Energy loss coefficient
Integrating \(\dot E=-\alpha E^2\) gives the stated law with \(\alpha=e^4B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\).
a.5. Radiated energy on escape
Its curvature radius is about 167 m, so flight time is R/c. Loss \(E_0-E(R/c)\simeq\alpha E_0^2R/c\simeq56\,\mathrm{MeV}\). The signed energy change is −56 MeV, while the requested lost energy is positive.
a.6. Time-dependent angular frequency
\(r=p/(eB)\), p≈E/c, hence \(\omega=c/r=ec^2B/E(t)=ec^2B(1+\alpha E_0t)/E_0\).
b.1. W mass constraint
Add their four-momenta and use zero individual masses: \[m_W^2c^2=2\left[p_\mu\sqrt{p_{\nu T}^2+p_{\nu z}^2}-\mathbf p_{\mu T}\cdot\mathbf p_{\nu T}-p_{\mu z}p_{\nu z}\right],\quad p_\mu=\sqrt{p_{\mu T}^2+p_{\mu z}^2}.\]
b.2. Two neutrino solutions
Let \(A=m_W^2c^2/2+\mathbf p_{\mu T}\cdot\mathbf p_{\nu T}\). Squaring \(p_\mu\sqrt{p_{\nu T}^2+z^2}=A+p_{\mu z}z\) gives \[p_{\mu T}^2z^2-2Ap_{\mu z}z+p_\mu^2p_{\nu T}^2-A^2=0.\] Check both roots in the unsquared equation. They are approximately +74.0 and −188.3 GeV/c.
b.3. Reconstructed top masses
For each root add the three final energies \(E_t=c(p_\mu+p_\nu+p_j)\) and vectors \(\mathbf p_t=\mathbf p_\mu+\mathbf p_\nu+\mathbf p_j\). Then \(m_t=c^{-2}\sqrt{E_t^2-c^2p_t^2}\). The exact-root candidates are about 169.3 and 311.2 GeV/c² respectively. Rounded fallback roots give nearby but different values.
b.4. Select the likely candidate
The dashed signal curve is about 0.1 near 169.3 GeV/c² and below 0.01 near 311.2 GeV/c², favouring the positive-pz candidate. The plotted normalized bin weight is roughly 0.1. It is not a posterior probability between the two candidates without an additional likelihood model.
b.5. Distance before decay
Its energy is about 272.6 GeV. Time dilation gives \(d=v\gamma\tau_0=(p_t/m_t)\tau_0=c\tau_0\sqrt{[E_t/(m_tc^2)]^2-1}\simeq2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm m\).

statement.text:
Physics of Live Systems

a.1. Flow in each generation
Find Qi in terms of ΔP,N,η,r0,ℓ0 and i.
a.2. Numerical inlet flow
Calculate Q0 in mL/hour.
a.3. Pressure amplitude transfer

For sinusoidal inlet pressure of angular frequency ω find Pout/Pin and the condition that low-frequency outlet oscillations are attenuated. Express the condition in η,ρ,E,h,r,ℓ.
a.4. Wall thickness bound
Assuming the same h at every level, estimate its maximum value for attenuation throughout the numerical tree.
b.1. Tumour volume fraction

An inextensible sphere initially contains normal tissue of density ρ0. A central tumour grows, with fixed normal-tissue mass. The densities are ρN=ρ0(1+p/KN), ρT=ρ0(1+p/KT), with common excess pressure p. Define v=VT/V, μ=MT/MN, κ=KN/KT. Find v(μ,κ), selecting the physical branch.
b.2. Central temperature
A spherical tumour of radius RT generates uniform heating power density P. Tumour and all surrounding tissue have conductivity k. Temperature far away is Tb=310.15 K. Find the steady centre temperature.
b.3. Heating all tumour cells
For RT=5.0 cm and k=0.60 W/(m K), find the threshold power density to raise every tumour cell from 37°C to above 43°C.
b.4. Flow reduction under compression
Only level N−1 vessels narrow by positive δr. Their collapse law is \(p/P_{cap}-1=(p_c/P_{cap}-1)(2-\delta r/\delta r_c)\delta r/\delta r_c\). At fixed whole-tree pressure drop and small p−Pcap, find the signed relative flow change δQ/Q in terms of v,KN,N,pc,δrc,rN−1,Pcap.

children.text: At level i, \(Q_i=Q_0/2^i\), while \(R_i=2^iR_0\). Each level therefore drops the same pressure Q0R0. Thus \[Q_i=\frac{\Delta P\pi r_0^4}{2^{i+3}N\ell_0\eta}.\]
Convert ΔP=25 mmHg to 3332 Pa. Then Q0≈\(4.04\times10^{-10}\) m³/s≈1.45 mL/hour, conventionally rounded to 1.5.

Complex impedances give \[\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}=\frac1{\sqrt{(1-\omega^2LC)^2+\omega^2C^2R^2}}.\] To quadratic order in ω, attenuation requires C²R²−2CL>0, or \(64\eta^2\ell^2/(3Ehr^3\rho)>1\). At equality attenuation first appears at fourth order.
The bound is \(h<64\eta^2\ell_i^2/(3Er_i^3\rho)=7.7\times10^{-5}2^{i/3}\,\mathrm m\). The strictest condition is at i=0, giving h less than about 77 μm.

Normal mass conservation gives p=KN v/(1−v). Eliminating p from the tumour mass relation yields \((1-\kappa)v^2-(1+\mu)v+\mu=0\). The branch tending to zero as μ→0 is \[v=\frac{1+\mu-\sqrt{(1+\mu)^2-4\mu(1-\kappa)}}{2(1-\kappa)}.\] At κ=1 the continuous limit is v=μ/(1+μ).
Conservation of heat gives \(T(r)-T_b=P R_T^3/(3kr)\) outside and \(T(r)-T_b=P R_T^2/(2k)-Pr^2/(6k)\) inside. Match temperature and heat flux at RT. At the centre \(T(0)=T_b+P R_T^2/(2k)\).

The coldest tumour point is its surface, not its centre. \(T(R_T)-T_b=PR_T^2/(3k)\). The threshold is \(P_{min}=3k(6\,\mathrm K)/R_T^2=4.32\,\mathrm{kW/m^3}\). Strictly exceeding 43°C requires power above this threshold.

Linearizing the collapse law gives \(\delta r=\delta r_c(p-P_{cap})/[2(p_c-P_{cap})]\). The last level's resistance increases by 4δr/r, while all N unperturbed levels contribute equally. Hence \[\frac{\delta Q}{Q}=-\frac{2}{N}\frac{K_Nv-(1-v)P_{cap}}{(1-v)(p_c-P_{cap})}\frac{\delta r_c}{r_{N-1}}.\] This applies on the narrowing side p>Pcap and is negative. Symmetry gives the same relative change in every level.

children.text: A lever with a pestle and a hollow water bucket pivots about a horizontal axis T. When horizontal, the pestle rests on rice in the mortar. The dry lever and pestle have mass \(M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), inertia \(I_L=12\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\), and centre G with TG horizontal in the horizontal configuration. Water enters at mass rate Φ. Use water density \(\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and the bucket geometry in the diagram: \(L=0.74\,\mathrm m\), \(a=0.20\,\mathrm m\), \(b=0.15\,\mathrm m\), \(h=0.12\,\mathrm m\), sloping end angle \(30^\circ\). The lever thickness is 8 cm. Neglect pivot friction, incoming-water impact and, when specified, water flow during motion. Assume water surfaces remain horizontal. Tilt α increases as the water bucket goes down and the pestle rises. During a working cycle water fills at α=0, the lever tips, water spills from α1 until empty at α2, inertia carries it to α0, then the empty lever falls back and pounds the rice. At β the spilling bucket counterbalances the dry lever. A sufficiently large inflow can sustain an elevated rest mode instead of pounding.

Find α1, when the initial 1.0 kg just begins to spill, and α2, when the bucket empties.
Find β and the remaining water mass m1 when total gravitational torque vanishes.

For very small constant inflow, neglect water added while moving and neglect changes of inertia. Sketch total torque μ against α over a complete cycle, explicitly labelling α=0, α1 and α2. Choose positive torque to increase α.
Explain geometrically the total work done by the gravitational torque over the cycle and the energy delivered to the rice.
Estimate α0 and Wpound from a piecewise-linear approximation to the torque graph. State the approximations.
Now retain inflow during motion and suppose the bucket always remains full to its spill edge. Sketch torque near β and identify the equilibrium.
Find the first-order torque near α=β+Δα. Use the source's approximation that the water moment arm can be fixed at its equilibrium value.

Find the minimum mass inflow Φ1 that can keep the bucket overflowing during a one-degree harmonic oscillation about β.

1.1. Dry centre position
The lever first lifts when the bucket contains 1.0 kg of water. Find TG.
1.2. Spilling and empty angles
Find α1, when the initial 1.0 kg just begins to spill, and α2, when the bucket empties.

children.text: The horizontal bucket-bottom length is \(d=L-h\cot30^\circ=0.5322\,\mathrm m\). With V=0.001 m³ the shallow-water depth c obeys \(V=bcd+bc^2\cot30^\circ/2\), giving c=0.01228 m. To the source's shallow-layer accuracy, the horizontal water moment arm is \(TH\simeq a+d/2+c\cot30^\circ/4=0.4714\,\mathrm m\). Balance \(M\,TG=m\,TH\), giving \(TG=0.0157\,\mathrm m\simeq0.016\,\mathrm m\).

At first spill the triangular water section has bottom length \(x=2V/(bh)=0.1111\,\mathrm m\). Geometry gives \(\tan\alpha_1=h/(x+h\cot30^\circ)\), hence \(\alpha_1=20.6^\circ\). The bucket is empty at \(\alpha_2=30.0^\circ\).

For a spilling triangular section, \(m=\rho bhx/2=9x\) in SI units. Its moment arm along the lever is \(TN=L+a-2h\cot30^\circ/3-x/3=0.8014-x/3\). Balance \(mTN=M\,TG=0.4714\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\), giving \(-3x^2+7.213x=0.4714\). Choose the geometric root x=0.0672 m, not the root larger than the bucket. Then m1≈0.605 kg and \(\beta=\arctan[h/(x+h\cot30^\circ)]=23.6^\circ\). The source accidentally prints TG=0.1571 m in one substitution, although its arithmetic and final result use 0.01571 m.

At α=0 the torque rises during filling from −4.62 N m to zero. On the outward constant-mass branch it rises to μ(α1)=+2.69 N m, then falls through μ(β)=0 to μ(α2)=−4.00 N m. Beyond α2, and throughout empty return, \(\mu=-Mg\,TG\cos\alpha=-4.62\cos\alpha\,\mathrm{N\,m}\). Thus the empty-return endpoint is μ(0)=−4.62 N m, different from the just-lifting endpoint at the same angle. Draw the path with arrows rather than a single-valued graph at α=0.

Infinitesimal work is \(dW=\mu\,d\alpha\), with α in radians. The signed enclosed area is \(W_{total}=\oint\mu\,d\alpha\). The pestle's impact energy is the kinetic energy acquired on empty return: \[W_{pound}=Mg\,TG\sin\alpha_0.\] This is the area between the empty-return torque curve and the α axis from 0 to α0. In the stipulated negligible-water-kinetic-energy model, the closed-cycle work supplies the impact energy.

Equate the positive outward area to the negative outward area at the turning point. A triangle of height 2.7 N m from 0 to β and a trapezoid falling to about −4 N m give \(23.6(2.7)/2\simeq4[(\alpha_0-23.6)+(\alpha_0-30)]/2\). The common degree-to-radian factor cancels only in this area equality. Thus α0≈34.7° and \(W_{pound}=4.62\sin34.7^\circ\simeq2.6\,\mathrm J\). These are graph-based estimates, not exact quadrature.

The filling and draining branches coincide when the bucket always spills. Torque decreases through zero as α increases through β, so a positive displacement has negative torque and vice versa. The equilibrium is stable.

The overflowing water mass is \(m(\alpha)=\rho bh^2(\cot\alpha-\cot30^\circ)/2\), so \(\Delta m=-\rho bh^2\Delta\alpha/(2\sin^2\beta)\). With TN≈M TG/m1≈0.779 m fixed, \[\mu\simeq-\frac{\rho bh^2g\,TN\cos\beta}{2\sin^2\beta}\Delta\alpha\simeq-47.2\Delta\alpha\,\mathrm{N\,m}.\] Δα is in radians. Including the smaller change of the centroid arm modifies this approximate coefficient by a few percent.

Treat the equilibrium water as a point mass: \(I_{eff}\simeq I_L+m_1TN^2\simeq12.4\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\). The linear equation is \(I_{eff}\ddot{\Delta\alpha}+47.2\Delta\alpha=0\). Hence \(\Delta\alpha(t)=\Delta\alpha(0)\cos(2\pi t/\tau)\), with \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{I_{eff}/47.2}\simeq3.2\,\mathrm s\).

The greatest refill rate occurs as the angle decreases fastest through β. For angular amplitude A in radians, \[\Phi_{min}=\frac{\pi\rho bh^2A}{\tau\sin^2\beta}.\] With A=π/180 and τ≈3.2 s, Φ1≈0.23 kg/s.

The limiting amplitude is \(\beta-\alpha_1\simeq3.0^\circ\). The required flow is proportional to amplitude, so \(\Phi_2\simeq3\Phi_1\simeq0.7\,\mathrm{kg/s}\). Above it the return can remain on the elevated oscillatory branch instead of striking the rice. This is the source's harmonic estimate.

Beyond α2, and throughout empty return, \(\mu=-Mg\,TG\cos\alpha=-4.62\cos\alpha\,\mathrm{N\,m}\). Thus the empty-return endpoint is μ(0)=−4.62 N m, different from the just-lifting endpoint at the same angle. Draw the path with arrows rather than a single-valued graph at α=0.
2.2. Work from the torque graph
Infinitesimal work is \(dW=\mu\,d\alpha\), with α in radians. The signed enclosed area is \(W_{total}=\oint\mu\,d\alpha\). The pestle's impact energy is the kinetic energy acquired on empty return: \[W_{pound}=Mg\,TG\sin\alpha_0.\] This is the area between the empty-return torque curve and the α axis from 0 to α0. In the stipulated negligible-water-kinetic-energy model, the closed-cycle work supplies the impact energy.
2.3. Maximum tilt and pounding estimate
Equate the positive outward area to the negative outward area at the turning point. A triangle of height 2.7 N m from 0 to β and a trapezoid falling to about −4 N m give \(23.6(2.7)/2\simeq4[(\alpha_0-23.6)+(\alpha_0-30)]/2\). The common degree-to-radian factor cancels only in this area equality. Thus α0≈34.7° and \(W_{pound}=4.62\sin34.7^\circ\simeq2.6\,\mathrm J\). These are graph-based estimates, not exact quadrature.
3.1.1. Elevated equilibrium stability
The filling and draining branches coincide when the bucket always spills. Torque decreases through zero as α increases through β, so a positive displacement has negative torque and vice versa. The equilibrium is stable.
3.1.2. Small-angle restoring torque
The overflowing water mass is \(m(\alpha)=\rho bh^2(\cot\alpha-\cot30^\circ)/2\), so \(\Delta m=-\rho bh^2\Delta\alpha/(2\sin^2\beta)\). With TN≈M TG/m1≈0.779 m fixed, \[\mu\simeq-\frac{\rho bh^2g\,TN\cos\beta}{2\sin^2\beta}\Delta\alpha\simeq-47.2\Delta\alpha\,\mathrm{N\,m}.\] Δα is in radians. Including the smaller change of the centroid arm modifies this approximate coefficient by a few percent.
3.1.3. Small-oscillation period
Treat the equilibrium water as a point mass: \(I_{eff}\simeq I_L+m_1TN^2\simeq12.4\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\). The linear equation is \(I_{eff}\ddot{\Delta\alpha}+47.2\Delta\alpha=0\). Hence \(\Delta\alpha(t)=\Delta\alpha(0)\cos(2\pi t/\tau)\), with \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{I_{eff}/47.2}\simeq3.2\,\mathrm s\).
3.2. Inflow for one-degree oscillations
The greatest refill rate occurs as the angle decreases fastest through β. For angular amplitude A in radians, \[\Phi_{min}=\frac{\pi\rho bh^2A}{\tau\sin^2\beta}.\] With A=π/180 and τ≈3.2 s, Φ1≈0.23 kg/s.
3.3. Inflow that prevents pounding
The limiting amplitude is \(\beta-\alpha_1\simeq3.0^\circ\). The required flow is proportional to amplitude, so \(\Phi_2\simeq3\Phi_1\simeq0.7\,\mathrm{kg/s}\). Above it the return can remain on the elevated oscillatory branch instead of striking the rice. This is the source's harmonic estimate.

statement.text:
Earthquake, Volcano and Tsunami

Specific constant-volume heat capacities are \(c_{Vm},c_{Vw}\). Part B studies the 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake, origin time 22:54:00 UTC and hypocentre 15 km deep. Part C studies a tsunami generated by ocean-floor uplift, with density \(\rho\) and local ocean depth \(d\).
A.1. Mixture equilibrium temperature
Find the temperature after the first, constant-volume mixing stage.
A.2. Mixture equilibrium pressure
Model the mixture as ideal gas with molar volume \(v_e\). Find its equilibrium pressure.
A.3. Eruption velocity scaling
Find the gas-eruption velocity in terms of pressure \(p\), total mass \(m\), volume \(V\), and an unknown dimensionless factor \(K\).
B.1. Crust P-wave velocity

Read the P-wave arrival at YOGI from the seismogram and determine crust speed.
B.2. Direct and reflected arrivals
Find DNP travel times for the direct crustal ray and the ray reflected at the crust-mantle boundary.
B.3. Mantle velocity

The earliest DNP arrival is about 22:55:15. Use a critically refracted head wave along the boundary to find mantle speed.
B.4. Continuously varying crust
Approximate the source at the surface and let \(v(z)=v_0+az\), \(a>0\). The ray parameter is \(p=\sin\theta(z)/v(z)\), with angle from the vertical. Find epicentral distance X.
B.5. Travel-time integral
Express the travel time as an integral over depth.
B.6. Three-layer travel time

Approximate the integral with three layers: \(v_1=6.65,v_2=6.97,v_3=6.99\,\mathrm{km/s}\), \(p=0.143\,\mathrm{s/km}\), and thicknesses \(\delta z_1=6,\delta z_2=9,\delta z_3=15\,\mathrm{km}\).
C.1. Uplift potential energy

A raised water box has area \(\lambda L/2\), with \(L\gg\lambda\), and height \(h\). Find its gravitational energy above the original ocean surface.
C.2. Shallow-water wave speed
Use energy and mass conservation to obtain tsunami speed up to a dimensionless factor.
C.3. Shoaling amplitude
The depth changes slowly. At depth \(d_0\), amplitude is \(A_0\). Use energy conservation to find amplitude \(A(d)\).

children.text: Conservation of internal energy gives \(m_wc_{Vw}(T_e-T_w)+m_mc_{Vm}(T_e-T_m)=0\), hence \[T_e=\frac{m_wc_{Vw}T_w+m_mc_{Vm}T_m}{m_wc_{Vw}+m_mc_{Vm}}.\]
The ideal-gas law gives \(p_e=RT_e/v_e\), with universal gas constant R.
Pressure times volume is energy. Dimensional balance therefore requires \(u=K\sqrt{pV/m}\).

The path is \(\sqrt{22.5^2+15^2}=27.04\,\mathrm{km}\). The first arrival is about 4.7 s after origin, giving \(v_c\simeq5.75\,\mathrm{km/s}\). Arrival picks around 4.5 to 5.5 s give roughly 4.9 to 6.0 km/s.

The direct distance is \(\sqrt{500^2+15^2}=500.225\,\mathrm{km}\). Reflect the source in the boundary to obtain reflected distance \(\sqrt{500^2+45^2}=502.021\,\mathrm{km}\). Divide by the same crust speed. At 5.75 km/s the times are 87.00 s and 87.31 s, respectively. Small differences from published rounded times reflect the graph-derived crust speed.

The crustal vertical travel totals \(2\times30-15=45\,\mathrm{km}\). If \(\sin i=v_c/v_m\), the time is \[75=500/v_m+45\sqrt{v_c^{-2}-v_m^{-2}}.\] Solve with \(v_m>v_c\), obtaining approximately \(v_m=7.1\,\mathrm{km/s}\).
The turning depth obeys \(p(v_0+az_t)=1\). Along a ray \(dx/dz=pv/\sqrt{1-p^2v^2}\). Thus \[X=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{p(v_0+az)}{\sqrt{1-p^2(v_0+az)^2}}dz=\frac2{ap}\sqrt{1-p^2v_0^2}.\]
Use \(dt=ds/v\), \(ds=dz/\cos\theta\): \[T(p)=2\int_0^{z_t}\frac{dz}{v(z)\sqrt{1-p^2v(z)^2}}.\] With slowness \(u=1/v\), the integrand is \(u^2/\sqrt{u^2-p^2}\).

Calculate \[T=2\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\delta z_i}{v_i\sqrt{1-p^2v_i^2}}.\] Direct evaluation of the supplied speeds gives about 184.1 s. The source first rounds the slownesses to 0.1504, 0.1435 and 0.1431 s/km and obtains 151.64 s. Near the turning point the cancellation makes early rounding significant. Both conventions must be explained rather than treating the source figure as uniquely precise.
The raised mass is \(\rho\lambda Lh/2\), with centre at height \(h/2\). Hence \(E_p=\rho g\lambda Lh^2/4\).

Mass continuity gives horizontal water speed \(U\sim hv/d\). Equate potential energy \(\sim\rho g\lambda Lh^2\) and kinetic energy \(\sim\rho d\lambda LU^2\). The result is \(v\sim\sqrt{gd}\), the shallow-water speed.

Energy per horizontal area scales as \(A^2\). Conservation of energy flux gives \(A^2\sqrt{gd}=A_0^2\sqrt{gd_0}\), and therefore \[A=A_0(d_0/d)^{1/4}.\] This assumes no dissipation, reflection, breaking or lateral focusing.

children.text: Model a homogeneous isotropic universe by an expanding uniform-density sphere of radius R(t)=a(t)Rs. Its mass-equivalent energy density is ρ, so total energy density is ρc². The first Friedmann equation is \(H^2=A_1\rho-kc^2/(R_s^2a^2)\), where H=ȧ/a and k is +1,0,−1 for closed, flat and open geometry. Adiabatic evolution has \(\dot\rho+A_2(\rho+p/c^2)H=0\), with p=wρc². Present values have subscript 0 and a0=1. Define critical mass density consistently with the first equation as ρc=H²/A1 and Ω=ρ/ρc. The source prints an extra c² in one definition of critical density, while its worked solution uses this dimensionally consistent definition. During scalar-field inflation, \(\ddot\phi+3H\dot\phi=-V^{\prime}\), \(H^2=(\dot\phi^2/2+V)/(3M_{pl}^2)\). Slow roll neglects φ̈ and kinetic energy. Define \(\epsilon=-\dot H/H^2\), \(\delta=-\ddot\phi/(H\dot\phi)\), ηV=δ+ε and dN=dln a=Hdt, with N=0 at the end. Thus N is negative before the end. Part D retains the source's requested numerical N=60 and discusses this sign convention explicitly.

statement.text:
Cosmic inflation
Model a homogeneous isotropic universe by an expanding uniform-density sphere of radius R(t)=a(t)Rs. Its mass-equivalent energy density is ρ, so total energy density is ρc². The first Friedmann equation is \(H^2=A_1\rho-kc^2/(R_s^2a^2)\), where H=ȧ/a and k is +1,0,−1 for closed, flat and open geometry. Adiabatic evolution has \(\dot\rho+A_2(\rho+p/c^2)H=0\), with p=wρc². Present values have subscript 0 and a0=1. Define critical mass density consistently with the first equation as ρc=H²/A1 and Ω=ρ/ρc. The source prints an extra c² in one definition of critical density, while its worked solution uses this dimensionally consistent definition. During scalar-field inflation, \(\ddot\phi+3H\dot\phi=-V^{\prime}\), \(H^2=(\dot\phi^2/2+V)/(3M_{pl}^2)\). Slow roll neglects φ̈ and kinetic energy. Define \(\epsilon=-\dot H/H^2\), \(\delta=-\ddot\phi/(H\dot\phi)\), ηV=δ+ε and dN=dln a=Hdt, with N=0 at the end. Thus N is negative before the end. Part D retains the source's requested numerical N=60 and discusses this sign convention explicitly.

a.1. First Friedmann coefficient
Use Newtonian gravity for a boundary test mass to determine A1.
a.2. Adiabatic continuity
Use the first law to determine A2.
a.3. Equations of state
Find w for radiation, nonrelativistic matter and constant energy density.
a.4. Flat-universe scale factors
For k=0 find a(t) in the three cases. Use a(0)=0 for radiation and matter, and a(t0)=1 for constant density.
a.5. Curvature-density relation
Express k through Ω,H,a,Rs and c.
a.6. Geometry ranges
Give the density-ratio range for each k.
b.1. Flatness problem
Find the time dependence of Ω−1 in radiation- and matter-dominated nearly flat universes.
b.2. Inflationary flattening
For a constant-density era and |Ω−1|≪1, find Ω−1 as a function of time.
b.3. Equivalent inflation conditions
Show that constant-density domination produces negative pressure, accelerated expansion and a decreasing comoving Hubble radius.
b.4. Slow-roll inflation bound
Show that decreasing (aH)⁻¹ means ε<1.
c.1. Potential slow-roll formulas
Estimate ε,ηV and dN/dφ using V,V′,V″.
d.1. End of monomial inflation
For V=Λ⁴(φ/Mpl)ⁿ with integer n and positive field, find φend when ε=1.
d.2. Observable constraints and e-fold sign
Using r=16ε and ns=1+2ηV−6ε at the start, express r and ns in N,n. Compare integer n to ns=0.968±0.006 and r<0.12 at the source's N=60.

children.text: For enclosed M=4πR³ρ/3, integrate R̈=−GM/R² to Ṙ²/2−GM/R=constant. Divide by R² and absorb the integration constant into curvature. This yields \(A_1=8\pi G/3\).
For E=ρVc² and V∝a³, dE=−pdV gives \(\dot\rho+3H(\rho+p/c^2)=0\). Therefore A2=3.

The continuity equation gives ρ∝a⁻³⁽¹⁺ʷ⁾. Radiation dilutes in number as a⁻³ and photon energy as a⁻¹, giving w=1/3. Nonrelativistic rest energy dilutes as a⁻³, giving w=0. Constant energy density has w=−1 and negative pressure.

Radiation has \(a=(2H_0t)^{1/2}\). Matter has \(a=(3H_0t/2)^{2/3}\). Constant density has \(a=e^{H_0(t-t_0)}\). In the first two cases the time origin is the Big Bang and H0 refers to the epoch with a=1.
Rearranging the first Friedmann equation gives \(k=(\Omega-1)H^2a^2R_s^2/c^2\). The source alternates Rs and R0 for the fixed reference radius.
For positive density, k=+1 corresponds to Ω>1, k=0 to Ω=1, and k=−1 to 0<Ω<1.

The exact curvature relation is Ω−1=kc²/(Rs²a²H²). In a nearly flat era with a∝tᵖ and H=p/t this scales as t²⁻²ᵖ. It grows as t in radiation domination and t²ᐟ³ in matter domination. The expansion laws are the nearly flat approximation used in this argument.
H is approximately constant and a∝exp(Ht), so \(\Omega(t)-1=[\Omega(t_i)-1]e^{-2H(t-t_i)}\). Curvature deviations decay exponentially.

Constant density implies p=−ρc². Differentiating Friedmann and using continuity gives \(\ddot a/a=-4\pi G(\rho+3p/c^2)/3\), hence positive acceleration. Since aH=ȧ, \(d[(aH)^{-1}]/dt=-\ddot a/\dot a^2<0\).
\(d[(aH)^{-1}]/dt=-(1+\dot H/H^2)/a=-(1-\epsilon)/a\). With a>0 this is negative exactly when ε<1.

From \(\dot H=-\dot\phi^2/(2M_{pl}^2)\), H²≈V/(3Mpl²) and 3Hφ̇≈−V′, obtain \[\epsilon\simeq\frac{M_{pl}^2}{2}\left(\frac{V^{\prime}}V\right)^2,\quad\eta_V\simeq M_{pl}^2\frac{V^{\prime\prime}}V,\quad\frac{dN}{d\phi}\simeq-\frac{V}{M_{pl}^2V^{\prime}}.\] These expressions require a monotonic field and the stated slow-roll approximation.
\(\epsilon=n^2M_{pl}^2/(2\phi^2)\), giving \(\phi_{end}=|n|M_{pl}/\sqrt2\). The usual positive-n rolling branch has n>0. The n=0 constant potential never reaches ε=1 by this mechanism.
d.2. Observable constraints and e-fold sign

Integrating dN/dφ gives \(\phi^2=M_{pl}^2(n^2/2-2nN)\). Therefore \[r=\frac{16n}{n-4N},\qquad n_s=1-\frac{2(n+2)}{n-4N}.\] With the literal N=+60 used by the source, ns=0.968 gives n≈−5.93, but n=−6 gives r≈0.390>0.12. No integer fits both constraints. This positive N conflicts with dN=Hdt and N=0 at the end for a pre-end epoch. If 60 means remaining e-folds, use N=−60 here, or replace denominators by n+240. Then n=1 gives r≈0.0664, ns≈0.9751, just outside the stated tilt interval, and n=2 gives r≈0.132>0.12. Again no positive integer satisfies both. The sign issue is kept explicit and this comparison uses self-review.

This positive N conflicts with dN=Hdt and N=0 at the end for a pre-end epoch. If 60 means remaining e-folds, use N=−60 here, or replace denominators by n+240. Then n=1 gives r≈0.0664, ns≈0.9751, just outside the stated tilt interval, and n=2 gives r≈0.132>0.12. Again no positive integer satisfies both. The sign issue is kept explicit and this comparison uses self-review.

children.text: The lower and upper slopes give \(R_{off}=10.0\,\Omega\), \(R_{on}=1.00\,\Omega\). The middle slope is −0.5 A/V, so \(R_{int}=2.00\,\Omega\), \(I_0=6.00\,\mathrm A\).

At a stationary state \(E=RI+U\). Intersections of \(I=(E-U)/R\) with the characteristic give the states. For R=3 Ω there is exactly one. For R=1 Ω there may be one, two at a corner, or three. The two-state corner cases must not be omitted.
The physical intersection lies on the intermediate branch. \(I=(E-R_{int}I_0)/(R-R_{int})=3.00\,\mathrm A\), and \(U=R_{int}(I_0-I)=6.00\,\mathrm V\).
Kirchhoff's law gives \(L\dot I=E-R_{int}I_0-(R-R_{int})I\). A perturbation obeys \(L\delta\dot I=-(R-R_{int})\delta I\). Because R−Rint=1 Ω>0 the state is stable, with decay time L/(R−Rint)=1 μs.

Voltage is continuous across the capacitor, so jumps are vertical. On the off branch voltage increases from Uh to Uth, jumps to the on branch at Uth, decreases to Uh, then jumps to the off branch. The middle-branch stationary state is unstable in this capacitive circuit. The branch equilibria lie outside the allowed branch intervals, so motion continues to each corner.

For branch resistance r, \(C\dot U=(E-U)/R-U/r\). Define \(U_r=Er/(R+r)\), \(t_r=CRr/(R+r)\). Then \(U(t)=U_r+[U(0)-U_r]e^{-t/t_r}\). Thus \[t_{on}=t_{R_{on}}\ln\frac{U_{th}-U_{on}}{U_h-U_{on}}=2.41\,\mu s,\quad t_{off}=t_{R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-U_h}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=3.71\,\mu s.\] Their sum is T=6.12 μs.

The on branch dominates. Estimating U by (Uh+Uth)/2 gives \(\overline P\sim[(U_h+U_{th})/2]^2t_{on}/(R_{on}T)\simeq19\,\mathrm W\). The source accepts justified estimates between 5 and 50 W. This is an estimate rather than an exact integral.
For the fundamental quarter-wave mode, \(s=cT/4=459\,\mathrm m\). Other odd quarter-wave lengths exceed 1 km.

Initially \(\widetilde U=12R_{off}/(R+R_{off})=9.23\,\mathrm V\). A short pulse raises U on the off branch but does not reach Uth, so current returns smoothly from above to its original value. A longer pulse reaches Uth, jumps to the on branch, decays there and jumps back at Uh. It then approaches the original off-branch state from below. The firing pulse is an all-or-nothing large excursion.
Using the off-branch exponential, \[\tau_{crit}=\frac{CRR_{off}}{R+R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-\widetilde U}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=0.936\,\mu s.\]
Yes. Since 1.00 μs exceeds 0.936 μs, the threshold is crossed and one large current excursion occurs before the original stationary state is recovered.

The lower and upper slopes give \(R_{off}=10.0\,\Omega\), \(R_{on}=1.00\,\Omega\). The middle slope is −0.5 A/V, so \(R_{int}=2.00\,\Omega\), \(I_0=6.00\,\mathrm A\).

a4. Inductive stability

b1. Capacitive limit cycle

The middle-branch stationary state is unstable in this capacitive circuit. The branch equilibria lie outside the allowed branch intervals, so motion continues to each corner.
b2. Oscillation period
For branch resistance r, \(C\dot U=(E-U)/R-U/r\). Define \(U_r=Er/(R+r)\), \(t_r=CRr/(R+r)\). Then \(U(t)=U_r+[U(0)-U_r]e^{-t/t_r}\). Thus \[t_{on}=t_{R_{on}}\ln\frac{U_{th}-U_{on}}{U_h-U_{on}}=2.41\,\mu s,\quad t_{off}=t_{R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-U_h}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=3.71\,\mu s.\] Their sum is T=6.12 μs.
b3. Power estimate
The on branch dominates. Estimating U by (Uh+Uth)/2 gives \(\overline P\sim[(U_h+U_{th})/2]^2t_{on}/(R_{on}T)\simeq19\,\mathrm W\). The source accepts justified estimates between 5 and 50 W. This is an estimate rather than an exact integral.
b4. Transmitter antenna

c1. Neuristor pulse sketches

The firing pulse is an all-or-nothing large excursion.
c2. Critical pulse duration

A brief engine misfire adds a velocity \(\Delta v\) radially towards Earth without changing the tangential velocity. Write \(\beta=\Delta v/v_0\). Ignore atmosphere, other bodies and changes in satellite mass. Conic orbits obey \(r=\ell/(1-\varepsilon\cos\theta)\), with \(\ell=L^2/(GMm^2)\) and \(\varepsilon^2=1+2EL^2/(G^2M^2m^3)\).

statement.text:
An ill fated satellite
A satellite of mass \(m\) is initially in a circular geosynchronous equatorial orbit of radius \(r_0\), speed \(v_0\), and period \(T_0=24.0\,\mathrm h\). Earth's radius is \(R_T=6.37\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), and surface gravity is \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). A brief engine misfire adds a velocity \(\Delta v\) radially towards Earth without changing the tangential velocity. Write \(\beta=\Delta v/v_0\). Ignore atmosphere, other bodies and changes in satellite mass. Conic orbits obey \(r=\ell/(1-\varepsilon\cos\theta)\), with \(\ell=L^2/(GMm^2)\) and \(\varepsilon^2=1+2EL^2/(G^2M^2m^3)\).


1.1. Geosynchronous radius
Calculate the initial orbital radius.
1.2.formula. Initial speed
Express \(v_0\) in terms of \(g,R_T,r_0\).
1.2.value. Initial speed value
Evaluate the initial speed.
1.3.L. Initial angular momentum
Find \(L_0\), using \(m,g,R_T,v_0\).
1.3.E. Initial energy
Find the initial total mechanical energy in terms of \(m,v_0\).
2.1.l. Semi-latus rectum
For \(0<\beta<1\), find \(\ell\) in terms of \(r_0,\beta\).
2.1.e. Eccentricity
Find the eccentricity for \(0<\beta<1\).
2.2. Major-axis angle
Find the angle between the major axis and the initial position vector.
2.3.min. Perigee radius
Find \(r_{\min}\) for \(0<\beta<1\).
2.3.max. Apogee radius
Find \(r_{\max}\) for \(0<\beta<1\).
2.3.values. Turning radii for beta = 1/4
Evaluate both radii for \(\beta=1/4\).
2.4. New orbital period
Find \(T\) in terms of \(T_0,\beta\), and evaluate it for \(\beta=1/4\).
3.1. Escape threshold
Find the minimum \(\beta_{\rm esc}\) needed to escape.
3.2. Closest approach at escape
Find the closest approach for \(\beta=\beta_{\rm esc}\).
4.1. Asymptotic speed

For \(\beta>1\), find the speed at infinite distance.
4.2. Impact parameter
Find the perpendicular distance \(b\) from Earth's centre to the outgoing asymptote.
4.3. Asymptotic direction
Find the angle \(\varphi\) between the initial outward radius and the outgoing asymptotic velocity, and evaluate it at \(\beta=3/2\).

children.text: Equate \(v_0^2/r_0=gR_T^2/r_0^2\) and use \(v_0=2\pi r_0/T_0\). Thus \[r_0=\left(\frac{gR_T^2T_0^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}=4.22\times10^7\,\mathrm m.\]
Circular orbits have potential energy twice the negative kinetic energy, hence \(E_0=-mv_0^2/2\).
The radial impulse exerts no torque, so \(L=L_0\), while \(E=mv_0^2(\beta^2-1)/2\). Thus \(\ell=r_0\).
Substitution of the new energy and unchanged angular momentum gives \(\varepsilon^2=\beta^2\), so \(\varepsilon=\beta\).
At the impulse point \(r=r_0=\ell\), so \(\cos\theta=0\). The angle is \(\alpha=\pi/2\).
The semi-major axis is \(a=r_0/(1-\beta^2)\). Kepler's law gives \[T=T_0(1-\beta^2)^{-3/2},\] or \(26.4\,\mathrm h\) for \(\beta=1/4\).
The minimum escape energy is zero. Since \(E=mv_0^2(\beta^2-1)/2\), \(\beta_{\rm esc}=1\).
The orbit is parabolic, with \(\varepsilon=1\) and \(\ell=r_0\), so \(r_{\min}=r_0/2\).
At infinity the potential vanishes. Energy conservation gives \(v_\infty=v_0\sqrt{\beta^2-1}\).
Conservation of angular momentum gives \(mv_\infty b=mr_0v_0\), hence \(b=r_0/\sqrt{\beta^2-1}\).
The asymptote satisfies \(\cos\theta=1/\beta\). With the diagram's outgoing-angle convention, \[\varphi=\pi/2+\arccos(1/\beta).\] At \(\beta=1.5\), this is \(2.41\,\mathrm{rad}=138^\circ\).

solution.text:
An ill fated satellite
1.1. Geosynchronous radius
Equate \(v_0^2/r_0=gR_T^2/r_0^2\) and use \(v_0=2\pi r_0/T_0\). Thus \[r_0=\left(\frac{gR_T^2T_0^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}=4.22\times10^7\,\mathrm m.\]
1.2.formula. Initial speed
Circular force balance gives \[v_0=R_T\sqrt{g/r_0}.\]
1.2.value. Initial speed value
Using the radius above gives \(v_0=3.07\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
1.3.L. Initial angular momentum
\(L_0=mr_0v_0=mgR_T^2/v_0\).
1.3.E. Initial energy
Circular orbits have potential energy twice the negative kinetic energy, hence \(E_0=-mv_0^2/2\).
2.1.l. Semi-latus rectum
The radial impulse exerts no torque, so \(L=L_0\), while \(E=mv_0^2(\beta^2-1)/2\). Thus \(\ell=r_0\).
2.1.e. Eccentricity
Substitution of the new energy and unchanged angular momentum gives \(\varepsilon^2=\beta^2\), so \(\varepsilon=\beta\).
2.2. Major-axis angle
At the impulse point \(r=r_0=\ell\), so \(\cos\theta=0\). The angle is \(\alpha=\pi/2\).
2.3.min. Perigee radius
The turning radii are \(\ell/(1\pm\varepsilon)\), giving \(r_{\min}=r_0/(1+\beta)\).
2.3.max. Apogee radius
\(r_{\max}=r_0/(1-\beta)\).
2.3.values. Turning radii for beta = 1/4
\(r_{\min}=3.38\times10^7\,\mathrm m\), \(r_{\max}=5.63\times10^7\,\mathrm m\).
2.4. New orbital period
The semi-major axis is \(a=r_0/(1-\beta^2)\). Kepler's law gives \[T=T_0(1-\beta^2)^{-3/2},\] or \(26.4\,\mathrm h\) for \(\beta=1/4\).
3.1. Escape threshold
The minimum escape energy is zero. Since \(E=mv_0^2(\beta^2-1)/2\), \(\beta_{\rm esc}=1\).
3.2. Closest approach at escape
The orbit is parabolic, with \(\varepsilon=1\) and \(\ell=r_0\), so \(r_{\min}=r_0/2\).
4.1. Asymptotic speed
At infinity the potential vanishes. Energy conservation gives \(v_\infty=v_0\sqrt{\beta^2-1}\).
4.2. Impact parameter
Conservation of angular momentum gives \(mv_\infty b=mr_0v_0\), hence \(b=r_0/\sqrt{\beta^2-1}\).
4.3. Asymptotic direction
The asymptote satisfies \(\cos\theta=1/\beta\). With the diagram's outgoing-angle convention, \[\varphi=\pi/2+\arccos(1/\beta).\] At \(\beta=1.5\), this is \(2.41\,\mathrm{rad}=138^\circ\).

statement.text:
Particles from the Sun

B1. Solar neutrino flux

B2. Converted neutrino fraction

B3. Energy transferred to an electron
