children.text: Integrate photon rate above the threshold and multiply by \(E_g\): \[P_{out}=\frac{2\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}.\]
The curve starts at \(\eta(0)=0\) with slope \(1/3\), rises to one maximum, then tends to zero with slope tending to zero from below. Both endpoints have zero efficiency.
Differentiation gives \(x_0^3-x_0^2-2x_0-2=0\). Its positive root is \(x_0\simeq2.27\), with \(\eta_{max}\simeq0.457\).
Build the sphere shell by shell, integrating \(-GM(r)\,dM/r\). The result is \(\Omega=-3GM^2/(5R)\).
\(\tau_{KH}=|\Omega|/L=3GM^2/(5RL)\simeq1.88\times10^7\) years, far below the solar-system age.
There are two neutrinos per reaction, giving \(\Phi_\nu=2L/(4\pi d^2\Delta E)=6.8\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).
B3. Energy transferred to an electron

Emission stops when \(v=c/n\), leaving total energy \(m_ec^2n/\sqrt{n^2-1}\). Add \(\alpha\Delta t\), then subtract the initial rest energy: \[E_{imp}=\alpha\Delta t+m_ec^2\left(\frac n{\sqrt{n^2-1}}-1\right).\]
B4. Core temperature from line broadening

The line-of-sight Doppler width obeys \(\Delta E_{rms}/E_\nu=v_{z,rms}/c\). Isotropy gives \(V_{rms}=\sqrt3v_{z,rms}=2.01\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}\). From \(mV_{rms}^2/2=3k_BT_c/2\), \(T_c=1.13\times10^7\,\mathrm K\).

solution.text:
Particles from the Sun
A1. Solar surface temperature
\(L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4\), so \(T_s=(L/(4\pi R^2\sigma))^{1/4}\simeq5760\,\mathrm K\).
A2. Incident cell power
With \(x=h\nu/(k_BT_s)\), \(\int_0^\infty x^3e^{-x}dx=6\). Hence \[P_{in}=\frac{12\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}.\]
A3. Photon spectrum
Divide spectral power by \(h\nu\): \[n_\gamma(\nu)=\frac{2\pi AR^2}{d^2c^2}\nu^2e^{-h\nu/(k_BT_s)}.\]
A4. Useful cell power
Integrate photon rate above the threshold and multiply by \(E_g\): \[P_{out}=\frac{2\pi AR^2(k_BT_s)^4}{d^2c^2h^3}x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}.\]
A5. Efficiency function
\[\eta(x_g)=\frac{x_g(x_g^2+2x_g+2)e^{-x_g}}6.\]
A6. Efficiency graph
The curve starts at \(\eta(0)=0\) with slope \(1/3\), rises to one maximum, then tends to zero with slope tending to zero from below. Both endpoints have zero efficiency.
A7. Best gap and efficiency
Differentiation gives \(x_0^3-x_0^2-2x_0-2=0\). Its positive root is \(x_0\simeq2.27\), with \(\eta_{max}\simeq0.457\).
A8. Silicon efficiency
\(k_BT_s\simeq0.496\,\mathrm{eV}\), so \(x_g\simeq2.24\) and \(\eta_{Si}\simeq0.457\).
A9. Gravitational solar energy
Build the sphere shell by shell, integrating \(-GM(r)\,dM/r\). The result is \(\Omega=-3GM^2/(5R)\).
A10. Kelvin-Helmholtz lifetime
\(\tau_{KH}=|\Omega|/L=3GM^2/(5RL)\simeq1.88\times10^7\) years, far below the solar-system age.
B1. Solar neutrino flux
There are two neutrinos per reaction, giving \(\Phi_\nu=2L/(4\pi d^2\Delta E)=6.8\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).
B2. Converted neutrino fraction
\(N_2=N_1(1-f)+N_1f/6\), so \(f=(6/5)(1-N_2/N_1)\).
B3. Energy transferred to an electron
Emission stops when \(v=c/n\), leaving total energy \(m_ec^2n/\sqrt{n^2-1}\). Add \(\alpha\Delta t\), then subtract the initial rest energy: \[E_{imp}=\alpha\Delta t+m_ec^2\left(\frac n{\sqrt{n^2-1}}-1\right).\]
B4. Core temperature from line broadening
The line-of-sight Doppler width obeys \(\Delta E_{rms}/E_\nu=v_{z,rms}/c\). Isotropy gives \(V_{rms}=\sqrt3v_{z,rms}=2.01\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}\). From \(mV_{rms}^2/2=3k_BT_c/2\), \(T_c=1.13\times10^7\,\mathrm K\).

statement.text:

A nonrelativistic particle of mass \(m\) moves without friction in the horizontal xy-plane. Across \(x=x_1\), potential changes from zero in region I to \(V_0\) in region II. It leaves \(O=(0,0)\) at speed \(v_1\), angle \(\theta_1\) to the x-axis, crosses at \((x_1,\alpha)\), then reaches \(P=(x_0,y_0)\) at speed \(v_2\), angle \(\theta_2\). Its fixed-energy action is \(\mathcal A=m\int v(s)\,ds\), stationary on the physical path. Ignore gravity and relativistic effects in every part. Use \(h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), \(m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\).

A1. Energy across the step
Find the speed in region II from energy conservation.
A2. Tangential momentum
Relate speeds to the two trajectory angles.
A3. Stationary action

Speeds are \(v_1=2.0000\times10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(v_2=1.9900\times10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}\). The screen is \(x_0-x_1=250.00\,\mathrm{mm}\) beyond the slit. Find the voltage accelerating electrons from rest to \(v_1\).

D3. Nearest interference minimum

children.text: \(mv_1^2/2=mv_2^2/2+V_0\), so \(v_2=\sqrt{v_1^2-2V_0/m}\), provided the trajectory can enter region II.
The potential force is normal to the boundary, so \(mv_1\sin\theta_1=mv_2\sin\theta_2\). Thus \(v_2=v_1\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2\).

\[\mathcal A=m v_1\sqrt{x_1^2+\alpha^2}+m v_2\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+(y_0-\alpha)^2}.\] Setting its derivative to zero gives \[\frac{v_1\alpha}{\sqrt{x_1^2+\alpha^2}}=\frac{v_2(y_0-\alpha)}{\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+(y_0-\alpha)^2}},\] which is the tangential-momentum relation.
The travel time is \(t=(n_1l_1+n_2l_2)/c\). Vary the crossing point along the interface. Its derivative vanishes when \(n_1\sin i_1=n_2\sin i_2\), Snell's law.
Across horizontal layers, \(n\sin i=n_0\). Since \(dy/dx=-\cot i\), \[\frac{dy}{dx}=-\sqrt{n(y)^2/n_0^2-1}.\]
\[\Delta\varphi_{CD}=\frac{2\pi md}{h}(v_1\sin\theta_1-v_2\sin\theta_2)=0.\] Stationary action means neighbouring paths interfere constructively to first order.
The incident and outgoing path differences subtract: \[\beta=\frac{m_ed}{h}(v_1-v_2)\sin\theta=5.13.\]

The nearest half-integer phase is \(5.5\times2\pi\). For outgoing angle \(\theta+\Delta\theta\), \(m_ed[v_1\sin\theta-v_2\sin(\theta+\Delta\theta)]/h=5.5\). Linearizing sine gives \(\Delta\theta\simeq-6.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad}\). Thus \(\Delta y=(x_0-x_1)\sec^2\theta\,\Delta\theta\simeq-16.2\,\mathrm{\mu m}\), below P.
Mean occupancy is \(N=IA\ell/v\). Set \(N=1\) and use \(v\simeq2\times10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}\): \(I_{min}=v/(A\ell)=4\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).

solution.text:
The Extremum Principle
A1. Energy across the step
\(mv_1^2/2=mv_2^2/2+V_0\), so \(v_2=\sqrt{v_1^2-2V_0/m}\), provided the trajectory can enter region II.
A2. Tangential momentum
The potential force is normal to the boundary, so \(mv_1\sin\theta_1=mv_2\sin\theta_2\). Thus \(v_2=v_1\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2\).
A3. Stationary action
\[\mathcal A=m v_1\sqrt{x_1^2+\alpha^2}+m v_2\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+(y_0-\alpha)^2}.\] Setting its derivative to zero gives \[\frac{v_1\alpha}{\sqrt{x_1^2+\alpha^2}}=\frac{v_2(y_0-\alpha)}{\sqrt{(x_0-x_1)^2+(y_0-\alpha)^2}},\] which is the tangential-momentum relation.
B1. Fermat and refraction
The travel time is \(t=(n_1l_1+n_2l_2)/c\). Vary the crossing point along the interface. Its derivative vanishes when \(n_1\sin i_1=n_2\sin i_2\), Snell's law.
B2. Graded-index beam slope
Across horizontal layers, \(n\sin i=n_0\). Since \(dy/dx=-\cot i\), \[\frac{dy}{dx}=-\sqrt{n(y)^2/n_0^2-1}.\]
B3. Beam trajectory
Integrate \(dx/dy=-n_0/\sqrt{(n_0-ky)^2-n_0^2}\). Using \(\int du/\sqrt{u^2-1}=\ln(u+\sqrt{u^2-1})\), \[x(y)=\frac{n_0}{k}\ln\left(1-\frac{ky}{n_0}+\sqrt{(1-ky/n_0)^2-1}\right).\]
B4. Bottom intersection
Substitute \(y=-10.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) in B3: \(x_0=30\ln[(4+\sqrt7)/3]=23.9\,\mathrm{cm}\).
C1. Wave phase and action
\(d\varphi=2\pi ds/\lambda=2\pi mv\,ds/h\), so \(\Delta\varphi=2\pi\Delta\mathcal A/h\).
C2. First-order phase difference
\[\Delta\varphi_{CD}=\frac{2\pi md}{h}(v_1\sin\theta_1-v_2\sin\theta_2)=0.\] Stationary action means neighbouring paths interfere constructively to first order.
D1. Electron accelerating voltage
Nonrelativistically \(eU_1=m_ev_1^2/2\), giving \(U_1=1.139\times10^3\,\mathrm V\).
D2. Two-slit phase
The incident and outgoing path differences subtract: \[\beta=\frac{m_ed}{h}(v_1-v_2)\sin\theta=5.13.\]
D3. Nearest interference minimum
The nearest half-integer phase is \(5.5\times2\pi\). For outgoing angle \(\theta+\Delta\theta\), \(m_ed[v_1\sin\theta-v_2\sin(\theta+\Delta\theta)]/h=5.5\). Linearizing sine gives \(\Delta\theta\simeq-6.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad}\). Thus \(\Delta y=(x_0-x_1)\sec^2\theta\,\Delta\theta\simeq-16.2\,\mathrm{\mu m}\), below P.
D4. Minimum electron flux
Mean occupancy is \(N=IA\ell/v\). Set \(N=1\) and use \(v\simeq2\times10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}\): \(I_{min}=v/(A\ell)=4\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\).

statement.text:
The Design of a Nuclear Reactor

Use \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

A1. Fission energy
For \({}^{235}\mathrm U+n\to{}^{94}\mathrm{Zr}+{}^{140}\mathrm{Ce}+2n\), estimate released energy, ignoring charge imbalance. Nuclear masses are 235.044 u, 93.9063 u, 139.905 u and neutron mass 1.00867 u. Use \(1\,\mathrm u=931.502\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^2\).
A2. Fissile number density
Find the number of uranium-235 atoms per unit fuel volume.
A3. Volumetric heating
Uniform neutron flux is \(\phi=2.000\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\), fission cross-section \(\sigma_f=5.400\times10^{-26}\,\mathrm{m^2}\). If 80 percent of fission energy becomes heat, find \(Q\). Use \(1\,\mathrm{MeV}=1.602\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm J\).
A4. Fuel temperature scale

A5. Largest fuel pin radius

B1. Centre-of-mass collision drawing

A neutron of mass 1 u and incoming laboratory velocity \(\mathbf v_b\) collides elastically with a stationary moderator atom of mass \(A\,\mathrm u\). Its outgoing laboratory velocity is \(\mathbf v_a\), and CM velocity is \(\mathbf v_m\). Draw the CM collision and label initial neutron, final neutron and initial moderator velocities, and neutron scattering angle \(\theta\).
B2. Post-collision CM speeds
Find neutron and moderator speeds \(v,V\) after collision in the CM frame.
B3. Neutron energy ratio
Derive \(G(\alpha,\theta)=E_a/E_b\), where \(\alpha=[(A-1)/(A+1)]^2\) and energies refer to the laboratory frame.
B4. Maximum moderator energy loss
Apply this model to a \(\mathrm{D_2O}\) molecule of mass 20 u. Find the maximum fractional neutron energy loss.
C1. Efficient reactor dimensions
Leakage rate is \(k_1[(2.405/R)^2+(\pi/H)^2]\psi\), and excess production rate is \(k_2\psi\), with \(k_1=1.021\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m\), \(k_2=8.787\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\). Minimize leakage for fixed cylindrical volume, then find steady-state dimensions.

children.text: The Design of a Nuclear Reactor
\(Q\) has units \(\mathrm{W/m^3}\), while \(\lambda\) has units \(\mathrm{W/(m\,K)}\), so \(F=Qa^2/\lambda\).

Subtract \(\mathbf v_m=\mathbf v_b/(A+1)\) from every laboratory velocity. Initial neutron is \(\mathbf v_b-\mathbf v_m\), final neutron \(\mathbf v_a-\mathbf v_m\), initial moderator \(-\mathbf v_m\). The outgoing CM momenta are equal and opposite. Mark \(\theta\) between incoming and outgoing neutron directions.
CM momentum gives \(v=AV\). Elastic energy conservation leaves the incoming CM speed magnitudes unchanged: \(v=Av_b/(A+1)\), \(V=v_b/(A+1)\).
Add CM translation to the outgoing neutron velocity: \(v_a^2=v^2+v_m^2+2vv_m\cos\theta\). Therefore \[G=\frac{A^2+1+2A\cos\theta}{(A+1)^2}=\frac{1+\alpha+(1-\alpha)\cos\theta}{2}.\]
Backscattering gives the minimum retained fraction \(\alpha\). Hence \(f_{loss}=1-(19/21)^2=80/441=0.1814\).

At fixed \(R^2H\), differentiating leakage gives \(H/R=\sqrt2\pi/2.405\). At the optimum the radial leakage term is twice the axial term. Steady balance yields \[R=2.405\sqrt{\frac{3k_1}{2k_2}}=3.175\,\mathrm m,\qquad H=\pi\sqrt{\frac{3k_1}{k_2}}=5.866\,\mathrm m.\]
Area per channel is \(s^2\), so \(F_n\simeq\pi R^2/s^2=387\). Total fuel mass is \(M=F_n\pi r_f^2H\rho\simeq9.89\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Boundary rounding is part of the estimate.

solution.text:
The Design of a Nuclear Reactor
A1. Fission energy
The mass defect is \(235.044-93.9063-139.905-1.00867=0.22403\,\mathrm u\). Thus \(E_f=208.7\,\mathrm{MeV}\).
A2. Fissile number density
\(N=0.00720\rho N_A/M_w=1.70\times10^{26}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\).
A3. Volumetric heating
The reaction rate is \(N\sigma_f\phi\). Hence \(Q=0.8E_fN\sigma_f\phi=4.92\times10^8\,\mathrm{W/m^3}\).
A4. Fuel temperature scale
\(Q\) has units \(\mathrm{W/m^3}\), while \(\lambda\) has units \(\mathrm{W/(m\,K)}\), so \(F=Qa^2/\lambda\).
A5. Largest fuel pin radius
Impose \(T_c\le T_m\). Thus \(a_u=\sqrt{4\lambda(T_m-T_s)/Q}=8.27\,\mathrm{mm}\).
B1. Centre-of-mass collision drawing
Subtract \(\mathbf v_m=\mathbf v_b/(A+1)\) from every laboratory velocity. Initial neutron is \(\mathbf v_b-\mathbf v_m\), final neutron \(\mathbf v_a-\mathbf v_m\), initial moderator \(-\mathbf v_m\). The outgoing CM momenta are equal and opposite. Mark \(\theta\) between incoming and outgoing neutron directions.
B2. Post-collision CM speeds
CM momentum gives \(v=AV\). Elastic energy conservation leaves the incoming CM speed magnitudes unchanged: \(v=Av_b/(A+1)\), \(V=v_b/(A+1)\).
B3. Neutron energy ratio
Add CM translation to the outgoing neutron velocity: \(v_a^2=v^2+v_m^2+2vv_m\cos\theta\). Therefore \[G=\frac{A^2+1+2A\cos\theta}{(A+1)^2}=\frac{1+\alpha+(1-\alpha)\cos\theta}{2}.\]
B4. Maximum moderator energy loss
Backscattering gives the minimum retained fraction \(\alpha\). Hence \(f_{loss}=1-(19/21)^2=80/441=0.1814\).
C1. Efficient reactor dimensions
At fixed \(R^2H\), differentiating leakage gives \(H/R=\sqrt2\pi/2.405\). At the optimum the radial leakage term is twice the axial term. Steady balance yields \[R=2.405\sqrt{\frac{3k_1}{2k_2}}=3.175\,\mathrm m,\qquad H=\pi\sqrt{\frac{3k_1}{k_2}}=5.866\,\mathrm m.\]
C2. Fuel channels and mass
Area per channel is \(s^2\), so \(F_n\simeq\pi R^2/s^2=387\). Total fuel mass is \(M=F_n\pi r_f^2H\rho\simeq9.89\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Boundary rounding is part of the estimate.

statement.text:
Two Problems in Mechanics
Part A: a wooden cylinder of radius \(r_1\), thickness \(h_1\), density \(\rho_1\), and total mass \(M\) contains a metal disk replacing wood. Its density is \(\rho_2>\rho_1\), radius \(r_2\), thickness \(h_2\), and axis B is parallel to cylinder axis S at distance \(d\). The disk is midway between the end faces. Known quantities are \(r_1,h_1,\rho_1,\rho_2,M\). Let the centre of mass C be distance \(b\) from S. Part B: a wheel-shaped space station of radius \(R\) rotates at angular speed \(\omega_{ss}\). Astronauts live on the inside rim. Ignore the station gravity and local floor curvature where specified. Earth has radius \(R_E\) and surface gravity \(g_E\).
A.1. Centre of mass offset


On a horizontal surface the cylinder is in stable equilibrium. Slowly incline the surface through \(\Theta\). The cylinder rolls without slipping and reaches equilibrium after rotating through the measured angle \(\phi\) shown. Determine \(b\).
A.2. Suspended-cylinder period

Suspend the cylinder at S, displace it through a small angle \(\varphi\), and measure period \(T\). Find the equation of motion and inertia \(I_S\).
A.3. Disk offset
Express \(d\) in terms of \(b\) and known quantities, allowing \(r_2,h_2\).
A.4. Geometrical inertia
Find \(I_S\) from geometry using \(b\), the known quantities, and optionally \(r_2,h_2\).
A.5. Hidden-disk dimensions
Determine \(r_2,h_2\) in terms of the measured \(b,T\) and known quantities.
B.1. Artificial gravity

Find the rotation rate producing gravity \(g_E\) at the rim.
B.2. Earth spring oscillator
A mass \(m\) on a spring of stiffness \(k\) moves only vertically. Find its angular frequency in uniform terrestrial gravity.
B.3. Station spring oscillator
Find the angular oscillation frequency when horizontal motion is constrained in the station.
B.4. Terrestrial gravity gradient
Include the first-order height dependence of Earth gravity. Find \(g_E(h)\) and angular oscillator frequency \(\widetilde\omega_E\). Ignore Earth rotation.
B.5. Indistinguishable frequencies
For which station radius do B.3 and B.4 coincide?
B.6. Small-height drop
Drop a mass from height \(H\ll R\). Assuming constant downward acceleration and \(d_x\ll H\), find horizontal velocity and displacement at the floor. Either consistent horizontal sign convention is allowed.
B.7. Return to the tower base
A sufficiently tall tower allows the released mass to hit its base, with zero relative horizontal displacement. Find the smallest nonzero height for this to occur.
B.8. Unconstrained oscillator trajectory

The spring hangs from a ring free to slide horizontally. Let y point towards the station centre and pull the mass to \(x=0,y=-d\), then release at rest. Neglect Coriolis feedback on vertical motion. Find \(x(t),y(t)\), and sketch the trajectory, marking amplitudes and cusps.

children.text: The centre of mass lies vertically above the contact point, so the common horizontal offset satisfies \(b\sin\phi=r_1\sin\Theta\). Hence \[b=r_1\sin\Theta/\sin\phi.\]
Define excess disk mass \(\Delta M=\pi r_2^2h_2(\rho_2-\rho_1)=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\). The uniform wood contribution has centre S, so \(Mb=\Delta M d\) and \(d=Mb/\Delta M\).
The parallel-axis theorem gives \[I_S=\tfrac12\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4+\tfrac12\Delta M r_2^2+\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}.\] Here \(\Delta M=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\).

Use \(I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2)\) and the previous inertia: \[r_2=\sqrt{\frac2{\Delta M}\left[\frac{MgbT^2}{4\pi^2}-\frac{\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4}{2}-\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}\right]},\qquad h_2=\frac{\Delta M}{\pi r_2^2(\rho_2-\rho_1)}.\] These require a physically admissible positive radicand and a disk fitting inside the wood.
Gravity shifts equilibrium without changing stiffness. Thus \(\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m}\).
The centrifugal force varies linearly with radius. After shifting equilibrium, \(m\ddot y+(k-m\omega_{ss}^2)y=0\). Hence \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\), assuming positive effective stiffness.
The downward magnitude is \(g_E(h)=g_E(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_E(1-2h/R_E)\). The upward variation reduces restoring stiffness, so \[\widetilde\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m-2g_E/R_E}.\]

The fall time is \(t_f=\sqrt{2H/(\omega_{ss}^2R)}\). Integrate the Coriolis acceleration magnitude \(2\omega_{ss}g_Et\): \[|v_x|=2H\omega_{ss},\qquad |d_x|=\frac13\sqrt{\frac{8H^3}{R}}.\] Relative to the rotating floor the mass falls behind the tower for the usual forward-positive convention.
B.7. Return to the tower base

In the inertial frame the mass moves straight at speed \(\omega_{ss}(R-H)\). Put \(u=\omega_{ss}t_f=\sqrt{R^2-(R-H)^2}/(R-H)\). Returning to the base requires \(\tan u=u\) with the correct angular branch and \(\cos u>0\). The first admissible nonzero root is \(u=7.72525\), between \(2\pi\) and \(5\pi/2\). Thus \(H/R=1-1/\sqrt{1+u^2}=0.87162\). The root near 4.493 has negative cosine and does not describe a tower inside the rim.

Write \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\). Then \(y=-d\cos\omega t\). Choosing \(\ddot x=-2\omega_{ss}\dot y\), integrate twice with zero initial velocity: \[x=\frac{2\omega_{ss}d}{\omega}\sin\omega t-2\omega_{ss}dt.\] The opposite horizontal sign is equivalent. The path has vertical extrema \(\pm d\), a drift, and cusps at \(y=-d\), separated horizontally by \(4\pi\omega_{ss}d/\omega\). The source prints an inconsistent sign for \(\dot y\). Differentiating the stated \(y(t)\) and using a single Coriolis convention resolves it.

solution.text:
Two Problems in Mechanics
A.1. Centre of mass offset
The centre of mass lies vertically above the contact point, so the common horizontal offset satisfies \(b\sin\phi=r_1\sin\Theta\). Hence \[b=r_1\sin\Theta/\sin\phi.\]
A.2. Suspended-cylinder period
The torque is \(-Mgb\sin\varphi\), so \(I_S\ddot\varphi=-Mgb\sin\varphi\simeq-Mgb\varphi\). Thus \[I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2).\]
A.3. Disk offset
Define excess disk mass \(\Delta M=\pi r_2^2h_2(\rho_2-\rho_1)=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\). The uniform wood contribution has centre S, so \(Mb=\Delta M d\) and \(d=Mb/\Delta M\).
A.4. Geometrical inertia
The parallel-axis theorem gives \[I_S=\tfrac12\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4+\tfrac12\Delta M r_2^2+\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}.\] Here \(\Delta M=M-\pi r_1^2h_1\rho_1\).
A.5. Hidden-disk dimensions
Use \(I_S=MgbT^2/(4\pi^2)\) and the previous inertia: \[r_2=\sqrt{\frac2{\Delta M}\left[\frac{MgbT^2}{4\pi^2}-\frac{\pi h_1\rho_1r_1^4}{2}-\frac{M^2b^2}{\Delta M}\right]},\qquad h_2=\frac{\Delta M}{\pi r_2^2(\rho_2-\rho_1)}.\] These require a physically admissible positive radicand and a disk fitting inside the wood.
B.1. Artificial gravity
Equate \(\omega_{ss}^2R=g_E\), giving \(\omega_{ss}=\sqrt{g_E/R}\).
B.2. Earth spring oscillator
Gravity shifts equilibrium without changing stiffness. Thus \(\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m}\).
B.3. Station spring oscillator
The centrifugal force varies linearly with radius. After shifting equilibrium, \(m\ddot y+(k-m\omega_{ss}^2)y=0\). Hence \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\), assuming positive effective stiffness.
B.4. Terrestrial gravity gradient
The downward magnitude is \(g_E(h)=g_E(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_E(1-2h/R_E)\). The upward variation reduces restoring stiffness, so \[\widetilde\omega_E=\sqrt{k/m-2g_E/R_E}.\]
B.5. Indistinguishable frequencies
Equate \(g_E/R=2g_E/R_E\), giving \(R=R_E/2\).
B.6. Small-height drop
The fall time is \(t_f=\sqrt{2H/(\omega_{ss}^2R)}\). Integrate the Coriolis acceleration magnitude \(2\omega_{ss}g_Et\): \[|v_x|=2H\omega_{ss},\qquad |d_x|=\frac13\sqrt{\frac{8H^3}{R}}.\] Relative to the rotating floor the mass falls behind the tower for the usual forward-positive convention.
B.7. Return to the tower base
In the inertial frame the mass moves straight at speed \(\omega_{ss}(R-H)\). Put \(u=\omega_{ss}t_f=\sqrt{R^2-(R-H)^2}/(R-H)\). Returning to the base requires \(\tan u=u\) with the correct angular branch and \(\cos u>0\). The first admissible nonzero root is \(u=7.72525\), between \(2\pi\) and \(5\pi/2\). Thus \(H/R=1-1/\sqrt{1+u^2}=0.87162\). The root near 4.493 has negative cosine and does not describe a tower inside the rim.
B.8. Unconstrained oscillator trajectory
Write \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m-\omega_{ss}^2}\). Then \(y=-d\cos\omega t\). Choosing \(\ddot x=-2\omega_{ss}\dot y\), integrate twice with zero initial velocity: \[x=\frac{2\omega_{ss}d}{\omega}\sin\omega t-2\omega_{ss}dt.\] The opposite horizontal sign is equivalent. The path has vertical extrema \(\pm d\), a drift, and cusps at \(y=-d\), separated horizontally by \(4\pi\omega_{ss}d/\omega\). The source prints an inconsistent sign for \(\dot y\). Differentiating the stated \(y(t)\) and using a single Coriolis convention resolves it.

statement.text:
Simplest model of gas discharge
An external ionizer creates \(Z_{ext}\) electron and singly charged ion pairs per unit volume per unit time. Recombination removes pairs at rate \(rn_en_i\), where \(r\) is constant. Initially both densities are zero. In part A ignore the electric field of the carriers. For current measurements a gas-filled tube has parallel electrodes of area \(S\), separation \(L\ll\sqrt S\), and voltage \(U\). Both carrier species have drift-speed magnitude \(v=\beta E\), and their densities are approximated as uniform.
A1. Density growth constants
Write \(n_e(t)=n_0+a\tanh(bt)\). Determine \(n_0,a,b\).
A2. Two ionizers
Two ionizers separately produce equilibrium electron densities \(12\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and \(16\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Find the density with both operating.
A3. Current-voltage law
With the ionizer operating for a long time, express total current in terms of \(U,\beta,L,S,Z_{ext},r,e\).
A4. Low-voltage resistivity
Find gas resistivity at sufficiently small voltage.
B1. Electron current constants

For part B neglect recombination, keep \(Z_{ext}\), and take uniform field. The cathode is at \(x=0\), anode at \(x=L\). Avalanches obey \(dN_e/dl=\alpha N_e\). Write \(I_e(x)=C_1e^{A_1x}+A_2\) and find \(A_1,A_2\).
B2. Ion current constants
Write \(I_i(x)=C_2+B_1e^{B_2x}\). Find \(B_1,B_2\).
B3. Anode boundary
State the ion-current boundary condition at the anode.
B4. Cathode boundary
Each ion striking the cathode releases on average \(\gamma\) electrons. State the boundary condition at \(x=0\).
B5. Finite total current
Find the total steady current while the subcritical solution remains finite.
B6. Critical gap length
Find the gap length above which secondary emission can maintain discharge without the external ionizer.

children.text: Pairs are created and destroyed together, so \(n_e=n_i=n\) and \(\dot n=Z_{ext}-rn^2\). The initial condition and substitution give \[n_0=0,\quad a=\sqrt{Z_{ext}/r},\quad b=\sqrt{rZ_{ext}}.\]
Rates add, not equilibrium densities. Thus \(n=\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}=20\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).

Each carrier current is \(I/2=en\beta US/L\). Pair balance is \(Z_{ext}SL=rn^2SL+I/(2e)\). The positive quadratic root gives \[I=\frac{e\beta^2U^2S}{rL^3}\left(\sqrt{1+\frac{4rZ_{ext}L^4}{\beta^2U^2}}-1\right).\]
Ion production gives \(-dI_i/dx=eZ_{ext}S+\alpha I_e\). Therefore \(B_1=-C_1\) and \(B_2=\alpha\).
No ions enter from beyond the anode, so \(I_i(L)=0\).

Total current \(I=I_e+I_i=C_2-eZ_{ext}S/\alpha\) is independent of position. Use \(C_2=C_1e^{\alpha L}\) and the cathode condition to obtain \[I=\frac{eZ_{ext}S}{\alpha}\left[\frac1{(1+\gamma)e^{-\alpha L}-\gamma}-1\right].\] The physical externally sustained branch has \(\gamma(e^{\alpha L}-1)<1\).

The avalanche feedback threshold is \(\gamma(e^{\alpha L}-1)=1\). Thus \[L_{cr}=\frac1\alpha\ln(1+1/\gamma).\] The linear model diverges at threshold and cannot predict the saturated discharge current.

solution.text:
Simplest model of gas discharge
A1. Density growth constants
Pairs are created and destroyed together, so \(n_e=n_i=n\) and \(\dot n=Z_{ext}-rn^2\). The initial condition and substitution give \[n_0=0,\quad a=\sqrt{Z_{ext}/r},\quad b=\sqrt{rZ_{ext}}.\]
A2. Two ionizers
Rates add, not equilibrium densities. Thus \(n=\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}=20\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).
A3. Current-voltage law
Each carrier current is \(I/2=en\beta US/L\). Pair balance is \(Z_{ext}SL=rn^2SL+I/(2e)\). The positive quadratic root gives \[I=\frac{e\beta^2U^2S}{rL^3}\left(\sqrt{1+\frac{4rZ_{ext}L^4}{\beta^2U^2}}-1\right).\]
A4. Low-voltage resistivity
As \(U\to0\), \(n\to\sqrt{Z_{ext}/r}\) and \(I=2e\beta US\sqrt{Z_{ext}/r}/L\). Hence \[\rho_{gas}=\frac1{2e\beta}\sqrt{r/Z_{ext}}.\]
B1. Electron current constants
Local balance gives \(dI_e/dx=eZ_{ext}S+\alpha I_e\), so \(A_1=\alpha\), \(A_2=-eZ_{ext}S/\alpha\).
B2. Ion current constants
Ion production gives \(-dI_i/dx=eZ_{ext}S+\alpha I_e\). Therefore \(B_1=-C_1\) and \(B_2=\alpha\).
B3. Anode boundary
No ions enter from beyond the anode, so \(I_i(L)=0\).
B4. Cathode boundary
The secondary-emission condition is \(I_e(0)=\gamma I_i(0)\).
B5. Finite total current
Total current \(I=I_e+I_i=C_2-eZ_{ext}S/\alpha\) is independent of position. Use \(C_2=C_1e^{\alpha L}\) and the cathode condition to obtain \[I=\frac{eZ_{ext}S}{\alpha}\left[\frac1{(1+\gamma)e^{-\alpha L}-\gamma}-1\right].\] The physical externally sustained branch has \(\gamma(e^{\alpha L}-1)<1\).
B6. Critical gap length
The avalanche feedback threshold is \(\gamma(e^{\alpha L}-1)=1\). Thus \[L_{cr}=\frac1\alpha\ln(1+1/\gamma).\] The linear model diverges at threshold and cannot predict the saturated discharge current.

statement.text:

On 17 January 2009 a camera recorded a meteor over the Baltic Sea. A 0.025 kg fragment was later found near Maribo. Use \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\), Earth's mass \(m_E=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), radius \(R_E=6.38\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), Sun's mass \(m_S=1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), and Earth-Sun distance \(a_E=1.50\times10^{11}\,\mathrm m\). During atmospheric heating, take the surface temperature to be a constant \(1000\,\mathrm K\).
1.1. Camera speed

The meteor travels on a straight track heading \(285^\circ\) clockwise from north towards the landing site, 195 km from the camera at azimuth \(230^\circ\). Frame 155 at 1.46 s has azimuth \(215^\circ\), altitude \(19.2^\circ\). Frame 161 at 2.28 s has azimuth \(221^\circ\), altitude \(14.7^\circ\). Find its mean speed, neglecting Earth curvature and gravity.
1.2a. Atmospheric deceleration
An entering sphere has mass \(m_M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), radius \(R_M=0.13\,\mathrm m\), temperature \(T_0=200\,\mathrm K\), and speed \(v_M=2.91\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Drag is \(F=k\rho_{\rm atm}Av^2\), with \(k=0.60\), \(\rho_{\rm atm}=4.1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and \(A=\pi R_M^2\). 1.3b. Heated-layer thickness

1.4a. Radioactive decay scheme

1.4b. Isochron proof

Earth has inertia \(I_E=0.83(2/5)m_ER_E^2\). Find the maximum axis tilt. Neglect orbital changes and use a 24 h initial day.

children.text: Intersect each horizontal camera bearing with the line through the landing site heading \(285^\circ\). The horizontal camera ranges are \(195\sin55^\circ/\sin70^\circ\) and \(195\sin55^\circ/\sin64^\circ\) km. Their heights are these ranges times \(\tan19.2^\circ\) and \(\tan14.7^\circ\). Combine the horizontal track displacement with the height difference and divide by \(0.82\,\mathrm s\). The result is about \(29.1\,\mathrm{km/s}\).
The dimensions of heat conduction give \(x=\sqrt{k_st/(\rho c)}\). Thus \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)=(1/2,-1/2,-1/2,1/2)\).

Rb decays as \(N_R(t)=N_R(0)e^{-\lambda t}\), while daughter Sr increases by \(N_R(0)-N_R(t)\). Divide by stable \(N_{86}\): \[\frac{N_{87\rm Sr}(t)}{N_{86}}=\frac{N_{87\rm Sr}(0)}{N_{86}}+(e^{\lambda t}-1)\frac{N_R(t)}{N_{86}}.\] This is the requested straight line with a common intercept.
The graph rises from approximately 0.700 to 0.712 over a horizontal span 0.25. Its slope is about 0.050. Therefore \(t=T_{1/2}\ln(1+a)/\ln2=3.4\times10^9\) years.
Its semi-major axis is the mean of the two distances. Kepler's law gives \(T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/(Gm_S)}=3.30\) years.

The asteroid mass is \(1.57\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{kg}\). Its largest angular momentum is \(m_av_aR_E\), perpendicular to Earth's spin. Hence \(\Delta\theta\simeq m_av_aR_E/(I_E\omega_E)=4.27\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
No angular momentum is added, but \(\Delta I=m_aR_E^2\). Thus \(\Delta T\simeq T\Delta I/I_E=6.84\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\).

Use \((I_E+m_aR_E^2)\omega_f=I_E\omega_E+m_av_aR_E\). To first order, \(\Delta T/T=\Delta I/I_E-\Delta L/L_E\), giving \(-3.62\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\). A retrograde impact changes the angular-momentum term's sign and lengthens the day.

The largest heliocentric speed at Earth's orbit approaches solar escape speed \(\sqrt{2Gm_S/a_E}\). A head-on encounter adds Earth's orbital speed \(\sqrt{Gm_S/a_E}\). Earth's gravity then adds escape-speed squared: \[v_{\max}=\sqrt{(\sqrt2+1)^2Gm_S/a_E+2Gm_E/R_E}\simeq72.8\,\mathrm{km/s}.\]

solution.text:
The Maribo Meteorite
1.1. Camera speed
Intersect each horizontal camera bearing with the line through the landing site heading \(285^\circ\). The horizontal camera ranges are \(195\sin55^\circ/\sin70^\circ\) and \(195\sin55^\circ/\sin64^\circ\) km. Their heights are these ranges times \(\tan19.2^\circ\) and \(\tan14.7^\circ\). Combine the horizontal track displacement with the height difference and divide by \(0.82\,\mathrm s\). The result is about \(29.1\,\mathrm{km/s}\).
1.2a. Atmospheric deceleration
Integrate \(m_M\dot v=-k\rho_{\rm atm}Av^2\): \[t=\frac{m_M}{k\rho_{\rm atm}\pi R_M^2v_M}\left(\frac1{0.9}-1\right)\simeq0.88\,\mathrm s.\]
1.2b. Energy available for melting
The mass cancels: \[\frac{E_{\rm kin}}{E_{\rm melt}}=\frac{v_M^2/2}{c(T_m-T_0)+L}\simeq2.1\times10^2.\]
1.3a. Thermal penetration powers
The dimensions of heat conduction give \(x=\sqrt{k_st/(\rho c)}\). Thus \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)=(1/2,-1/2,-1/2,1/2)\).
1.3b. Heated-layer thickness
\(x=\sqrt{k_st/(\rho c)}=1.6\,\mathrm{mm}\), and \(x/R_M=0.012\).
1.4a. Radioactive decay scheme
\[{}^{87}_{37}\mathrm{Rb}\longrightarrow{}^{87}_{38}\mathrm{Sr}+{}^0_{-1}e+\bar\nu_e.\] This is beta-minus decay.
1.4b. Isochron proof
Rb decays as \(N_R(t)=N_R(0)e^{-\lambda t}\), while daughter Sr increases by \(N_R(0)-N_R(t)\). Divide by stable \(N_{86}\): \[\frac{N_{87\rm Sr}(t)}{N_{86}}=\frac{N_{87\rm Sr}(0)}{N_{86}}+(e^{\lambda t}-1)\frac{N_R(t)}{N_{86}}.\] This is the requested straight line with a common intercept.
1.4c. Radiometric age
The graph rises from approximately 0.700 to 0.712 over a horizontal span 0.25. Its slope is about 0.050. Therefore \(t=T_{1/2}\ln(1+a)/\ln2=3.4\times10^9\) years.
1.5. Comet Encke period
Its semi-major axis is the mean of the two distances. Kepler's law gives \(T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/(Gm_S)}=3.30\) years.
1.6a. Maximum pole-impact tilt
The asteroid mass is \(1.57\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{kg}\). Its largest angular momentum is \(m_av_aR_E\), perpendicular to Earth's spin. Hence \(\Delta\theta\simeq m_av_aR_E/(I_E\omega_E)=4.27\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
1.6b. Radial equatorial impact
No angular momentum is added, but \(\Delta I=m_aR_E^2\). Thus \(\Delta T\simeq T\Delta I/I_E=6.84\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\).
1.6c. Tangential equatorial impact
Use \((I_E+m_aR_E^2)\omega_f=I_E\omega_E+m_av_aR_E\). To first order, \(\Delta T/T=\Delta I/I_E-\Delta L/L_E\), giving \(-3.62\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\). A retrograde impact changes the angular-momentum term's sign and lengthens the day.
1.7. Maximum impact speed
The largest heliocentric speed at Earth's orbit approaches solar escape speed \(\sqrt{2Gm_S/a_E}\). A head-on encounter adds Earth's orbital speed \(\sqrt{Gm_S/a_E}\). Earth's gravity then adds escape-speed squared: \[v_{\max}=\sqrt{(\sqrt2+1)^2Gm_S/a_E+2Gm_E/R_E}\simeq72.8\,\mathrm{km/s}.\]

children.text: A silver nanoparticle of radius \(R=10.0\,\mathrm{nm}\) has one free electron per silver atom. Its positive ion sphere is fixed. Model its electrons as a uniformly charged sphere which can shift by \(x_p\ll R\) along \(x\). All relative permittivities are one. Use \(\rho_{Ag}=1.049\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), molar mass \(M_{Ag}=0.1079\,\mathrm{kg/mol}\), \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), \(m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\epsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}\), and \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Electron charge is \(-e\).

nodes.alt: Original five-panel silver nanoparticle and vessel model showing the displaced charge distributions, external field and illumination geometry.

children.text: Find particle volume and mass, ion number and charge density, electron concentration \(n\), total electron charge \(Q\), and total electron mass \(m_0\).

Create a spherical neutral cavity inside a uniformly charged sphere of density \(\rho\) by adding a smaller sphere of density \(-\rho\), centred at \(\mathbf x_d\). Prove the cavity field is uniform, \(\mathbf E=A(\rho/\epsilon_0)\mathbf x_d\), and find \(A\).
Find the restoring force and work for displacing the electron cloud by \(x_p\), using \(n,R,e,\epsilon_0\).
Apply \(\mathbf E_0=-E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\). Find \(x_p\) and the electron charge \(-\Delta Q\) transported through the central yz-plane.
Match \(W_{el}=\Delta Q^2/(2C)\). Find \(C\) and its numerical value.
Find the equivalent applied voltage \(V_0\) in terms of \(R,E_0\).
If the electron cloud moves at velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf x}\), find its kinetic energy and conventional current through the yz-plane.
Find the LC resonance angular frequency.
Find the resonance angular frequency and vacuum wavelength.

An oscillating field drives cloud velocity \(v\). Each electron loses all its kinetic energy in a collision, with mean collision interval \(\tau=5.24\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm s\gg1/\omega_p\). Find average Joule power and mean-square current explicitly in terms of \(\langle v^2\rangle\).
Find and evaluate the equivalent resistance for collision heating.
The scattered power is \(P_{scat}=Q^2x_0^2\omega_p^4/(12\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\). Find \(R_{scat}=P_{scat}/\langle I^2\rangle\) and its numerical value.
The equivalent LCR series circuit is driven by \(V=V_0\cos\omega_pt\). Derive both mean power losses in terms of \(E_0\).

The particle concentration is \(n_{np}=7.3\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) in a vessel \(h\times h\times a=10\times10\times1.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). Light enters through area \(h^2\) at the same intensity. All nanoparticle Joule heating converts water at \(20^\circ\mathrm C\) to steam at \(100^\circ\mathrm C\), without heating bulk water. Use \(c_w=4.181\times10^3\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\) and \(L_w=2.260\times10^6\,\mathrm{J/kg}\). Find steam mass per second.

statement.text:
Plasmonic Steam Generator
A silver nanoparticle of radius \(R=10.0\,\mathrm{nm}\) has one free electron per silver atom. Its positive ion sphere is fixed. Model its electrons as a uniformly charged sphere which can shift by \(x_p\ll R\) along \(x\). All relative permittivities are one. Use \(\rho_{Ag}=1.049\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), molar mass \(M_{Ag}=0.1079\,\mathrm{kg/mol}\), \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), \(m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(\epsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}\), and \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Electron charge is \(-e\).

2.1. Particle and electron properties
Find particle volume and mass, ion number and charge density, electron concentration \(n\), total electron charge \(Q\), and total electron mass \(m_0\).
2.2. Neutral cavity field
Create a spherical neutral cavity inside a uniformly charged sphere of density \(\rho\) by adding a smaller sphere of density \(-\rho\), centred at \(\mathbf x_d\). Prove the cavity field is uniform, \(\mathbf E=A(\rho/\epsilon_0)\mathbf x_d\), and find \(A\).
2.3. Restoring force and work
Find the restoring force and work for displacing the electron cloud by \(x_p\), using \(n,R,e,\epsilon_0\).
2.4. Static displacement and separated charge
Apply \(\mathbf E_0=-E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\). Find \(x_p\) and the electron charge \(-\Delta Q\) transported through the central yz-plane.
2.5a. Equivalent capacitance
Match \(W_{el}=\Delta Q^2/(2C)\). Find \(C\) and its numerical value.
2.5b. Equivalent voltage
Find the equivalent applied voltage \(V_0\) in terms of \(R,E_0\).
2.6a. Kinetic energy and current
If the electron cloud moves at velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf x}\), find its kinetic energy and conventional current through the yz-plane.
2.6b. Equivalent inductance
Use \(W_{kin}=LI^2/2\) to find and evaluate \(L\).
2.7a. Plasmon angular frequency
Find the LC resonance angular frequency.
2.7b. Resonance values
Find the resonance angular frequency and vacuum wavelength.
2.8a. Collision heating
An oscillating field drives cloud velocity \(v\). Each electron loses all its kinetic energy in a collision, with mean collision interval \(\tau=5.24\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm s\gg1/\omega_p\). Find average Joule power and mean-square current explicitly in terms of \(\langle v^2\rangle\).
2.8b. Heating resistance
Find and evaluate the equivalent resistance for collision heating.
2.9. Scattering resistance
The scattered power is \(P_{scat}=Q^2x_0^2\omega_p^4/(12\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\). Find \(R_{scat}=P_{scat}/\langle I^2\rangle\) and its numerical value.
2.10a. Resonant absorbed and scattered power
The equivalent LCR series circuit is driven by \(V=V_0\cos\omega_pt\). Derive both mean power losses in terms of \(E_0\).
2.10b. Illumination values
Use incident intensity \(S=\epsilon_0cE_0^2/2=1.00\,\mathrm{MW/m^2}\). Evaluate \(E_0,P_{heat},P_{scat}\).
2.11a. Steam mass rate
The particle concentration is \(n_{np}=7.3\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) in a vessel \(h\times h\times a=10\times10\times1.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). Light enters through area \(h^2\) at the same intensity. All nanoparticle Joule heating converts water at \(20^\circ\mathrm C\) to steam at \(100^\circ\mathrm C\), without heating bulk water. Use \(c_w=4.181\times10^3\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\) and \(L_w=2.260\times10^6\,\mathrm{J/kg}\). Find steam mass per second.
2.11b. Steam efficiency
Find thermodynamic efficiency \(\eta=P_{st}/P_{tot}\).

children.text: \[V=\frac43\pi R^3,\quad M=\rho_{Ag}V,\quad N=MN_A/M_{Ag},\quad n=\rho_{Ag}N_A/M_{Ag}.\] The ion charge density is \(en\), electron charge is \(Q=-eN\), and electron mass is \(m_0=m_eN\). Numerically \(V=4.19\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), \(M=4.39\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(N=2.45\times10^5\), \(n=5.85\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), \(en=9.38\times10^9\,\mathrm{C/m^3}\), \(Q=-3.93\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm C\), \(m_0=2.23\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{kg}\).

Inside a uniform sphere Gauss's law gives \(\mathbf E=\rho\mathbf r/(3\epsilon_0)\). Superpose the displaced negative sphere: \(\mathbf E=\rho[\mathbf r-(\mathbf r-\mathbf x_d)]/(3\epsilon_0)=\rho\mathbf x_d/(3\epsilon_0)\). Thus \(A=1/3\).
The induced inner field is \(enx_p/(3\epsilon_0)\). Multiply by \(-enV\): \[F_x=-\frac{4\pi R^3n^2e^2}{9\epsilon_0}x_p,\qquad W_{el}=\frac{2\pi R^3n^2e^2}{9\epsilon_0}x_p^2.\]
The total internal field vanishes, so \(x_p=3\epsilon_0E_0/(en)\). A cylinder of cross-section \(\pi R^2\) and length \(x_p\) crosses the plane: \(-\Delta Q=-en\pi R^2x_p\).

\[P_{heat}=\frac{m_enV}{2\tau}\langle v^2\rangle,\qquad\langle I^2\rangle=(en\pi R^2)^2\langle v^2\rangle.\] The factor one half in the source's collision model comes from kinetic energy, not from averaging the sinusoid a second time.

At resonance the reactances cancel. With \(R_t=R_{heat}+R_{scat}\), \[\langle I^2\rangle=\frac{8R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2},\quad P_{heat}=\frac{8R_{heat}R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2},\quad P_{scat}=\frac{8R_{scat}R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2}.\]

There are \(n_{np}h^2a=7.3\times10^{11}\) particles, giving \(P_{st}=4.98\,\mathrm{kW}\). Specific steam-production energy is \(c_w(100-20)+L_w=2.59\times10^6\,\mathrm{J/kg}\). The source rounds this to \(2.62\times10^6\) and reports \(\dot m=1.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/s}\). Direct use of the supplied constants gives \(1.92\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/s}\), also accepted.

solution.text:
Plasmonic Steam Generator
2.1. Particle and electron properties
\[V=\frac43\pi R^3,\quad M=\rho_{Ag}V,\quad N=MN_A/M_{Ag},\quad n=\rho_{Ag}N_A/M_{Ag}.\] The ion charge density is \(en\), electron charge is \(Q=-eN\), and electron mass is \(m_0=m_eN\). Numerically \(V=4.19\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), \(M=4.39\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(N=2.45\times10^5\), \(n=5.85\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), \(en=9.38\times10^9\,\mathrm{C/m^3}\), \(Q=-3.93\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm C\), \(m_0=2.23\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{kg}\).
2.2. Neutral cavity field
Inside a uniform sphere Gauss's law gives \(\mathbf E=\rho\mathbf r/(3\epsilon_0)\). Superpose the displaced negative sphere: \(\mathbf E=\rho[\mathbf r-(\mathbf r-\mathbf x_d)]/(3\epsilon_0)=\rho\mathbf x_d/(3\epsilon_0)\). Thus \(A=1/3\).
2.3. Restoring force and work
The induced inner field is \(enx_p/(3\epsilon_0)\). Multiply by \(-enV\): \[F_x=-\frac{4\pi R^3n^2e^2}{9\epsilon_0}x_p,\qquad W_{el}=\frac{2\pi R^3n^2e^2}{9\epsilon_0}x_p^2.\]
2.4. Static displacement and separated charge
The total internal field vanishes, so \(x_p=3\epsilon_0E_0/(en)\). A cylinder of cross-section \(\pi R^2\) and length \(x_p\) crosses the plane: \(-\Delta Q=-en\pi R^2x_p\).
2.5a. Equivalent capacitance
Substitution gives \[C=\frac94\pi\epsilon_0R=6.26\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm F.\]
2.5b. Equivalent voltage
\(V_0=\Delta Q/C=4RE_0/3\).
2.6a. Kinetic energy and current
\[W_{kin}=\frac12m_en\frac{4\pi R^3}{3}v^2,\qquad I=-en\pi R^2v.\]
2.6b. Equivalent inductance
\[L=\frac{4m_e}{3\pi Rne^2}=2.57\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm H.\]
2.7a. Plasmon angular frequency
\[\omega_p=(LC)^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{3\epsilon_0m_e}}.\]
2.7b. Resonance values
\(\omega_p=7.88\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), \(\lambda_p=2\pi c/\omega_p=239\,\mathrm{nm}\).
2.8a. Collision heating
\[P_{heat}=\frac{m_enV}{2\tau}\langle v^2\rangle,\qquad\langle I^2\rangle=(en\pi R^2)^2\langle v^2\rangle.\] The factor one half in the source's collision model comes from kinetic energy, not from averaging the sinusoid a second time.
2.8b. Heating resistance
\[R_{heat}=P_{heat}/\langle I^2\rangle=\frac{2m_e}{3\pi ne^2R\tau}=2.46\,\Omega.\]
2.9. Scattering resistance
Use \(\langle v^2\rangle=\omega_p^2x_0^2/2\) and \(Q=-4\pi enR^3/3\): \[R_{scat}=\frac{8\omega_p^2R^2}{27\pi\epsilon_0c^3}=2.45\,\Omega.\]
2.10a. Resonant absorbed and scattered power
At resonance the reactances cancel. With \(R_t=R_{heat}+R_{scat}\), \[\langle I^2\rangle=\frac{8R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2},\quad P_{heat}=\frac{8R_{heat}R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2},\quad P_{scat}=\frac{8R_{scat}R^2E_0^2}{9R_t^2}.\]
2.10b. Illumination values
\(E_0=\sqrt{2S/(\epsilon_0c)}=27.4\,\mathrm{kV/m}\), \(P_{heat}=6.82\,\mathrm{nW}\), and \(P_{scat}=6.81\,\mathrm{nW}\).
2.11a. Steam mass rate
There are \(n_{np}h^2a=7.3\times10^{11}\) particles, giving \(P_{st}=4.98\,\mathrm{kW}\). Specific steam-production energy is \(c_w(100-20)+L_w=2.59\times10^6\,\mathrm{J/kg}\). The source rounds this to \(2.62\times10^6\) and reports \(\dot m=1.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/s}\). Direct use of the supplied constants gives \(1.92\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/s}\), also accepted.
2.11b. Steam efficiency
The incident power is \(h^2S=10.0\,\mathrm{kW}\). Hence \(\eta=4.98/10.0=0.498\).

The historical data and idealizations below are those of the 2013 problem.

statement.text:
The Greenlandic Ice Sheet
Model Greenland as a rectangular island of width \(2L\), length \(5L\), with a flat bed at sea level. Ice height H(x) is independent of y, symmetric about the divide x=0, and vanishes at x=±L. Use \(\rho_i=917\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\rho_w=998\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(g=9.82\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), basal friction stress \(S_b=100\,\mathrm{kPa}\). Neglect atmospheric pressure. The integral \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u}\,du=2/3\) may be used. In the dynamical model, incompressible ice flows in the xz plane. Central snowfall adds ice thickness c per year, balanced by melting at the coasts. Near the divide take H≈Hm constant, vx independent of z, vz independent of x and vz=0 at the bed. The historical data and idealizations below are those of the 2013 problem.

3.1. Hydrostatic pressure
Find p(x,z) at height z above the bed.
3.2a. Slab force balance
For x>0, balance horizontal pressure force on a slab of base ΔxΔy against \(S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Write \(S_b=kH\,dH/dx\) and determine k.
3.2b. Ice height profile
Find H(x) and the maximum height Hm. Show the scaling with L.
3.2c. Volume scaling exponent
The island area is A=10L². Find γ in \(V_{ice}\propto A^\gamma\), and derive the volume coefficient.
3.3. Horizontal ice velocity
Use mass conservation in the central region to find vx(x).
3.4. Vertical ice velocity
Using \(\partial_xv_x+\partial_zv_z=0\), find vz(z).
3.5. Particle trajectory
A particle starts at \((x_i,H_m)\). Find its path z(x) in the central approximation.
3.6. Age at the divide
Find the age τ(z) of ice at height z above ground at x=0.
3.7a. Accumulation rates
A 3060 m core has the end of the ice age at depth 1492 m, 11,700 years ago. The ice age began 120,000 years ago at depth 3040 m. Assume Hm=3060 m throughout and constant rates c_ig and c_ia in each period. Find both in m/year.
3.7b. Temperature transition

The supplied graphs relate \(\delta^{18}O=1000(R_{ice}/R_{ref}-1)\) per mille to temperature, with R=[18O]/[16O] and an equatorial-ocean reference. Use the core and calibration plots to estimate the temperature change at the ice-age/interglacial transition.
3.8. Uniform sea level rise
Use Greenland area \(A_G=1.71\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), ocean area \(A_O=3.61\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) and the height profile to find the mean rise after all ice melts.
3.9. Local gravitational tide
Model Greenland ice as a point mass at Earth's surface. Copenhagen is 3500 km along the surface from it. With a global ocean, no rotation, \(M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(R_E=6.38\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), find the sea-level difference between Copenhagen and the point antipodal to Greenland. Work to first order in sea height.

children.text: Integrating \(\partial p/\partial z=-\rho_i g\) with zero surface pressure gives \(p=\rho_i g[H(x)-z]\).

The integrated pressure force per transverse length is \(\rho_i gH^2/2\). Its decrease across the slab gives \(-\rho_i gH H^{\prime}\Delta x\Delta y=S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Thus \(k=-\rho_i g\), including the sign on the positive-x side.
Integrate \(H H^{\prime}=-S_b/(\rho_i g)\) from the coast: \[H(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2S_b}{\rho_i g}(L-|x|)},\qquad H_m=\sqrt{\frac{2S_bL}{\rho_i g}}\propto L^{1/2}.\]
\(V_{ice}=5L\int_{-L}^{L}H(x)dx=(20/3)H_mL^2=(2/3)AH_m\). Since Hm∝L^(1/2), volume scales as L^(5/2) and \(\gamma=5/4\).
Snowfall on a strip from 0 to x supplies volume cx per unit transverse length per year. Outward transport is Hm vx. Thus \(v_x=cx/H_m\).
Dividing the velocities gives \(dz/dx=-z/x\), hence \(xz=H_mx_i\) and \(z=H_mx_i/x\).

For the interglacial period, \(c_{ig}=3060\ln(3060/1568)/11700=0.175\,\mathrm{m/year}\). At the period boundary a particle currently at z=20 m was at \(20(3060/1568)\) m. Equivalently \(c_{ia}=3060\ln(1568/20)/(120000-11700)=0.123\,\mathrm{m/year}\). The two age intervals must be treated separately.
The isotope signal rises from approximately −43.5 to −34.5 per mille. The calibration maps these to roughly −40°C and −28°C, giving a warming of about 12 K. Graph-reading uncertainty is expected.

solution.text:
The Greenlandic Ice Sheet
3.1. Hydrostatic pressure
Integrating \(\partial p/\partial z=-\rho_i g\) with zero surface pressure gives \(p=\rho_i g[H(x)-z]\).
3.2a. Slab force balance
The integrated pressure force per transverse length is \(\rho_i gH^2/2\). Its decrease across the slab gives \(-\rho_i gH H^{\prime}\Delta x\Delta y=S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Thus \(k=-\rho_i g\), including the sign on the positive-x side.
3.2b. Ice height profile
Integrate \(H H^{\prime}=-S_b/(\rho_i g)\) from the coast: \[H(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2S_b}{\rho_i g}(L-|x|)},\qquad H_m=\sqrt{\frac{2S_bL}{\rho_i g}}\propto L^{1/2}.\]
3.2c. Volume scaling exponent
\(V_{ice}=5L\int_{-L}^{L}H(x)dx=(20/3)H_mL^2=(2/3)AH_m\). Since Hm∝L^(1/2), volume scales as L^(5/2) and \(\gamma=5/4\).
3.3. Horizontal ice velocity
Snowfall on a strip from 0 to x supplies volume cx per unit transverse length per year. Outward transport is Hm vx. Thus \(v_x=cx/H_m\).
3.4. Vertical ice velocity
\(dv_z/dz=-c/H_m\), and the bed condition fixes \(v_z=-cz/H_m\).
3.5. Particle trajectory
Dividing the velocities gives \(dz/dx=-z/x\), hence \(xz=H_mx_i\) and \(z=H_mx_i/x\).
3.6. Age at the divide
Integrate \(dz/dt=-cz/H_m\) from Hm to z: \[\tau(z)=\frac{H_m}{c}\ln\frac{H_m}{z}.\]
3.7a. Accumulation rates
For the interglacial period, \(c_{ig}=3060\ln(3060/1568)/11700=0.175\,\mathrm{m/year}\). At the period boundary a particle currently at z=20 m was at \(20(3060/1568)\) m. Equivalently \(c_{ia}=3060\ln(1568/20)/(120000-11700)=0.123\,\mathrm{m/year}\). The two age intervals must be treated separately.
3.7b. Temperature transition
The isotope signal rises from approximately −43.5 to −34.5 per mille. The calibration maps these to roughly −40°C and −28°C, giving a warming of about 12 K. Graph-reading uncertainty is expected.
3.8. Uniform sea level rise
\(L=\sqrt{A_G/10}=4.14\times10^5\,\mathrm m\), \(H_m\simeq3030\,\mathrm m\), \(V_{ice}=(2/3)A_GH_m=3.45\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Meltwater volume is multiplied by \(\rho_i/\rho_w\). The rise is \(h=(\rho_i/\rho_w)V_{ice}/A_O=8.79\,\mathrm m\).
3.9. Local gravitational tide
Let \(M_i=\rho_iV_{ice}\simeq3.17\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}\). At angular distance θ, separation from the ice is \(r=2R_E\sin(\theta/2)\). Constant potential gives \(gh-GM_i/r=\text{constant}\). Thus \[h_{CPH}-h_{opp}=\frac{M_iR_E}{2M_E}\left[\csc\left(\frac{3500\times10^3}{2R_E}\right)-1\right]\simeq4.56\,\mathrm m.\] The ocean is locally higher near the ice. Its loss on melting partially offsets the uniform rise.

solution.text:
Part A. Single pipe
A.i
Write the force balance for the droplet. Since \(d\ll r\), the force \(\pi\Delta p\,d^2/4\) from the excess pressure inside the tube is negligible. Gravity, \(4\pi r_{\max}^3\rho g/3\), is balanced by the capillary force. Just before separation, the water forms a neck with a vertical tangent near the nozzle. The capillary force across the neck's horizontal cross-section is \(\pi\sigma d\), so
\[r_{\max}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{3\sigma d}{4\rho g}}.\]
A.ii
Since \(d\ll r\), the tube's effect on the droplet capacitance is negligible. Its potential is both \(\varphi\) and \(Q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)\), hence
\[Q=4\pi\epsilon_0\varphi r.\]
A.iii
The excess pressure is the sum of capillary pressure \(2\sigma/r\), which increases the pressure, and electrostatic pressure \(\epsilon_0 E^2/2=\epsilon_0\varphi^2/(2r^2)\), which decreases it. The excess pressure changes sign when
\[\frac{\epsilon_0\varphi_{\max}^2}{2r^2}=\frac{2\sigma}{r},\qquad\varphi_{\max}=2\sqrt{\frac{\sigma r}{\epsilon_0}}.\]
The source derives the electrostatic pressure as follows. A surface charge of density \(\sigma\) and area \(S\) feels \(F=\sigma S\bar E\), where \(\bar E\) excludes that surface element's own field. The force is perpendicular to the surface, so \(F/S\) is a pressure. Gauss's law gives the field jump \(\Delta E=\sigma/\epsilon_0\). The field inside the conductor vanishes: \(\bar E-\Delta E/2=0\). Outside, \(E=\bar E+\Delta E/2\). Thus \(\bar E=E/2=\Delta E/2\), giving the stated pressure. Here the source reuses the symbol sigma for surface charge density.
Alternatively, consider a virtual displacement of a capacitor's surface and compare pressure work \(p\Delta V\) with the change in electric-field energy \(\epsilon_0E^2\Delta V/2\).
A third derivation requires the mechanical work \(dA\), also denoted \(dW\) in the source, for an infinitesimal droplet inflation to vanish. Energy conservation gives
\[dW+dW_{\mathrm{el}}=\sigma\,d(4\pi r^2)+\frac12\varphi_{\max}^2\,dC_d,\qquad C_d=4\pi\epsilon_0r,\]
\[dW_{\mathrm{el}}=\varphi_{\max}\,dq=4\pi\epsilon_0\varphi_{\max}^2\,dr.\]
Setting \(dW=0\) recovers the same critical potential.
Part B. Two pipes
B.i
Relative to the surrounding electrode, whose potential is \(-U/2\) with \(U=q/C\), the earthed droplet is at \(U/2\). Either sign convention is acceptable if used consistently. The long cylindrical electrode effectively shields the potential of the external surroundings. Using Part A
\[Q=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0qr_{\max}}C.\]
B.ii
The droplet's charge has the same sign as the capacitor's opposite plate, connected to the farther electrode. Falling into the bowl therefore increases the capacitor charge by \(Q\)
\[dq=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}\,dN=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0r_{\max}n}{C}q\,dt,\qquad dN=n\,dt.\]
Solving this linear differential equation
\[q=q_0e^{\gamma t},\qquad\gamma=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0r_{\max}n}{C}=\frac{\pi\epsilon_0n}{C}\sqrt[3]{\frac{6\sigma d}{\rho g}}.\]
B.iii
The droplets reach the bowls if their mechanical energy \(mgH\), with \(m\) the droplet mass, overcomes the electric repulsion. The initial total potential is zero: the electrode contributes \(U/2\), while the droplet itself contributes \(-U/2\). Its motion is not affected by its own field, so the external potential changes from \(U/2\) to \(-U/2\). The change in electrostatic energy obeys \(UQ\le mgH\), with \(Q=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}\). Therefore
\[U_{\max}=\frac{mgH}{2\pi\epsilon_0U_{\max}r_{\max}},\]
\[U_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{H\sigma d}{2\epsilon_0r_{\max}}}=\sqrt[6]{\frac{H^3g\sigma^2\rho d^2}{6\epsilon_0^3}}.\]

statement.text:
A Three-body Problem and LISA
Two gravitating masses M and m move in coplanar circular orbits of radii R and r about their common centre O, with \(MR=mr\). A third infinitesimal mass \(\mu\) is placed in the same plane and rotates so its position relative to M and m is stationary. It is not collinear with them and does not perturb their motion. G denotes the gravitational constant.

1.1. Binary angular velocity
Find the angular velocity of the line joining M and m.
1.2.1. Distance to M
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to M in terms of R and r.
1.2.2. Distance to m
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to m.
1.2.3. Distance to O
Find distance \(\rho\) from \(\mu\) to the common centre.
1.3. Restricted radial oscillation
Now take M = m. Give the infinitesimal mass a small radial perturbation along its line from O. Under the source's assumed conservation of its angular momentum, find the radial oscillation frequency in terms of \(\omega_0\).
1.4. LISA relative speed

The source describes three spacecraft at the corners of an equilateral triangle of arm length \(L=5.0\) million kilometres. Their plane rolls once per year as they orbit the Sun, trailing Earth by \(20^\circ\). Find the relative speed of two spacecraft in their common plane, using 365 days per year.

children.text: Force balance for either mass, together with the centre-of-mass relation, gives \[\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{(R+r)^3}}.\]

In the co-rotating configuration, the acceleration is \(-\omega_0^2\mathbf r_\mu\). Equate this to the vector sum of the two gravitational accelerations. Comparing coefficients of the two nonparallel relative-position vectors using \(M\mathbf r_M+m\mathbf r_m=0\) gives equal inverse-cube distances to the two masses, each equal to \((R+r)^{-3}\). Thus the triangle is equilateral and both distances are R + r.
The same equilateral configuration gives R + r. There are two mirror positions, the usual triangular Lagrange points.
Use the cosine rule in a triangle with sides r and R+r and included angle \(60^\circ\): \[\rho=\sqrt{R^2+Rr+r^2}.\]

Here R = r and \(\rho_0=\sqrt3R\). In the stipulated radial model the attraction is \(-2GM\rho/(R^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}\). Conserved angular momentum gives centrifugal term \(\rho_0^4\omega_0^2/\rho^3\). Linearizing their sum around \(\rho_0\) yields \[\ddot\xi=-\frac74\omega_0^2\xi,\qquad\omega_{rad}=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}\omega_0.\] This is the restricted radial calculation requested. It does not establish stability of the unrestricted equal-mass triangular three-body configuration.

For rigid rotation in the triangle plane, the relative-position vector has fixed length L and rotates with \(\omega=2\pi/T\). Hence \[v_{rel}=\omega L=\frac{2\pi(5.0\times10^9\,\mathrm m)}{365\times86400\,\mathrm s}=996\,\mathrm{m/s}.\] The common heliocentric translation cancels. These are the mission parameters supplied in the historical problem, not a statement of the current mission design.

At every surface point the two potentials cancel if \(q\to q\), \(q^{\prime}=-qR/d\), and \(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\). These follow either from the two axial points or from the general surface-distance ratio.
The image gives an attractive force towards the centre with magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)^2}.\]
The real-charge field points towards A for positive \(q\), while the image field opposes it. Thus \[E_A=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{r^2}-\frac{R/d}{(r-d+R^2/d)^2}\right].\]

The total charge seen at leading order is \(q+q^{\prime}=q(1-R/d)\). Therefore \[E_A\simeq\frac{q(1-R/d)}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}.\] Expanding one order further gives a correction \(-2qR(1-R^2/d^2)/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\).
Only in the limit \(d\to R^+\), when the real and image charges coincide at the surface with opposite signs.

The charge-centre distance is \(s=\sqrt{l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha}\). The force points towards the sphere centre and has magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rs}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2-R^2)^2}.\] Draw this central force at the bob.
Geometry gives \(\sin\gamma=l\sin\alpha/s\). The restoring-component magnitude is \[F_\perp=\frac{q^2Rl\sin\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0(l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha-R^2)^2}.\]

This is \(q\) times their potential at its position, without a half factor: \[U_1=-\frac{q^2R}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
The sphere surface has zero total potential, so its induced-charge potential is minus that of \(q\). The pair-energy half factor gives \(U_2=-U_1/2\), or \[U_2=\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]

solution.text:
Image of a charge in a metallic object
1a. Sphere potential
Grounding fixes \(V=0\).
1b.q. Image charge
At every surface point the two potentials cancel if \(q\to q\), \(q^{\prime}=-qR/d\), and \(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\). These follow either from the two axial points or from the general surface-distance ratio.
1b.d. Image position
\(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\), lying inside the sphere.
1c. Force magnitude
The image gives an attractive force towards the centre with magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)^2}.\]
2a. Field behind the sphere
The real-charge field points towards A for positive \(q\), while the image field opposes it. Thus \[E_A=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{r^2}-\frac{R/d}{(r-d+R^2/d)^2}\right].\]
2b. Far field
The total charge seen at leading order is \(q+q^{\prime}=q(1-R/d)\). Therefore \[E_A\simeq\frac{q(1-R/d)}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}.\] Expanding one order further gives a correction \(-2qR(1-R^2/d^2)/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\).
2c. Complete screening
Only in the limit \(d\to R^+\), when the real and image charges coincide at the surface with opposite signs.
3a. Pendulum force
The charge-centre distance is \(s=\sqrt{l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha}\). The force points towards the sphere centre and has magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rs}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2-R^2)^2}.\] Draw this central force at the bob.
3b. Tangential force magnitude
Geometry gives \(\sin\gamma=l\sin\alpha/s\). The restoring-component magnitude is \[F_\perp=\frac{q^2Rl\sin\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0(l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha-R^2)^2}.\]
3c. Small-oscillation angular frequency
Linearize \(mL\ddot\alpha=-F_\perp\). The result is \[\omega=\frac{|q|}{(l-L)^2-R^2}\sqrt{\frac{Rl}{4\pi\epsilon_0mL}}.\] The ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega/(2\pi)\).
4a. External-induced interaction energy
This is \(q\) times their potential at its position, without a half factor: \[U_1=-\frac{q^2R}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
4b. Induced-charge mutual energy
The sphere surface has zero total potential, so its induced-charge potential is minus that of \(q\). The pair-energy half factor gives \(U_2=-U_1/2\), or \[U_2=\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
4c. Total interaction energy
\[U=U_1+U_2=-\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\] An independent derivation integrates the attractive force from infinity: \(U=-\int_d^\infty q^2Rx/[4\pi\epsilon_0(x^2-R^2)^2],dx\). Use \(\int_d^\infty x(x^2-R^2)^{-2}dx=1/[2(d^2-R^2)]\). The self-energy of the external point charge is excluded.

solution.text:
2. Chimney physics
1.a. Draft and minimum height
Let \(p_0\) be ambient pressure at the furnace level. Hydrostatics gives \(p_\mathrm{Air}(z)=p_0-\rho_a gz\). At minimum height smoke exit pressure equals the outside pressure. Bernoulli between the nearly stationary furnace gas and the exit gives
\[\frac12\rho_s v^2+\rho_sgh+p_0-\rho_agh=p_0,\qquad v^2=2gh\left(\frac{\rho_a}{\rho_s}-1\right).\]
Equal-pressure ideal-gas densities satisfy \(\rho_a/\rho_s=T_\mathrm{Smoke}/T_\mathrm{Air}\). To carry the produced gas, \(v\ge B/A\). Thus
\[h_{\min}=\frac{B^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2gA^2\Delta T}.\]
1.b. Different climates
Absolute temperatures must be in kelvin. Keeping \(B,A\) and furnace temperature fixed, \(h\propto T_\mathrm{Air}/(T_\mathrm{Smoke}-T_\mathrm{Air})\). Hence
\[h_\mathrm{warm}=100\,\mathrm m\frac{303.15/(673.15-303.15)}{243.15/(673.15-243.15)}\simeq145\,\mathrm m.\]
1.c and 1.d. Flow and pressure profiles
Continuity with fixed density and cross-section makes \(v=B/A\) constant throughout the chimney. In the idealized model it jumps from nearly zero in the furnace to this value at entry. Smoke pressure drops at entry by \(\rho_s v^2/2=(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh\), then falls linearly:
\[p_\mathrm{Smoke}(z)=p_0-(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh-\rho_sgz,\qquad0<z<h.\]
At the top it matches ambient pressure. Draw the entry discontinuity and the different slopes rather than a continuously accelerating constant-area flow.
2. Solar-chimney efficiency
Write mass flow as \(\dot M=A\rho_h v\). The solar heating power is \(GS=\dot M c\Delta T\), while kinetic power is \(\dot Mv^2/2=\dot Mgh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}\). Their ratio is
\[\eta=\frac{gh}{cT_\mathrm{Air}}.\]
The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope g/(c T_Air), within the assumptions of the chimney model. It should not be extrapolated to efficiencies above one.
3. Prototype numbers
\[\eta=\frac{9.81\times195}{1012\times295}\simeq0.0064=0.64\%,\qquad P=GS\eta\simeq45\,\mathrm{kW}.\]
A typical sunny-day duration is not specified in the statement. The official estimate assumes eight hours, giving \(E\simeq360\,\mathrm{kWh}\). For any chosen duration \(t_d\), use \(E=GS\eta t_d\). The numeric field states the eight-hour convention.
4. Temperature rise and mass flow
Eliminate mass flow between \(\dot M=A\rho_h\sqrt{2gh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}}\) and \(\dot M=GS/(c\Delta T)\). This gives
\[\Delta T=\left[\frac{G^2S^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2ghA^2c^2\rho_h^2}\right]^{1/3}\simeq9.1\,\mathrm K,\qquad \dot M=\frac{GS}{c\Delta T}\simeq760\,\mathrm{kg/s}.\]
These are ideal available kinetic-energy figures, not an additional claim about actual electrical output or turbine efficiency. The original solution cites W. W. Christie's Chimney design and theory (1902), and Schlaich, Bergermann, Schiel and Weinrebe, Design of Commercial Solar Updraft Tower Systems (2005). Its original references and equations remain in the linked PDF.

children.text: CHERENKOV LIGHT AND RING IMAGING COUNTER

Every emitted sphere has radius \((c/n)(t_1-t)\), proportional to its centre's distance \(v(t_1-t)\) behind B. The common tangent envelope is a cone with vertex B. In the selected plane its two sides are straight tangent lines extending backwards from B. Draw the endpoint cap if restricting emission to the finite segment AB.
The right triangle between B, a wave centre and its tangent point gives \(\sin\varphi=1/(\beta n)\). Thus \(\varphi=\arcsin[1/(\beta n)]=\pi/2-\theta\).

Parallel Cherenkov rays at a given azimuth focus to one point of the focal plane. Their fixed angle theta around IS generates a circle. The line through C parallel to IS intersects that plane at O. If F is the axial focus, \(FO=f\alpha\) to first order, and ring radius \(r=f\theta\). The ray diagram must show these constructions.

With \(K=Mc/p\), \(\beta=1/\sqrt{1+K^2}\). The exact threshold is \(P_{min}=(\sqrt{1+K^2}-1)/a\), approximately \(K^2/(2a)\). This gives about 16 atm for protons, 4.6 atm for kaons and 0.36 atm for pions. Radiation requires pressure above the threshold.
For small theta and small \(n-1\), \(\theta^2\simeq2aP-K^2\). Set \(\theta_\pi=2\theta_K\), giving \[aP_{1/2}=\frac{4K_K^2-K_\pi^2}{6}.\] The pressure is about 6.0 atm.

The angles are \(\theta_K\simeq0.0277\,\mathrm{rad}=1.6^\circ\), \(\theta_\pi\simeq0.0554\,\mathrm{rad}=3.2^\circ\). Protons do not radiate because this pressure is below their approximately 16 atm threshold.

Differentiate \(\cos\theta=1/(n\beta)\) at fixed n. To leading order, \[\frac{d\theta}{dp}\simeq\frac{K^2}{\theta p}.\] The values are about \(0.51^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\) for kaons and \(0.020^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\) for pions.
The angular separation is about \(1.6^\circ\) and the sum-width coefficient is \(0.53^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\). Therefore \(\Delta p<1.6/(10\times0.53)\simeq0.30\,\mathrm{GeV}/c\).
At threshold \(\beta=1/n\). Relativistic kinetic energy gives \[T_{min}=Mc^2\left[\frac1{\sqrt{1-1/n^2}}-1\right]\simeq0.517Mc^2.\]
Thresholds are \(1.96\,\mathrm{GeV}\) for alpha particles and \(0.264\,\mathrm{MeV}\) for electrons. Only electrons can exceed their threshold at the given radioactive energies.

\(\delta n=0.02(n-1)\), and differentiating the Cherenkov relation gives \(\delta\theta=\delta n/(n\tan\theta)\simeq\delta n/\theta\). With \(n=1.00162\), \(\theta\simeq0.055\,\mathrm{rad}\), this is \(0.033^\circ\).

The full visible angular spread from 6.1 corresponds to an approximate dispersion half width \(0.017^\circ\). Momentum spread contributes \(0.020\times0.3=0.006^\circ\). Dispersion is about three times larger. The source treats the spectral half-span as a half-width estimate, not a specified exact spectral line shape.
Long-wavelength red light has lower n and smaller theta. Short-wavelength blue/violet light has larger theta. The ordering is red, then a white overlap region, then blue/violet at the outside.

Its unstretched separation is d and \(C_0=\epsilon_0A/d\). The isolated plates carry fixed charges \(\pm Q\). children.text: Only the other plate's field acts on a given plate. Its field is \(Q/(2\epsilon_0A)\), so \(F_E=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0A)\), independent of gap.
Balance spring and electrical forces: \(kx=F_E\), hence \(x=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0Ak)\).
The final gap is \(d-x\). Thus \[V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\] This requires the gap to remain positive.
The gaps are \(d-x\) and \(d+x\). Therefore \(Q_+=\epsilon_0AV/(d-x)\), \(Q_-=\epsilon_0AV/(d+x)\). The central faces carry opposite signs.
The two attractions oppose each other: \[F_E=\frac{\epsilon_0AV^2}{2}\left[\frac1{(d-x)^2}-\frac1{(d+x)^2}\right].\]
Binomial expansion gives \(F_E\simeq2\epsilon_0AV^2x/d^3\). The electrical force is destabilizing.
Both springs supply restoring force, totalling \(-2kx\). Hence \[k_{eff}=2k-2\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3.\] Stable centring requires this coefficient to be positive.

In the car frame, inertial force balances the restoring force: \(Ma=k_{eff}x\). Thus \[a=\frac{2x}{M}(k-\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3).\] The signed acceleration in the +x direction is minus this value. This states explicitly the coordinate convention behind the sign in the source.

The isolated central conductor and its connected capacitor plate have zero net charge. With \(C_+=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), \(C_-=\epsilon_0A/(d+x)\), charge balance gives \(C_+(V_S-V)+C_-(V_S+V)+C_SV_S=0\). Therefore \[V_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{C_S(d^2-x^2)+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]
The ratio is \(\epsilon_0AV^2/(kd^3)=7.6\times10^{-9}\). Thus electric forces can be neglected in the transient mechanical motion. The same smallness holds in state beta.
In the accelerating frame the displacement obeys \(M\ddot x+2kx=Ma\), starting with zero displacement and relative velocity. Thus \[x(t)=\frac{Ma}{2k}[1-\cos(\sqrt{2k/M}\,t)],\qquad x_{max}=Ma/k.\]
At the first displacement maximum, \(x_{max}=Mg/k\). Combine with 3.2 to get \[C_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0A}{d}\left(\frac{VMg}{kV_Sd}-1\right)=8.0\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm F.\]

For an estimated gap \(l\), the initial relative velocity is zero and closing distance is \(gt_1^2/2\). Thus \(t_1=\sqrt{2l/g}\). A plausible \(l=0.4\) to \(1\,\mathrm m\) gives \(t_1\simeq0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\). This estimate depends on the chosen gap and is self-review.

The threshold is reached at the first displacement maximum, half a mechanical period: \[t_2=\pi\sqrt{M/(2k)}=0.013\,\mathrm s.\] It is much shorter than the estimated \(0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\), so this idealized model triggers in time. It omits the real inflation time.

Capacitive accelerometer

Only the other plate's field acts on a given plate. Its field is \(Q/(2\epsilon_0A)\), so \(F_E=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0A)\), independent of gap.
1.2. Equilibrium displacement

The final gap is \(d-x\). Thus \[V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\] This requires the gap to remain positive.
1.4. Capacitance ratio
\(C=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), so \[C/C_0=\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right)^{-1}.\]
1.5. Stored energy
\(U=Q^2(d-x)/(2\epsilon_0A)+kx^2/2\). Substitution gives \[U=\frac{Q^2d}{2\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{4\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\]

\[V_S\simeq\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{d^2C_S+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]

children.text: Tidal torques transfer Earth's spin angular momentum to the Moon's orbit. Treat the Moon as a point mass on a circular orbit about Earth's centre. The spin and orbital axes are parallel. Ignore the Sun and Earth's motion about the common centre of mass. All moments and torques refer to Earth's axis. Suffix 1 denotes present quantities and suffix 2 denotes the final synchronous state. Use \(M_E=6.0\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(M_M=7.3\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(D_1=3.8\times10^8\,\mathrm m\), \(\omega_{E1}=7.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(\omega_{M1}=2.7\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and \(G=6.7\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}\). Model Earth by density \(\rho_i=1.3\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) for \(r<r_i=3.5\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), and \(\rho_o=4.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) up to \(r_o=6.4\times10^6\,\mathrm m\). Give numerical results to two significant figures.
Express \(L_2\), when both angular frequencies equal \(\omega_2\).
Write the conservation equation, neglecting the final Earth spin.
Find \(D_2\) using \(L_1,M_E,M_M,G\). Neglect final Earth spin throughout section 2.
Give \(D_2\) in metres and in units of \(D_1\).
Give \(\omega_2\) and the final day in present days.
Find final Earth spin divided by final Moon orbital angular momentum.

statement.text:
Evolution of Earth-Moon system
Tidal torques transfer Earth's spin angular momentum to the Moon's orbit. Treat the Moon as a point mass on a circular orbit about Earth's centre. The spin and orbital axes are parallel. Ignore the Sun and Earth's motion about the common centre of mass. All moments and torques refer to Earth's axis. Suffix 1 denotes present quantities and suffix 2 denotes the final synchronous state. Use \(M_E=6.0\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(M_M=7.3\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(D_1=3.8\times10^8\,\mathrm m\), \(\omega_{E1}=7.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(\omega_{M1}=2.7\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and \(G=6.7\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}\). Model Earth by density \(\rho_i=1.3\times10^4\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) for \(r<r_i=3.5\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), and \(\rho_o=4.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) up to \(r_o=6.4\times10^6\,\mathrm m\). Give numerical results to two significant figures.
1a. Present angular momentum
Express \(L_1\) using \(I_E,I_{M1},\omega_{E1},\omega_{M1}\).
1b. Synchronous angular momentum
Express \(L_2\), when both angular frequencies equal \(\omega_2\).
1c. Angular momentum conservation
Write the conservation equation, neglecting the final Earth spin.
2a. Final circular orbit
Write the gravitational circular-orbit equation.
2b. Final separation
Find \(D_2\) using \(L_1,M_E,M_M,G\). Neglect final Earth spin throughout section 2.
2c. Final angular frequency
Find \(\omega_2\) using the same parameters.
2d. Layered Earth inertia
Derive \(I_E\) for the two-density model.
2e. Earth inertia value
Evaluate the moment of inertia.
2f. Total angular momentum value
Evaluate the present angular momentum.
2g. Final separation value
Give \(D_2\) in metres and in units of \(D_1\).
2h. Final day
Give \(\omega_2\) and the final day in present days.
2i. Neglected spin ratio
Find final Earth spin divided by final Moon orbital angular momentum.
3a. Near-bulge force

Model the tidal bulges as two point masses \(m=3.6\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{kg}\) on opposite points of Earth's surface. Their line leads the Earth-Moon line by \(\theta=3^\circ\). Find the force magnitude from the nearer bulge.
3b. Far-bulge force
Find the force from the farther bulge.
3c. Near-bulge torque
Find the magnitude of the nearer-bulge torque.
3d. Far-bulge torque
Find the magnitude of the farther-bulge torque.
3e. Net tidal torque
Find the leading nonzero net torque for \(r_o\ll D_1\). You may use \((1+u)^a\simeq1+au\).
3f. Torque value
Evaluate the torque.
3g. Annual recession
Find the increase in separation per year, using \(1\,\mathrm{yr}=3.1\times10^7\,\mathrm s\).
3h. Spin slowdown and day length
Find the annual change in spin frequency and in the day length.
4a. System energy
Find total rotational plus gravitational energy in terms of the present parameters.
4b. Annual mechanical energy change
Express \(\Delta E\) in terms of \(\Delta D_1,\Delta\omega_{E1}\), then evaluate it for one year.
4c. Mass of tidal water
Assume all Earth is covered by a layer of water of thickness \(h=0.5\,\mathrm m\), density \(10^3\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\). Find its mass.
4d. Annual tidal heat
The layer rises by \(0.5\,\mathrm m\) twice daily, with 10 percent of gravitational energy dissipated when it falls. Use \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\) and 365 days per year. Find annual heat and compare with 4b.

children.text: Add a uniform outer-density sphere and an inner sphere of excess density: \[I_E=\frac{8\pi}{15}[\rho_or_o^5+(\rho_i-\rho_o)r_i^5].\]
The ratio is \(I_E/(M_MD_2^2)\simeq1/260\), validating the approximation.
The law of cosines gives \(s_-^2=D_1^2+r_o^2-2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), hence \(F_c=GmM_M/s_-^2\).
The lever arm supplies another factor \(D_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-\). Thus \(\tau_c=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-^3\).
The leading terms cancel in \(\tau_c-\tau_f\). The next terms give \[\tau=6GmM_Mr_o^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/D_1^3.\]
Differentiate \(L_M=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED}\). Then \(\Delta D=2\tau\Delta t\sqrt{D_1/(GM_E)}/M_M=0.034\,\mathrm m\) per year.

Angular momentum conservation gives \(\Delta\omega_{E1}=-\tau\Delta t/I_E=-1.6\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Since \(P_E=2\pi/\omega_E\), \(\Delta P_E/P_E=-\Delta\omega_E/\omega_E\), giving \(\Delta P_E=1.9\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\) per year.
The circular orbit has energy \(-GM_EM_M/(2D_1)\). Thus \[E=\frac12I_E\omega_{E1}^2-\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1}.\]
The heat is \(Q=0.1M_{\rm water}g(0.5\,\mathrm m)\times2\times365=9.3\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J\). It is comparable to the mechanical energy loss.

solution.text:
Evolution of Earth-Moon system
1a. Present angular momentum
The two parallel contributions add: \(L_1=I_E\omega_{E1}+I_{M1}\omega_{M1}\).
1b. Synchronous angular momentum
\(L_2=(I_E+I_{M2})\omega_2\).
1c. Angular momentum conservation
\(I_E\omega_{E1}+I_{M1}\omega_{M1}=I_{M2}\omega_2=L_1\).
2a. Final circular orbit
\(\omega_2^2D_2^3=GM_E\).
2b. Final separation
Since \(L_1=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED_2}\), \[D_2=\frac{L_1^2}{GM_EM_M^2}.\]
2c. Final angular frequency
Combine \(\omega_2=\sqrt{GM_E/D_2^3}\) with part 2b: \(\omega_2=G^2M_E^2M_M^3/L_1^3\).
2d. Layered Earth inertia
Add a uniform outer-density sphere and an inner sphere of excess density: \[I_E=\frac{8\pi}{15}[\rho_or_o^5+(\rho_i-\rho_o)r_i^5].\]
2e. Earth inertia value
\(I_E=8.0\times10^{37}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\).
2f. Total angular momentum value
Use \(I_{M1}=M_MD_1^2\). The result is \(L_1=3.4\times10^{34}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}\).
2g. Final separation value
\(D_2=5.4\times10^8\,\mathrm m=1.4D_1\).
2h. Final day
\(\omega_2=1.6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), corresponding to about 46 present days.
2i. Neglected spin ratio
The ratio is \(I_E/(M_MD_2^2)\simeq1/260\), validating the approximation.
3a. Near-bulge force
The law of cosines gives \(s_-^2=D_1^2+r_o^2-2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), hence \(F_c=GmM_M/s_-^2\).
3b. Far-bulge force
\(s_+^2=D_1^2+r_o^2+2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), so \(F_f=GmM_M/s_+^2\).
3c. Near-bulge torque
The lever arm supplies another factor \(D_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-\). Thus \(\tau_c=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-^3\).
3d. Far-bulge torque
\(\tau_f=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_+^3\), acting opposite to \(\tau_c\).
3e. Net tidal torque
The leading terms cancel in \(\tau_c-\tau_f\). The next terms give \[\tau=6GmM_Mr_o^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/D_1^3.\]
3f. Torque value
\(\tau=4.1\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
3g. Annual recession
Differentiate \(L_M=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED}\). Then \(\Delta D=2\tau\Delta t\sqrt{D_1/(GM_E)}/M_M=0.034\,\mathrm m\) per year.
3h. Spin slowdown and day length
Angular momentum conservation gives \(\Delta\omega_{E1}=-\tau\Delta t/I_E=-1.6\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Since \(P_E=2\pi/\omega_E\), \(\Delta P_E/P_E=-\Delta\omega_E/\omega_E\), giving \(\Delta P_E=1.9\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\) per year.
4a. System energy
The circular orbit has energy \(-GM_EM_M/(2D_1)\). Thus \[E=\frac12I_E\omega_{E1}^2-\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1}.\]
4b. Annual mechanical energy change
\[\Delta E=I_E\omega_{E1}\Delta\omega_{E1}+\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1^2}\Delta D_1\simeq-9.0\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J.\]
4c. Mass of tidal water
\(M_{\rm water}=4\pi r_o^2h\rho_{\rm water}=2.6\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{kg}\).
4d. Annual tidal heat
The heat is \(Q=0.1M_{\rm water}g(0.5\,\mathrm m)\times2\times365=9.3\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J\). It is comparable to the mechanical energy loss.
