children.text: Three absolute electrical measurements are considered. Use vacuum permeability \(\mu_0\). In the Kelvin method, a closed \(N\)-turn circular coil of radius \(a\) and resistance \(R\) rotates at angular speed \(\omega\) about its vertical diameter in a horizontal field \(B_0\). Its inductance is negligible. At \(t=0\) its normal points along \(B_0\). A slowly responding magnetic needle at its centre measures the time-averaged field. In the Lorenz method, two conducting discs of radius \(b\) share a shaft rotating at \(\omega\). Each is centred in an \(N\)-turn coil of radius \(a\gg b\), carrying opposite currents \(I\). The coils are far apart. Brushes and a null galvanometer connect the disc rims as shown. Finally, an Ampere balance uses six single-turn coils of radius \(a\), in series. On each side of the balance, a moving coil is midway between two fixed coils at distances \(h\ll a\). Currents give a net upward force on coil 2 and downward force on coil 5. The equal arm lengths are \(d\). A mass \(m\) at horizontal distance \(x\) balances the electromagnetic torque. Ignore interactions between opposite sides and approximate neighbouring wire segments as straight.

statement.text:
Absolute measurements of electrical quantities
Three absolute electrical measurements are considered. Use vacuum permeability \(\mu_0\). In the Kelvin method, a closed \(N\)-turn circular coil of radius \(a\) and resistance \(R\) rotates at angular speed \(\omega\) about its vertical diameter in a horizontal field \(B_0\). Its inductance is negligible. At \(t=0\) its normal points along \(B_0\). A slowly responding magnetic needle at its centre measures the time-averaged field. In the Lorenz method, two conducting discs of radius \(b\) share a shaft rotating at \(\omega\). Each is centred in an \(N\)-turn coil of radius \(a\gg b\), carrying opposite currents \(I\). The coils are far apart. Brushes and a null galvanometer connect the disc rims as shown. Finally, an Ampere balance uses six single-turn coils of radius \(a\), in series. On each side of the balance, a moving coil is midway between two fixed coils at distances \(h\ll a\). Currents give a net upward force on coil 2 and downward force on coil 5. The equal arm lengths are \(d\). A mass \(m\) at horizontal distance \(x\) balances the electromagnetic torque. Ignore interactions between opposite sides and approximate neighbouring wire segments as straight.

1.emf. Induced emf
Find the emf as a function of time.
1.power. Average power
Find the average dissipated power.
2. Kelvin resistance
The needle deflects by a small angle \(\theta\) relative to \(B_0\). Determine \(R\).
3. Two-disc emf

Find the total emf between rims 1 and 4.
4. Lorenz resistance
Find the resistance measured when the galvanometer reads zero.
5. Force between neighbouring coils

Find the force magnitude between coils 1 and 2.
6. Current from balance
Determine the current in terms of the balance parameters.
7. Restoring displacement
The balance has mass \(M\) and its centre of gravity is a distance \(l\) below the pivot, excluding the suspended coils and added mass. Find the largest small upward displacement \(\delta z\) of coil 2, with coil 5 moving down, for which the balance remains restoring. Use \(\delta z\ll h\), small angles, and expand \((1\pm u)^{-1}\simeq1\mp u+u^2\).

children.text: Faraday's law applied to \(N\pi a^2B_0\cos\omega t\) gives \[\mathcal E=N\pi a^2B_0\omega\sin\omega t.\]
With negligible inductance, \(i=\mathcal E/R\), and the mean of \(\sin^2\) is \(1/2\). Thus \(\overline P=(N\pi a^2B_0\omega)^2/(2R)\).

The rotating current produces an average transverse field \(\overline B_y=\mu_0N^2\pi aB_0\omega/(4R)\), and zero mean parallel field. Therefore \[R=\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\tan\theta}\simeq\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\theta}.\]
Each coil produces \(B=\mu_0NI/(2a)\). Radial integration of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) gives \(B\omega b^2/2\) per disc. The two contributions add: \[\mathcal E=\mu_0Nb^2\omega I/(2a).\]
The force per unit length between parallel wires is \(\mu_0I^2/(2\pi h)\). Multiply by \(2\pi a\) to get \(F=\mu_0aI^2/h\).
Four equal force contributions give \(mgx=4Fd\). Thus \[I=\sqrt{\frac{mghx}{4\mu_0ad}}.\]

The gravitational restoring torque is \(Mgl\sin\delta\phi+mgx\cos\delta\phi\). The magnetic torque is \(2\mu_0aI^2d[1/(h-\delta z)+1/(h+\delta z)]\cos\delta\phi\). Use \(\delta\phi\simeq\delta z/d\), cancel the equilibrium torque and keep the leading displacement terms. The restoring condition on the specified side is \[0<\delta z<\frac{Mlh^2}{mxd}.\] The upper bound is a small-displacement estimate and is valid only if it is much smaller than \(h\).

solution.text:
Absolute measurements of electrical quantities
1.emf. Induced emf
Faraday's law applied to \(N\pi a^2B_0\cos\omega t\) gives \[\mathcal E=N\pi a^2B_0\omega\sin\omega t.\]
1.power. Average power
With negligible inductance, \(i=\mathcal E/R\), and the mean of \(\sin^2\) is \(1/2\). Thus \(\overline P=(N\pi a^2B_0\omega)^2/(2R)\).
2. Kelvin resistance
The rotating current produces an average transverse field \(\overline B_y=\mu_0N^2\pi aB_0\omega/(4R)\), and zero mean parallel field. Therefore \[R=\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\tan\theta}\simeq\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\theta}.\]
3. Two-disc emf
Each coil produces \(B=\mu_0NI/(2a)\). Radial integration of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) gives \(B\omega b^2/2\) per disc. The two contributions add: \[\mathcal E=\mu_0Nb^2\omega I/(2a).\]
4. Lorenz resistance
At null, \(IR=\mathcal E\), so \(R=\mu_0Nb^2\omega/(2a)\).
5. Force between neighbouring coils
The force per unit length between parallel wires is \(\mu_0I^2/(2\pi h)\). Multiply by \(2\pi a\) to get \(F=\mu_0aI^2/h\).
6. Current from balance
Four equal force contributions give \(mgx=4Fd\). Thus \[I=\sqrt{\frac{mghx}{4\mu_0ad}}.\]
7. Restoring displacement
The gravitational restoring torque is \(Mgl\sin\delta\phi+mgx\cos\delta\phi\). The magnetic torque is \(2\mu_0aI^2d[1/(h-\delta z)+1/(h+\delta z)]\cos\delta\phi\). Use \(\delta\phi\simeq\delta z/d\), cancel the equilibrium torque and keep the leading displacement terms. The restoring condition on the specified side is \[0<\delta z<\frac{Mlh^2}{mxd}.\] The upper bound is a small-displacement estimate and is valid only if it is much smaller than \(h\).

children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES

A two-level atom of mass m moves along +x with speed v. Ground-state internal energy is zero and excited-state energy is \(\hbar\omega_0\). A laser photon travels along -x with laboratory frequency \(\omega_L\), energy \(\hbar\omega_L\), and momentum \(-\hbar q\), where \(q=\omega_L/c>0\). Assume \(v/c\ll1\) and \(\hbar q/(mv)\ll1\). Keep first-order corrections appropriate to the observable and discard their products. Absorption is followed by spontaneous emission with equal probability along either x direction. Part I uses a resonant incident beam. All atomic energies exclude the constant rest energy.

nodes.alt: Original moving two-level atom, incident counterpropagating photon and the laboratory x axis.

children.text: Write the resonance condition for the counterpropagating photon.
Find the atomic laboratory momentum immediately after absorption.
Find total atomic kinetic plus internal energy after absorption.
If the spontaneous photon is emitted along -x, find its laboratory energy.
Find that emitted photon's signed laboratory momentum.
Find the final atom momentum for this emission direction.
Find its final energy after backward emission.
If emission is along +x, find the photon's laboratory energy.
Find the forward photon momentum, retaining its first-order Doppler correction.
Find the final atomic momentum at the stipulated atomic-momentum order.
Find the final atomic energy consistently with momentum and energy conservation.
Average the two equally likely photon energies.
Find its mean momentum at the retained order relative to the atomic momentum.
Find mean atomic energy after emission.
Find the mean final atomic momentum.
Find the mean atomic energy change in one complete absorption-emission cycle.
Find the mean atomic momentum change in one complete cycle.
Now a resonant laser beam of laboratory frequency \(\omega_L^{\prime}\) travels along +x with the atom. Find mean energy change per cycle.
Find mean momentum change per co-propagating cycle.

nodes.alt: Original two counterpropagating beams and an atomic gas travelling in the positive x direction.

children.text: For N atoms at rest, a beam produces excited population \(N_{exc}=N\Omega_R^2/[(\omega_0-\omega_L)^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2]\), with lifetime \(\Gamma^{-1}\). Thus cycles occur at rate \(\Gamma N_{exc}\). Two opposite beams of the same arbitrary frequency illuminate atoms moving at v. Find their total force, treating the two beam rates independently in this supplied model.
Expand the two-beam force to first order in v.
For \(v>0\), when does the force speed up the atoms?
When is the force zero for the symmetric pair?
For \(v>0\), when does the force slow the atoms?
If the atoms instead move at velocity \(-v\), what detuning gives cooling?
For red detuning and initial velocity \(v_0\), find velocity after time \(\tau\). Use b for the per-atom coefficient defined in 8a.
The atoms initially have thermal equilibrium temperature \(T_0\). Find their temperature after time tau in this deterministic low-velocity model.

children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
The approaching atom sees a blueshift: \(\omega_0=\omega_L(1+v/c)\) to first order.
Energy conservation gives \(E_{at}=mv^2/2+\hbar\omega_L\). Equivalently, \((mv-\hbar q)^2/(2m)+\hbar\omega_0\) reduces to this at the retained order.
Backward Doppler redshift cancels the incident resonance blueshift, leaving \(E_\gamma\simeq\hbar\omega_L\).
The emitted backward momentum restores the incident loss: \(p_{at}=mv\) to retained order.
The atom returns to its internal ground state and original momentum, so \(E_{at}=mv^2/2\).
The emitted light is Doppler blueshifted in addition to the incident resonance shift: \(E_\gamma=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)\).
\(p_{at}=mv-2\hbar q\). The extra photon Doppler term is a product of the two small ratios when compared with mv, so it is discarded here.

Expand \((mv-2\hbar q)^2/(2m)\) to first order in recoil relative to mv: \[E_{at}=\frac12mv^2-2\hbar qv.\] This also follows from 1c minus 3a. The official solution's corresponding expression loses a factor two in the kinetic-energy change. The native key uses the conservation-consistent result.
The residual \(\hbar qv/c\) is a product of the two small ratios relative to mv, so the retained mean emitted momentum is zero.
Average 2d and the corrected 3d: \[\overline E_{at}=mv^2/2-\hbar qv.\] The source's half-sized average loss inherits the factor error in 3d.
Average mv and \(mv-2\hbar q\), yielding \(mv-\hbar q\).

\[\Delta E=-\hbar qv=-\hbar\omega_Lv/c.\] It equals v times mean momentum transfer to the retained order. The official answer has an erroneous factor one half, inconsistent with both conservation and 5b.

The resonance condition is \(\omega_0=\omega_L^{\prime}(1-v/c)\). Reversing the photon momentum reverses the first-order work, giving \(\Delta E=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}v/c\). This corrects the same factor-one-half error in the official answer.

Let \(\delta=\omega_0-\omega_L\), \(q=\omega_L/c\), \(D=\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\). The +x beam is seen at \(\omega_L-qv\), and the -x beam at \(\omega_L+qv\). Thus \[F=N\Gamma\hbar q\Omega_R^2\left[\frac1{(\delta+qv)^2+D}-\frac1{(\delta-qv)^2+D}\right].\]

Writing \(D_0=\delta^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\), the denominator difference is \(-4\delta qv/D_0^2\). Hence \[F=-Nbv,\qquad b=\frac{4\hbar q^2\Omega_R^2\Gamma\delta}{D_0^2}.\] Here b is the damping coefficient per atom, not the total coefficient Nb.
Blue detuning, \(\omega_L>\omega_0\), gives \(\delta<0\) and positive force.
At exact resonance \(\omega_L=\omega_0\), the two rates are equal. The force is also zero at v = 0 for any detuning.
Red detuning, \(\omega_L<\omega_0\), gives positive b and a force opposite to v.
The linear force is odd in v. The same red-detuning condition \(\omega_L<\omega_0\) gives a force opposing either velocity sign.
Total mass is Nm, so \(Nm\dot v=-Nbv\). Therefore \[v(\tau)=v_0e^{-b\tau/m}.\] Dividing a total force coefficient by the single-atom mass without cancelling N would be inconsistent.

Every velocity component in the one-dimensional model is reduced by \(e^{-b\tau/m}\). Since temperature is proportional to mean-square velocity, \[T(\tau)=T_0e^{-2b\tau/m}.\] Recoil diffusion and other heating prevent the model from describing arbitrarily low temperatures.

DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
1a. Absorption resonance
The approaching atom sees a blueshift: \(\omega_0=\omega_L(1+v/c)\) to first order.
1b. Momentum after absorption

\(p_\gamma=-\hbar\omega_L/c=-\hbar q\).

\(p_\gamma=E_\gamma/c=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)/c\).

\(p_{at}=mv-2\hbar q\). The extra photon Doppler term is a product of the two small ratios when compared with mv, so it is discarded here.

6b. Co-propagating momentum transfer
\(\Delta p=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}/c\).
7a. Two-beam force
Let \(\delta=\omega_0-\omega_L\), \(q=\omega_L/c\), \(D=\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\). The +x beam is seen at \(\omega_L-qv\), and the -x beam at \(\omega_L+qv\). Thus \[F=N\Gamma\hbar q\Omega_R^2\left[\frac1{(\delta+qv)^2+D}-\frac1{(\delta-qv)^2+D}\right].\]

Blue detuning, \(\omega_L>\omega_0\), gives \(\delta<0\) and positive force.
8c. Zero force condition
At exact resonance \(\omega_L=\omega_0\), the two rates are equal. The force is also zero at v = 0 for any detuning.
8d. Cooling condition
Red detuning, \(\omega_L<\omega_0\), gives positive b and a force opposite to v.

children.text: An atomic probe microscope measures the vertical displacement \(z\) of a cantilever by reflecting a laser onto a photodetector. The cantilever obeys \(m\ddot z+b\dot z+kz=F\), with \(k=m\omega_0^2\) and weak damping \(0<b/m\ll\omega_0\). A piezoelectric tube supplies F. A lock-in amplifier multiplies its input by the reference \(V_R=V_{R0}\sin\omega t\), then retains only the dc component. A phase shifter and photodetector complete the measurement circuit as shown. Throughout, the source calls \(\omega=\omega_0\) resonance, appropriate in the stated weak-damping limit.

nodes.alt: Original atomic probe microscope, photodetector, phase shifter, piezotube and lock-in circuit with labelled reference signals.

children.text: For \(F=F_0\sin\omega t\), write \(z=A\sin(\omega t-\phi)\), with \(A>0\), \(0\le\phi\le\pi\). Find A.
Find \(\tan\phi\), state the phase quadrant, and give A and phi at \(\omega=\omega_0\).
The input is \(V_i=V_{i0}\sin(\omega_it-\phi_i)\), with all listed constants positive. What frequency condition is necessary for a nonzero dc output? State the additional phase condition.
At the matching frequency, find the magnitude of the dc output.

The phase shifter changes the reference to \(V_R^{\prime}=V_{R0}\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\). The piezotube produces \(F=c_1V_R^{\prime}\), and the detector produces \(V_i=c_2z\). Find the dc output magnitude at \(\omega_0\), taking \(c_1,c_2>0\).

A small mass change shifts natural frequency by \(\Delta\omega_0\), producing phase change \(\Delta\phi=\pi/1800\) at the original drive frequency. Find the mass change for \(m=1.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(b/m=1.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). You may use first-order binomial and tangent expansions.
A sample exerts additional force \(f(h)\), where h is tip-sample separation. Near equilibrium \(h_0\), write \(f(h)=f(h_0)+c_3(h-h_0)\). Find the new natural frequency.

A tip with charge \(Q=6e\) passes over a trapped electron of charge \(q=e\), where \(e=-1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\). The maximum small positive shift \(\Delta\omega_0\) occurs directly over the electron. Find tip-electron distance \(d_0\), ignoring polarization and using Coulomb constant \(k_e\).
Evaluate the distance in nm for \(\Delta\omega_0=20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(m=10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(k_e=9.0\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\).

statement.text:
Atomic Probe Microscope
An atomic probe microscope measures the vertical displacement \(z\) of a cantilever by reflecting a laser onto a photodetector. The cantilever obeys \(m\ddot z+b\dot z+kz=F\), with \(k=m\omega_0^2\) and weak damping \(0<b/m\ll\omega_0\). A piezoelectric tube supplies F. A lock-in amplifier multiplies its input by the reference \(V_R=V_{R0}\sin\omega t\), then retains only the dc component. A phase shifter and photodetector complete the measurement circuit as shown. Throughout, the source calls \(\omega=\omega_0\) resonance, appropriate in the stated weak-damping limit.

a.amplitude. Displacement amplitude
For \(F=F_0\sin\omega t\), write \(z=A\sin(\omega t-\phi)\), with \(A>0\), \(0\le\phi\le\pi\). Find A.
a.phase. Phase relation
Find \(\tan\phi\), state the phase quadrant, and give A and phi at \(\omega=\omega_0\).
b.frequency. Lock-in frequency condition
The input is \(V_i=V_{i0}\sin(\omega_it-\phi_i)\), with all listed constants positive. What frequency condition is necessary for a nonzero dc output? State the additional phase condition.
b.output. Lock-in output magnitude
At the matching frequency, find the magnitude of the dc output.
c. Phase-shifted microscope signal
The phase shifter changes the reference to \(V_R^{\prime}=V_{R0}\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\). The piezotube produces \(F=c_1V_R^{\prime}\), and the detector produces \(V_i=c_2z\). Find the dc output magnitude at \(\omega_0\), taking \(c_1,c_2>0\).
d. Detectable mass change
A small mass change shifts natural frequency by \(\Delta\omega_0\), producing phase change \(\Delta\phi=\pi/1800\) at the original drive frequency. Find the mass change for \(m=1.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(b/m=1.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). You may use first-order binomial and tangent expansions.
e. Force-gradient frequency
A sample exerts additional force \(f(h)\), where h is tip-sample separation. Near equilibrium \(h_0\), write \(f(h)=f(h_0)+c_3(h-h_0)\). Find the new natural frequency.
f.formula. Trapped-charge depth
A tip with charge \(Q=6e\) passes over a trapped electron of charge \(q=e\), where \(e=-1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\). The maximum small positive shift \(\Delta\omega_0\) occurs directly over the electron. Find tip-electron distance \(d_0\), ignoring polarization and using Coulomb constant \(k_e\).
f.value. Charge depth value
Evaluate the distance in nm for \(\Delta\omega_0=20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(m=10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(k_e=9.0\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\).

children.text: Equating sine and cosine coefficients after substitution gives \[A=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{m^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+b^2\omega^2}}.\]

\[\tan\phi=\frac{b\omega}{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}.\] The phase is below \(\pi/2\) for \(\omega<\omega_0\), and above it for \(\omega>\omega_0\). At \(\omega_0\), \(A=F_0/(b\omega_0)\) and \(\phi=\pi/2\). The exact amplitude maximum is at \(\sqrt{\omega_0^2-b^2/(2m^2)}\), whose weak-damping difference from \(\omega_0\) is neglected in the source.
Product-to-sum gives a difference-frequency term and a sum-frequency term. A dc term is possible only if \(\omega=\omega_i\). It is nonzero only when \(\cos\phi_i\ne0\).
The signed dc component is \(V_{i0}V_{R0}\cos\phi_i/2\), so its magnitude is \(V_{i0}V_{R0}|\cos\phi_i|/2\). The absolute value is required when the question asks for magnitude.

The cantilever lags its drive by \(\pi/2\), cancelling the phase-shifter advance. Thus the detector signal is in phase with the original reference. Its amplitude is \(c_1c_2V_{R0}/(b\omega_0)\), giving \[V_{dc}=\frac{c_1c_2V_{R0}^2}{2b\omega_0}.\]

With fixed k, \(\Delta\omega_0=-\omega_0\Delta m/(2m)\). Linearizing the phase at fixed drive gives \(\Delta\phi=-2m\Delta\omega_0/b\). Thus \[\Delta m=(b/\omega_0)\Delta\phi=1.7\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{kg}.\] The rendered source gives \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), not the 0.1 produced by its faulty text extraction.
The constant force moves the equilibrium, while the gradient changes stiffness to \(k-c_3\). Thus \[\omega_0^{\prime}=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-c_3/m},\] assuming \(k-c_3>0\).
Directly over the charge, \(f=k_eqQ/h^2\), so \(c_3=-2k_eqQ/d_0^3\). To first order \(\Delta\omega_0=-c_3/(2m\omega_0)\), giving \[d_0=\left(\frac{k_eqQ}{m\omega_0\Delta\omega_0}\right)^{1/3}.\]

solution.text:
Atomic Probe Microscope
a.amplitude. Displacement amplitude
Equating sine and cosine coefficients after substitution gives \[A=\frac{F_0}{\sqrt{m^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+b^2\omega^2}}.\]
a.phase. Phase relation
\[\tan\phi=\frac{b\omega}{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}.\] The phase is below \(\pi/2\) for \(\omega<\omega_0\), and above it for \(\omega>\omega_0\). At \(\omega_0\), \(A=F_0/(b\omega_0)\) and \(\phi=\pi/2\). The exact amplitude maximum is at \(\sqrt{\omega_0^2-b^2/(2m^2)}\), whose weak-damping difference from \(\omega_0\) is neglected in the source.
b.frequency. Lock-in frequency condition
Product-to-sum gives a difference-frequency term and a sum-frequency term. A dc term is possible only if \(\omega=\omega_i\). It is nonzero only when \(\cos\phi_i\ne0\).
b.output. Lock-in output magnitude
The signed dc component is \(V_{i0}V_{R0}\cos\phi_i/2\), so its magnitude is \(V_{i0}V_{R0}|\cos\phi_i|/2\). The absolute value is required when the question asks for magnitude.
c. Phase-shifted microscope signal
The cantilever lags its drive by \(\pi/2\), cancelling the phase-shifter advance. Thus the detector signal is in phase with the original reference. Its amplitude is \(c_1c_2V_{R0}/(b\omega_0)\), giving \[V_{dc}=\frac{c_1c_2V_{R0}^2}{2b\omega_0}.\]
d. Detectable mass change
With fixed k, \(\Delta\omega_0=-\omega_0\Delta m/(2m)\). Linearizing the phase at fixed drive gives \(\Delta\phi=-2m\Delta\omega_0/b\). Thus \[\Delta m=(b/\omega_0)\Delta\phi=1.7\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{kg}.\] The rendered source gives \(k=1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}\), not the 0.1 produced by its faulty text extraction.
e. Force-gradient frequency
The constant force moves the equilibrium, while the gradient changes stiffness to \(k-c_3\). Thus \[\omega_0^{\prime}=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-c_3/m},\] assuming \(k-c_3>0\).
f.formula. Trapped-charge depth
Directly over the charge, \(f=k_eqQ/h^2\), so \(c_3=-2k_eqQ/d_0^3\). To first order \(\Delta\omega_0=-c_3/(2m\omega_0)\), giving \[d_0=\left(\frac{k_eqQ}{m\omega_0\Delta\omega_0}\right)^{1/3}.\]
f.value. Charge depth value
\(\omega_0=10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), giving \(d_0=41\,\mathrm{nm}\).

statement.text:

Use one rotation in 24 hours and one year of 365.25 days. After part A use the empirical hmax=21 km irrespective of your estimate. For solar averaging replace the Sun by a uniform circular ring in the ecliptic plane. Set z perpendicular to that plane, with origin at Earth's centre. Near Earth all distances r,|z| are much smaller than the ring radius.

a.1. Flattening dimensions
In \(h_{max}\propto G^{-1}\omega^\beta M_E^\gamma R^\delta\), find β,γ,δ.
a.2. Flattening estimate
Assume the dimensionless factor is one and evaluate hmax.
b.1. Ring field on its axis

Find the direction and leading magnitude of the Sun-ring gravitational field at coordinate z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane
Find the leading field at radial distance r in the ecliptic plane, giving direction and a derivation.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap

Imagine the spheroid as a full sphere of radius Re minus two equal excess polar regions. Find the mass m of one removed region in hmax,ME,Rp.
c.2. Solar torque
The torque on the removed regions equals that on two point masses 2m/5 at the endpoints of the polar diameter. Find the torque magnitude on Earth to first order in hmax/R, and state its sense.
d.1. Solar-only precession period
Derive the precession period T1 in MS,dSE,ω,hmax,R,α.
d.2. Solar-only numerical period
Evaluate T1 in years using hmax=21 km.
e.1. Lunar correction factor
Now approximate the Moon's orbit as a circle in the ecliptic plane. Find T2/T1 after adding its averaged torque.
e.2. Combined numerical period
Evaluate T2 in years.

children.text: Using [G]=L³M^−1T^−2, dimensional balance gives time exponent 2−β=0, mass exponent 1+γ=0 and length exponent δ−3=1. Thus β=2, γ=−1, δ=4.
b.1. Ring field on its axis
The exact potential is \(\Phi(z)=-GM_S/\sqrt{d_{SE}^2+z^2}\). Thus \(g_z=-GM_Sz/(d_{SE}^2+z^2)^{3/2}\simeq-GM_Sz/d_{SE}^3\). It points toward the ecliptic plane for either sign of z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane

Symmetry and the mass-free divergence condition near the centre give \(2g_r/r+\partial_zg_z=0\), so \[g_r=GM_Sr/(2d_{SE}^3),\] radially outwards. Alternatively expand the ring potential through r²: \(\Phi(r)=-GM_S/d_{SE}-GM_Sr^2/(4d_{SE}^3)\), then differentiate. The axial restoring field and in-plane outward field have opposite signs.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap
The spheroid volume is \(4\pi R_e^2R_p/3\). Half the difference from a sphere is \(2\pi R_e^2h_{max}/3\). Multiply by density \(3M_E/(4\pi R_e^2R_p)\) to obtain \(m=M_Eh_{max}/(2R_p)\).

A complete sphere has zero torque, so Earth's torque is opposite that on the removed masses. Both the vertical restoring and radial outward fields contribute. Their combined torque magnitude is \(6GmM_SR^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha/(5d_{SE}^3)\). Substitute m≈MEhmax/(2R): \[|\tau|=\frac{3GM_EM_SR h_{max}}{5d_{SE}^3}\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.\] If the north axis lies in +xz, this torque is along −y, giving retrograde precession.

To leading order the spin angular momentum is \(L=(2/5)M_ER^2\omega\). The magnitude changes slowly compared with direction. Precession gives \(|\dot{\mathbf L}|=\Omega_1L\sin\alpha=|\tau|\). Hence \[T_1=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_1}=\frac{4\pi d_{SE}^3R\omega}{3GM_Sh_{max}\cos\alpha}.\]
The model gives \(T_1\simeq8.06\times10^4\) years. This is larger than the observed precession period because the Moon has not yet been included.

The same ring calculation applies and torque coefficients add as M/d³. Thus \[\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{M_S/d_{SE}^3}{M_S/d_{SE}^3+M_M/d_{ME}^3}.\] The lunar torque makes precession faster and the period shorter.
The ratio is approximately 0.315. Multiplying the solar-only period gives \(T_2\simeq2.54\times10^4\) years in this homogeneous-Earth, coplanar-circular-orbit model.

children.text: Waves and phase transitions in spin systems
Torque is \(\dot{\mathbf L}=\gamma\mathbf L\times\mathbf B\). Compare with \(\dot{\mathbf L}=\omega_L\hat z\times\mathbf L\), giving \(\omega_L=-\gamma B\).
The equatorial field of ring 1 is \(\mathbf B_1=-\mu_0\boldsymbol\mu_1/(4\pi d^3)\). Thus U=−μ2·B1 gives \(J_0=\mu_0\gamma^2/(4\pi d^3)\), positive.
The terms containing Si are \(-J\mathbf S_i\cdot(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1})\). Comparing with −γSi·Bi,eff gives \(\mathbf B_{i,eff}=(J/\gamma)(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1})\).
Apply magnetic torque: \[\frac{d\mathbf S_i}{dt}=J\mathbf S_i\times(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1}).\] Each spin keeps constant magnitude because its derivative is perpendicular to itself.

Linearization gives \(\dot S_{ix}=JS(2S_{iy}-S_{i-1,y}-S_{i+1,y})\) and \(\dot S_{iy}=-JS(2S_{ix}-S_{i-1,x}-S_{i+1,x})\). Take equal-amplitude quadrature waves Sx=δScos(kai−ωt), Sy=δSsin(kai−ωt). Then \[\omega=2JS[1-\cos(ka)].\] The opposite phase convention can reverse signed frequency. The field checks its positive branch.
\(\omega\simeq JSa^2k^2\). With E=ℏω,p=ℏk, compare E=(JSa²/ℏ)p² with p²/(2meff), giving \(m_{eff}=\hbar/(2JSa^2)\).

The spin wave has no y momentum, so pin cosθin=pout cosθout. Its x momentum is ps=pin sinθin−pout sinθout and energy Es=(pin²−pout²)/(2mn). Thus \[m_{eff}=m_n\frac{\sin^2(\theta_{in}-\theta_{out})}{\cos^2\theta_{out}-\cos^2\theta_{in}}=m_n\frac{\sin(\theta_{in}-\theta_{out})}{\sin(\theta_{in}+\theta_{out})}.\] Choose physical angles giving positive energy loss and mass. If angles are instead measured from the chain, convert them before using this expression.
The ±z states have energies −h and +h. Boltzmann weights give \(p_\uparrow/p_\downarrow=e^{2h/(k_BT)}\). For negative h the labels remain ±z, so up is then anti-aligned with the field.

Normalize the two Boltzmann weights to obtain \(\bar s=p_\uparrow-p_\downarrow=\tanh[h/(k_BT)]\). All curves are odd through the origin. For a large field range they saturate near ±1, for a small range they are nearly linear with slope 1/(kBT), and the intermediate range gives a smooth unsaturated S-shaped curve.
All spins align, with either global sign, so every bond contributes −J̃. For an open chain Eg=−J̃(N−1)≈−J̃N. A periodic chain has exactly N bonds.

The explicitly prescribed replacement gives \(\tilde J_{eff}=\tilde J\bar s\). This matches the official scheme's single-counted energy ansatz. For comparison, a thermodynamically consistent local-field decoupling uses both neighbours, field 2J̃s̄ and an additive correction NJ̃s̄². Those are different approximations, so the next items use the one requested here.

For the source ansatz, \(\bar s=\tanh[\tilde J\bar s/(k_BT)]\). The zero solution always exists. Nonzero roots appear when the right-hand slope at zero exceeds one, giving \(T_c=\tilde J/k_B\). Above Tc only zero exists, below Tc there are also two opposite roots. This is the transition of the stated approximation, not an exact 1D transition.

Expand tanh x≈x−x³/3. The roots are \(\bar s=0\) and \(\bar s\simeq\pm\sqrt{3(T_c-T)/T_c}\). Keeping cubic-order temperature factors gives ±√[3(T/Tc)²(1−T/Tc)]. Draw the full roots from the implicit equation, not the near-critical expansion down to T=0: nonzero branches approach ±1 with zero slope at zero temperature and merge with vertical tangents at Tc. The zero branch persists below Tc but is unstable in the mean-field picture.
c.7. Magnetic phases in the approximation

The approximate model is paramagnetic above Tc and ferromagnetic below Tc, where it supports spontaneous nonzero s̄. The exact infinite one-dimensional short-range chain orders only at zero temperature.

The zero branch persists below Tc but is unstable in the mean-field picture.
c.7. Magnetic phases in the approximation
The approximate model is paramagnetic above Tc and ferromagnetic below Tc, where it supports spontaneous nonzero s̄. The exact infinite one-dimensional short-range chain orders only at zero temperature.

children.text: Use the intercepting disc and the absorbed fraction: \(P_0=(1-a)\pi R_E^2F_s\).
Equate absorbed disc power to emission over 4πRE²: \(T_{g0}=[(1-a)F_s/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}\simeq255\,\mathrm K\), about −18°C.

Let PE be ground emission and PA the emission of each atmospheric face. Surface balance gives PE=PA+tswP0. Top-of-atmosphere balance gives tlwPE+PA=P0. Hence \(T_g=[(1+t_{sw})/(1+t_{lw})]^{1/4}T_{g0}\simeq286\,\mathrm K\), about 13°C.
The relative coordinate has reduced mass μ=mAmB/(mA+mB). Thus \(\omega_d=\sqrt{k(m_A+m_B)/(m_Am_B)}\).

For fixed incoming lab frequency fin, the molecule sees f′≈fin(1+v/c). Thus if fin=f0 the observed shift is +f0v/c, the convention used in the official solution. If f0 instead denotes the molecule's rest-frame absorption resonance, the resonant laboratory incident frequency is \(f=f_0/(1+v/c)\simeq f_0-f_0v/c\), with shift −f0v/c. The source wording mixes these descriptions. Both yield the same symmetric thermal line profile below, so this signed convention item uses self-review.
The Gaussian integral is √(2πkBT/m), so \(C=\sqrt{m/(2\pi k_BT)}\).
Use |v|=c|f−f0|/f0 and the constant Jacobian c/f0. Thus \[p_2(f)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{mc^2(f-f_0)^2}{2k_BT f_0^2}\right].\] If normalized, the prefactor is (c/f0)√[m/(2πkBT)].
The curve is a symmetric Gaussian centred at zero, decaying to zero in both tails. The 1/e points are \(f_*-f_0=\pm f_0\sqrt{2k_BT/(mc^2)}\). The field checks the positive half-width.
Balance upward minus downward pressure forces on area A and height dz against weight ρgA dz. This gives \(dp/dz=-\rho g\).
Adiabatic enthalpy change balances gravitational potential: cp dT+μairg dz=0. Equivalently combine pVγ=constant with hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus \(\Gamma_a=\mu_{air}g/c_p\).

Parcel and environment temperatures become T−Γaδz and T−Γδz. At equal pressure ρ∝1/T, so net buoyancy acceleration is \[\delta\ddot z=\frac gT(\Gamma-\Gamma_a)\delta z.\] Stability requires Γ<Γa, with \(\omega=\sqrt{g(\mu_{air}g/c_p-\Gamma)/T}\). Equality is neutral, while Γ>Γa gives exponential growth. This sign follows the defined positive lapse rate.
For evaporated mass m, ΔS=Lm/T while ΔV≈(m/μw)RT/ps. Thus \(d p_s/dT=\mu_w Lp_s/(RT^2)\).

The water partial pressure is \(p_w\simeq\phi(\mu_{air}/\mu_w)p\), and dry adiabatic ascent gives p=pi(T/Ti)cp/R. Solve \[\phi\frac{\mu_{air}}{\mu_w}p_i(T_l/T_i)^{7/2}=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T_l-1/T_i)\right]\] for the first lower-temperature crossing. With Ti=290.15 K the root is Tl≈286.8 K, or 13.7°C. The total-mass definition of φ changes this only slightly beyond the dilute approximation.

Snell gives internal entry α′=arcsin(sinα/n) and internal exit β′=φ−α′. The external exit angle is β=arcsin(nsinβ′). Therefore \[\delta=\alpha+\arcsin\{n\sin[\varphi-\arcsin(\sin\alpha/n)]\}-\varphi.\] A transmitted ray requires the exit sine magnitude no greater than one.

The (α,δ) pairs in degrees are approximately (20,27.5),(25,24.6),(30,23.0),(35,22.2),(40,21.8),(45,22.0),(50,22.5),(55,23.4),(60,24.7),(65,26.5),(70,28.7). Draw a smooth curve with a minimum close to α=41°. Label both axes in degrees.

The random crystal orientations concentrate rays near minimum deviation. Symmetric passage gives \(\delta_{min}=2\arcsin[n\sin(\varphi/2)]-\varphi\simeq21.8^\circ\), the familiar approximately 22° halo.

The relative coordinate has reduced mass μ=mAmB/(mA+mB). Thus \(\omega_d=\sqrt{k(m_A+m_B)/(m_Am_B)}\).
b.2. Vibrational photon
Harmonic-oscillator adjacent levels differ by \(E_p=\hbar\omega_d\).
b.3. Doppler-shift convention

b.4. Velocity normalization

c.2. Ideal-gas gradient
Ideal gas gives ρ=μairp/(RT), hence \(dp/dz=-\mu_{air}gp/(RT)\).
c.3. Isothermal barometric law
Integrate dp/p=−μairg dz/(RT) to obtain \(p(z)=p_0e^{-\mu_{air}gz/(RT)}\).
c.4. Dry adiabatic lapse rate
Adiabatic enthalpy change balances gravitational potential: cp dT+μairg dz=0. Equivalently combine pVγ=constant with hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus \(\Gamma_a=\mu_{air}g/c_p\).
c.5. Buoyancy stability

At equal pressure ρ∝1/T, so net buoyancy acceleration is \[\delta\ddot z=\frac gT(\Gamma-\Gamma_a)\delta z.\] Stability requires Γ<Γa, with \(\omega=\sqrt{g(\mu_{air}g/c_p-\Gamma)/T}\). d.1. Clausius-Clapeyron slope
For evaporated mass m, ΔS=Lm/T while ΔV≈(m/μw)RT/ps. Thus \(d p_s/dT=\mu_w Lp_s/(RT^2)\).
d.2. Saturation-pressure law
Integration of dps/ps=(μwL/R)dT/T² gives \[p_s(T)=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T-1/T_0)\right].\]

e.1. Prism deviation law

The (α,δ) pairs in degrees are approximately (20,27.5),(25,24.6),(30,23.0),(35,22.2),(40,21.8),(45,22.0),(50,22.5),(55,23.4),(60,24.7),(65,26.5),(70,28.7). Draw a smooth curve with a minimum close to α=41°. Label both axes in degrees.

statement.text:
Geometry of Water Fountain
A hemispherical fountain sprayer of radius \(r\) is at height \(h\) above horizontal ground. Its radius is small compared with the water range, so treat it as a point source. All holes eject water at speed \(v_0\), at elevation \(0<\theta<\pi/2\) above horizontal. There are \(\rho(\theta)\) holes per unit hemisphere area. Ignore air resistance and use gravitational acceleration \(g\). Part A assumes uniform hole density. Part B seeks uniform coverage on the ground.

A.1. Projectile position
Find \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), with the ground at \(y=0\).
A.2. Water trajectory
Eliminate time to obtain \(y(x,\theta)\) using just one type of trigonometric function.
A.3. Trajectory envelope
Derive the minimal boundary enclosing all trajectories and sketch it over the trajectories.
A.4. Landing range
Find the positive landing range \(R(\theta)\).
A.5. Zero-height range
Show that as \(h\to0\), \(R=v_0^2\sin(2\theta)/g\).
B.1. Ground annulus
Express the elemental ground annulus area in terms of \(R,R_{\mathrm{prime}}=dR/d\theta,d\theta\), taking \(R_{\mathrm{prime}}>0\).
B.2. Hole density
Determine the angular hole density up to an overall constant for uniform ground coverage. Use \(R_{\mathrm{prime}}>0\).
B.3. Flat-source distribution
For \(h=0\) and \(0<\theta<45^\circ\), find the explicit angular dependence for uniform coverage.

children.text: Horizontal acceleration vanishes and vertical acceleration is \(-g\), hence \[x=v_0t\cos\theta,\qquad y=h+v_0t\sin\theta-\tfrac12gt^2.\]

For fixed \(x\), maximize the preceding quadratic in \(u=\tan\theta\). The maximum occurs at \(u=v_0^2/(gx)\), giving \[y_{\rm env}=h+\frac{v_0^2}{2g}-\frac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}.\] Equivalently its discriminant in \(u\) vanishes. Sketch this downward parabola tangent to every trajectory, with vertex at \(x=0,y=h+v_0^2/(2g)\).
Solve \(y(t)=0\) for the positive time, then multiply by \(v_0\cos\theta\): \[R=\frac{v_0\cos\theta}{g}\left(v_0\sin\theta+\sqrt{v_0^2\sin^2\theta+2gh}\right).\]
For \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), the square root becomes \(v_0\sin\theta\). Thus \(R=2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g=v_0^2\sin(2\theta)/g\).
The annulus has area \(dA_W=2\pi R\,dR=2\pi RR_{\mathrm{prime}}\,d\theta\). If the angle branch decreases in range, use \(|R_{\mathrm{prime}}|\).

The hemisphere band area is \(2\pi r^2\cos\theta\,d\theta\). Equal water delivery per ground area requires \(\rho\,2\pi r^2\cos\theta\,d\theta\propto2\pi RR_{\mathrm{prime}}\,d\theta\), so \[\rho(\theta)\propto\frac{RR_{\mathrm{prime}}}{r^2\cos\theta}.\]

With \(R=v_0^2\sin2\theta/g\) and \(R_{\mathrm{prime}}=2v_0^2\cos2\theta/g\), \[\rho\propto\frac{v_0^4}{g^2r^2}\frac{\sin4\theta}{\cos\theta}.\] The requested angular shape is \(\sin4\theta/\cos\theta\). Restricting the angle avoids two launch angles delivering water to the same ring.

solution.text:
Geometry of Water Fountain
A.1. Projectile position
Horizontal acceleration vanishes and vertical acceleration is \(-g\), hence \[x=v_0t\cos\theta,\qquad y=h+v_0t\sin\theta-\tfrac12gt^2.\]
A.2. Water trajectory
Substitute \(t=x/(v_0\cos\theta)\) and \(\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta\): \[y=h+x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}(1+\tan^2\theta).\]
A.3. Trajectory envelope
For fixed \(x\), maximize the preceding quadratic in \(u=\tan\theta\). The maximum occurs at \(u=v_0^2/(gx)\), giving \[y_{\rm env}=h+\frac{v_0^2}{2g}-\frac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}.\] Equivalently its discriminant in \(u\) vanishes. Sketch this downward parabola tangent to every trajectory, with vertex at \(x=0,y=h+v_0^2/(2g)\).
A.4. Landing range
Solve \(y(t)=0\) for the positive time, then multiply by \(v_0\cos\theta\): \[R=\frac{v_0\cos\theta}{g}\left(v_0\sin\theta+\sqrt{v_0^2\sin^2\theta+2gh}\right).\]
A.5. Zero-height range
For \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), the square root becomes \(v_0\sin\theta\). Thus \(R=2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g=v_0^2\sin(2\theta)/g\).
B.1. Ground annulus
The annulus has area \(dA_W=2\pi R\,dR=2\pi RR_{\mathrm{prime}}\,d\theta\). If the angle branch decreases in range, use \(|R_{\mathrm{prime}}|\).
B.2. Hole density
The hemisphere band area is \(2\pi r^2\cos\theta\,d\theta\). Equal water delivery per ground area requires \(\rho\,2\pi r^2\cos\theta\,d\theta\propto2\pi RR_{\mathrm{prime}}\,d\theta\), so \[\rho(\theta)\propto\frac{RR_{\mathrm{prime}}}{r^2\cos\theta}.\]
B.3. Flat-source distribution
With \(R=v_0^2\sin2\theta/g\) and \(R_{\mathrm{prime}}=2v_0^2\cos2\theta/g\), \[\rho\propto\frac{v_0^4}{g^2r^2}\frac{\sin4\theta}{\cos\theta}.\] The requested angular shape is \(\sin4\theta/\cos\theta\). Restricting the angle avoids two launch angles delivering water to the same ring.

children.text: At the common internal incidence angle, Snell gives \(n_a<n_b\). Thus \(c/n_a>c/n_b\), so ray a travels faster.

If the rod angle is \(\theta_1\), side reflection requires \(\cos\theta_1>n_2/n_1\), whereas far-end reflection requires \(\sin\theta_1>n_2/n_1\). Using \(n_3\sin\theta=n_1\sin\theta_1\), \[\arcsin(n_2/n_3)<\theta<\arcsin(\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}/n_3).\] Numerically \(45.58^\circ<\theta<53.00^\circ\).
B.2.i. Oil at the far end
The far-end medium has index greater than the rod. Total internal reflection there is impossible. No incident-angle interval returns all the light to the polymer.

Side reflection requires \(\theta_1<\arccos(1.33/1.50)=27.54^\circ\), while far-end reflection requires \(\theta_1>\arcsin(1.33/1.50)=62.46^\circ\). These intervals do not intersect, so no total-return interval exists.

At the side-wall critical angle, the core angle to the axis satisfies \(\sin\theta_{\rm core}=\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}/n_1\). Entry refraction gives \[\sin\theta_a=\frac{\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}}{n_3}.\] If this exceeds one, all physical entry angles are accepted.

Let \(a=25\,\mu\mathrm m\), bend radius \(R=10000\,\mu\mathrm m\). Conservation of the ray impact parameter between inner and outer core radii requires \(\sin\phi_{\rm inner}=(R+a)\sin\phi_{\rm outer}/(R-a)\). Set \(\sin\phi_{\rm outer}=n_2/n_1\). Entry refraction then gives \[\sin\theta_{a,\rm bend}=\frac1{n_3}\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2\left(\frac{R+a}{R-a}\right)^2}.\] It is smaller than the straight value. The original occultation, spectrum and radio-image figures provide the observational data.
A.1. Lunar angular motion
Find the lunar motion against background stars in one hour, one minute, and one second. Express each in degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds.
A.2. One lunar diameter
How long does the Moon take to move by its own angular diameter?
B.1. Occultation oscillations

What causes the intensity oscillations? Options: A, telescope diffraction pattern. B, mount instability. C, lunar surface features. D, atmosphere. Explain your choice.
B.2. Component reappearance

B.3. Angular component separation
Estimate the projected angular separation from the occultation graph and the lunar angular speed.
C.1. Spectral redshift

Compare corresponding Balmer-line wavelengths in the laboratory and 3C 273 spectra. Estimate \(z=(\lambda-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0\).
C.2. Gravitational-redshift hypothesis
If \(z=(1-2GM/(c^2r))^{-1/2}-1\), find the required mass for a source at the edge of the Galaxy, \(r\sim3\times10^{21}\,\mathrm m\), and at the edge of the Solar System, \(r\sim1.5\times10^{13}\,\mathrm m\). Explain why these are implausible.
C.3. Cosmological distance
Instead use \(z\simeq v/c\) and Hubble law \(v=Hd\). Find the distance and compare it with the Galaxy.
D.1. Spectral luminosity
The flux is \(F_\nu=25000\nu^{-0.3}\,\mathrm{Jy}\), with frequency in Hz and \(1\,\mathrm{Jy}=10^{-26}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,Hz^{-1}}\). Find \(L_\nu=4\pi d^2F_\nu\).
D.2. Integrated radio luminosity
Integrate over \(10^7<\nu<10^{11}\,\mathrm{Hz}\).
D.3. Luminosity comparison
Compare with the stated solar luminosity and \(L_{MW}=1.5\times10^{10}L_\odot\).
E.1. Annihilation photon energy
Explain why electron-positron annihilation \(e^++e^-\to2\gamma\) at rest does not directly produce the observed optical and radio emission. Estimate photon energy and wavelength.
E.2. Accretion power
One solar mass falls from infinity to Schwarzschild radius \(R_s=2GM/c^2\) each year. Estimate Newtonian potential-energy power and compare it with D.
F.1. Minimum-energy ratio

For particle energy \(U_e\propto B^{-3/2}\) and field energy \(U_B\propto B^2\), minimize \(U=U_e+U_B\) at fixed volume and show \(U_e/U_B=4/3\).
F.2. Jet magnetic field
Take the jet energy to be half the energy radiated in one second in D.2, and volume \(10^{45}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Estimate its magnetic field.

children.text: The angular rate is \(360^\circ/(27.3\times24\,\mathrm h)\). In one hour: \(0.54945^\circ=32.967\) arcmin \(=1978.02\) arcsec. In one minute: \(0.0091575^\circ=0.54945\) arcmin \(=32.967\) arcsec. In one second: \(0.000152625^\circ=0.0091575\) arcmin \(=0.54945\) arcsec. The source solution labels its final per-second result in degrees where arcseconds are intended.
Divide \(30\) arcminutes by \(0.54945\) arcminutes per minute to obtain \(54.6\,\mathrm{min}\).

The published key selects A. Physically, lunar occultation fringes are Fresnel diffraction at the lunar limb, recorded by the telescope. They should not be attributed to the telescope aperture alone. The other proposed instrumental and surface explanations do not account for the coherent occultation fringes. This wording discrepancy is retained for self-review.

C. The two components can have different projected separations normal to the lunar limb at disappearance and reappearance. Their reappearance times coincide because their positions align along the local limb. This constrains the two-dimensional structure.

The disappearance times differ by roughly half a minute. Multiply by \(32.97\) arcseconds per minute to obtain about \(16.5\) arcseconds, conventionally estimated as \(15\) arcseconds. Graph reading and projection limit precision.

For example, the rest H-gamma line at \(434\,\mathrm{nm}\) appears near \(500\,\mathrm{nm}\). Corresponding line ratios are approximately \(1.158\), giving \(z\simeq0.158\). Accept reasonable estimates from several lines.

Solve for \[M=\frac{c^2r}{2G}\left[1-(1+z)^{-2}\right].\] At \(z=0.158\), this gives about \(2.6\times10^{17}M_\odot\) and \(1.3\times10^9M_\odot\), respectively. Either would dominate and severely disrupt the containing Galaxy or Solar System.
\(d=zc/H=0.158\times300000/75=632\,\mathrm{Mpc}\), thousands of times the Galactic size. This is the stated low-redshift approximation, without a modern cosmological-distance correction.

Using \(d=632\,\mathrm{Mpc}=1.953\times10^{25}\,\mathrm m\), \[L_\nu=1.198\times10^{30}\nu^{-0.3}\,\mathrm{W/Hz}.\] Rounding \(d\) to \(2\times10^{25}\,\mathrm m\) gives the published coefficient \(1.25\times10^{30}\). The luminosity has units W/Hz, not the flux units printed in the answer sheet.

\[L=\frac{1.198\times10^{30}}{0.7}\left[(10^{11})^{0.7}-(10^7)^{0.7}\right]\simeq8.56\times10^{37}\,\mathrm W.\] The rounded-distance convention gives \(8.94\times10^{37}\,\mathrm W\), conventionally \(9\times10^{37}\,\mathrm W\).

The supplied benchmarks give \(L/L_\odot\simeq(2.2\text{ to }2.4)\times10^{11}\), and \(L/L_{MW}\simeq15\). These are comparisons using the given luminosity benchmarks. The solar value is a bolometric luminosity, so it should not be described as the actual solar radio-band luminosity.

Each photon has \(E=m_ec^2=0.511\,\mathrm{MeV}=8.19\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm J\), and \(\lambda=h/(m_ec)=2.43\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm m=0.00243\,\mathrm{nm}\). This is gamma radiation, far above optical and radio frequencies. The source sheet has an incorrect wavelength conversion and calls it X-rays. Reprocessing is outside this simple direct-emission comparison.

The model releases \(GM\dot M/R_s=\dot Mc^2/2\). With \(\dot M=2\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg/yr}\), \(P=2.85\times10^{39}\,\mathrm W\), enough to supply the radio luminosity even with losses. The source numerical value uses \(\dot Mc^2\), dropping its own factor one-half. This estimate is a Newtonian energy scale, not a relativistic accretion-efficiency calculation.
At the stationary point \(dU/dB=(-3U_e/2+2U_B)/B=0\), so \(U_e=4U_B/3\). It is a minimum because both energy contributions grow at opposite ends of the positive B range.

Use energy, not power: \(U\simeq4.3\text{ to }4.5\times10^{37}\,\mathrm J\). From \(U=7U_B/3\), \(U_B=3U/7\), so \[B=\sqrt{\frac{2\mu_0(3U/7)}{V}}\simeq2.2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm T.\] The source rounds the luminosity to \(10^{38}\,\mathrm W\), yielding \(2.3\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm T\).

children.text: Hydrostatic balance and the gas law give \(dp/dh=-\rho g\), \(\rho=\mu p/(RT)\). Integrate: \[p(h)=p(0)\exp\left[-\frac\mu R\int_0^h\frac{g(s)}{T(s)}ds\right].\]
For constant g0, \(p_{sta}=p_0e^{-h/h_0}\), with \(h_0=RT/(\mu g_0)=12414\,\mathrm m\).

\(g(h)=g_0(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_0(1-2h/R_E)\). Its integral is \(g_0h(1-h/R_E)\), giving \[p_{imp}=p_0\exp[-h(1-h/R_E)/h_0].\] The exact isothermal result is \(p_0\exp[-h/(h_0(1+h/R_E))]\). It rolls without slipping on a horizontal turntable, assumed large enough that it never falls off. In the laboratory, its horizontal centre position is \(\mathbf R\), velocity \(\mathbf v\), and spin \(\boldsymbol\omega\). statement.text:
A Ball on a Turntable
A ball of mass m, radius r and spherically symmetric mass distribution has inertia I about any central axis. It rolls without slipping on a horizontal turntable, assumed large enough that it never falls off. In the laboratory, its horizontal centre position is \(\mathbf R\), velocity \(\mathbf v\), and spin \(\boldsymbol\omega\). The turntable rotates about upward \(\hat{\mathbf z}\) at signed rate \(\Omega\). Initial \(\mathbf R_0,\mathbf v_0,\Omega_0\) are known, including vector directions. Write \(J\mathbf a=\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf a\), \(\alpha=I/(I+mr^2)\), and \(\delta=I_d/(mr^2)\), where \(I_d\) is turntable inertia. Part A fixes \(\Omega=\Omega_0\). Part B lets the table rotate freely. Part C adds uniformly distributed surface charge Q and vertical uniform field \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\), with B positive. Use the standard cross product. The source preamble has a typo in its z component.

A.1. Rolling constraint
Express the laboratory ball velocity from the no-slip constraint.
A.2. Ball acceleration
Use force and torque equations to find the centre acceleration.
A.3. Velocity-position relation
Integrate the acceleration relation to express velocity using initial data and current position.
A.4. Explicit trajectory
Give the full trajectory for the prescribed initial data.
A.5. Return to a table mark
For a uniform solid ball, \(I=2mr^2/5\), choose circle radius \(R_t=R_0\). When does it return closest to the table mark initially beneath it?
B.1. Freely rotating constraint
Find velocity and acceleration when the table rate varies.
B.2. Table angular acceleration
Find signed angular acceleration in terms of the current position and initial data.
B.3. Table speed versus radius
Find the table speed as a function of R alone.
B.4. Maximum possible table speed
Find the maximum possible speed at fixed initial radius and rate.
B.5. Conic trajectories
Find the conserved vertical angular momentum, remove constant ball spin, and derive the trajectory equation in coordinates with x along c. List the possible trajectory types.
C.1. Charged-ball equations

Take \(I=mr^2/10\). Find the Newton and spin equations and the electromagnetic torque due to surface-charge rotation.
C.2. Magnetic acceleration
Eliminate friction and spin to find the ball acceleration for constant table rate.
C.3. Removing the gyroscopic term
Write \(\ddot{\mathbf R}-\gamma\dot{\mathbf R}\times\hat{\mathbf z}+\beta\mathbf R=0\). Find beta and gamma. Transform with \(x=\rho\cos\eta,y=\rho\sin\eta\) to remove first derivatives and classify the resulting radial equation.
C.4. Expanding spiral
Use \(x(0)=1,y(0)=0,\dot x(0)=1,\dot y(0)=-1\) in the linearly growing case \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}=0\). Find beta, gamma, table rates, charge sign and sketch the trajectory. The source leaves the condition beta prime equals zero implicit in this part.
C.5. Spiral energy growth
For the C.4 spiral, find leading total energy change after N much greater than one revolutions and the change per revolution. In this part use \(m=r=1\) and the explicit local value \(I=1/11\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\). Explain any inconsistency with the preceding inertia.

children.text: The bottom contact velocity equals the local table velocity: \(\mathbf v-r\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\Omega\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf R\). Thus \[\mathbf v=\Omega J\mathbf R+r\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}.\]

If friction is \(\mathbf F\), then \(m\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf F\) and \(I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=-rJ\mathbf F\). Differentiate the rolling constraint and eliminate friction to get \(\dot{\mathbf v}=\alpha\Omega J\mathbf v\).
Constant \(\alpha\Omega\) allows direct integration: \[\mathbf v=\mathbf v_0+\alpha\Omega J(\mathbf R-\mathbf R_0).\]

Put \(q=\alpha\Omega\). Then \[\mathbf R(t)=\mathbf R_0+\frac{\sin qt}{q}\mathbf v_0+\frac{1-\cos qt}{q}J\mathbf v_0.\] It is a circle of radius \(|\mathbf v_0/q|\), centred at \(\mathbf R_c=\mathbf R_0+J\mathbf v_0/q\). The q=0 limit is straight-line motion.
A.5. Return to a table mark

The ball-circle angular rate is \(q=2\Omega/7\). Both the ball and the mark certainly return together at \(t=14\pi/|\Omega|\). An earlier coincidence depends on the specified initial velocity direction and the second intersection of the two equal-radius circles. The source gives \(14\pi/(9|\Omega|)\) for a special crossing configuration, not a universal first-return time. To determine the actual earliest time for the given vectors solve \(\mathbf R(t)=\mathcal R(\Omega t)\mathbf R_0\) with the explicit A.4 trajectory. A tangent, coincident-circle or differently oriented initial geometry can change the earlier solutions.

Combining the rolling and spin equations still gives \[\dot{\mathbf v}=\alpha(\dot\Omega J\mathbf R+\Omega J\mathbf v).\] Integrating, \(\mathbf v=\alpha\Omega J\mathbf R+\mathbf c\), where \(\mathbf c=\mathbf v_0-\alpha\Omega_0J\mathbf R_0\) is constant.

Table torque is \(I_d\dot\Omega=-m(\mathbf R\times\dot{\mathbf v})_z\). Substitution yields \[(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\dot\Omega=-\alpha m\Omega\,\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R.\] This determines the sign as well as the magnitude.

Since \(\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf R=\tfrac12dR^2/dt\), integration gives \[\Omega^2=\Omega_0^2\frac{I_d+\alpha mR_0^2}{I_d+\alpha mR^2}.\] The sign of the rotation remains that of the initial rate when it is nonzero.
The denominator is smallest at R=0, giving \[|\Omega|_{max}=|\Omega_0|\sqrt{1+\alpha mR_0^2/I_d}.\] This is an upper bound. A particular trajectory need not pass through the centre.

Total vertical angular momentum is \(M_z=I_d\Omega+m(\mathbf R\times\mathbf v)_z+I\omega_z\). The last term is constant, so define \(L=M_z-I\omega_z\). With \(\mathbf c=c\hat{\mathbf x}\), \[L=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)-mcy.\] Put \(C=\Omega_0^2(I_d+\alpha mR_0^2)\). Combining with B.3 gives \[(L+mcy)^2=C[I_d+\alpha m(x^2+y^2)].\] This is a conic: ellipse if \(C\alpha m>m^2c^2\), parabola if equal, hyperbola if smaller, with degenerate cases separately possible. Squaring loses the sign constraint \(L+mcy=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\), so retain the branch consistent with the initial data. Several signs and coefficient expansions in the source solution are inconsistent. The conserved-form equation avoids them.

The uniform surface charge has magnetic moment \(\boldsymbol\mu=Qr^2\boldsymbol\omega/3\). Thus \[m\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf F+Q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,\quad I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=-rJ\mathbf F+\frac{Qr^2}{3}\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf B.\]

Differentiate the rolling relation and substitute the C.1 equations. With \(A=I+mr^2\), \[A\ddot{\mathbf R}=\left(\frac{4Qr^2B}{3}-I\Omega\right)\dot{\mathbf R}\times\hat{\mathbf z}-\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3}\mathbf R.\] Every coefficient retains the signed table rate and charge.

\[\gamma=\frac{4Qr^2B/3-I\Omega}{I+mr^2},\qquad\beta=\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3(I+mr^2)}.\] The numerator of beta includes Omega, omitted in one source line. A rotating-frame substitution with \(\eta=-\gamma t/2+\phi\) gives \(\ddot\rho+\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}\rho=0\), \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}=\beta+\gamma^2/4\), for solutions with a fixed direction in that rotating frame. More generally the two rotating Cartesian components each satisfy that oscillator equation. Positive beta prime gives harmonic components, zero gives linear components, negative gives exponential components. A general polar radius also has an angular-momentum term, so the scalar radial form is not universal.

The initial phase rate is -1, so \(\gamma=2\), while \(\beta=-1\). The solution is \[x=(1+t)\cos t,\qquad y=-(1+t)\sin t.\] It spirals clockwise with linearly increasing radius. For \(I=mr^2/10\), \(\alpha=1/11\) and \(\gamma=4\beta/\Omega-\alpha\Omega\), so \(\Omega=-11\pm\sqrt{77}\). Both table rates are negative. Since beta is proportional to Q times Omega and B is positive, Q is positive. The source says negative, contradicting its own beta formula. Initial data alone do not determine beta and gamma without the specified linearly growing case.

For \(\rho=1+t\), \(v^2=1+\rho^2\). The horizontal spin from rolling is \(\boldsymbol\omega_h=J\mathbf v+\Omega\mathbf R\), so \(\omega_h^2=1+(1+\Omega)^2\rho^2\). Vertical spin is constant. Thus \[\Delta E=\tfrac12[1+I(1+\Omega)^2][(1+t)^2-1].\] At \(t\simeq2\pi N\), \(\Delta E\simeq2\pi^2N^2[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\), with per-revolution increment \(\simeq4\pi^2N[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\). The source replaces the signed factor by \((1+|\Omega|)^2\), which is inconsistent with the rolling constraint for the clockwise spiral. Its explicit inertia 1/11 also differs from the earlier 1/10 mass distribution. Treat this part as a local changed-inertia evaluation. If recomputing C.4 for I=1/11, use \(\alpha=1/12\) and \(\Omega=-12\pm4\sqrt6\).

Table torque is \(I_d\dot\Omega=-m(\mathbf R\times\dot{\mathbf v})_z\). Substitution yields \[(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\dot\Omega=-\alpha m\Omega\,\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R.\] This determines the sign as well as the magnitude.
B.3. Table speed versus radius
Since \(\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf R=\tfrac12dR^2/dt\), integration gives \[\Omega^2=\Omega_0^2\frac{I_d+\alpha mR_0^2}{I_d+\alpha mR^2}.\] The sign of the rotation remains that of the initial rate when it is nonzero.
B.4. Maximum possible table speed
The denominator is smallest at R=0, giving \[|\Omega|_{max}=|\Omega_0|\sqrt{1+\alpha mR_0^2/I_d}.\] This is an upper bound. A particular trajectory need not pass through the centre.
B.5. Conic trajectories
Total vertical angular momentum is \(M_z=I_d\Omega+m(\mathbf R\times\mathbf v)_z+I\omega_z\). The last term is constant, so define \(L=M_z-I\omega_z\). With \(\mathbf c=c\hat{\mathbf x}\), \[L=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)-mcy.\] Put \(C=\Omega_0^2(I_d+\alpha mR_0^2)\). Combining with B.3 gives \[(L+mcy)^2=C[I_d+\alpha m(x^2+y^2)].\] This is a conic: ellipse if \(C\alpha m>m^2c^2\), parabola if equal, hyperbola if smaller, with degenerate cases separately possible. Squaring loses the sign constraint \(L+mcy=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\), so retain the branch consistent with the initial data. Several signs and coefficient expansions in the source solution are inconsistent. The conserved-form equation avoids them.
C.1. Charged-ball equations
The uniform surface charge has magnetic moment \(\boldsymbol\mu=Qr^2\boldsymbol\omega/3\). Thus \[m\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf F+Q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,\quad I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=-rJ\mathbf F+\frac{Qr^2}{3}\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf B.\]
C.2. Magnetic acceleration
Differentiate the rolling relation and substitute the C.1 equations. With \(A=I+mr^2\), \[A\ddot{\mathbf R}=\left(\frac{4Qr^2B}{3}-I\Omega\right)\dot{\mathbf R}\times\hat{\mathbf z}-\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3}\mathbf R.\] Every coefficient retains the signed table rate and charge.
C.3. Removing the gyroscopic term
\[\gamma=\frac{4Qr^2B/3-I\Omega}{I+mr^2},\qquad\beta=\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3(I+mr^2)}.\] The numerator of beta includes Omega, omitted in one source line. A rotating-frame substitution with \(\eta=-\gamma t/2+\phi\) gives \(\ddot\rho+\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}\rho=0\), \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}=\beta+\gamma^2/4\), for solutions with a fixed direction in that rotating frame. More generally the two rotating Cartesian components each satisfy that oscillator equation. Positive beta prime gives harmonic components, zero gives linear components, negative gives exponential components. A general polar radius also has an angular-momentum term, so the scalar radial form is not universal.
C.4. Expanding spiral
The initial phase rate is -1, so \(\gamma=2\), while \(\beta=-1\). The solution is \[x=(1+t)\cos t,\qquad y=-(1+t)\sin t.\] It spirals clockwise with linearly increasing radius. For \(I=mr^2/10\), \(\alpha=1/11\) and \(\gamma=4\beta/\Omega-\alpha\Omega\), so \(\Omega=-11\pm\sqrt{77}\). Both table rates are negative. Since beta is proportional to Q times Omega and B is positive, Q is positive. The source says negative, contradicting its own beta formula. Initial data alone do not determine beta and gamma without the specified linearly growing case.
C.5. Spiral energy growth
For \(\rho=1+t\), \(v^2=1+\rho^2\). The horizontal spin from rolling is \(\boldsymbol\omega_h=J\mathbf v+\Omega\mathbf R\), so \(\omega_h^2=1+(1+\Omega)^2\rho^2\). Vertical spin is constant. Thus \[\Delta E=\tfrac12[1+I(1+\Omega)^2][(1+t)^2-1].\] At \(t\simeq2\pi N\), \(\Delta E\simeq2\pi^2N^2[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\), with per-revolution increment \(\simeq4\pi^2N[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\). The source replaces the signed factor by \((1+|\Omega|)^2\), which is inconsistent with the rolling constraint for the clockwise spiral. Its explicit inertia 1/11 also differs from the earlier 1/10 mass distribution. Treat this part as a local changed-inertia evaluation. If recomputing C.4 for I=1/11, use \(\alpha=1/12\) and \(\Omega=-12\pm4\sqrt6\).

statement.text:
Cavitation
A spherical bubble in infinite, homogeneous, inviscid, incompressible water contains vapour and possibly air. Neglect gravity, translation and air migration except where a question explicitly includes them. Vapour pressure remains at \(p_v\) through rapid evaporation and condensation, and water temperature is constant. Bubble radius is R, far-field pressure \(p_\infty\), water density \(\rho=997\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), surface tension \(\sigma=72.8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N/m}\), and \(p_v=2340\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Unless stated otherwise \(p_\infty=101\,\mathrm{kPa}\). Air is ideal with adiabatic exponent \(\gamma=1.4\), reference partial pressure q0 at radius R0, and atmospheric density \(\delta=1.29\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\). For dissolved air, Henry law is \(u=Hq\), \(H=0.24\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^2/m^2}\). Diffusivity is \(\kappa=2\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}\), with outward flux \(-\kappa\partial u/\partial r\). The supplied half-line heat-equation kernel is \([e^{-(x-y)^2/(4t)}-e^{-(x+y)^2/(4t)}]/\sqrt{4\pi t}\). Useful integrals are \(\int_0^\infty e^{-bx^2}dx=\sqrt\pi/(2\sqrt b)\) and \(\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-bx^2}dx=\sqrt\pi/(4b^{3/2})\). Several numerical values in the retained solution use different constants from the statement. Use the statement constants here.

A.1. Collapse time scale
Estimate the collapse time of a pure-vapour bubble with R0=1 mm, no surface tension, and the stated pressures. Set the dimensionless factor to one.
A.2. Critical pressure
A bubble with \(R_0=10^{-5}\,\mathrm m\) starts in equilibrium at 101 kPa. Find q0, then lower pressure gradually with isothermal air. Find the critical external pressure for unbounded growth.
B.1. Bubble equation of motion
Derive the radius equation and insert adiabatic air pressure.
B.2. Exposure to vacuum
A 10 micrometre nucleus initially in equilibrium at 101 kPa is suddenly exposed to vacuum. Estimate its asymptotic growth speed and the time scale to reach that regime.
B.3. Pressure-jump rebound
A 10 micrometre gas bubble starts in equilibrium at \(p^-_\infty=1600\,\mathrm{Pa}\), then the far pressure jumps to 101 kPa. Estimate minimum radius before rebound.
B.4. Final-collapse exponent
For pure vapour with complete collapse at time T, find alpha in \(R\sim(T-t)^\alpha\).
B.5. Bubble resonance
Find the natural radial frequency of an equilibrium bubble of radius R0=0.1 mm.
B.6. Standing-wave force
A small bubble at x=0 is driven by \(p=p_0+A\sin[k(x+a)]\sin\omega t\), \(\omega=2\pi f,k=\omega/c\). Find the mean force, treating the small response linearly away from resonance.
C.1. Diffusive dissolution

C.2. Air trapped in a crevice

A conical wall crevice has aperture alpha and water contact angle theta as shown. State mechanical and diffusive equilibrium and when the pocket survives.

children.text: Dimensional analysis using the positive driving pressure gives \[T\sim R_0\sqrt{\rho/(p_\infty-p_v)}=1.01\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm s.\] The retained solution prints 0.1 s, a factor of 1000 too large.

Laplace balance gives \(q_0=p_\infty-p_v+2\sigma/R_0=113220\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Isothermal conservation gives \(q=q_0R_0^3/R^3\), hence \(p_\infty(R)=p_v+q_0R_0^3/R^3-2\sigma/R\). Its minimum occurs at \(R_c=\sqrt{3q_0R_0^3/(2\sigma)}=48.3\,\mu\mathrm m\). Therefore \(p_c=p_v-4\sigma/(3R_c)\simeq331\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The published q0 and threshold use different surface-tension data.

Incompressibility gives radial water speed \(v(r,t)=R^2\dot R/r^2\). Integrate the radial Euler equation from R to infinity and add the Laplace jump. The Rayleigh-Plesset equation without viscosity is \[\rho(R\ddot R+\tfrac32\dot R^2)=p_v+q_0(R_0/R)^{3\gamma}-p_\infty-2\sigma/R.\] The vapour term stays constant while the air term changes adiabatically.

The formal large-radius limit is \(\dot R_\infty=\sqrt{2p_v/(3\rho)}=1.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\), but one must first check whether the initial bubble can reach that branch. With the adiabatic air law from B.1, \(q_0=113220\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and \(x=R/R_0\), integration of the radius equation gives \[\dot R^2=\frac2\rho\left[\frac{p_v}{3}(1-x^{-3})+\frac{q_0}{3(1-\gamma)}(x^{-3\gamma}-x^{-3})-\frac\sigma{R_0}(x^{-1}-x^{-3})\right].\] The right-hand side first returns to zero at \(x=5.26846\), after about \(7.06\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\). The bubble therefore reaches about 52.7 micrometres and rebounds. It cannot cross the negative-square-speed interval to the formal unbounded branch. Thus the stated adiabatic model has no accessible terminal growth speed or settling time for these initial data. If the air is instead kept isothermal, the critical pressure from A.2 is positive, vacuum lies below it and unbounded expansion is possible. Its formal limiting speed is then 1.25 m/s. The source's initial estimate \(\dot R_\infty/\ddot R(0)\simeq1.2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm s\) is not a settling time, even in that alternative model. State the thermal assumption and compare both interpretations. This part requires self-review.

Initial balance gives \(q_0=1600-2340+14560=13820\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Multiply the motion equation by \(R^2\dot R\) and integrate. At a turning point, with \(x=R/R_0\), \[0=\frac{p_\infty-p_v}{3}(x^3-1)+\frac\sigma{R_0}(x^2-1)+\frac{q_0}{3(\gamma-1)}(x^{3-3\gamma}-1).\] Select the smaller positive root, excluding initial x=1. It gives a radius of about 3 micrometres. The source estimate 0.4 micrometres uses a much smaller q0 that is inconsistent with the statement. The source small-radius asymptotic formula is not reliable at the corrected moderate compression.
The dominant inward kinetic-energy balance gives \(\dot R\sim-R^{-3/2}\). Integrating yields \(R^{5/2}\propto T-t\), so \(\alpha=2/5\).

Linearize with \(R=R_0(1+y)\): \[\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=0,\quad\omega_0^2=\frac{3\gamma q_0-2\sigma/R_0}{\rho R_0^2},\quad q_0=p_\infty-p_v+2\sigma/R_0.\] Hence \(f_0=\omega_0/(2\pi)\simeq32.6\,\mathrm{kHz}\).

The external pressure drives \(\rho R_0^2(\ddot y+\omega_0^2y)=-A\sin(ka)\sin\omega t\). Thus \(y=-A\sin(ka)\sin\omega t/[\rho R_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)]\). Average \(F_x=-\langle V\partial_xp\rangle\) with \(V\simeq4\pi R_0^3(1+3y)/3\): \[\langle F_x\rangle=\frac{\pi R_0A^2k\sin(2ka)}{\rho(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}=\frac{fA^2R_0\sin(4\pi fa/c)}{2\rho c(f_0^2-f^2)}.\] Below resonance bubbles are driven towards pressure antinodes. The retained solution loses the minus sign in the pressure forcing and consequently reverses the force. At resonance the undamped steady linear formula fails.

The spherical diffusion equation is \(u_t=\kappa(u_{rr}+2u_r/r)\). The quasi-steady profile gives outward air loss \(dm/dt=-4\pi\kappa RH(q-p_\infty)\). Mechanical equilibrium requires \(q=p_\infty+2\sigma/R\). With \(m=(4\pi/3)\delta(q/p_\infty)R^3\) and \(\epsilon=2\sigma\delta/p_\infty\), integration gives \[T=\frac{\delta R_0^3+\epsilon R_0^2}{6\sigma\kappa H}\simeq7\,\mathrm s.\] Direct integration of \(\delta R^2+(2/3)\epsilon R\) produces epsilon with coefficient one, not four as printed in the retained solution. The stated q=170 kPa is also not in mechanical equilibrium at R0 with the other given constants, which instead imply 115.56 kPa. Using a fixed prescribed q throughout gives a different approximate diffusion-only model. The self-consistent equilibrium estimate above explains this limitation rather than imposing a unique numerical key.
C.2. Air trapped in a crevice

The interface obeys \(p_v+q=p_\infty\pm2\sigma/R\) with curvature sign chosen from the geometry, and \(u=Hq\). A curvature that opposes diffusive squeezing allows a stable trapped pocket. With the source contact-angle convention its geometric condition is \(2\theta>\pi+\alpha\). The angle convention and curvature orientation are essential.

children.text: A door hinge is a thin hollow open-ended cylinder of radius \(r\), height \(h\) and thickness \(\Delta r\ll r\), pressing on its base with the weight of the whole door, mass \(M\). Its upper end turns with the rigid door, while its lower rim sticks. For shear angle \(\alpha\), \(dF=G\alpha\,dS\). Find torsional coefficient \(\kappa=\tau/\theta\). Use \(r=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(h=3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(\Delta r=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(G=8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

Use \(\mu_s=0.75\), \(\mu_k=0.55\), \(M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). For slow opening, find the angular speed giving 20 Hz sound pulses. Assume the pure-slip oscillation frequency is much greater than 20 Hz. Give a formula and numerical value.

statement.text:
Creaking Door
A block of mass \(m\) is attached to an ideal spring of constant \(k\). The other end is driven right at speed \(u\). Floor friction coefficients satisfy \(\mu_k<\mu_s\). Let \(x\) be spring elongation, \(x_k=\mu_kmg/k\), and \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). Pure slip has kinetic friction throughout. Stick-slip alternates static and kinetic friction and can create creaking pulses.

a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude
Initially the block slides at speed \(0<v_0<u\) and \(x(0)=x_k\). Find the period and elongation amplitude.
a2. Elongation sketch
Sketch \(x(t)\) for \(0<t<3T_0\).
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
Now start the block at rest, still with \(x(0)=x_k\). Sketch laboratory velocity \(v(t)\) for three periods, and mark \(v=u\).
c. Mean elongation
For the initial conditions of b, find long-time mean elongation.
d. Stick-slip period
Find the new oscillation period.
e. Critical driving speed
Suppose the oscillation amplitude loses a small fraction \(\eta\ll1\) per pure-slip period through additional spring dissipation. Find the critical speed above which periodic stick-slip is impossible.
f. Hinge torsional stiffness

A door hinge is a thin hollow open-ended cylinder of radius \(r\), height \(h\) and thickness \(\Delta r\ll r\), pressing on its base with the weight of the whole door, mass \(M\). Its upper end turns with the rigid door, while its lower rim sticks. For shear angle \(\alpha\), \(dF=G\alpha\,dS\). Find torsional coefficient \(\kappa=\tau/\theta\). Use \(r=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(h=3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(\Delta r=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(G=8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
g. Audible door speed
Use \(\mu_s=0.75\), \(\mu_k=0.55\), \(M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). For slow opening, find the angular speed giving 20 Hz sound pulses. Assume the pure-slip oscillation frequency is much greater than 20 Hz. Give a formula and numerical value.

children.text: Since \(\dot x=u-v\), the moving equation gives \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2(x-x_k)=0\). Thus \[T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\qquad A=(u-v_0)\sqrt{m/k}.\] The minimum block speed stays positive for the stated initial conditions.
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.

The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
In the frame of the driven end, the slip arc and uniform stick segment are symmetric about \(x_k\). Their mean displacement is zero, giving \(\overline x=\mu_kmg/k\).

Put \(q=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The stuck distance in the driven frame is \(2(x_s-x_k)\), so \(t_{stick}=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/(ku)\). The slipping phase misses angle \(2\arctan q\) of a full oscillator cycle. Therefore \[T=2\sqrt{m/k}\,[q+\pi-\arctan q].\]

At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]

Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).

Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

solution.text:
Creaking Door
a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude
Since \(\dot x=u-v\), the moving equation gives \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2(x-x_k)=0\). Thus \[T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\qquad A=(u-v_0)\sqrt{m/k}.\] The minimum block speed stays positive for the stated initial conditions.
a2. Elongation sketch
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
c. Mean elongation
In the frame of the driven end, the slip arc and uniform stick segment are symmetric about \(x_k\). Their mean displacement is zero, giving \(\overline x=\mu_kmg/k\).
d. Stick-slip period
Put \(q=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The stuck distance in the driven frame is \(2(x_s-x_k)\), so \(t_{stick}=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/(ku)\). The slipping phase misses angle \(2\arctan q\) of a full oscillator cycle. Therefore \[T=2\sqrt{m/k}\,[q+\pi-\arctan q].\]
e. Critical driving speed
At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]
f. Hinge torsional stiffness
Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).
g. Audible door speed
Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

children.text: Equipartition gives mvz²/2=3kBT/2, so vz≈\(5.26\times10^{2}\) m/s.

Transverse acceleration magnitude is μs|Gx|/m. Its deflection during the magnet and subsequent drift is \(\mu_s|G_x|[l_2^2/2+l_2l_3]/(mv_z^2)\). Two opposite moments double this: \[\Delta x=\frac{2\mu_s|G_x|l_2(l_2/2+l_3)}{mv_z^2}.\] The pre-magnet distance l1 has no effect.

Superpose the two wire fields. Let \(D_\pm=x^2+(y\pm a)^2\). Then \[\mathbf B=\frac{\mu I_0a}{\pi D_+D_-}[(x^2-y^2+a^2)\hat x+2xy\hat y].\] This sign matches the stated upper +z and lower −z currents.
c.2. Field direction on a circular boundary

At R, y=0 and B points +x. At P0=(xc,√(xc²+a²)) the x component vanishes and the field points +y for xc>0. More generally on this right-hand circular arc the field is normal to the circle, as its cross product with (x−xc,y) vanishes.
Set y=0 in C1: \(\mathbf B=\mu I_0a\hat x/[\pi(x^2+a^2)]\). The permeability in this model remains μ from the original magnetic circuit.

Differentiate Bx. For x>0 the gradient is negative, \(dB_x/dx=-2\mu I_0ax/[\pi(x^2+a^2)^2]\). The force magnitude is \(2\mu_s\mu I_0a|x|/[\pi(x^2+a^2)^2]\), with opposite signs for opposite moments. The field checks x>0.
e.1. Field and gradient at P
The right intersections are xR=xc+√(xc²+a²) and xQ=xd+√(xd²+a²). Thus xP=(xR+xQ)/2≈0.01624 m. Substitution gives B≈0.160 T and gradient magnitude ≈17.3 T/m. The signed gradient is negative.
Invert B1: \(\mu_s=m\Delta x\,v_z^2/[2|G_x|l_2(l_2/2+l_3)]\). With |Gx|≈17.34 T/m this gives μs≈\(1.04\times10^{-23}\) J/T.

Each spot displacement is xspot=Δx/2=0.10 cm and scales as vz⁻². Linear error propagation gives |δxspot|/xspot=2|δvz|/vz. Interpreting 20% as ±20% gives ±0.04 cm, hence positions from 0.06 to 0.14 cm in magnitude. If 20% is the full speed width, use ±10% and half this spot uncertainty. The source accepts both conventions.

Under the ±20% speed convention the inferred splitting uncertainty is ±40%, so \(\mu_s=(1.04\pm0.42)\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/T}\). The full interval is approximately 0.62 to \(1.46\times10^{-23}\) J/T. A full-width 20% convention gives half that uncertainty. The source omits the factor \(10^{-23}\) in its final line, restored here.

children.text: A Mechanical Model for Phase Transitions

A bead of mass m slides on a ring of radius R rotating about its vertical diameter at angular speed \(\omega\). Angle \(\theta\) is measured from the downward vertical, with \(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\). Let \(\omega_c=\sqrt{g/R}\). In the stated rotating-frame model, the only forces are gravity, the radial normal N, centrifugal force and opposing tangential force \(-fkN\), with \(f=\operatorname{sgn}\dot\theta\). Use this simplified force diagram, omitting any additional forces. For B.1 through B.9 set k=0. Landau free energy has the form \(V(\mathcal M)=a(T)\mathcal M^2+b(T)\mathcal M^4\), with b positive and a changing sign at the transition. Expansions \(\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+\cdots\), \(\cos\theta=1-\theta^2/2+\theta^4/24+\cdots\) may be used.

Expansions \(\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+\cdots\), \(\cos\theta=1-\theta^2/2+\theta^4/24+\cdots\) may be used.


A.1. Radial and tangential equations
Write both equations of motion, with angle increasing counterclockwise.
B.1. Equilibrium branches
Find equilibrium angles in terms of \(\omega,\omega_c\).
B.2. Equilibrium-angle plot
Sketch equilibrium angles against \(\omega/\omega_c\).
B.3. Normal-reaction plot
Sketch normal-reaction magnitude at stable equilibrium against the rotation-rate ratio.
B.4. Effective-potential coefficients
With \(F_\theta=-R^{-1}dV/d\theta\), \(V(0)=0\), and \(V=P+Q\cos\theta+S\sin^2\theta\), determine P,Q,S.
B.5. Quartic expansion
Find \(a(\omega),b(\omega)\) in \(V\simeq a\theta^2+b\theta^4\).
B.6. Potential plots
Sketch V against angle for \(\omega/\omega_c=0.9\) and 5, without detailed plotting calculations.
B.7. Critical-exponent analogy

B.8. Small-oscillation frequency

B.9. Frequency plot
Sketch the small-oscillation frequency against rotation rate.
