children.text: A Mechanical Model for Phase Transitions

With N directed towards the centre, \[mR\dot\theta^2=N-mg\cos\theta-mR\omega^2\sin^2\theta,\] \[mR\ddot\theta=mR\omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-mg\sin\theta-fkN.\] These are the stipulated two-component model.

The tangential equation gives \(\sin\theta_0(\omega^2\cos\theta_0-\omega_c^2)=0\). The branch \(\theta_0=0\) always exists. For \(\omega>\omega_c\), additional branches are \(\theta_0=\pm\arccos(\omega_c^2/\omega^2)\). The zero branch becomes unstable above threshold.
The stable zero branch continues to ratio 1, where it bifurcates continuously into two symmetric stable branches approaching \(\pm\pi/2\). Show the remaining zero branch as unstable above 1.

Below threshold the bead sits at the bottom and \(N=mg\). Above threshold substitute \(\cos\theta_0=\omega_c^2/\omega^2\) in the radial equation to get \(N=mR\omega^2\). The curve is continuous at the threshold and then quadratic.
Integrating the tangential force gives \[V=mgR(1-\cos\theta)-\tfrac12mR^2\omega^2\sin^2\theta.\] Thus \(P=mgR,Q=-mgR,S=-mR^2\omega^2/2\).

Expand both cosine and sine squared through fourth order: \[a=\frac{mgR}{2}(1-\omega^2/\omega_c^2),\qquad b=\frac{mgR}{6}(\omega^2/\omega_c^2-1/4).\] In particular the quartic coefficient is positive near the transition.

At 0.9, V has one minimum at zero. At 5, the zero-angle point is a local maximum between symmetric minima at \(\pm\arccos(1/25)\). Use the full potential on the allowed interval for the distant minima, since a small-angle quartic expansion is not accurate there.

Near threshold, \(1-\theta_0^2/2\simeq\omega_c^2/\omega^2\), so \(\theta_0\simeq\pm\sqrt2(1-\omega_c^2/\omega^2)^{1/2}\). Thus magnetization corresponds to \(\theta_0\), reduced temperature to \(\omega_c^2/\omega^2\), and the exponent is \(\beta=1/2\). Equivalently use \(\sin\theta_0\) and reduced temperature \(\omega_c^4/\omega^4\).

At zero below threshold, \(\Omega_0=\sqrt{\omega_c^2-\omega^2}\). At the nonzero stable branches above threshold, \(\Omega_0=\omega\sqrt{1-\omega_c^4/\omega^4}\). Both tend to zero at threshold, where a harmonic approximation has zero stiffness.

The curve starts at \(\Omega_0=\omega_c\) for zero rotation, decreases to zero at \(\omega_c\), then rises and approaches \(\Omega_0\sim\omega\). Both sides have the square-root softening near threshold.

With zero velocity and acceleration in the stipulated limiting-force model, \[\frac{\omega^2}{\omega_c^2}=\frac{\sin\theta_0+k\cos\theta_0}{\sin\theta_0(\cos\theta_0-k\sin\theta_0)}=\frac{\tan(\theta_0+\alpha)}{\sin\theta_0}.\] Thus \(x=\theta_0+\alpha,y=\theta_0\). The equality prescribes a directional limiting friction force. True static friction would allow an interval bounded by this force rather than a unique equilibrium equality.

Using \(\tan(\theta_0+\alpha)\simeq\theta_0+k\) and \(\sin\theta_0\simeq\theta_0\), \[\theta_0\simeq k/[(\omega/\omega_c)^2-1].\] The estimates are \(-0.0667\) and \(-0.0980\) radians, rounded to \(-0.07,-0.10\) in the source. Exact roots of the limiting-force equation are approximately \(-0.0665,-0.0971\) radians.

children.text: Model a neutral air molecule as a fixed point charge +q inside a uniform spherical negative cloud of total charge −q,mass m,radius r. Its small natural vibration frequency is ω0. Light drives E=E0cosωt ŷ and cloud displacement y=y0cosωt. Use the negative charge sign in its force. For low-frequency radiation assume ω≪ω0. Mean optical intensity is I=cε0E0²/2. Molecule number density is n0 and scattered power per molecule is s. For numerical estimates take q=e=\(1.602\times10^{-19}\) C,m=me=\(9.109\times10^{-31}\) kg,ε0=\(8.854\times10^{-12}\) SI,c=\(3.0\times10^{8}\) m/s,n0=\(2.54\times10^{25}\) m⁻³,ω0=\(1.25\times10^{16}\) rad/s and ω=\(3.25\times10^{15}\) rad/s. children.text: The restoring acceleration is −ω0²y and the electric force is −qE. Hence \(\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=-(qE_0/m)\cos\omega t\).

Substitute y=y0cosωt to obtain \(y_0=qE_0/[m(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)]\). This signed coefficient is negative below resonance. The nonnegative amplitude is its absolute value. The steady particular solution excludes free oscillations and resonance.

The dipole vector points from negative to positive charge, so \(\mathbf p=-qy\hat y\simeq[q^2E_0/(m\omega_0^2)]\cos\omega t\hat y\). Its oscillation amplitude is q²E0/(mω0²), and its instantaneous magnitude takes the absolute value of the cosine. This distinguishes the signed sinusoid from the nonnegative magnitude.
Inside the uniform cloud the field grows linearly with displacement. Action and reaction give restoring force \(-q^2y/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). Therefore \(\omega_0=q/\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0mr^3}\).
Matching dimensions in s=kp0αωβε0γcδ gives α=2,β=4,γ=−1,δ=−3. Thus \(s=k p_0^2\omega^4/(\epsilon_0c^3)\).
Balance power in a slab of area A and thickness dx: I(x)A−I(x+dx)A=n0sA dx. Hence \(dI/dx=-n_0s\). Since s∝E0²∝I this is dI/dx=−I/L.
Combine B2 with I=cε0E0²/2 to obtain \[L=\frac{6\pi\epsilon_0^2m^2c^4}{n_0q^4}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\omega}\right)^4,\qquad I(x)=I_0e^{-x/L}.\]
Substitution of the supplied molecular and optical data gives approximately L=130 km. The source uses rounded constants and a ten-percent numerical acceptance range.

Let θ=d/R. In the source projection construction the local horizontal through the observer intersects the mountain radius at radius (R+h)secθ. Similar triangles give \[H^{\prime}=R+h-\frac{(R+h)^2}{R+H}\sec(d/R).\] To leading order in h/R,H/R,d/R, \(H^{\prime}\simeq H-h-d^2/(2R)\). The full source construction gives approximately 6096 m for Kanchenjunga and 4534 m for Everest. Both extend above the local horizontal. Show Earth centre, observer radius, mountain radius and the observer's tangent line.

For equal effective luminosities, \[\frac{I_E}{I_K}=\left(\frac{75}{170}\right)^2e^{-(170-75)/130}\simeq0.093.\] The distances and L must use the same units. This exceeds 0.05, so Everest is visible in this model.
\(L_p=1/(8n\pi r^2)\). Each particle has mass 4πr³ρ/3, so n=ρp/(4πr³ρ/3), giving \(L_p=r\rho/(6\rho_p)\). Convert ρp=\(5\times10^{-9}\) kg/m³ and ρ=3000 kg/m³ to obtain Lp=50 km.

The total attenuation has exponent −d/L−d/Lp. Thus \(I_K/I_{ref}=e^{-75/50}\simeq0.223\), while \(I_E/I_{ref}=0.093e^{-170/50}\simeq0.0031\). Kanchenjunga remains above 5%, while Everest does not. The reference remains the unpolluted Kanchenjunga intensity, rather than being reset after pollution.

statement.text:
Water-hammer effect
A nonviscous liquid flows one-dimensionally in a rigid pipe of length L and radius R. A reservoir feeds its upstream end B at depth h below the free surface, and a valve at downstream end A opens to atmosphere Pa. Water has reference density ρ0=1000 kg/m³ and bulk modulus B=2.2 GPa, defined for the finite element by \(\Delta P=-B\Delta V/V_0\). Initially flow velocity is v0 in +x with pressure P0. A pressure front moves upstream at positive laboratory speed c. Valve closure changes downstream fluid velocity to v1≤0 in A. The short valve has opening radius r, cone angle β, and a contracted atmospheric jet of radius rc=r√Cc. Its inlet and contracted-jet streamlines are parallel. Contraction data (r/R,Cc at 45°,Cc at 90°) are (0,.746,.611),(.2,.747,.616),(.3,.748,.622),(.4,.749,.631),(1,1,1). For C and D treat c and ρ0 as constants, neglect valve length, use β=90° and use the incompressible steady-valve relation locally. In D additionally approximate reservoir pressure Ph by P0, as requested for the wave-reflection model, without resetting the given initial flow to zero.

a.1. Wave pressure and speed
Find α,β,γ in ΔPs=αρ0c(v1−v0) and c=β+√(γB/ρ0). State the small-flow-speed limit.
a.2. Sudden-closure magnitude
Calculate c and ΔPs for v0=4.0 m/s and v1=0.
b.1. Valve pressure relation

Find ΔPin=Pin−Pa in terms of ρ0,vin,r,R,Cc.
c.1. Fully open initial flow
Find P0 and v0 in terms of ρ0,g,h,Pa.
c.2. First round trip after closure
At t=0 close the valve instantly. Let τ=2L/c and Ph=P0+ρ0gh. Find pipe pressure and velocity just before t=τ/2 and just before t=τ, explaining the reflected wave.
d.1. Finite-step closure recursion
At times 0,τ,2τ,3τ set rn/R to .4,.3,.2,0 respectively. Let ΔPn=Pn−P0, v4=0 and ΔP0=0. Enforcing Ph≈P0, derive ΔPn/(ρ0c) from the previous step and an equation for vn for n=1,2,3.
d.2. Graphical pressure-velocity construction
For v0=4.0 m/s plot ΔP against X=ρ0cv in MPa. Draw the straight lines and valve curves for all four steps, label their intersections, and estimate (Xn,ΔPn). You may use c≈1500 m/s.

children.text: In the front frame continuity gives ρ0(c+v0)=ρ1(c+v1). Momentum gives ΔPs=−ρ0(c+v0)(v1−v0). The finite-volume modulus gives ΔPs=B(ρ1−ρ0)/ρ1. Combining yields c+v0=√(B/ρ0). Thus \(\alpha=-(1+v_0/c),\ \beta=-v_0,\ \gamma=1\). For v0≪c, c≈√(B/ρ0) and ΔPs≈−ρ0cΔv. A density-based linearized modulus changes higher-order terms, as discussed in the source.

The acoustic speed relative to water is √(B/ρ0)=1483 m/s, and the upstream laboratory front speed is 1479 m/s. At source precision c≈\(1.5\times10^{3}\) m/s. The pressure rise is v0√(ρ0B)≈5.93 MPa. The field checks the pressure in MPa.

Continuity gives \(v_c=v_{in}R^2/(C_cr^2)\). Bernoulli between the parallel sections gives \[\Delta P_{in}=\frac{\rho_0v_{in}^2}{2}\left[\frac1{C_c^2}\left(\frac Rr\right)^4-1\right].\] This applies for nonzero opening, not at the fully closed limit with zero flow.
At r=R, Cc=1 so inlet and outlet speeds agree and P0=Pa. Bernoulli from the reservoir free surface gives \(v_0=\sqrt{2gh}\).
c.2. First round trip after closure

Just before τ/2 the compression front has nearly reached B, leaving virtually the whole pipe at \(P=P_0+\rho_0cv_0\), v=0. The fixed-pressure reservoir reflects an expansion of amplitude Ph−P1. Just before τ the return front has nearly reached A, leaving \(P=P_h\) and \(v=-v_0+gh/c\). The infinitesimal regions ahead of each front retain the previous state. At the exact closed boundary velocity remains zero until the incoming front reflects, so the stated limits refer to the pipe interior.

After each reservoir reflection, the arriving valve-side velocity is \(v_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}/(\rho_0c)\). The next upstream wave therefore gives \[\frac{\Delta P_n}{\rho_0c}=v_{n-1}-v_n-\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}.\] For n<4 set \(k_n=(R/r_n)^4/C_n^2-1\) and use ΔPn=ρ0knvn²/2. Thus \[\frac{k_n}{2c}v_n^2+v_n+\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}-v_{n-1}=0.\] Choose the nonnegative root. For n=4 use v4=0 directly in the recursion.

Each step line is \(\Delta P=-X+X_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}\). The valve parabola is \(\Delta P=k_nX^2/(2\rho_0c^2)\), with kn≈97.1,318,1646 for the first three openings. Starting at (6,0) MPa, intersections are approximately (5.37,0.624), (3.75,0.997), (1.695,1.06) and (0,0.643) MPa. The fourth curve is the vertical line X=0. Slow staged closure keeps these peaks well below the 6 MPa sudden-closure estimate. The source's first graphical table contains a mistyped 5.8 MPa coordinate, corrected by its appendix to 5.37 MPa.

children.text: Ray tracing and generation of entangled light

For a plane wave in a nonmagnetic dielectric use \(\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf H\), \(\mathbf k\times\mathbf E=\omega\mathbf B\), \(\mathbf k\times\mathbf H=-\omega\mathbf D\), energy density \(u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf B)/2\) and Poynting vector S=E×H. Ray speed is |S|/u. In A take D=εE. In B the optic axis is z and D=(εEx,εEy,ε′Ez), with no=c√(μ0ε), ne=c√(μ0ε′). Initially k=k(sinθ,0,cosθ). A signed angle from E to D, or from S to k, is positive clockwise in the source xz view. For refraction the interface is yz, incident medium isotropic with index n, and the crystal axes x2,z2 are rotated by φ as shown. In C a nonzero quadratic polarization \(P_i^{NL}=\sum_{jk}\chi^{(2)}_{ijk}E_jE_k\) couples three waves. Positive frequencies satisfy ω≥ω2 and ω1≥ω2. Use photon energy ℏω and momentum ℏk. The specified entangled pair is \((|x'_ay'_b\rangle+|y'_ax'_b\rangle)/\sqrt2\). Linear polarizers at a,b have axes at α,β measured from x′, and perpendicular settings add π/2.

a.2. Isotropic index
Find n.
a.3. Isotropic ray
Find the energy-flow direction and ray speed.

b.2. Polarizations and walk-off angle

b.3. Arbitrary propagation azimuth

b.4. Extraordinary energy flow

children.text: Ray tracing and generation of entangled light
Eliminate B,H from Maxwell equations. With k·E=0, k²E=ω²μ0εE. Thus \(v_p=\omega/k=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon}\).
E,H,k are mutually orthogonal and E×H points along k. The electric and magnetic energy densities are equal, so u=|S|/vp. Thus Ŝ=k̂ and vr=vp=1/√(μ0ε).

The ordinary mode has D̂=±ŷ, B̂=±(−cosθ,0,sinθ) and n=no. The extraordinary mode has D̂=±(cosθ,0,−sinθ), B̂=±ŷ with correlated signs and \[n(\theta)=\frac{n_on_e}{\sqrt{n_o^2\sin^2\theta+n_e^2\cos^2\theta}}.\] At θ=0 or π both indices equal no. For a genuinely anisotropic crystal these are the optic-axis directions.

The ordinary mode has Ê=±ŷ and α=0. The extraordinary direction is \[\hat E=\pm\frac{(n_e^2\cos\theta,0,-n_o^2\sin\theta)}{\sqrt{n_e^4\cos^2\theta+n_o^4\sin^2\theta}}.\] Comparing slopes of E and D gives \[\tan\alpha=\frac{(n_o^2-n_e^2)\tan\theta}{n_e^2+n_o^2\tan^2\theta}.\] Overall sign of polarization is immaterial.

Let \(\hat t=(\hat k-\cos\theta\hat z)/\sin\theta\). The same two indices apply. Ordinary Ê is ±(k̂×ẑ)/sinθ. Extraordinary Ê is proportional to \(n_e^2\cos\theta\hat t-n_o^2\sin\theta\hat z\), normalized as in B2. At sinθ=0 choose any two transverse orthogonal polarizations, since the modes are degenerate. This vector form avoids the inconsistent expanded z coefficient printed in one source formula.

Ordinary light has αr=0, vr=c/no and Ŝ=k̂. For extraordinary light αr=α, and with \(D=n_e^2\cos^2\theta+n_o^2\sin^2\theta\), \(W=\sqrt{n_e^4\cos^2\theta+n_o^4\sin^2\theta}\), \[\hat S=(n_o^2\sin\theta,0,n_e^2\cos\theta)/W,\qquad v_r=\frac{cW}{n_on_e\sqrt D}=v_p/\cos\alpha_r.\] The extraordinary ray index is \(n_s=\sqrt{n_e^2(\hat S\cdot\hat x)^2+n_o^2(\hat S\cdot\hat z)^2}\). For ordinary light ns=no.

Write s=n sinθ1. Differentiating optical travel time at the interface gives \(s^2=(P_3-P_1\tan\theta_2)^2/(P_1\tan^2\theta_2-2P_3\tan\theta_2+P_2)\). Therefore \[A=P_1(s^2-P_1),\quad\bar B=-2P_3(s^2-P_1),\quad C=P_2s^2-P_3^2.\] Select the root consistent with the unsquared Fermat equation and forward energy flow. At φ=0, \(\tan\theta_2=n_es/[n_o\sqrt{n_o^2-s^2}]\). At φ=π/2, \(\tan\theta_2=n_os/[n_e\sqrt{n_e^2-s^2}]\).

Products of plane-wave phases yield sum and difference components. Matching gives \(\omega=\omega_1\pm\omega_2\), \(\mathbf k=\mathbf k_1\pm\mathbf k_2\), with consistent signs. Multiplication by ℏ gives energy and momentum conservation. Decay of the pump photon uses \(\omega=\omega_1+\omega_2\) and \(\mathbf k=\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2\).

The same-polarization channels o→o+o and e→e+e are impossible. Their parent index at the larger frequency exceeds either daughter index, while momentum matching would require a frequency-weighted average of the daughter indices. No cross-polarization channel is universally excluded without additional information relating no and ne.

Put ν=Ω−Ωe, so Ω−Ωo=−ν. The ordinary longitudinal component is \(k_{2z}=K_o-
u/u_o-q^2/(2K_o)\). The source angular approximation gives \(k_{1z}=K_e+
u/u_e+N_eq_{x'}+[N_e\cot	heta-1]q^2/(2K_e)\). Sum these and impose Kp=Ke+Ko. Completing the square gives \[M= rac{K_o(1-N_e\cot	heta)+K_e}{2K_eK_o},\quad N=- rac{N_e}{2M},\quad L=-
u(1/u_o-1/u_e)+ rac{N_e^2}{4M}.\] The centre is qx′=−N. Its tilt magnitude is |N|/Ko and cone half-angle is √(L/M)/Ko, provided L≥0. Signs describe the chosen x′ direction. The source changes coefficient letters mid-derivation and has some dimensional typos in its final angle formula. These expressions follow its stated longitudinal expansion. A general expansion retaining curvature of ne(θ) requires further second angular derivatives.

The joint transmission amplitude is (cosαsinβ+sinαcosβ)/√2. Squaring gives \[P(\alpha,\beta)=P(\alpha_\perp,\beta_\perp)=\tfrac12\sin^2(\alpha+\beta),\] \[P(\alpha,\beta_\perp)=P(\alpha_\perp,\beta)=\tfrac12\cos^2(\alpha+\beta).\] The field checks P(α,β).

The four normalized joint probabilities give \(E=-\cos[2(\alpha+\beta)]\). Therefore S is the indicated absolute-value combination of these cosines with sums of angles. At the specified settings S=2√2>2. The source incorrectly simplifies its own C4 probabilities to a difference of angles in one line, but both the consistent sum convention and a reversed b-axis convention give the same S for these settings. The field checks the numerical S.

children.text: A small spherical permanent magnet can be treated as a point dipole m=q_mδm, represented by south and north magnetic charges −qm,+qm with displacement δm from south to north. The north pole defines its position. A monopole produces \(\mathbf B=\mu_0q_m\hat r/(4\pi r^2)\) and experiences force qmB. Write B=−∇Φ. A uniform conducting film extends infinitely in xy, occupies −d≤z≤0, has conductivity σ, and lies height h below the source, with h≫d. Neglect displacement current and take induced volume current uniform across d. In A a north monopole appears at (0,0,h) at t=0 and remains there. Neglect propagation delay. Initially its image above the film calculation is +qm at (0,0,−h), and below-film calculation uses −qm at the real source position. The supplied film equation is ∂²B′z/∂z²=μ0σ∂B′z/∂t after neglecting lateral derivatives in the thin-film approximation. In B a source moves along +x at fixed h for its whole prior history and is at x=0 now. In C take a type-I superconductor with σ→∞ and a horizontally fixed dipole m x̂ of mass M0 in gravity −g ẑ. Ignore orientation coupling and air damping.

statement.text:
Magnetic levitation
A small spherical permanent magnet can be treated as a point dipole m=q_mδm, represented by south and north magnetic charges −qm,+qm with displacement δm from south to north. The north pole defines its position. A monopole produces \(\mathbf B=\mu_0q_m\hat r/(4\pi r^2)\) and experiences force qmB. Write B=−∇Φ. A uniform conducting film extends infinitely in xy, occupies −d≤z≤0, has conductivity σ, and lies height h below the source, with h≫d. Neglect displacement current and take induced volume current uniform across d. In A a north monopole appears at (0,0,h) at t=0 and remains there. Neglect propagation delay. Initially its image above the film calculation is +qm at (0,0,−h), and below-film calculation uses −qm at the real source position. The supplied film equation is ∂²B′z/∂z²=μ0σ∂B′z/∂t after neglecting lateral derivatives in the thin-film approximation. In B a source moves along +x at fixed h for its whole prior history and is at x=0 now. In C take a type-I superconductor with σ→∞ and a horizontally fixed dipole m x̂ of mass M0 in gravity −g ẑ. Ignore orientation coupling and air damping.

a.1. Initial field above the film
Find total B(ρ,z) at t=0 for z≥0 away from the monopole.
a.2. Initial field below the film
Find the initial total field for z≤−d.
a.3. Initial surface flux
Find initial magnetic flux through either film surface.
a.4. Induced current density
Find the initial induced volume current j(ρ) using the thin-film approximation.
a.5. First-order surface evolution
Integrate the film equation across thickness to obtain a first-order equation near z≈0.
a.6. Surface evolution solution
Find the general form of B′z near the surface for t>0.
a.7. Receding image speed
Show the induced field represents a downward-moving image and find its speed.
b.1. Hopping-source images
Approximate motion by hops vτ at times −nτ,n≥0. Each hop creates +qm at the new position and −qm at the old. Give present image positions for both types.
b.2. Image monopole potential
Write and evaluate the image-potential sum Φ+(x,z) in the y=0 plane as τ tends to zero.
b.3. Lift and drag on a vertical dipole

The moving dipole has fixed moment m ẑ. Find its force at the present position (0,0,h).
b.4. Copper image speed
For σ=\(5.9\times10^{7}\) Ω⁻¹m⁻¹,d=0.50 cm,h=5.0 cm calculate v0.
b.5. Skin-depth correction
The skin depth is δ=√[2/(ωμ0σ)] with ω=max(v,v0)/h. Estimate v0(v) in low- and high-speed regimes, replacing film thickness by skin depth if smaller.
b.6. Crossover speed
Find vc where the low- and high-speed estimates meet.
c.1. Superconducting equilibrium height
Find h0 for the horizontal dipole of mass M0.
c.2. Vertical oscillation frequency
Find angular frequency Ω of small vertical oscillations.
c.3. Micromagnet height
A sphere has R=1.0 μm,ρ0=7400 kg/m³,magnetization M=0.75 T/μ0 and g=9.8 m/s². Calculate h0.
c.4. Micromagnet oscillations
Calculate Ω for that sphere.

children.text: a.1. Initial field above the film

Sum the real and positive image fields: \[\mathbf B=\frac{\mu_0q_m}{4\pi}\left[\frac{\boldsymbol\rho+(z-h)\hat z}{(\rho^2+(z-h)^2)^{3/2}}+\frac{\boldsymbol\rho+(z+h)\hat z}{(\rho^2+(z+h)^2)^{3/2}}\right].\]
a.2. Initial field below the film
The negative image at the source cancels its field in the lower region, so B=0.

At z=0 the two normal components cancel pointwise, and below the film the field vanishes. The total flux through any patch of either surface is zero. The source writes B′z=0 in one explanation, but it is the total Bz that vanishes, not the image contribution by itself.

Ampère's law across the film gives \(\mathbf j=(\hat z\times\mathbf B_{above})/(\mu_0d)\). Thus \[\mathbf j=\frac{q_m}{2\pi d}\frac{\hat z\times\boldsymbol\rho}{(h^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}}.\] The current is azimuthal and produces the opposing initial normal field.

The induced normal field is even about the midplane, so its derivatives at opposite faces are opposite. Neglect variation of its time derivative across d. Integration gives \(2\partial_zB_z^{\prime}=\mu_0\sigma d\,\partial_tB_z^{\prime}\), or \(\partial_tB_z^{\prime}=v_0\partial_zB_z^{\prime}\), with v0=2/(μ0σd).
The characteristic solution is \(B_z^{\prime}(\rho,z;t)=f(\rho,z+v_0t)\), with f determined by the initial induced field.
The initial image field depends on z+h. Replacing z by z+v0t places the image at zimage=−h−v0t. Thus the downward speed is \(v_0=2/(\mu_0\sigma d)\).
Positive images are at \((-nv\tau,0,-h-nv_0\tau)\). Negative images are at \((-(n+1)v\tau,0,-h-nv_0\tau)\). Their differing lateral positions retain the history of motion.

Put H=z+h. The sum is \[\Phi_+=\frac{\mu_0q_m}{4\pi}\sum_{n\ge0}\left[\frac1{\sqrt{(x+nv\tau)^2+(H+nv_0\tau)^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{(x+(n+1)v\tau)^2+(H+nv_0\tau)^2}}\right].\] Its continuum limit is \(\mu_0q_mv/(4\pi)\int_0^\infty(x+vt)[(x+vt)^2+(H+v_0t)^2]^{-3/2}dt\). Evaluation gives \[\Phi_+=\frac{\mu_0q_mv}{4\pi(Hv-v_0x)}\left[\frac H{\sqrt{x^2+H^2}}-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right].\] At a removable zero of the denominator use the integral or its continuous limit.
b.3. Lift and drag on a vertical dipole

Form the image-dipole potential \(\Phi_T=\delta_m\partial_z\Phi_+\), differentiate for the field, then take the north-minus-south force while holding the image source fixed during field differentiation. This yields \[F_z=\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{32\pi h^4}\left(1-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right),\quad F_x=-\frac{v_0}{v}F_z,\quad F_y=0.\] Lift is positive and drag negative for v>0. Both vanish continuously as v tends to zero.

At low v the skin depth exceeds d, so v0(v)=2/(μ0σd), the B4 constant. At high v, δ<d and ω≈v/h, so \[v_0(v)=\frac2{\mu_0\sigma\delta}=\sqrt{\frac{2v}{\mu_0\sigma h}}=\sqrt{v_0dv/h}.\] This is an effective-thickness estimate beyond the uniform-through-thickness low-speed model.
Set δ=d with ω=vc/h: \(v_c=2h/(\mu_0\sigma d^2)=v_0h/d\). For the copper dimensions it is about 54 m/s.

For a perfect diamagnetic plane the horizontal image has the same horizontal moment at z=−h. Its repulsive force is \(F_z=3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi h^4)\). Balance M0g to obtain \[h_0=[3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi M_0g)]^{1/4}.\]
The derivative of the magnetic force at h0 is −4M0g/h0. Thus \(\Omega=\sqrt{4g/h_0}\). This is angular frequency in rad/s.
Use m=(4πR³/3)M and M0=(4πR³/3)ρ0. Then \(h_0=[\mu_0M^2R^3/(16\rho_0g)]^{1/4}\simeq25\,\mathrm{\mu m}\).

Using h0≈25 μm, \(\Omega\simeq1.25\times10^3\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), or f≈200 Hz. The source loosely labels the angular frequency in kHz and substitutes a rounded 30 μm in one line. Angular frequency and cycles per second are distinguished here.

Evaluation gives \[\Phi_+=\frac{\mu_0q_mv}{4\pi(Hv-v_0x)}\left[\frac H{\sqrt{x^2+H^2}}-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right].\] At a removable zero of the denominator use the integral or its continuous limit.
b.3. Lift and drag on a vertical dipole
Form the image-dipole potential \(\Phi_T=\delta_m\partial_z\Phi_+\), differentiate for the field, then take the north-minus-south force while holding the image source fixed during field differentiation. This yields \[F_z=\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{32\pi h^4}\left(1-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right),\quad F_x=-\frac{v_0}{v}F_z,\quad F_y=0.\] Lift is positive and drag negative for v>0. Both vanish continuously as v tends to zero.
b.4. Copper image speed
\(v_0=2/(\mu_0\sigma d)\simeq5.4\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
b.5. Skin-depth correction
At low v the skin depth exceeds d, so v0(v)=2/(μ0σd), the B4 constant. At high v, δ<d and ω≈v/h, so \[v_0(v)=\frac2{\mu_0\sigma\delta}=\sqrt{\frac{2v}{\mu_0\sigma h}}=\sqrt{v_0dv/h}.\] This is an effective-thickness estimate beyond the uniform-through-thickness low-speed model.
b.6. Crossover speed
Set δ=d with ω=vc/h: \(v_c=2h/(\mu_0\sigma d^2)=v_0h/d\). For the copper dimensions it is about 54 m/s.
c.1. Superconducting equilibrium height
For a perfect diamagnetic plane the horizontal image has the same horizontal moment at z=−h. Its repulsive force is \(F_z=3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi h^4)\). Balance M0g to obtain \[h_0=[3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi M_0g)]^{1/4}.\]
c.2. Vertical oscillation frequency
The derivative of the magnetic force at h0 is −4M0g/h0. Thus \(\Omega=\sqrt{4g/h_0}\). This is angular frequency in rad/s.
c.3. Micromagnet height
Use m=(4πR³/3)M and M0=(4πR³/3)ρ0. Then \(h_0=[\mu_0M^2R^3/(16\rho_0g)]^{1/4}\simeq25\,\mathrm{\mu m}\).
c.4. Micromagnet oscillations
Using h0≈25 μm, \(\Omega\simeq1.25\times10^3\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), or f≈200 Hz. The source loosely labels the angular frequency in kHz and substitutes a rounded 30 μm in one line. Angular frequency and cycles per second are distinguished here.

Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface gives \(E(r)=\Delta q/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x\,r)\), radially outward for positive charge.
The core potential is \(\Delta q\ln(b/a)/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x)\). Hence \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)\).
Between the conductors \(B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)\). Integrating flux per unit length gives \(L_x=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)\).

Appending a short cell with series iωLx dx and shunt iωCx dx must leave the semi-infinite impedance unchanged. To first order this gives Lx−CxZ0²=0. Thus \(Z_0=\ln(b/a)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}/(2\pi)\). Since √(μ0/ε0)/(2π)=59.96 Ω, \(b/a=\exp[50\sqrt4/59.96]\simeq5.30\).

Replace the plane by opposite charge and opposite return current in an image wire 2d away. To leading order \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2d/a)\), \(L_x=\mu\ln(2d/a)/(2\pi)\). Therefore \[Z_0=\frac{\ln(2d/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}.\]
Voltage continuity gives Vi+Vr=Vt, current continuity gives (Vi−Vr)/Z0=Vt/Z1. Thus \(\Gamma=(Z_1-Z_0)/(Z_1+Z_0)\). The reflected current has the opposite propagation direction.
A π shift means Γ<0, occurring for Z1<Z0. At Z1=Z0 reflection vanishes, so a reflected phase is not defined.
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

With electron charge −e, \(\phi_n=V_g-ne/C_g\). Integrate the potential while adding charge −e, or average the initial and final potentials: \[\Delta E_n=-e(\phi_n+\phi_{n+1})/2=\frac{e^2}{C_g}(n+1/2)-eV_g.\] The voltage source's work must be included.

Addition energies are spaced by e²/Cg. As a gate threshold is crossed, N increments and ΔEN resets from approximately zero to approximately e²/Cg. Thus \(E_c=e^2/C_g\), understood as the supremum of this sawtooth if exact degeneracy is assigned to the lower-N state.
Thermal excitations must be much smaller than the addition energy: \(k_BT\ll E_c=e^2/C_g\). Near a particular gate degeneracy the actual ΔEN, rather than its maximum, sets the stricter condition.

\(\tau\sim R_tC_t\). Requiring \(h/(R_tC_t)\ll e^2/C_g\) gives \(R_t\gg hC_g/(e^2C_t)\), which is stronger than h/e² because Cg≫Ct. This uses the specifically requested junction-capacitance time estimate.

Tune the OFF series LC resonance: \(L_0=1/(\omega^2C_0)=6.33\,\mu H\), giving Zoff=0 and Γoff=−1. In the ON state \(Z_{on}=i\omega L_0+[1/R_{on}+i\omega C_0]^{-1}\simeq(158+6.3i)\,\Omega\). Thus Γon≈0.520+0.0145i and ΔΓ≈1.52. The contrast can exceed one because it is a difference of complex amplitudes.

Tune \(\omega_{rf}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}\), so the OFF admittance vanishes and Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(Z_{on}=1/(i\omega_{rf}C_q)=-iZ_CC_0/C_q\). Make its magnitude comparable to Z0: \(Z_C\sim Z_0C_q/C_0\). At equality Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2 in the stated phasor convention.

Add a capacitor Cm in series between the transmission line and the entire parallel LC-dot network. At the same OFF resonance the network remains open, so Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(-i[1/(\omega C_q)+1/(\omega C_m)]\). Set its magnitude to Z0: \[C_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0\omega C_q-1}\simeq\frac1{Z_0\omega}.\] The assumed inequality ensures Cm>0. Then Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2. The source's +i uses the opposite phasor sign and does not change the contrast.

children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei
Longitudinal lengths contract by 1/γ while particle number and transverse area are invariant. Thus \(n^{\prime}=\gamma n\).
The swept volume per time is Av, so \(F_p=\gamma nAv\).
Injected particle rate is αV/μpp, hence \(\gamma_2n_2A_2v_2-\gamma_1n_1A_1v_1=\alpha V/\mu_{pp}\).

Each particle's model energy transforms by γ, while the number flux has another γ. Thus \(F_E=\gamma^2nAv\epsilon_{av}\). Material injected at rest adds only rest energy, so \(F_E(s_2)-F_E(s_1)=\alpha Vc^2\).
Energy injection is αVc² and rest-mass flux increases by αV. Their contributions cancel in Pj for any segment. Thus \(dP_j/ds=0\).

Rearrange \(P_j=(\gamma-1)\dot Mc^2+(13/4)\gamma^2AvP\): \[\dot M=\frac{P_j-(13/4)\gamma^2AvP}{(\gamma-1)c^2}.\] Substitution gives approximately \(2.8\times10^{19}\) kg/s and \(5.2\times10^{19}\) kg/s at the inlet and outlet. The displayed inputs support only about two significant figures.

The model momentum flux is \(\Pi(s)=F_E(s)v(s)/c^2=[P_j+\dot M(s)c^2]v(s)/c^2\). The net increase is Π2−Π1, approximately \(2.01\times10^{27}\) N with the supplied numerical inputs. The source quotes \(1.9\times10^{27}\) N after rounding. The phrase total momentum flux in this task refers to this difference, not either endpoint alone.

The end forces are P1A1−P2A2. The sloping wall contributes an outward axial component, giving \[F_{Pr}=P_1A_1-P_2A_2+\int_{r_1}^{r_2}2\pi rP[s(r)]\,dr,\quad s(r)=s_1+\frac{s_2-s_1}{r_2-r_1}(r-r_1).\] The integral is about \(9.71\times10^{26}\) N and the net force about \(8.10\times10^{26}\) N with the supplied inputs. The source rounds these to \(9.8\times10^{26}\) N and \(8.2\times10^{26}\) N.

The model would require Π=FPr. With the quoted rounded results, \(|1.9-0.82|/0.82\times100\%\simeq132\%\). \[u=U/V=\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon.\] Physical distributions must have cutoffs or decay sufficiently rapidly for this integral to exist.

A particle incident at θ carries normal momentum (ε/c)cosθ and reverses it. The incident flux includes c cosθ and solid-angle weight sinθ dθdφ/(4π). X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei

Longitudinal lengths contract by 1/γ while particle number and transverse area are invariant. Thus \(n^{\prime}=\gamma n\).
a.2. Particle flux
The swept volume per time is Av, so \(F_p=\gamma nAv\).
a.3. Mass-loading continuity
Injected particle rate is αV/μpp, hence \(\gamma_2n_2A_2v_2-\gamma_1n_1A_1v_1=\alpha V/\mu_{pp}\).
a.4. Energy balance
Each particle's model energy transforms by γ, while the number flux has another γ. Thus \(F_E=\gamma^2nAv\epsilon_{av}\). Material injected at rest adds only rest energy, so \(F_E(s_2)-F_E(s_1)=\alpha Vc^2\).
a.5. Jet-power derivative
Energy injection is αVc² and rest-mass flux increases by αV. Their contributions cancel in Pj for any segment. Thus \(dP_j/ds=0\).
a.6. End mass fluxes

a.7. Momentum flux increase

statement.text:
Tippe top
Model a tippe top as an axisymmetric truncated sphere of radius R with a stem. Its centre of mass C is displaced from geometric centre O by αR along the axis, with 0<α<1. Before the stem touches, the floor contact A satisfies \(\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{CA}=\alpha R\hat3-R\hat z\). The inertial XYZ frame has Z upward. The intermediate xyz frame rotates about Z by azimuth φ, with z=Z and symmetry axis \(\hat3=\sin\theta\hat x+\cos\theta\hat z\). Tilting xyz about y by θ gives the 123 frame, with 2=y and \(\hat1=\cos\theta\hat x-\sin\theta\hat z\). The axial spin angle is ψ. Principal inertias are I1=I2 and I3. The top has mass m, centre position s and sliding contact velocity vA=vx xhat+vy yhat. Kinetic friction is \(\mathbf F_f=-\mu_kN\mathbf v_A/|\mathbf v_A|\) when sliding, and the normal force is N. Initially the top is spun without a translational impulse. Unless asked otherwise consider θ<π/2 and no stem contact. The rotating derivative rule is \((d\mathbf A/dt)_{inertial}=(d\mathbf A/dt)_{rot}+\boldsymbol\omega_{frame}\times\mathbf A\).

a.1. Force diagram
Find total external force and draw free-body diagrams projected onto xz and xy. Indicate vA and its relation to friction.
a.2. Torque about centre of mass
Find the total torque in xyz.
a.3. No vertical contact velocity
Use the contact condition (s+a)·zhat=0 to prove vA·zhat=0.
a.4. Angular velocity in both frames

Find total angular velocity in xyz and in 123 in terms of the Euler-angle derivatives.
a.5. Energy in contact variables
Find total energy in Euler-angle derivatives and vx,vy. Identify rotational, translational and gravitational terms.
a.6. Vertical angular momentum rate
Find dLz/dt about C.
a.7. Energy transfer and dissipation
Which forces transfer energy while the centre rises? Find the total energy-change rate and identify force and torque components relevant to the terms in A5.
a.8. Energy sketches through inversion

Sketch ET,Ug,KT,KR through phases I initially upright θ≈0, II tilting, III first stem contact θ>π/2, IV spinning inverted, V resting inverted. Axes need not have equal scales.
a.9. Transverse inertia identity
Show \(\mathbf L\times\hat3=k(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3)\) and find k.
a.10. Jellett integral
Find a time-dependent vector v such that λ=L·v remains constant before stem contact, and prove its derivative vanishes.

children.text: \[\mathbf F_{ext}=(N-mg)\hat z+\mathbf F_f.\] Weight acts at C downward, N acts at A upward, and tangential friction acts at A opposite vA. The xy sketch must show opposite vA and Ff arrows. No absolute horizontal direction is prescribed.
a.2. Torque about centre of mass

Gravity has no torque about C. The contact torque is \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf a\times(N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\), or \[\tau_x=R(1-\alpha\cos\theta)F_{f,y},\quad\tau_y=R(\alpha\cos\theta-1)F_{f,x}-\alpha RN\sin\theta,\quad\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}.\]

The material velocity at contact is \(\mathbf v_A=\dot{\mathbf s}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a\). Although a labels the instantaneous geometric contact rather than one fixed material point, \(\dot{\mathbf a}=\alpha R\dot{\hat3}\) and \(\dot{\hat3}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3\). The difference between adot and ω×a is horizontal. Therefore \(\mathbf v_A\cdot\hat z=(\dot{\mathbf s}+\dot{\mathbf a})\cdot\hat z=d[(\mathbf s+\mathbf a)\cdot\hat z]/dt=0\).
a.4. Angular velocity in both frames

Add the precession, tilt and spin: \(\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\phi\hat z+\dot\theta\hat2+\dot\psi\hat3\). Thus \[\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\psi\sin\theta\hat x+\dot\theta\hat y+(\dot\phi+\dot\psi\cos\theta)\hat z\] and \[\boldsymbol\omega=-\dot\phi\sin\theta\hat1+\dot\theta\hat2+(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)\hat3.\]

\(U_g=mgR(1-\alpha\cos\theta)\), \(K_R=[I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2]/2\). The centre velocity is \[\dot{\mathbf s}=[v_x+R\dot\theta(1-\alpha\cos\theta)]\hat x+[v_y-R\sin\theta(\alpha\dot\phi+\dot\psi)]\hat y+\alpha R\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat z.\] Hence KT=m|sdot|²/2 and ET=KT+KR+Ug. Squaring the displayed components gives the requested explicit expression.
The z axis is fixed in inertial space, so \(\dot L_z=\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}\).

Contact-force power splits into centre work \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\dot{\mathbf s}\) and torque power \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\). Their sum is contact power \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\mathbf v_A\). Since vAz=0, \[\dot E_T=\mathbf F_f\cdot\mathbf v_A=-\mu_kN|\mathbf v_A|\le0.\] Gravity exchanges kinetic and potential energy, with \(\dot U_g=mg\alpha R\sin\theta\dot\theta\). The normal force can do centre-of-mass work but has zero total rigid-body power at contact. Frictional Fy and its x,z torque components change vertical angular momentum and facilitate spin-to-tilt energy transfer. Friction dissipates total energy while rotational energy supplies the gravitational rise.

ET decreases under sliding friction and approaches the final gravitational energy at rest. Ug rises during inversion and becomes constant when the stem-supported height settles. KT starts near zero, rises transiently and returns near zero in phase IV and to zero in V. KR is initially dominant, decreases overall as energy is transferred and dissipated, and vanishes in V. The source sketches it monotonically falling as a qualitative typical history, rather than a theorem for every possible trajectory. Draw all components consistently with ET=Ug+KT+KR. The spherical-contact formula for Ug ceases to apply once support transfers to the stem.
Axisymmetry gives \(\mathbf L=I_1\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I_1)(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\hat3)\hat3\). Cross with 3hat: the second term vanishes and k=I1.

Choose \(\mathbf v=\mathbf a=\alpha R\hat3-R\hat z\), or its negative, which changes only the convention for λ. Then \[\dot\lambda=\dot{\mathbf L}\cdot\mathbf a+\alpha R\mathbf L\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3).\] The first term vanishes because contact torque is a×F. By A9, \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3=(\mathbf L\times\hat3)/I_1\), so the second term also vanishes. It is essential to differentiate the moving vector a: torque perpendicular to a alone would not prove conservation.

statement.text:
Optical trap of neutral atoms
Model a neutral sodium atom as a massive +e core and a −e electron cloud. In a static field E0 uhat its induced moment is p0=αE0 uhat. In a laser field E(r,t)=E0(r)cos(ωt)uhat, write the moment as p=α(ω)E0(r)cos[ωt+φ(ω)]uhat. Use the positive-amplitude convention α≥0 and phase −π≤φ≤0, so a passive response lags the field. This is equivalent to the source's signed-amplitude convention. Intensity is I=ε0cE0²/2. The electron equation is \(\ddot x+\gamma_\omega\dot x+\omega_0^2x=-eE_0\cos\omega t/m_e\), and p=−ex. Larmor power is \(P_L=e^2a^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\). Use e=\(1.602\times10^{-19}\) C, me=\(9.109\times10^{-31}\) kg, ε0=\(8.854\times10^{-12}\) F/m, c=\(2.998\times10^{8}\) m/s, kB=\(1.381\times10^{-23}\) J/K and ħ=\(1.055\times10^{-34}\) J s.

1.1. Power absorbed by induced dipole
Increase a uniform field very slowly from zero. Find instantaneous absorbed power in E and pdot.
1.2. Static induced potential
Find total work in raising the field from zero to E0 and the induced potential energy.
2.1. Mean optical potential
Find the time-averaged induced potential in α,φ,ε0,c,I.
3.1. Photon scattering rate
The scattering rate is mean absorbed power divided by ħω. Find it.
4.1. Oscillator polarizability
Solve the driven oscillator for α and the phase relations in the stated positive-amplitude convention.
5.1. Radiative damping
An electron moves in a circular orbit of angular frequency ω and speed v. Equate Larmor radiation to the work of damping force −me γω v and find γω.
6.1. Trap-to-scattering ratio
Define γ=γω0. Find Udip/(ħΓsc) in terms of ω,ω0,γ.
7.1. Gaussian trap depth

For ω<ω0 a Gaussian beam has \(I(\rho,z)=2P\exp[-2\rho^2/D(z)^2]/[\pi D(z)^2]\), \(D(z)=D_0\sqrt{1+z^2/z_R^2}\), \(z_R=\pi D_0^2/\lambda\). Find the positive trap depth in c,ω,ω0,γ,P,D0.
7.2. Equivalent trap temperature
Use P=4 mW, λ=985 nm, D0=6 μm, sodium λ0=589 nm. Evaluate depth as temperature using the explicit convention Udepth=kBT0.
8.1. Trap frequencies
Expand the Gaussian potential near its bottom as \(-U_{depth}+m\Omega_\rho^2\rho^2/2+m\Omega_z^2z^2/2\). Find both frequencies using Udepth=kBT0.
9.1. Condensate size estimate
For U(z)=Umin+mΩz²z²/2 estimate size z0 by balancing potential energy against uncertainty kinetic energy. State your width convention.
9.2. Lowest energy estimate
Find the lowest energy scale and distinguish the uncertainty estimate from the exact oscillator ground-state value.
9.3. Characteristic velocity
Estimate a characteristic condensate speed along z.
10.1. Initial condensate aspect ratio

Extend the oscillator estimate to 3D and find radial-to-axial size ratio. State whether radial width denotes one transverse axis or √〈x²+y²〉.
10.2. Condensate expansion velocity ratio
Find the radial-to-axial characteristic expansion-speed ratio using the same convention as 10.1.
10.3. Late condensate aspect ratio
Assume free expansion with constant characteristic velocities and final dimensions much larger than their initial values. Find the late aspect ratio.
10.4. Late thermal-cloud shape
Find the late thermal-cloud aspect ratio and compare with the condensate.

children.text: The two charge forces do total work \(dW=\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf p\), giving \(P_{abs}=\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\).

For p=αE, \(W=\int_0^{E_0}E\alpha dE=\alpha E_0^2/2=\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The induced mechanical trapping potential is \(U_{ind}=-\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The factor one half accounts for inducing the dipole.
\(\langle\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\rangle=-\alpha\omega E_0^2\sin\phi/2\). Thus \[\Gamma_{sc}=-\frac{\alpha I\sin\phi}{\hbar\epsilon_0c}.\] With the lag convention sinφ≤0, this is nonnegative.

Put \(D=\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\omega^2\omega^2}\). Then \[\alpha=\frac{e^2}{m_eD},\quad\cos\phi=\frac{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}{D},\quad\sin\phi=-\frac{\gamma_\omega\omega}{D}.\] The source instead permits a negative α and shifts φ by π. The observable products αcosφ and αsinφ agree.

The ratio is \(\tfrac12\cot\phi=-(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)/(2\gamma_\omega\omega)\). With \(\gamma_\omega=\gamma(\omega/\omega_0)^2\), \[\frac{U_{dip}}{\hbar\Gamma_{sc}}=-\frac{\omega_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{2\gamma\omega^3}.\] It is negative for red detuning ω<ω0.
The deepest point is ρ=z=0. Replace e²/(ε0me) by 6πc³γ/ω0² to obtain \[U_{depth}=\frac{6c^2\gamma P(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{\omega_0^2D_0^2[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^6/\omega_0^4]}.\]

\(\omega=2\pi c/\lambda\), \(\omega_0=2\pi c/\lambda_0\), γ≈\(6.4\times10^{7}\) s^−1. These give Udepth/kB≈4.13 μK. The source also accepts thermal-energy conventions f kBT0, with f=1/2 or 3/2, but this field fixes f=1.

Using the source's estimate pz0≈ħ gives \(E-U_{min}\sim m\Omega_z^2z_0^2/2+\hbar^2/(2mz_0^2)\), minimized at \(z_0\sim\sqrt{\hbar/(m\Omega_z)}\). If z0 means exact rms width, use Δz=√[ħ/(2mΩz)]. Numerical width factors depend on this choice.

The source's pz0≈ħ estimate yields \(E_{min}-U_{min}\sim\hbar\Omega_z\). The exact quantum harmonic oscillator gives \(E_{min}-U_{min}=\hbar\Omega_z/2\). Both convey the requested scale and the source accepts the exact result.
The uncertainty estimate gives \(v_z\sim\hbar/(mz_0)\sim\sqrt{\hbar\Omega_z/m}\). This is a typical or rms scale, not signed mean velocity, which vanishes. The exact rms speed is √[ħΩz/(2m)].

For per-axis widths, \(x_0/z_0=\sqrt{\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). If \(\rho_0=\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}\), then \(\rho_0/z_0=\sqrt{2\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). The initially tighter radial confinement makes a cigar-shaped cloud. The source accepts either explicit width convention.
For one transverse component, \(v_x/v_z=\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). For combined radial rms speed, \(v_\rho/v_z=\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). Confinement and velocity width vary oppositely.

The late width ratio is the velocity ratio. Per-axis \(x_L/z_L\to\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\), or combined radial \(\rho_L/z_L\to\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). The condensate expands faster in the initially tightly confined direction, reversing the visible anisotropy.

Maxwell velocities have equal Cartesian rms components. Thus late per-axis widths satisfy xL/zL=1 and the cloud is spherical, unlike the condensate. A combined radial rms width √〈x²+y²〉 divided by axial rms width is √2 even for a sphere. This geometric convention must not be confused with visible anisotropy. The source's quoted ratio 1 refers to equal widths along individual directions.

2.1. Mean optical potential

3.1. Photon scattering rate

children.text: An elevator is anchored at Earth's equator and co-rotates with Earth. Use Earth's mass \(M=5.98\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), radius \(R=6370\,\mathrm{km}\), geostationary radius \(R_G=42300\,\mathrm{km}\), angular speed \(\omega=7.27\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), Sun's mass \(M_S=2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), Earth-Sun distance \(R_E=1.5\times10^8\,\mathrm{km}=1\,\mathrm{AU}\), and Earth orbital speed \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\). Use \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{SI}\), \(g=GM/R^2\), \(GM=\omega^2R_G^3\) in symbolic derivations, and the supplied rounded values in estimates. Ignore atmospheric effects.
A homogeneous cylindrical cable has constant area A and density \(\rho\). Both ends have zero tension, and the bottom is at the equator. Find the height of its top above the surface.
At what distance from the centre is the stress largest?
Find maximum stress in terms of \(\rho,R_G,R,g\). For steel, density is \(7900\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), tensile strength 5.0 GPa. Evaluate maximum stress divided by tensile strength.

children.text: A nanotube has 27 carbon-carbon bonds parallel to its axis. Nearest-neighbour length \(a=0.142\,\mathrm{nm}\), spacing between closest parallel bonds \(b=0.246\,\mathrm{nm}\). Bond energy is \(V(x)=V_0(e^{-4x/a}-2e^{-2x/a})\), where \(V_0=4.93\,\mathrm{eV}\), and x is extension from equilibrium. Find P and Q in \(V(x)\simeq P+Qx^2\). Ignore non-nearest interactions and changes in bond angles.
Find the spring constant of a bond.
Estimate the nanotube Young modulus using the source model.
Assume the bond breaks when its harmonic elastic energy reaches \(V_0\). Find \(x_{max}\).
Estimate its tensile strength in the same effective-area convention.
Carbon molar mass is 12 g/mol. Find effective solid-cylinder density. Use \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
A tapered tower has constant density \(\rho\), constant tensile stress \(\sigma\) and surface area \(A_S\). Find its cross-section \(A(h)\) at height h above the ground.
If the upper and lower end cross-sections are equal, find the top radius from Earth centre.
Find \(A_G/A_S\) for nanotube strength 130 GPa and density \(1300\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).
Terminate the tower with a counterweight of mass \(m_C\) at height \(h_C\) above geostationary radius. Find its mass in terms of \(h_C\) and the tapered-tower parameters.
Find the radius at which a payload released from rest relative to the tower can escape Earth.

The tower top is 107000 km from Earth centre. Assume tower motion is in Earth's orbital plane and neglect Earth gravity at release. Find the minimum and maximum solar distances attainable by releasing a payload from rest relative to the tower, in AU.

children.text: Radial force balance gives \(d\sigma/dr=\rho GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integrate from R, where stress is zero. Setting it to zero again at top radius H gives \(RH^2+R^2H-2R_G^3=0\), after discarding the trivial zero-length root. Thus \[H=\frac R2\left[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1\right],\qquad h_{top}=H-R\simeq1.45\times10^5\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The derivative changes sign where gravitational and centrifugal accelerations balance, so \(r=R_G\).
Integrating to \(R_G\) gives \[\sigma_{max}=\rho gR^2\left[\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right].\] For steel this is about 383 GPa, or 76.5 times its strength.
Expand each exponential to second order. Linear terms cancel and \(V=-V_0+4V_0x^2/a^2\), so \(P=-V_0\), \(Q=4V_0/a^2\).

The circumference has 27 parallel-bond spacings, so \(d=27b/\pi\). Using effective solid area \(A=\pi d^2/4\), one axial chain contributes \(ka/A\) to the modulus. For 27 parallel chains, \[E=27\frac{ka}{A}\simeq342\,\mathrm{GPa}.\] This is the source's effective solid-cylinder convention. A shell-wall-area convention would give a different quoted modulus.
The maximum strain is \(x_{max}/a=1/2\). Thus \(\sigma_0=E/2=171\,\mathrm{GPa}\). This extrapolation of the harmonic approximation is the estimate requested, not a measured strength.
An axial repeat length \(3a/2\) contains \(2\times27\) atoms. Divide their mass by \((\pi d^2/4)(3a/2)\), giving \(\rho\simeq1440\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).

Force balance now reads \(\sigma\,dA/dr=\rho A GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integration gives \[A(h)=A_S\exp\left\{\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left[\frac1R+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}-\frac1{R+h}-\frac{(R+h)^2}{2R_G^3}\right]\right\}.\]
The exponential in 3.1 must return to zero. This gives the same nontrivial root as 1.1: \[H=\frac R2[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1]\simeq151000\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The maximum area is at \(R_G\). Substitute h equal to \(R_G-R\) in 3.1: \[\frac{A_G}{A_S}=\exp\left[\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left(\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right)\right]\simeq1.623.\]

Let \(r_C=R_G+h_C\). The counterweight is pulled down by both gravity and cable tension: \(m_C\omega^2r_C=GMm_C/r_C^2+\sigma A(r_C-R)\). Thus \[m_C=\frac{\sigma A(r_C-R)}{\omega^2r_C-GM/r_C^2},\qquad h_C>0.\] Insert A from 3.1 for an explicit function of h_C. A counterweight at or below GEO cannot supply the required positive upward effective force.
The inertial release speed is \(\omega r\). Set \(\omega^2r^2/2-GM/r=0\) to find \[r_C=(2GM/\omega^2)^{1/3}=2^{1/3}R_G\simeq53200\,\mathrm{km}.\]

Release adds or subtracts \(v_t=\omega r_t=7.78\,\mathrm{km/s}\) to Earth's given orbital speed. For tangential heliocentric speed \(v=v_E\pm v_t\), energy and angular momentum give the other turning radius \[r_2=\frac{v^2R_E^2}{2GM_S-v^2R_E}.\] Prograde release maximizes aphelion, about 5.3 AU. Retrograde release minimizes perihelion, about 0.43 AU. The source's solar-distance estimates retain the supplied \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), even though that is not exactly the circular speed from its rounded \(M_S,R_E\).

4.2. Solar distance extrema
Release adds or subtracts \(v_t=\omega r_t=7.78\,\mathrm{km/s}\) to Earth's given orbital speed. For tangential heliocentric speed \(v=v_E\pm v_t\), energy and angular momentum give the other turning radius \[r_2=\frac{v^2R_E^2}{2GM_S-v^2R_E}.\] Prograde release maximizes aphelion, about 5.3 AU. Retrograde release minimizes perihelion, about 0.43 AU. The source's solar-distance estimates retain the supplied \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), even though that is not exactly the circular speed from its rounded \(M_S,R_E\).

children.text: a1.1. Temperature profile with Joule heating
Heat balance gives \(kS T^{\prime\prime}=-\rho I^2/S\). Integrate and impose both temperatures: \[T(x)=T_1+(T_2-T_1)x/L+\frac{\rho I^2}{2kS^2}x(L-x).\]
a1.2. Heat current along a leg
Differentiate A1.1: \(q=kS(T_1-T_2)/L+(\rho I^2/S)(x-L/2)\). With R=ρL/S and K=kS/L, \(q(0)=K(T_1-T_2)-RI^2/2\) and \(q(L)=K(T_1-T_2)+RI^2/2\). Half the Joule heat flows to each end.
\(q_2=\pi_2I\), with the positive quantities denoting received and rejected heat in the generator cycle.
The ideal efficiency is P/q1=(T1−T2)/T1. Substitute the preceding heat and power to obtain π1=αT1. At any junction \(\pi=\alpha T\).
Add the conductive, Peltier and split Joule contributions: \[q_1=K(T_1-T_2)+\alpha T_1I-RI^2/2,\quad q_2=K(T_1-T_2)+\alpha T_2I+RI^2/2.\] Their difference is load power α(T1−T2)I−RI².
The circuit current is \(I=\alpha(T_1-T_2)/[R(1+m)]\). Divide I²RL by q1 to get \[\eta=\frac{m(T_1-T_2)}{(KR/\alpha^2)(1+m)^2+T_1(1+m)-(T_1-T_2)/2}.\]

Power is proportional to m/(1+m)² and peaks at m=1. Substitution gives \[\eta_P=\frac{T_1-T_2}{4/Z+(3T_1+T_2)/2}.\] The source prints T1−T1 in one numerator, a typographical error corrected by its derivation.
Differentiate A3.3 with respect to m. The positive stationary root is \(M=\sqrt{1+Z(T_1+T_2)/2}\). It is larger than one for Z>0.
At m=M the efficiency simplifies to \[\eta_{max}=\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1}\frac{M-1}{M+T_2/T_1},\qquad M=\sqrt{1+Z(T_1+T_2)/2}.\]
Minimize KR=(kASA+kBSB)(ρA/SA+ρB/SB). Setting the derivative with respect to SB/SA to zero gives \(S_B/S_A=\sqrt{\rho_Bk_A/(\rho_Ak_B)}\).
a5.2. Best material figure of merit
a6.1. Numerical efficiency at maximum power
The matched materials give Zm=α²/(4ρk)=0.00315 K⁻¹. With m=1, ηopt≈0.0586, or 5.86%. Using rounded Z=0.0032 gives the source's approximately 5.84% to 5.9%. Carnot is 120/423≈28.4%, so ηopt/ηc≈0.21.
M=√(1+0.00315×363)≈1.46. The maximum efficiency is approximately 0.060, or 6.0%. It uses a different load from maximum power.
The upper Peltier term removes heat while conduction from the warm sink and half the Joule heat oppose cooling: \[q_C=\alpha T_1I-K(T_2-T_1)-RI^2/2.\]
At fixed temperatures qC is largest at I=αT1/R. Its zero at the minimum attainable temperature gives \(\Delta T_{max}=ZT_{1,min}^2/2\).
The positive solution of ZmT1²/2+T1−T2=0 is \(T_{1,min}=[\sqrt{1+2Z_mT_2}-1]/Z_m\simeq222\,\mathrm K\).
b2.2. Working current at the limit
The pair resistance is R=2ρL/S=0.004 Ω. Thus \(I_w=\alpha T_{1,min}/R\simeq23.3\,\mathrm A\).
The required source power is \(P=\alpha(T_2-T_1)I+RI^2\). Therefore \[\beta=\frac{\alpha T_1I-K(T_2-T_1)-RI^2/2}{\alpha(T_2-T_1)I+RI^2}.\]
Let TM=(T1+T2)/2. Differentiate β and take the positive root: \[I_\beta=\frac{\alpha(T_2-T_1)}{R(\sqrt{1+ZT_M}-1)}.\] This differs from the maximum-cooling-power current.

With \(s=\sqrt{1+ZT_M}\), substitution gives \[\beta_{max}=\frac{T_1}{T_2-T_1}\frac{s-T_2/T_1}{s+1}.\] Positive cooling at the optimum requires s>T2/T1. This tends to the Carnot COP as Z tends to infinity.

children.text: Symmetry gives concentric circles. Circulation \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\) implies \(v=\kappa/r\), directed according to the circulation.
The free-surface slope obeys \(g\,dz/dr=v^2/r=\kappa^2/r^3\). Integrating, \[z(r)=z_0-\kappa^2/(2gr^2).\] The constant follows from liquid volume and the formula excludes the core.

Each moves at \(\kappa/r_0\) perpendicular to their connecting line. They trace full circles about their midpoint, remaining diametrically opposite at radius \(r_0/2\), with common angular speed \(2\kappa/r_0^2\). By contrast, opposite-circulation vortices translate together.
The coarse-grained lattice rotates rigidly. A and B trace circles about the beaker centre. The central vortex C stays at the centre.
The number per area is \(2/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Summing circulation inside a circle gives \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\pi r^2\,2/(\sqrt3u^2)\), so \[v=2\pi\kappa r/(\sqrt3u^2).\]
The angular velocity \(2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\) is independent of radius. Rigid rotation preserves separation: \(AB(t)=AB(0)\).
Rigid-body angular speed is \(\Omega=2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Integrating \(g\,dz/dr=\Omega^2r\) gives \[z=z_0+2\pi^2\kappa^2r^2/(3gu^4).\]
Circulation times oriented area times density gives \(P=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), normal to the loop by the circulation right-hand rule.

The two long opposite filaments each contribute kinetic energy. Integrating from core a to separation b, or using the two-wire inductance analogue, gives \[U=2\pi\rho\kappa^2d\ln(b/a).\] End corrections are smaller for \(b\ll d\).

The difference between old and new flow is the flow of a rectangular loop. Thus \(|\Delta P|=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), perpendicular to both the filament and its displacement. Its sign is fixed by the oriented loop formed by the new filament and the negative old filament.

For length d, electric force is \(\lambda d\mathbf E\). Momentum changes perpendicular to filament displacement, so the constant drift is perpendicular to E, with magnitude \(|\lambda|E/(2\pi\kappa\rho)\). Choose the sign using C.3. The path is a straight line, with no ordinary mass-times-acceleration law for the vortex.

Total charge is fixed at \(-2\pi R_0|\lambda|\), so force is constant and parallel to initial momentum. From \(P=P_0+2\pi ER_0|\lambda|t\), \[R(t)=\sqrt{R_0^2+ER_0|\lambda|t/(\pi\rho\kappa)}.\] The centre moves along the ring axis in the force direction. Charge density decreases as the ring grows.

Work and momentum balance imply \(v=dU/dP\). With the given U and P, \[v\simeq\frac{\kappa}{2R(t)}\ln\frac{R(t)}a.\] Differentiating the approximate energy exactly adds a 1 inside the logarithmic bracket, which is beyond leading-logarithm accuracy. As R grows the speed decreases in the large-log regime. Replacing the slowly varying logarithm by \(\ln(R_0/a)\) gives the further approximation in the source.
With no external force momentum stays constant, hence radius and speed stay constant: \(v(t)=v_*\) for \(t>t_*\).

An opposite-circulation image across the wall enforces zero normal flow. Its distance is \(2h_0\). The vortex translates parallel to the wall at constant speed \(\kappa/(2h_0)\), with direction fixed by the image circulation.

Use three images: opposite circulation across each wall and equal circulation across both. At \((h_0,h_0)\) the net components are opposite with magnitudes \(\kappa/(4h_0)\). The speed is \(\kappa/(2\sqrt2h_0)\), tangent to the corner trajectory.

Energy conservation for the four-image arrangement implies \[(x^2+y^2)/(x^2y^2)=2/h_0^2.\] The curve passes through \((h_0,h_0)\), tangent to the direction with opposite x and y components. It approaches one wall at a fixed distance as it travels far along it, with direction set by the circulation.
For \(x\to\infty\), the trajectory invariant yields \(y\to h_0/\sqrt2\). Only the nearest-wall image matters, giving \[v_\infty=\kappa/(2y)=\kappa/(\sqrt2h_0).\]

Each moves at \(\kappa/r_0\) perpendicular to their connecting line. They trace full circles about their midpoint, remaining diametrically opposite at radius \(r_0/2\), with common angular speed \(2\kappa/r_0^2\). By contrast, opposite-circulation vortices translate together.
B.2. Lattice trajectories
The coarse-grained lattice rotates rigidly. A and B trace circles about the beaker centre. The central vortex C stays at the centre.
B.3. Lattice velocity
The number per area is \(2/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Summing circulation inside a circle gives \(2\pi rv=2\pi\kappa\pi r^2\,2/(\sqrt3u^2)\), so \[v=2\pi\kappa r/(\sqrt3u^2).\]
B.4. Lattice spacing in time
The angular velocity \(2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\) is independent of radius. Rigid rotation preserves separation: \(AB(t)=AB(0)\).
B.5. Smoothed lattice surface
Rigid-body angular speed is \(\Omega=2\pi\kappa/(\sqrt3u^2)\). Integrating \(g\,dz/dr=\Omega^2r\) gives \[z=z_0+2\pi^2\kappa^2r^2/(3gu^4).\]
C.1. Rectangular-loop momentum
Circulation times oriented area times density gives \(P=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), normal to the loop by the circulation right-hand rule.
C.2. Rectangular-loop energy
The two long opposite filaments each contribute kinetic energy. Integrating from core a to separation b, or using the two-wire inductance analogue, gives \[U=2\pi\rho\kappa^2d\ln(b/a).\] End corrections are smaller for \(b\ll d\).
C.3. Shifted-filament momentum
The difference between old and new flow is the flow of a rectangular loop. Thus \(|\Delta P|=2\pi\kappa\rho bd\), perpendicular to both the filament and its displacement. Its sign is fixed by the oriented loop formed by the new filament and the negative old filament.
D.1. Charged straight filament
For length d, electric force is \(\lambda d\mathbf E\). Momentum changes perpendicular to filament displacement, so the constant drift is perpendicular to E, with magnitude \(|\lambda|E/(2\pi\kappa\rho)\). Choose the sign using C.3. The path is a straight line, with no ordinary mass-times-acceleration law for the vortex.
D.2. Charged-ring radius
Total charge is fixed at \(-2\pi R_0|\lambda|\), so force is constant and parallel to initial momentum. From \(P=P_0+2\pi ER_0|\lambda|t\), \[R(t)=\sqrt{R_0^2+ER_0|\lambda|t/(\pi\rho\kappa)}.\] The centre moves along the ring axis in the force direction. Charge density decreases as the ring grows.
D.3. Charged-ring velocity
Work and momentum balance imply \(v=dU/dP\). With the given U and P, \[v\simeq\frac{\kappa}{2R(t)}\ln\frac{R(t)}a.\] Differentiating the approximate energy exactly adds a 1 inside the logarithmic bracket, which is beyond leading-logarithm accuracy. As R grows the speed decreases in the large-log regime. Replacing the slowly varying logarithm by \(\ln(R_0/a)\) gives the further approximation in the source.
D.4. Field switched off
With no external force momentum stays constant, hence radius and speed stay constant: \(v(t)=v_*\) for \(t>t_*\).
E.1. One flat wall
An opposite-circulation image across the wall enforces zero normal flow. Its distance is \(2h_0\). The vortex translates parallel to the wall at constant speed \(\kappa/(2h_0)\), with direction fixed by the image circulation.
E.2. Right-angle corner
Use three images: opposite circulation across each wall and equal circulation across both. At \((h_0,h_0)\) the net components are opposite with magnitudes \(\kappa/(4h_0)\). The speed is \(\kappa/(2\sqrt2h_0)\), tangent to the corner trajectory.
E.3. Corner trajectory
Energy conservation for the four-image arrangement implies \[(x^2+y^2)/(x^2y^2)=2/h_0^2.\] The curve passes through \((h_0,h_0)\), tangent to the direction with opposite x and y components. It approaches one wall at a fixed distance as it travels far along it, with direction set by the circulation.
E.4. Long-time corner speed
For \(x\to\infty\), the trajectory invariant yields \(y\to h_0/\sqrt2\). Only the nearest-wall image matters, giving \[v_\infty=\kappa/(2y)=\kappa/(\sqrt2h_0).\]

children.text: Evolution of a supermassive black-hole binary
Integrate the transverse gravitational impulse along the undeflected straight path. It gives Δp⊥=2GMm/(bv), hence α=2GM/(bv²)=2b1/b and k=2.
The star keeps its speed in the hole frame. To order α², its longitudinal momentum change has magnitude mvα²/2. The hole receives drag \(\Delta p_x=-mv\alpha^2/2=-2G^2M^2m/(b^2v^3)\).
The rate in an annulus db is 2πbvn db. Therefore \[F_{DF}=-\frac{4\pi G^2M^2\rho}{v^2}\ln\frac R{b_1}.\] The negative sign is relative to the velocity. The logarithm comes from db/b.
Angular momentum gives bσ=rmvp. Energy gives vp²=σ²+2GM2/rm. Thus \(b=r_m\sqrt{1+2GM_2/(\sigma^2r_m)}\).
Use M2=2M and rm≈a. Strong focusing gives bmax²≈4GMa/σ². The rate πbmax²nσ gives \(\Delta t\simeq m\sigma/(4\pi GM\rho a)\). This approximate cross section sets the numerical convention used below.
Each ejected star takes approximately mvbin²/2=GmM/(8a). Divide by the B3 interval: \(\dot E\simeq-\pi G^2M^2\rho/(2\sigma)\). Since dE/da=GM²/(4a²), \(\dot a\simeq-2\pi G\rho a^2/\sigma\).
Integrate da/a²=−(2πGρ/σ)dt. The halving time is \(T_{SS}=\sigma/(2\pi G\rho a_1)\simeq7.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Gy}\).
Using ω²=GM/(4a³) and I=2Ma² yields \(\dot E=-64G^4M^5/(5c^5a^5)\). Divide by dE/da=GM²/(4a²): \(\dot a=-256G^3M^3/(5c^5a^3)\).
Integration gives \(T_{GW}=5c^5(a_2^4-r_g^4)/(1024G^3M^3)\simeq5c^5a_2^4/(1024G^3M^3)\). The approximation neglects rg⁴.
The enclosed stellar mass is M*(r)=σ²r/G. Therefore v²=GM*(r)/r=σ² and v=σ.
Circular kinetic energy is constant, while dU/da=Mσ²/a. The energy-loss rate is FDFσ=−GM²σlnΛ/a². Thus \(\dot a\simeq-GM\ln\Lambda/(a\sigma)\).

A mass-equivalence estimate M*(a1)≈M gives \(a_1\simeq GM/\sigma^2\simeq10.8\,\mathrm{pc}\). Equating the actual forces instead gives GM/(4σ²)≈2.7 pc. Both are legitimate within the source's estimate criterion. Use the 10.8 pc convention consistently below.
Integrate D2: \(T_1=\sigma(a_0^2-a_1^2)/(2GM\ln\Lambda)\simeq0.121\,\mathrm{Gy}\). The a1² correction is negligible.

Equate the B4 and C1 energy-loss magnitudes. Then \[a_2^5=\frac{128G^2M^3\sigma}{5\pi c^5\rho_1}.\] For a1=10.8 pc, ρ1≈\(6.3\times10^{3}\)M☉/pc³ and a2≈0.018 pc. The alternative 2.7 pc formation convention gives a2≈0.010 pc.

\[T_2\simeq\frac\sigma{2\pi G\rho_1}\left(\frac1{a_2}-\frac1{a_1}\right)\simeq0.063\,\mathrm{Gy},\quad T_3\simeq\frac{5c^5a_2^4}{1024G^3M^3}\simeq0.016\,\mathrm{Gy}.\] At the transition T3≈σ/(8πGρ1a2), one quarter of the dominant term in T2. The alternative a1 convention gives 0.0068 and 0.0017 Gy.

Add T1+T2+T3≈0.121+0.063+0.016=0.20 Gy. The alternative force-equivalence estimate gives approximately 0.13 Gy. Both use the stated replenished stellar population approximation. Depletion of stars on intersecting orbits would invalidate a constant slingshot rate, the final-parsec issue mentioned in the source.

solution.text:
Evolution of a supermassive black-hole binary
a.1. Weak scattering coefficient
Integrate the transverse gravitational impulse along the undeflected straight path. It gives Δp⊥=2GMm/(bv), hence α=2GM/(bv²)=2b1/b and k=2.
a.2. Longitudinal impulse
The star keeps its speed in the hole frame. To order α², its longitudinal momentum change has magnitude mvα²/2. The hole receives drag \(\Delta p_x=-mv\alpha^2/2=-2G^2M^2m/(b^2v^3)\).
a.3. Dynamical friction
The rate in an annulus db is 2πbvn db. Therefore \[F_{DF}=-\frac{4\pi G^2M^2\rho}{v^2}\ln\frac R{b_1}.\] The negative sign is relative to the velocity. The logarithm comes from db/b.
a.4. Coulomb logarithm
b1=GM/v²≈10.8 pc, so lnΛ≈ln(20000/10.8)≈7.53.
b.1. Circular binary energy
Use Mvbin²/a=GM²/(4a²). Then \(v_{bin}=\sqrt{GM/(4a)}\) and \(E=2(Mv_{bin}^2/2)-GM^2/(2a)=-GM^2/(4a)\).
b.2. Gravitational focusing
Angular momentum gives bσ=rmvp. Energy gives vp²=σ²+2GM2/rm. Thus \(b=r_m\sqrt{1+2GM_2/(\sigma^2r_m)}\).
b.3. Collision interval
Use M2=2M and rm≈a. Strong focusing gives bmax²≈4GMa/σ². The rate πbmax²nσ gives \(\Delta t\simeq m\sigma/(4\pi GM\rho a)\). This approximate cross section sets the numerical convention used below.
b.4. Slingshot shrinkage
Each ejected star takes approximately mvbin²/2=GmM/(8a). Divide by the B3 interval: \(\dot E\simeq-\pi G^2M^2\rho/(2\sigma)\). Since dE/da=GM²/(4a²), \(\dot a\simeq-2\pi G\rho a^2/\sigma\).
b.5. Radius-halving time
Integrate da/a²=−(2πGρ/σ)dt. The halving time is \(T_{SS}=\sigma/(2\pi G\rho a_1)\simeq7.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Gy}\).
c.1. Radiative shrinkage
Using ω²=GM/(4a³) and I=2Ma² yields \(\dot E=-64G^4M^5/(5c^5a^5)\). Divide by dE/da=GM²/(4a²): \(\dot a=-256G^3M^3/(5c^5a^3)\).
c.2. Radiative merger time
Integration gives \(T_{GW}=5c^5(a_2^4-r_g^4)/(1024G^3M^3)\simeq5c^5a_2^4/(1024G^3M^3)\). The approximation neglects rg⁴.
c.3. Hubble-time radius
\(a_H=[1024G^3M^3t_H/(5c^5)]^{1/4}\simeq0.098\,\mathrm{pc}\).
d.1. Galaxy circular speed
The enclosed stellar mass is M*(r)=σ²r/G. Therefore v²=GM*(r)/r=σ² and v=σ.
d.2. Frictional orbital decay
Circular kinetic energy is constant, while dU/da=Mσ²/a. The energy-loss rate is FDFσ=−GM²σlnΛ/a². Thus \(\dot a\simeq-GM\ln\Lambda/(a\sigma)\).
d.3. Binary formation radius
A mass-equivalence estimate M*(a1)≈M gives \(a_1\simeq GM/\sigma^2\simeq10.8\,\mathrm{pc}\). Equating the actual forces instead gives GM/(4σ²)≈2.7 pc. Both are legitimate within the source's estimate criterion. Use the 10.8 pc convention consistently below.
d.4. Initial sinking time
Integrate D2: \(T_1=\sigma(a_0^2-a_1^2)/(2GM\ln\Lambda)\simeq0.121\,\mathrm{Gy}\). The a1² correction is negligible.
d.5. Transition to radiation
Equate the B4 and C1 energy-loss magnitudes. Then \[a_2^5=\frac{128G^2M^3\sigma}{5\pi c^5\rho_1}.\] For a1=10.8 pc, ρ1≈\(6.3\times10^{3}\)M☉/pc³ and a2≈0.018 pc. The alternative 2.7 pc formation convention gives a2≈0.010 pc.
d.6. Late-stage durations
\[T_2\simeq\frac\sigma{2\pi G\rho_1}\left(\frac1{a_2}-\frac1{a_1}\right)\simeq0.063\,\mathrm{Gy},\quad T_3\simeq\frac{5c^5a_2^4}{1024G^3M^3}\simeq0.016\,\mathrm{Gy}.\] At the transition T3≈σ/(8πGρ1a2), one quarter of the dominant term in T2. The alternative a1 convention gives 0.0068 and 0.0017 Gy.
d.7. Total evolution time
Add T1+T2+T3≈0.121+0.063+0.016=0.20 Gy. The alternative force-equivalence estimate gives approximately 0.13 Gy. Both use the stated replenished stellar population approximation. Depletion of stars on intersecting orbits would invalidate a constant slingshot rate, the final-parsec issue mentioned in the source.

statement.text:
Space Debris
A rocket stage is axisymmetric about body axis x, with principal inertias \(J_x<J_y=J_z\). Its centre of mass is C. Let angular momentum magnitude be L, making angle \(\theta\) with x. Initially the tank is empty and external torques vanish. Residual fuel of negligible mass can later dissipate energy without external torque. The stage subsequently travels in a circular polar orbit of period \(T=100\,\mathrm{min}\). Its only conducting component is a nonmagnetic spherical tank shell, radius \(R=4\,\mathrm m\), thickness \(D=2\,\mathrm{mm}\), resistivity \(\rho=2.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\mathrm m\). Ignore shell self-inductance. In the orbital XY plane, \(\mathbf r=R_O(\cos u,\sin u,0)\), Earth magnetic dipole points along negative Y, and the equatorial field magnitude is \(B_0=20\,\mu\mathrm T\). Use \(\mathbf B=\mu_0[3(\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf r)\mathbf r/r^5-\boldsymbol\mu/r^3]/(4\pi)\).

A.1. Angular-velocity components

Find \(\omega_x,\omega_y\) in terms of L, angle and inertias.
A.2. Rotational energy
Find \(E_x,E_y\) and total E as a function of L and \(\cos\theta\).
A.3. Maximum axis excursion
With initial angle \(\theta_0\), find the largest angle between the symmetry axis and its initial direction.
A.4. Precessing reference frame

A frame has y1 along fixed L and rotates so that x always lies in its x1y1 plane. Find its rate \(\Omega(t)\), and the stage relative spin magnitude and angle to x.
B.1. Dissipative end state
For residual fuel sloshing with no external torque and initial \(0<\theta_1<\pi/2\), find the final angle \(\theta_2\).
B.2. Final angular speed
Initially \(\omega_1=1\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), at \(\gamma_1=30^\circ\) to x. Use \(J_x=4200,J_y=15000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\). Find the final speed.
C.1. Induced magnetic moment

For a uniform field with constant derivative \(\dot{\mathbf B}\) directed along y, find the shell magnetic-moment components.
C.2. Shell torque
The field is at angle \(\alpha\) to its derivative as in the diagram. Find torque components.
C.3. Orbital magnetic field

Find all inertial field components along the orbit.
C.4. Torque on the rotating stage
The stage rotates at signed angular speed \(\omega\) along Z. Find torque versus u.
C.5. Slow spin evolution
Assume spin changes negligibly during one orbit. Find \(\omega(t)\) from initial \(\omega_2\).
C.6. Steady period ratio
Find orbital period divided by stage rotation period in steady state.

children.text: Energy and L conservation keep \(\cos^2\theta\), hence the continuous branch of \(\theta\), fixed. The axis precesses on a cone about L. For the source acute-angle convention the maximum is \(\psi=2\theta_0\). For a directed axis with an obtuse initial angle the corresponding expression is \(2\min(\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0)\).

The relative spin must lie along x. Resolving \(\boldsymbol\omega=\boldsymbol\Omega+\boldsymbol\omega_s\), \(\Omega\sin\theta=L\sin\theta/J_y\). Thus \[\Omega=L/J_y,\quad\omega_s=L\cos\theta_0(1/J_x-1/J_y),\quad\gamma_s=0\] for the acute-angle convention. Both rates are constant.
L is fixed, and the coefficient of \(\cos^2\theta\) in E is positive. Its minimum is at \(\cos\theta_2=0\), hence \(\theta_2=\pi/2\). The stage rotates about a transverse maximum-inertia axis.
\(L=\omega_1\sqrt{J_x^2\cos^2\gamma_1+J_y^2\sin^2\gamma_1}\) stays fixed. The final speed is \(L/J_y=0.556\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).

Slice the shell into rings normal to the derivative. Faraday emf is \(\pi R^2\sin^2\phi\,\dot B\), resistance \(2\pi\rho\sin\phi/(D\,d\phi)\), and moment element \(-\pi DR^4\dot B\sin^3\phi\,d\phi/(2\rho)\). Since \(\int_0^\pi\sin^3\phi\,d\phi=4/3\), \[\boldsymbol\mu=-K\dot{\mathbf B},\qquad K=2\pi DR^4/(3\rho).\] Thus \((\mu_x,\mu_y,\mu_z)=(0,-K\dot B,0)\).
Torque is \(\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B\). In the source axes it has \(M_x=M_y=0\), \(M_z=K B\dot B\sin\alpha\). Its invariant vector form is \(K\mathbf B\times\dot{\mathbf B}\).
Substitution in the dipole field gives \[B_X=-\tfrac32B_0\sin2u,\quad B_Y=\tfrac12B_0(3\cos2u-1),\quad B_Z=0.\] At u=0 this agrees with the given equatorial field.
C.4. Torque on the rotating stage

The derivative relevant to shell currents is the material derivative \(\mathbf q=\dot{\mathbf B}_E-\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf B_E\), not just the orbital derivative. Use \(\mathbf M=K\mathbf B_E\times\mathbf q\). Then \[M_X=M_Y=0,\quad M_Z=K B_0^2\left[\frac{3\pi}{T}(3-\cos2u)-\frac\omega2(5-3\cos2u)\right].\]

Orbit-average the cosine to zero: \(J_y\dot\omega=KB_0^2(9\pi/T-5\omega/2)\). Thus \[\omega(t)=\frac{18\pi}{5T}+\left(\omega_2-\frac{18\pi}{5T}\right)e^{-\delta t},\quad\delta=\frac{5\pi DB_0^2R^4}{3J_y\rho}.\] For the initial positive spin this remains positive and equals its magnitude.

The equilibrium rate is \(18\pi/(5T)\). Hence \(T/T_s=T\omega_\infty/(2\pi)=9/5=1.8\). The source final paragraph has a denominator typo in the angular-rate sentence. Its preceding evolution formula and final period ratio agree.

solution.text:
Space Debris
A.1. Angular-velocity components
Project angular momentum: \(\omega_x=L\cos\theta/J_x\), \(\omega_y=L\sin\theta/J_y\).
A.2. Rotational energy
\(E_x=L^2\cos^2\theta/(2J_x)\), \(E_y=L^2\sin^2\theta/(2J_y)\). Hence \[E=\frac{L^2}{2J_y}+\frac{L^2}{2}(J_x^{-1}-J_y^{-1})\cos^2\theta.\]
A.3. Maximum axis excursion
Energy and L conservation keep \(\cos^2\theta\), hence the continuous branch of \(\theta\), fixed. The axis precesses on a cone about L. For the source acute-angle convention the maximum is \(\psi=2\theta_0\). For a directed axis with an obtuse initial angle the corresponding expression is \(2\min(\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0)\).
A.4. Precessing reference frame
The relative spin must lie along x. Resolving \(\boldsymbol\omega=\boldsymbol\Omega+\boldsymbol\omega_s\), \(\Omega\sin\theta=L\sin\theta/J_y\). Thus \[\Omega=L/J_y,\quad\omega_s=L\cos\theta_0(1/J_x-1/J_y),\quad\gamma_s=0\] for the acute-angle convention. Both rates are constant.
B.1. Dissipative end state
L is fixed, and the coefficient of \(\cos^2\theta\) in E is positive. Its minimum is at \(\cos\theta_2=0\), hence \(\theta_2=\pi/2\). The stage rotates about a transverse maximum-inertia axis.
B.2. Final angular speed
\(L=\omega_1\sqrt{J_x^2\cos^2\gamma_1+J_y^2\sin^2\gamma_1}\) stays fixed. The final speed is \(L/J_y=0.556\,\mathrm{rad/s}\).
C.1. Induced magnetic moment
Slice the shell into rings normal to the derivative. Faraday emf is \(\pi R^2\sin^2\phi\,\dot B\), resistance \(2\pi\rho\sin\phi/(D\,d\phi)\), and moment element \(-\pi DR^4\dot B\sin^3\phi\,d\phi/(2\rho)\). Since \(\int_0^\pi\sin^3\phi\,d\phi=4/3\), \[\boldsymbol\mu=-K\dot{\mathbf B},\qquad K=2\pi DR^4/(3\rho).\] Thus \((\mu_x,\mu_y,\mu_z)=(0,-K\dot B,0)\).
C.2. Shell torque
Torque is \(\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B\). In the source axes it has \(M_x=M_y=0\), \(M_z=K B\dot B\sin\alpha\). Its invariant vector form is \(K\mathbf B\times\dot{\mathbf B}\).
C.3. Orbital magnetic field
Substitution in the dipole field gives \[B_X=-\tfrac32B_0\sin2u,\quad B_Y=\tfrac12B_0(3\cos2u-1),\quad B_Z=0.\] At u=0 this agrees with the given equatorial field.
C.4. Torque on the rotating stage
The derivative relevant to shell currents is the material derivative \(\mathbf q=\dot{\mathbf B}_E-\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf B_E\), not just the orbital derivative. Use \(\mathbf M=K\mathbf B_E\times\mathbf q\). Then \[M_X=M_Y=0,\quad M_Z=K B_0^2\left[\frac{3\pi}{T}(3-\cos2u)-\frac\omega2(5-3\cos2u)\right].\]
C.5. Slow spin evolution
Orbit-average the cosine to zero: \(J_y\dot\omega=KB_0^2(9\pi/T-5\omega/2)\). Thus \[\omega(t)=\frac{18\pi}{5T}+\left(\omega_2-\frac{18\pi}{5T}\right)e^{-\delta t},\quad\delta=\frac{5\pi DB_0^2R^4}{3J_y\rho}.\] For the initial positive spin this remains positive and equals its magnitude.
C.6. Steady period ratio
The equilibrium rate is \(18\pi/(5T)\). Hence \(T/T_s=T\omega_\infty/(2\pi)=9/5=1.8\). The source final paragraph has a denominator typo in the angular-rate sentence. Its preceding evolution formula and final period ratio agree.
