statement.text:
Mechanics of a Deformable Lattice
An N by N lattice, \(N>1\), contains \(N^2\) identical uniform equilateral triangular plates of side l and mass M. Equal-length massless rods connect freely hinged vertices. Four tubes confine the N edge vertices to slide along rails. The tubes form a diamond with fixed 60 and 120 degree corners. The top tube is horizontal, with top-left vertex A(0,0) fixed. The lattice has one degree of freedom \(0\le\alpha\le60^\circ\). Triangles are indexed \((m,n)\), \(0\le m,n<N\), with vertices A,B,C in the diagrams. Motion lies in the xy plane, y positive upward, and potential zero at y=0. A plate has central inertia \(Ml^2/12\). Use gravitational acceleration g.


A.1. Four-plate potential

For N=2, find total potential energy as a function of angle.
A.2. Four-plate equilibrium
Find the equilibrium angle for N=2.
A.3. Four-plate oscillation
Find kinetic energy in terms of \(\Delta\dot\alpha\) for small oscillations and the ordinary frequency.
B.1. General lattice equilibrium
Find the equilibrium angle for arbitrary N.
B.2. Large-lattice scaling
At equilibrium as \(N\to\infty\), find exponents in \(\Delta E_p\propto N^{\gamma_1}\), \(E_k\propto N^{\gamma_2}\), and \(f_{E}^{\prime}\propto N^{\gamma_3}\), for fixed small angle and angular-speed perturbations.
C.1. Optimal force point

Choose one of the \(3N^2\) vertices where a force can maintain \(\alpha=60^\circ\) with minimum magnitude.
C.2. Minimum holding force
Find this force magnitude and its direction \(\theta_F\) as shown in the diagram.

children.text: The first plate centre is at \(y_{00}=-l\sin(\pi/6+\alpha)/\sqrt3\); each row is lower by \(\sqrt3l\cos\alpha\). Thus \[E_p=4Mg\,y_{00}-2\sqrt3Mgl\cos\alpha=-\frac23Mgl(4\sqrt3\cos\alpha+3\sin\alpha).\]
Zero first derivative of the potential gives \(4\sqrt3\sin\alpha_E=3\cos\alpha_E\), so \(\alpha_E=\arctan(\sqrt3/4)=0.40864\,\mathrm{rad}\). The second derivative is positive.

Plate-centre coordinates are \[x_{mn}=(2m+n)l\cos\alpha+\frac l{\sqrt3}\cos(\alpha+\pi/6),\quad y_{mn}=-\sqrt3nl\cos\alpha-\frac l{\sqrt3}\sin(\alpha+\pi/6).\] Differentiate and sum \(M(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)/2\) over four plates. This gives \(164Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2/57\). Plate spin adds \(Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2/6\). Therefore \[E_k=\frac{347}{114}Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2.\] Also \(\Delta E_p=\sqrt{57}Mgl(\Delta\alpha)^2/3\). Taking the ratio of the two quadratic coefficients yields \[f_E=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{38\sqrt{57}}{347}\frac gl}.\]

The potential curvature grows as \(N^3\). Since \(\alpha_{E}^{\prime}\sim1/N\), differentiated centre coordinates remain order l per plate even at indices of order N. Each plate contributes order one translational and rotational inertia, so total inertia grows as \(N^2\). Hence \((\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3)=(3,2,1/2)\). The small-angle limit is taken locally about each equilibrium before comparing N scaling.
Virtual work requires \(F|\partial\mathbf r/\partial\alpha|\ge|\partial E_p/\partial\alpha|\). The largest vertex displacement per angle is at C(N-1,N-1), so choose that vertex.

At \(\alpha=\pi/3\), \(dE_p/d\alpha=3(N-1)N^2Mgl/4\). The C(N-1,N-1) derivative is \((3N-2)l(-\sqrt3/2,1/2)\). A force along that derivative supplies positive virtual work, giving \[F_{min}=\frac{3(N-1)N^2}{4(3N-2)}Mg,\qquad\theta_F=5\pi/6.\] The force is 150 degrees from positive x, rather than necessarily perpendicular to the line from the fixed vertex.

solution.text:
Mechanics of a Deformable Lattice
A.1. Four-plate potential
The first plate centre is at \(y_{00}=-l\sin(\pi/6+\alpha)/\sqrt3\); each row is lower by \(\sqrt3l\cos\alpha\). Thus \[E_p=4Mg\,y_{00}-2\sqrt3Mgl\cos\alpha=-\frac23Mgl(4\sqrt3\cos\alpha+3\sin\alpha).\]
A.2. Four-plate equilibrium
Zero first derivative of the potential gives \(4\sqrt3\sin\alpha_E=3\cos\alpha_E\), so \(\alpha_E=\arctan(\sqrt3/4)=0.40864\,\mathrm{rad}\). The second derivative is positive.
A.3. Four-plate oscillation
Plate-centre coordinates are \[x_{mn}=(2m+n)l\cos\alpha+\frac l{\sqrt3}\cos(\alpha+\pi/6),\quad y_{mn}=-\sqrt3nl\cos\alpha-\frac l{\sqrt3}\sin(\alpha+\pi/6).\] Differentiate and sum \(M(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)/2\) over four plates. This gives \(164Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2/57\). Plate spin adds \(Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2/6\). Therefore \[E_k=\frac{347}{114}Ml^2(\Delta\dot\alpha)^2.\] Also \(\Delta E_p=\sqrt{57}Mgl(\Delta\alpha)^2/3\). Taking the ratio of the two quadratic coefficients yields \[f_E=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{38\sqrt{57}}{347}\frac gl}.\]
B.1. General lattice equilibrium
Summing plate heights gives \[E_p=-\frac{N^2Mgl}{6}\left[\sqrt3(3N-2)\cos\alpha+3\sin\alpha\right].\] Differentiate: \[\alpha_{E}^{\prime}=\arctan\frac{\sqrt3}{3N-2}.\]
B.2. Large-lattice scaling
The potential curvature grows as \(N^3\). Since \(\alpha_{E}^{\prime}\sim1/N\), differentiated centre coordinates remain order l per plate even at indices of order N. Each plate contributes order one translational and rotational inertia, so total inertia grows as \(N^2\). Hence \((\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3)=(3,2,1/2)\). The small-angle limit is taken locally about each equilibrium before comparing N scaling.
C.1. Optimal force point
Virtual work requires \(F|\partial\mathbf r/\partial\alpha|\ge|\partial E_p/\partial\alpha|\). The largest vertex displacement per angle is at C(N-1,N-1), so choose that vertex.
C.2. Minimum holding force
At \(\alpha=\pi/3\), \(dE_p/d\alpha=3(N-1)N^2Mgl/4\). The C(N-1,N-1) derivative is \((3N-2)l(-\sqrt3/2,1/2)\). A force along that derivative supplies positive virtual work, giving \[F_{min}=\frac{3(N-1)N^2}{4(3N-2)}Mg,\qquad\theta_F=5\pi/6.\] The force is 150 degrees from positive x, rather than necessarily perpendicular to the line from the fixed vertex.

children.text: A thin-walled cylinder of mass M and inner radius R rotates about a fixed horizontal axis OZ. A smaller uniform solid cylinder of mass m and radius r<R rolls inside it, with parallel axes and moment of inertia Icm=mr²/2. Contact is rough and rolling has no slip except for the short initial skid in 1.8. Gravity is g. Measure θ, the angle of the small centre from the downward vertical, and φ, the outer-cylinder rotation, in the same positive counterclockwise sense. ψ is the small cylinder's absolute spin angle. Initially both angles are zero and the small cylinder is at the bottom. Use \(I_{cm}=mr^2/2\), and let \(\theta=0\) denote the lowest centre position.

children.text: Find ψ in terms of θ,φ,R,r.
Find the angular acceleration of the small cylinder in terms of the angular accelerations of θ and φ.
Derive an equation for θdouble-dot with general Icm.
If the outer cylinder is constrained to rotate at constant angular speed, find the small-oscillation period.
Find the stable equilibrium angle for 1.4.
For constant outer angular acceleration α, find the stable equilibrium angle and its existence condition.

The shell initially rotates steadily at Ω while the small centre is stationary at the bottom. Stop and hold the shell abruptly. After a very short skid, the small cylinder rolls without slip. statement.text:
Rolling Cylinders
A thin-walled cylinder of mass M and inner radius R rotates about a fixed horizontal axis OZ. A smaller uniform solid cylinder of mass m and radius r<R rolls inside it, with parallel axes and moment of inertia Icm=mr²/2. Contact is rough and rolling has no slip except for the short initial skid in 1.8. Gravity is g. Measure θ, the angle of the small centre from the downward vertical, and φ, the outer-cylinder rotation, in the same positive counterclockwise sense. ψ is the small cylinder's absolute spin angle. Initially both angles are zero and the small cylinder is at the bottom. Use \(I_{cm}=mr^2/2\), and let \(\theta=0\) denote the lowest centre position.

1.1. Rolling constraint
Find ψ in terms of θ,φ,R,r.
1.2. Spin acceleration
Find the angular acceleration of the small cylinder in terms of the angular accelerations of θ and φ.
1.3. Driven centre equation
Derive an equation for θdouble-dot with general Icm.
1.4. Period with fixed rotation rate
If the outer cylinder is constrained to rotate at constant angular speed, find the small-oscillation period.
1.5. Steady-rotation equilibrium
Find the stable equilibrium angle for 1.4.
1.6. Accelerating-shell equilibrium
For constant outer angular acceleration α, find the stable equilibrium angle and its existence condition.
1.7. Freely rotating outer cylinder
Release the outer cylinder so it rotates freely during small oscillations. Derive the oscillation period.
1.8. Abrupt stop and full ascent
The shell initially rotates steadily at Ω while the small centre is stationary at the bottom. Stop and hold the shell abruptly. After a very short skid, the small cylinder rolls without slip. In the high-friction, locally-flat approximation, find the minimum Ω needed to reach the top while maintaining contact.

children.text: Contact velocities obey \((R-r)\dot\theta+r\dot\psi=R\dot\phi\). Integrate with the stated initial angles: \[\psi=R\phi/r-(R-r)\theta/r.\]

Tangential translation gives \(m(R-r)\ddot\theta=f-mg\sin\theta\). Spin torque gives \(I_{cm}\ddot\psi=fr\). Eliminating f using 1.2 yields \[(m+I_{cm}/r^2)(R-r)\ddot\theta=-mg\sin\theta+(I_{cm}R/r^2)\ddot\phi.\]
Put φdouble-dot=0 and Icm=mr²/2. Then \(\ddot\theta=-2g\theta/[3(R-r)]\), giving \[T=2\pi\sqrt{3(R-r)/(2g)}.\]
With no angular acceleration, the gravitational tangential force must vanish. The stable bottom equilibrium is θ=0.
At equilibrium \(g\sin\theta_{eq}=R\alpha/2\), so \(\theta_{eq}=\arcsin(R\alpha/(2g))\) on the branch with cosθ>0. It exists for |Rα|≤2g, with marginal restoration at equality.

Its torque equation is \(MR^2\ddot\phi=-fR\). Combining this with the rolling constraint and the small-cylinder equations gives \[\ddot\theta=-\frac{g(2M+m)}{(R-r)(3M+m)}\sin\theta.\] Thus \[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(R-r)(3M+m)}{g(2M+m)}}.\] The M→∞ limit agrees with 1.4.

Before stopping, spin speed is RΩ/r. A friction impulse J gives mv=J and \(I(\omega-R\Omega/r)=-Jr\). At rolling onset v=rω, so v0=RΩ/3. Thereafter energy conservation gives top speed \(v_t^2=v_0^2-8g(R-r)/3\). The contact condition at the top is \(v_t^2\ge g(R-r)\). Thus \[\Omega_{min}=\frac{\sqrt{33g(R-r)}}R.\] Energy is lost during the skid and cannot be conserved across the abrupt-stop stage.

solution.text:
Rolling Cylinders
1.1. Rolling constraint
Contact velocities obey \((R-r)\dot\theta+r\dot\psi=R\dot\phi\). Integrate with the stated initial angles: \[\psi=R\phi/r-(R-r)\theta/r.\]
1.2. Spin acceleration
Differentiate twice: \[\ddot\psi=\frac Rr\ddot\phi-\frac{R-r}{r}\ddot\theta.\]
1.3. Driven centre equation
Tangential translation gives \(m(R-r)\ddot\theta=f-mg\sin\theta\). Spin torque gives \(I_{cm}\ddot\psi=fr\). Eliminating f using 1.2 yields \[(m+I_{cm}/r^2)(R-r)\ddot\theta=-mg\sin\theta+(I_{cm}R/r^2)\ddot\phi.\]
1.4. Period with fixed rotation rate
Put φdouble-dot=0 and Icm=mr²/2. Then \(\ddot\theta=-2g\theta/[3(R-r)]\), giving \[T=2\pi\sqrt{3(R-r)/(2g)}.\]
1.5. Steady-rotation equilibrium
With no angular acceleration, the gravitational tangential force must vanish. The stable bottom equilibrium is θ=0.
1.6. Accelerating-shell equilibrium
At equilibrium \(g\sin\theta_{eq}=R\alpha/2\), so \(\theta_{eq}=\arcsin(R\alpha/(2g))\) on the branch with cosθ>0. It exists for |Rα|≤2g, with marginal restoration at equality.
1.7. Freely rotating outer cylinder
Its torque equation is \(MR^2\ddot\phi=-fR\). Combining this with the rolling constraint and the small-cylinder equations gives \[\ddot\theta=-\frac{g(2M+m)}{(R-r)(3M+m)}\sin\theta.\] Thus \[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(R-r)(3M+m)}{g(2M+m)}}.\] The M→∞ limit agrees with 1.4.
1.8. Abrupt stop and full ascent
Before stopping, spin speed is RΩ/r. A friction impulse J gives mv=J and \(I(\omega-R\Omega/r)=-Jr\). At rolling onset v=rω, so v0=RΩ/3. Thereafter energy conservation gives top speed \(v_t^2=v_0^2-8g(R-r)/3\). The contact condition at the top is \(v_t^2\ge g(R-r)\). Thus \[\Omega_{min}=\frac{\sqrt{33g(R-r)}}R.\] Energy is lost during the skid and cannot be conserved across the abrupt-stop stage.

children.text: Electrons in a superconductor can lower their energy by Δ per electron by forming an opposite-spin, opposite-momentum Cooper pair. First model an electron as a uniformly charged ring with charge −e, mass m and radius r. Its angular velocity points along the ring normal n̂. The Bohr magneton is μB=eℏ/(2me)=\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV/T. In B write the common two-electron kinetic energy as K0=p1²/(2me)+p2²/(2me). Ignore orbital effects there. In C ignore spins and minimize the normalized real-wavefunction functional \[F=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi\left(-\alpha\psi-\frac{\hbar^2}{4m_e}\psi^{\prime\prime}+\frac{e^2B_z^2x^2}{m_e}\psi\right)dx,\qquad\alpha>0.\] In D, spin-orbit coupling gives opposite internal fields +Bz ẑ and −Bz ẑ to opposite-momentum electrons. These internal fields act on spin only. An external in-plane field Bx x̂ is perpendicular to them, and orbital effects of this in-plane field are ignored.

statement.text:
Magnetic field effects on superconductors
Electrons in a superconductor can lower their energy by Δ per electron by forming an opposite-spin, opposite-momentum Cooper pair. First model an electron as a uniformly charged ring with charge −e, mass m and radius r. Its angular velocity points along the ring normal n̂. The Bohr magneton is μB=eℏ/(2me)=\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV/T. In B write the common two-electron kinetic energy as K0=p1²/(2me)+p2²/(2me). Ignore orbital effects there. In C ignore spins and minimize the normalized real-wavefunction functional \[F=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi\left(-\alpha\psi-\frac{\hbar^2}{4m_e}\psi^{\prime\prime}+\frac{e^2B_z^2x^2}{m_e}\psi\right)dx,\qquad\alpha>0.\] In D, spin-orbit coupling gives opposite internal fields +Bz ẑ and −Bz ẑ to opposite-momentum electrons. These internal fields act on spin only. An external in-plane field Bx x̂ is perpendicular to them, and orbital effects of this in-plane field are ignored.

a1. Ring angular momentum
Find the magnitude and direction of angular momentum for angular speed ω.
a2. Orbital magnetic moment
Relate ring magnetic moment to its angular momentum.
a3. Orientation energy
If n̂ makes angle θ to a uniform field Bz ẑ, find U with U=0 at θ=π/2.
a4. Classical spin estimate
Use the ring gyromagnetic relation for spin projection ±ℏ/2. Find energies for spins parallel and antiparallel to B.
a5. Quantum spin energies
Quantum mechanics doubles the A4 values. Give both energies at B=1 T and use this convention subsequently.
b1. Pair energy
Find ES for a Cooper pair in a uniform field when only spin is affected.
b2. Normal-state minimum
Find the minimum energy EN of two unpaired electrons in an in-plane field Bx>0.
b3. Paramagnetic threshold
Find BP above which the normal state is preferred in this pair model.
c1. Optimal Gaussian
For \(\psi=(2\lambda/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-\lambda x^2}\), find λ minimizing F. You may use Gaussian normalization and ⟨x²⟩=1/(4λ).
c2. Orbital critical field
Find the critical |Bz| where the superconducting state is no longer energetically favoured.
d1. Ising pair energy

Find EI for the opposite-momentum pair in the internal fields of magnitude Bz>0.
d2. Normal energy in crossed fields
Find the minimum normal-state energy E∥ under external Bx.
d3. Enhanced Ising threshold
Find BI such that E∥<EI for |Bx|>BI.

children.text: The ring inertia is mr². Thus \(\mathbf L=mr^2\omega\hat{\mathbf n}\), with direction given by the right-hand rule.
The signed current is I=−eω/(2π), so \(\boldsymbol\mu=I\pi r^2\hat{\mathbf n}=-e\mathbf L/(2m)\). The magnetic moment is antiparallel to angular momentum.
Integrate magnetic torque or use \(U=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B\). Thus \(U=er^2\omega B_z\cos\theta/2\). The positive sign follows because the ring charge is negative.
With the classical factor one, \(U_{up}=+\mu_BB/2\) and \(U_{down}=-\mu_BB/2\). These are estimates before the quantum spin factor is applied.
The corrected energies are U′up=+μBB=+\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV and U′down=−μBB=−\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV. Magnetic moment parallel to B means spin antiparallel to B.
Opposite spin Zeeman energies cancel, so \(E_S=K_0-2\Delta\).
Both magnetic moments align with the field, lowering each electron energy by μBBx. Thus \(E_N=K_0-2\mu_BB_x\).
EN<ES when 2μBBx>2Δ. Thus \(B_P=\Delta/\mu_B\). This simplified two-electron criterion differs from the full condensation-energy Pauli limit by a factor √2.

The expectation is \(F=-\alpha+\hbar^2\lambda/(4m_e)+e^2B_z^2/(4m_e\lambda)\). Set its derivative to zero with λ>0, obtaining \(\lambda=e|B_z|/\hbar\). The second derivative is positive. The field checks Bz>0.
At the minimum \(F_{min}=-\alpha+e\hbar|B_z|/(2m_e)\). Setting it to zero gives \(B_c=2m_e\alpha/(e\hbar)=\alpha/\mu_B\).
The two spins are opposite but each magnetic moment aligns with its own opposite internal field. Thus \(E_I=K_0-2\Delta-2\mu_BB_z\).
d2. Normal energy in crossed fields
The two total fields are (Bx,0,±Bz), both of magnitude \(\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}\). Align each magnetic moment with its own total field, giving \(E_\parallel=K_0-2\mu_B\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}\).
At equality \(\sqrt{B_I^2+B_z^2}=B_z+\Delta/\mu_B\). Therefore \[B_I=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta^2+2\Delta\mu_BB_z}}{\mu_B}.\] It can greatly exceed BP when the internal spin-orbit field is large.

solution.text:
Magnetic field effects on superconductors
a1. Ring angular momentum
The ring inertia is mr². Thus \(\mathbf L=mr^2\omega\hat{\mathbf n}\), with direction given by the right-hand rule.
a2. Orbital magnetic moment
The signed current is I=−eω/(2π), so \(\boldsymbol\mu=I\pi r^2\hat{\mathbf n}=-e\mathbf L/(2m)\). The magnetic moment is antiparallel to angular momentum.
a3. Orientation energy
Integrate magnetic torque or use \(U=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B\). Thus \(U=er^2\omega B_z\cos\theta/2\). The positive sign follows because the ring charge is negative.
a4. Classical spin estimate
With the classical factor one, \(U_{up}=+\mu_BB/2\) and \(U_{down}=-\mu_BB/2\). These are estimates before the quantum spin factor is applied.
a5. Quantum spin energies
The corrected energies are U′up=+μBB=+\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV and U′down=−μBB=−\(5.788\times10^{-5}\) eV. Magnetic moment parallel to B means spin antiparallel to B.
b1. Pair energy
Opposite spin Zeeman energies cancel, so \(E_S=K_0-2\Delta\).
b2. Normal-state minimum
Both magnetic moments align with the field, lowering each electron energy by μBBx. Thus \(E_N=K_0-2\mu_BB_x\).
b3. Paramagnetic threshold
EN<ES when 2μBBx>2Δ. Thus \(B_P=\Delta/\mu_B\). This simplified two-electron criterion differs from the full condensation-energy Pauli limit by a factor √2.
c1. Optimal Gaussian
The expectation is \(F=-\alpha+\hbar^2\lambda/(4m_e)+e^2B_z^2/(4m_e\lambda)\). Set its derivative to zero with λ>0, obtaining \(\lambda=e|B_z|/\hbar\). The second derivative is positive. The field checks Bz>0.
c2. Orbital critical field
At the minimum \(F_{min}=-\alpha+e\hbar|B_z|/(2m_e)\). Setting it to zero gives \(B_c=2m_e\alpha/(e\hbar)=\alpha/\mu_B\).
d1. Ising pair energy
The two spins are opposite but each magnetic moment aligns with its own opposite internal field. Thus \(E_I=K_0-2\Delta-2\mu_BB_z\).
d2. Normal energy in crossed fields
The two total fields are (Bx,0,±Bz), both of magnitude \(\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}\). Align each magnetic moment with its own total field, giving \(E_\parallel=K_0-2\mu_B\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}\).
d3. Enhanced Ising threshold
At equality \(\sqrt{B_I^2+B_z^2}=B_z+\Delta/\mu_B\). Therefore \[B_I=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta^2+2\Delta\mu_BB_z}}{\mu_B}.\] It can greatly exceed BP when the internal spin-orbit field is large.

b. Classical Hall resistance

Because (−ŷ)×ẑ=−x̂, electron drift is along −x. Conventional current is along +x.
\(I=Ne v_s/L=NeE_y/(BL)\) and VH=EyW. Hence \(R_H=BLW/(Ne)=\phi/(Ne)\), as a positive resistance magnitude.

children.text: Study charged particles in the terrestrial magnetosphere. Use \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(\epsilon_0=8.9\times10^{-12}\), \(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\), \(e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), electron mass \(m=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), proton mass \(m_p=1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(k=1.38\times10^{-23}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), \(h=6.626\times10^{-34}\), \(R_E=6.4\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), and equatorial surface dipole strength \(B_0=3.1\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm T\). For a dipole directed down the z axis, use \[\mathbf B_d=\frac{B_0R_E^3}{r^5}[-3xz\hat{\mathbf x}-3yz\hat{\mathbf y}+(x^2+y^2-2z^2)\hat{\mathbf z}],\quad r\ge R_E.\] The original statement prints a plus sign on the x term, inconsistent with an axial dipole and the later solution. The corrected dipole convention is explicit here. Dayside reconnection permits some solar-wind particles to reach the magnetotail and subsequently precipitate into the thermosphere.

The corrected dipole convention is explicit here. Dayside reconnection permits some solar-wind particles to reach the magnetotail and subsequently precipitate into the thermosphere.
a.i. Electron gyro-orbit

An electron starts at the origin with velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf y}\) perpendicular to uniform \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\). Find its trajectory.
a.ii. Current and magnetic moment
Find the current magnitude and the electron orbital magnetic-moment vector.
a.iii. Helical pitch
If the initial velocity makes angle \(0<\theta<90^\circ\) with B, find the helix pitch.
b.i. Diamagnetic current
In uniform B along z, ions and electrons have equal temperature and density \(n(x)=n_0+\alpha x\), with \(\alpha>0\). Explain the current generation with a sketch. Pressure is \(p=2knT\).
b.ii. Plasma magnetization
For Maxwellian ions and electrons, find beta in the signed magnetization \(M=\beta n(x)kT/B\). You may use \(\int_0^\infty xe^{-x}dx=1\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi\).
c. Diamagnetic field ratio
At \((x,y,z)=(10R_E,0,R_E)\), use \(p(z)=p_0e^{-(z/a)^2}\), \(p_0=3\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{Pa}\), \(a=2R_E\), and local \(B_{dia}=\mu_0M\). Calculate the ratio of diamagnetic and dipole field magnitudes, noting the different field-axis orientation from part b.
d.i. Adiabatic magnetic moment

For a slowly varying magnetic mirror, \(\langle B_r\rangle=-r_c(dB/ds)/2\), with \(|B_r|\ll B_z\). Derive the gyro-averaged parallel force and show that \(\mu=mv_\perp^2/(2B)\) is conserved.
d.ii. Mirror confinement
At the field minimum Bmin the pitch angle is theta. The mirror maximum is Bmax. Find the trapping condition.
e. Auroral loss cone

A particle starts at the equator at x=6RE with pitch theta. In the dipole approximation and ignoring drift, determine the pitch-angle condition for it to reach below 200 km near latitude 60 degrees.
f.i. Atmospheric stratification
Assume isothermal ideal gas with \(\rho_0g/P_0=0.13\,\mathrm{km^{-1}}\). Find density versus altitude and the oxygen-density ratio at 160 and 220 km.
f.ii. Auroral colours

Oxygen excited states lie 1.96 and 4.17 eV above ground, with lifetimes 110 s and 0.8 s. Collision frequency is \(\nu=10^9\rho/\rho_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Predict colours at 160 and 220 km.
g. Solar-wind compression
Find the minimum solar-wind speed pushing the dayside magnetopause to geosynchronous radius. The wind has field \(B_s=5\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm T\) and density 50 protons per cubic centimetre. Ignore inner plasma pressure and changes of the dipole. Use the stated energy-density balance with magnetic pressure \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\).

children.text: Let \(\omega_c=eB/m>0\), \(r_c=mv/(eB)\). Newton gives \(\dot v_x=-\omega_cv_y,\dot v_y=\omega_cv_x\). With the prescribed initial conditions, \[x=r_c(\cos\omega_ct-1),\quad y=r_c\sin\omega_ct,\quad z=0.\] It is a circle centred at \((-r_c,0)\), not at the initial position. The source unshifted circle misses the origin condition.
\(I=e/T=e^2B/(2\pi m)\). The conventional current circulates opposite to the electron, so \[\boldsymbol\mu=-\frac{mv_\perp^2}{2B}\hat{\mathbf B}.\] It is diamagnetic.
The parallel speed stays \(v\cos\theta\); multiply it by \(2\pi m/(eB)\). The pitch is \(2\pi mv\cos\theta/(eB)\), with orbit radius \(mv\sin\theta/(eB)\).

Opposite gyration senses and more guiding centres on the denser side produce charge currents in the same transverse direction. Magnetization is \(\mathbf M=-(p/B)\hat{\mathbf z}\), so \(\mathbf j_M=\nabla\times\mathbf M=(2kT\alpha/B)\hat{\mathbf y}\). Draw excess conventional current along positive y. This satisfies \(\mathbf j\times\mathbf B=\nabla p\).
For either species, \(\langle mv_\perp^2/2\rangle=kT\). Each therefore contributes \(-nkT/B\) along B. Together \(M=-2nkT/B=-p/B\), giving beta=-2.

Use \(|\mathbf B_d|^2=B_0^2(30^2+98^2)/101^5\). Then \(|B_{dia}|/|B_d|=\mu_0p/|B_d|^2\simeq0.306\). The source value about one divides by the squared x component alone. That is not the total dipole-field magnitude. The local magnetization opposes the total local field, so use its full magnitude unless a projected-component ratio is explicitly requested.

Gyro-averaging the axial Lorentz force gives \(F_\parallel=-\mu\,dB/ds\), where mu is the positive moment magnitude. Then \(d(mv_\parallel^2/2)/dt=-\mu\,dB/dt\). Total kinetic energy is constant, while perpendicular energy is \(\mu B\). Its derivative must be \(\mu\,dB/dt\), so \(B\,d\mu/dt=0\). Thus mu is adiabatically conserved under the stated slow-field approximation.

At reflection \(v_\parallel=0\). Energy and mu conservation give \(\sin^2\theta\ge B_{min}/B_{max}\). Thus \[\theta\ge\arcsin\sqrt{B_{min}/B_{max}}.\] The source final arcsine omits the square root, although its preceding velocity inequality requires it.

The initial strength is \(B_i=B_0/216\). At \(r=R_E+200\,\mathrm{km}\), latitude 60 degrees, \(B_L=B_0(R_E/r)^3\sqrt{1+3\sin^260^\circ}\). To avoid mirroring above that level, \(\sin^2\theta<B_i/B_L\), yielding roughly \(\theta<3.0^\circ\). Neglecting the 200 km altitude gives about 2.9 degrees. A single ideal dipole line from 6RE reaches the surface nearer 66 degrees, so the source specified latitude is an approximate target-field estimate rather than an exact field-line intersection.

With constant g over the height range, hydrostatic balance gives \(\rho(H)=\rho_0e^{-0.13H}\), H in km. Hence \(\rho(160)/\rho(220)=e^{7.8}=2.44\times10^3\). Keeping inverse-square gravity instead gives \(\rho/\rho_0=\exp[-(\rho_0gR_E/P_0)(1-R_E/(R_E+H))]\).

At 160 km, \(\nu\simeq0.93\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), quenching the long-lived first state while the short-lived second state can radiate to the first. The photon has energy 2.21 eV and wavelength about 562 nm, green. At 220 km, \(\nu\simeq3.8\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), so the first state survives and can radiate to ground at about 633 nm, red. The source assumes the lower excited state is more populated to identify the dominant red light. Other lines can still occur.

For a 24-hour period, \(r_g^3=gR_E^2(86400/(2\pi))^2\), so \(r_g\simeq6.59R_E\). Local dipole field is \(B_m=B_0(R_E/r_g)^3\). The model balance is \(\rho_sv^2/2+B_s^2/(2\mu_0)=B_m^2/(2\mu_0)\), with \(\rho_s=50\times10^6m_p\). Hence \[v=\sqrt{(B_m^2-B_s^2)/(\mu_0\rho_s)}\simeq330\,\mathrm{km/s}.\] This uses the source energy-density convention. A fluid momentum-flux pressure convention would replace the one-half kinetic factor and give a different threshold.

Hence \[v=\sqrt{(B_m^2-B_s^2)/(\mu_0\rho_s)}\simeq330\,\mathrm{km/s}.\] This uses the source energy-density convention. A fluid momentum-flux pressure convention would replace the one-half kinetic factor and give a different threshold.

children.text: Bright transmission requires 2ntcosθ=mλ. Since 2t/λ=33921.3026, the highest accessible integer is 33921. Thus m1=33921, m2=33920 and m3=33919.
Use \(\theta_i=\arccos(m_i\lambda/(2t))\), obtaining approximately 0.242°, 0.502° and 0.668°. The source rounding gives 0.241°, 0.502° and 0.667°.
\(D_i=2f\tan\theta_i\simeq2f\theta_i\), with angles in radians. The diameters are approximately 2.53, 5.26 and 6.99 mm.
At half maximum Fsin²(ε/4)=1. Thus \(\epsilon=4\arcsin(1/\sqrt F)\simeq4/\sqrt F=0.211\,\mathrm{rad}\).

Each new centre crossing increases optical order by one. Hence \(2t(n_{air}-1)/\lambda\simeq10\), giving \(n_{air}\simeq1+10\lambda/(2t)=1.000295\). The fractional initial order and endpoint counting limit the precision of this estimate.

With ν0=c/λ, \[
u_a=
u_0- rac{\Delta E_1+\Delta E_2}{2h},\quad
u_b=
u_0- rac{\Delta E_2-\Delta E_1}{2h},\] \[
u_c=
u_0+ rac{\Delta E_2-\Delta E_1}{2h},\quad
u_d=
u_0+ rac{\Delta E_1+\Delta E_2}{2h}.\] Each level is displaced by half its full gap.

Paraxial interference gives \(|\Delta\lambda|/\lambda=|D_j^2-D_i^2|/(8f^2)\), and \(|\Delta\nu|=c|\Delta\lambda|/\lambda^2\). Thus \[\Delta E_1=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_2^2-D_1^2)=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_4^2-D_3^2),\] \[\Delta E_2=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_4^2-D_2^2)=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_3^2-D_1^2).\] Experimental rounding makes alternative pairs slightly different.

Divide the E-derived gaps by μBB. Pairs (D2,D1) and (D4,D2) give gk1≈0.68 and gk2≈1.99. Alternative pairs give about 0.72 and 1.95. These are consistent with theoretical 2/3 and 2 within the supplied measurement precision.
The full energy span is (gk1+gk2)μBB≈hcΔλ/λ². Thus \(B=4\pi m_ec\Delta\lambda/[e\lambda^2(g_{k1}+g_{k2})]\). Using the source sum 2.67 gives B≈0.277 T, or 2770 gauss.

The free spectral range is c/(2t)=\(1.5\times10^{10}\) Hz. The LED width is approximately cΔλ/λ²=\(1.42\times10^{13}\) Hz, giving N≈2tΔλ/λ²≈947. The source rounds the bandwidth first and reports 946. Exact endpoint counting depends on the specified band edges.
\(\Delta\nu=c\epsilon/(4\pi nt)\simeq c/(\pi nt\sqrt F)\simeq5.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}\). This is the individual linewidth, not the 15 GHz free spectral range.

Fabry-Perot etalon and Zeeman splitting
a.i. First three orders
Bright transmission requires 2ntcosθ=mλ. Since 2t/λ=33921.3026, the highest accessible integer is 33921. Thus m1=33921, m2=33920 and m3=33919.
a.ii. Ring angles
Use \(\theta_i=\arccos(m_i\lambda/(2t))\), obtaining approximately 0.242°, 0.502° and 0.668°. The source rounding gives 0.241°, 0.502° and 0.667°.
a.iii. Ring diameters
\(D_i=2f\tan\theta_i\simeq2f\theta_i\), with angles in radians. The diameters are approximately 2.53, 5.26 and 6.99 mm.
b.i. Phase linewidth
At half maximum Fsin²(ε/4)=1. Thus \(\epsilon=4\arcsin(1/\sqrt F)\simeq4/\sqrt F=0.211\,\mathrm{rad}\).
b.ii. Resolving power
\(|\Delta\delta|=4\pi nt|\Delta\lambda|/\lambda^2\). Thus \(\lambda/\Delta\lambda=4\pi nt/(\lambda\epsilon)\simeq\pi nt\sqrt F/\lambda=1.01\times10^6\).
c. Air refractive index
Each new centre crossing increases optical order by one. Hence \(2t(n_{air}-1)/\lambda\simeq10\), giving \(n_{air}\simeq1+10\lambda/(2t)=1.000295\). The fractional initial order and endpoint counting limit the precision of this estimate.
d. Four Zeeman frequencies
With ν0=c/λ, \[\nu_a=\nu_0-\frac{\Delta E_1+\Delta E_2}{2h},\quad\nu_b=\nu_0-\frac{\Delta E_2-\Delta E_1}{2h},\] \[\nu_c=\nu_0+\frac{\Delta E_2-\Delta E_1}{2h},\quad\nu_d=\nu_0+\frac{\Delta E_1+\Delta E_2}{2h}.\] Each level is displaced by half its full gap.
e. Splittings from ring diameters
Paraxial interference gives \(|\Delta\lambda|/\lambda=|D_j^2-D_i^2|/(8f^2)\), and \(|\Delta\nu|=c|\Delta\lambda|/\lambda^2\). Thus \[\Delta E_1=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_2^2-D_1^2)=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_4^2-D_3^2),\] \[\Delta E_2=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_4^2-D_2^2)=\frac{hc}{8\lambda f^2}(D_3^2-D_1^2).\] Experimental rounding makes alternative pairs slightly different.
f. Measured Landé factors
Divide the E-derived gaps by μBB. Pairs (D2,D1) and (D4,D2) give gk1≈0.68 and gk2≈1.99. Alternative pairs give about 0.72 and 1.95. These are consistent with theoretical 2/3 and 2 within the supplied measurement precision.
g. Solar magnetic field
The full energy span is (gk1+gk2)μBB≈hcΔλ/λ². Thus \(B=4\pi m_ec\Delta\lambda/[e\lambda^2(g_{k1}+g_{k2})]\). Using the source sum 2.67 gives B≈0.277 T, or 2770 gauss.
h.i. LED transmitted comb
The free spectral range is c/(2t)=\(1.5\times10^{10}\) Hz. The LED width is approximately cΔλ/λ²=\(1.42\times10^{13}\) Hz, giving N≈2tΔλ/λ²≈947. The source rounds the bandwidth first and reports 946. Exact endpoint counting depends on the specified band edges.
h.ii. Individual comb linewidth
\(\Delta\nu=c\epsilon/(4\pi nt)\simeq c/(\pi nt\sqrt F)\simeq5.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}\). This is the individual linewidth, not the 15 GHz free spectral range.

children.text: A phase point specifies the coordinate and momentum of a system, and its trajectory has arrows in the direction of time. For a one-coordinate system the phase portrait is a collection of curves in a two-dimensional plane. Unless specified otherwise use axes \((x,p)\), with \(p=m\dot x\), and neglect air resistance. For a pendulum use \((\alpha,\dot\alpha)\), where \(\alpha\) is measured from the downward vertical.
Draw the phase trajectory of a free particle reflecting elastically from walls at \(x=\pm L/2\).
For mass \(m\) under \(F=-kx\), find the phase-trajectory equation and its parameters.
Draw a harmonic-oscillator phase trajectory and indicate its time direction.

A mass \(m\) at the end of a massless rigid rod of length \(L\) swings in gravity \(g\). Draw its phase portrait at arbitrary angle. How many qualitatively different non-equilibrium trajectory types occur, and what conditions distinguish them?

A block of mass \(m\) on a horizontal surface is attached to a spring of constant \(k\). Static and kinetic friction coefficients both equal \(\mu\). Initially \(x=A_0>0\), velocity zero. Write its equation of motion.
B2. Damped phase portrait and equilibria
Draw the phase trajectory and find equilibrium points.
Must the block stop at zero extension? Find the width of its possible final-rest region.
Find the drop in successive positive-side turning amplitudes while full cycles continue.
Find the time between successive positive maxima and the sequence \(A(t_n)\).
B5. Motion graph and cycle count
Sketch \(x(t)\), and estimate the number of oscillations before rest.

children.text: The speed is constant between impacts, giving horizontal segments \(p=\pm p_0\), \(-L/2<x<L/2\). At each wall momentum reverses instantaneously. The top segment runs right and the bottom segment left, with the wall jumps closing a clockwise rectangle.
Energy conservation gives \(p^2/(2m)+kx^2/2=E\), or \[\frac{x^2}{2E/k}+\frac{p^2}{2mE}=1.\] The semiaxes are \(\sqrt{2E/k}\) in x and \(\sqrt{2mE}\) in p.
Draw the ellipse centred on the origin. At positive p the coordinate increases, so the trajectory is clockwise. The origin itself is the equilibrium point.

Energy is \(E=mL^2\dot\alpha^2/2+mgL(1-\cos\alpha)\). There are three types: closed librations for \(0<E<2mgL\), separatrices for \(E=2mgL\), and continuous rotations for \(E>2mgL\). Plot both rotational directions and both branches of each separatrix. Centres are at \(\alpha=2n\pi\), saddles at \((2n+1)\pi\). The separatrix approaches a top equilibrium only asymptotically. Equilibrium points are excluded from the count.

nodes.alt: Original pendulum energy and phase portrait showing oscillations, separatrices and rotations.

children.text: While moving, \[m\ddot x=-kx-\mu mg\,\operatorname{sgn}(\dot x).\] At rest it remains stuck if \(|kx|\le\mu mg\). The moving equation alone must not be used to force motion through the sticking region.
B2. Damped phase portrait and equilibria

Define \(c=\mu mg/k\), \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). For positive velocity, \((x+c)^2+(p/(m\omega_0))^2\) is constant. For negative velocity replace \(x+c\) by \(x-c\). Join alternating half-ellipses at turning points with clockwise arrows. Their centres are \((-c,0)\) and \((c,0)\), but the actual static equilibria comprise the entire segment \(p=0,|x|\le c\).

nodes.alt: Original clockwise sliding-friction phase trajectory with alternating shifted half-ellipses.

children.text: It need not stop at zero. Static friction permits any \(-c\le x_f\le c\), whose width is \(2c=2\mu mg/k\).
Each half-cycle reduces turning-distance magnitude by \(2c\). A full cycle therefore gives \(\Delta A=4c=4\mu mg/k\).

Each moving half-cycle lasts \(\pi/\omega_0\). Thus \(t_n=nT\), \(T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\), and \(A(t_n)=A_0-4n\mu mg/k\), until sticking interrupts the next half-cycle. The envelope is linear rather than exponential.
B5. Motion graph and cycle count

Draw sinusoidal arcs around alternating shifted centres, under a linearly decreasing envelope, then a horizontal line at the final position in \([-c,c]\). The rough full-cycle estimate is \(N\simeq A_0/(4c)=kA_0/(4\mu mg)\), which is not an exact integer count near the last partial cycle. More precisely, if \(A_0>c\), the number of moving half-cycles is \(\lceil(A_0-c)/(2c)\rceil\). If \(A_0\le c\), the block never starts.

children.text: In the two-slit electron interference experiment, a monochromatic point source \(S\) emits electrons through an electron biprism onto a screen. The biprism consists of a grounded cylindrical wire mesh with a thin central filament \(F\), directed into the figure. \(S_1,S_2\) are virtual sources separated by \(d\). The source-to-biprism distance is \(\ell\), and the biprism-to-screen distance is \(L\). The diagram is not to scale. Experiments were performed by Mollenstedt and colleagues, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi, and Tonomura and colleagues.

nodes.alt: Original electron biprism ray diagram: source S and virtual sources S1 and S2 separated by d, filament F in grounded mesh, distances ell and L, screen, transverse x axis, propagation z axis, filament radius a and mesh radius b.

children.text: Take the filament cross-section centre as origin \(O\). Find the potential \(V(x,z)\) near the filament in terms of filament surface potential \(V_a\), filament radius \(a\), and mesh radius \(b\). Ignore mirror charges.

An incoming electron plane wave has wave-vector component \(k_z\). Find its induced transverse component \(k_x\) due to the biprism in terms of electron charge, \(v_z,V_a,k_z,a,b\), with \(|k_x|\ll k_z\). Use \(\mathbf k=2\pi\mathbf p/h\).
Before \(S\), electrons are accelerated from a field-emission tip through potential \(V_0\). Find the nonrelativistic wavelength using rest mass \(m\), charge and \(V_0\).

Use \(v_z=c/2\), \(V_a=10\,\mathrm V\), \(V_0=50\,\mathrm{kV}\), \(a=0.5\,\mu\mathrm m\), \(b=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(\ell=25\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(L=1.5\,\mathrm m\), \(h=6.6\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), electron charge magnitude \(e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), rest mass \(m=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(c=3\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
Find the interference fringe spacing on the screen.
If the electron wave is spherical instead of planar, is its fringe spacing larger, equal or smaller than in d.ii?
Find the percentage wavelength error caused by using the nonrelativistic approximation in part c.
Find the separation \(d\) of the apparent double slits.

Conventions: use positive e for the electron-charge magnitude. The transverse deflection changes sign on opposite sides of the filament, so the automatic k_x fields ask for its magnitude. Retain the supplied v_z for deflection and V_0 for wavelengths, as the official calculation does.

statement.text:
Question 2: Electron biprism
In the two-slit electron interference experiment, a monochromatic point source \(S\) emits electrons through an electron biprism onto a screen. Experiments were performed by Mollenstedt and colleagues, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi, and Tonomura and colleagues.

a

b

c.i

c.ii
Find the wavelength including relativity.
Use \(v_z=c/2\), \(V_a=10\,\mathrm V\), \(V_0=50\,\mathrm{kV}\), \(a=0.5\,\mu\mathrm m\), \(b=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(\ell=25\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(L=1.5\,\mathrm m\), \(h=6.6\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\), electron charge magnitude \(e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), rest mass \(m=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(c=3\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
d.i
Calculate \(k_x\).
d.ii
Find the interference fringe spacing on the screen.
d.iii
If the electron wave is spherical instead of planar, is its fringe spacing larger, equal or smaller than in d.ii?
d.iv
Find the percentage wavelength error caused by using the nonrelativistic approximation in part c.
d.v
Find the separation \(d\) of the apparent double slits.
Conventions: use positive e for the electron-charge magnitude. The transverse deflection changes sign on opposite sides of the filament, so the automatic k_x fields ask for its magnitude. Retain the supplied v_z for deflection and V_0 for wavelengths, as the official calculation does.

children.text: For line charge density \(\lambda_q\), Gauss's law gives \(E_r=\lambda_q/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\). Integrate with \(V(b)=0\) and eliminate \(\lambda_q\) using \(V(a)=V_a\):

With electron charge \(-e\), the force is \(F_x=e\,\partial V/\partial x=-eV_ax/[(x^2+z^2)\ln(b/a)]\). To leading small-deflection order, treat \(x\) and \(v_z\) as constant during transit. The near-filament straight-line approximation extends the impulse integral to infinite limits:

Equivalently, solve the transverse equation of motion for the small slope \(|dx/dz|=\pi eV_a/[mv_z^2\ln(b/a)]\) in a nonrelativistic trajectory treatment, then use \(k_x/k_z\simeq dx/dz\). In the relativistic form use \(p_z=\gamma mv_z\), so the same impulse-to-wave-vector result follows. The positive source result is the magnitude, although an intermediate impulse is evaluated at positive \(x\) with an inconsistent sign.

\[V(r)=\frac{\lambda_q}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac br=V_a\frac{\ln(b/r)}{\ln(b/a)},\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+z^2}.\]
b. Transverse impulse
With electron charge \(-e\), the force is \(F_x=e\,\partial V/\partial x=-eV_ax/[(x^2+z^2)\ln(b/a)]\). To leading small-deflection order, treat \(x\) and \(v_z\) as constant during transit. The near-filament straight-line approximation extends the impulse integral to infinite limits:
\[\Delta p_x=\frac1{v_z}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F_x\,dz=-\operatorname{sgn}(x)\frac{\pi eV_a}{v_z\ln(b/a)}.\]
\[|k_x|=\frac{2\pi}{h}|\Delta p_x|=\frac{2\pi^2 eV_a}{hv_z\ln(b/a)}.\]
Equivalently, solve the transverse equation of motion for the small slope \(|dx/dz|=\pi eV_a/[mv_z^2\ln(b/a)]\) in a nonrelativistic trajectory treatment, then use \(k_x/k_z\simeq dx/dz\). \[\lambda_\mathrm{nr}=\frac h{\sqrt{2meV_0}},\qquad \lambda_\mathrm{rel}=\frac h{\sqrt{2meV_0\left(1+\dfrac{eV_0}{2mc^2}\right)}}.\]

a. Aligned lens geometry

b. Perfect alignment image

children.text: Place observer, lens and source on an axis, with the lens between the others. Draw a ray reaching transverse radius \(r_E\) at the lens plane, then bending towards the observer. Label \(\theta_E\) at the observer, total bend \(\alpha\) at the lens, distances \(D_L,D_S,D_S-D_L\). The source-side angle is \(\alpha-\theta_E\). Rotational symmetry creates equivalent rays at all azimuths.

children.text: Rotational symmetry turns a point image into a circular Einstein ring, centred on the projected lens position, with angular radius \(\theta_E\). A finite-size source broadens the ring.

For an ideal point source and point lens there are two images, on opposite sides of the lens along the line to the unlensed source. For a small-angle source offset \(\beta\), the lens equation is \(\beta=\theta-\theta_E^2/\theta\), with roots \(\theta_\pm=[\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2+4\theta_E^2}]/2\). A resolved extended source produces distorted arcs, rather than a complete ring. Show the two rays in the plane containing observer, lens and source. The official marking notes favour arcs and discuss incomplete rings. Those describe an extended or resolved source. For the ideal point-source, point-lens model, the two-image lens-equation result above is the consistent limit. Compare the geometry as well as the sketch.
Zero asymptotic kinetic energy requires \(mv_{esc}^2/2-GMm/r=0\), so \(v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).

The substitution gives \(r_S=2GM/c^2\), the same radius as in general relativity. The Newtonian argument reproduces the expression but does not derive an event horizon or the behaviour of light inside it.
Both angles are very small. Small-angle approximations for sine and tangent are valid for both. Neither angle is irrelevant to the geometry.

solution.text:
Gravitational lensing
a. Aligned lens geometry
Place observer, lens and source on an axis, with the lens between the others. Draw a ray reaching transverse radius \(r_E\) at the lens plane, then bending towards the observer. Label \(\theta_E\) at the observer, total bend \(\alpha\) at the lens, distances \(D_L,D_S,D_S-D_L\). The source-side angle is \(\alpha-\theta_E\). Rotational symmetry creates equivalent rays at all azimuths.

b. Perfect alignment image
Rotational symmetry turns a point image into a circular Einstein ring, centred on the projected lens position, with angular radius \(\theta_E\). A finite-size source broadens the ring.
c. Misalignment image
For an ideal point source and point lens there are two images, on opposite sides of the lens along the line to the unlensed source. For a small-angle source offset \(\beta\), the lens equation is \(\beta=\theta-\theta_E^2/\theta\), with roots \(\theta_\pm=[\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2+4\theta_E^2}]/2\). A resolved extended source produces distorted arcs, rather than a complete ring. Show the two rays in the plane containing observer, lens and source. The official marking notes favour arcs and discuss incomplete rings. Those describe an extended or resolved source. For the ideal point-source, point-lens model, the two-image lens-equation result above is the consistent limit. Compare the geometry as well as the sketch.
d.escape. Newtonian escape speed
Zero asymptotic kinetic energy requires \(mv_{esc}^2/2-GMm/r=0\), so \(v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).
d.radius. Schwarzschild radius
The substitution gives \(r_S=2GM/c^2\), the same radius as in general relativity. The Newtonian argument reproduces the expression but does not derive an event horizon or the behaviour of light inside it.
e. Radius from deflection
Because \(\alpha=2r_S/r_E\), \(r_S=\alpha r_E/2\).
f. Angular approximation choice
Both angles are very small. Small-angle approximations for sine and tangent are valid for both. Neither angle is irrelevant to the geometry.
g. Radius from measurable distances
\(r_E\simeq D_L\theta_E\), and \(\alpha\simeq\theta_E+r_E/(D_S-D_L)=\theta_ED_S/(D_S-D_L)\). Therefore \[r_S=\frac{\theta_E^2D_LD_S}{2(D_S-D_L)}.\]
h. Einstein angular radius
\[\theta_E=\sqrt{\frac{4GM}{c^2}\frac{D_S-D_L}{D_LD_S}}=7.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad},\] about 0.014 arcseconds.

7.RC. Resistance-capacitance product

children.text: Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder gives \(\mathbf E=\lambda\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\).
Integrating \(-E_r\) gives \(f(r)=-\lambda\ln(r/r_*)/(2\pi\epsilon_0)\), where any reference length \(r_*\) is absorbed in K. There is no finite choice \(V(\infty)=0\) for an isolated infinite line.

Superposition gives \[V=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac{(x-b)^2+y^2}{(x+b)^2+y^2}.\] Fixed nonzero potential means a fixed ratio of distances, hence coaxial families of circular cylinders parallel to z. The zero-potential surface is the plane \(x=0\).

The appropriate equivalent line charges lie at \(x=\pm4a\). Their distance ratio on each surface is 3 or 1/3, and \(\lambda=\pi\epsilon_0V_0/\ln3\). In the exterior, \[V=\frac{V_0}{4\ln3}\ln\frac{(x-4a)^2+y^2}{(x+4a)^2+y^2}.\] Inside the left cylinder \(V=+V_0/2\), inside the right \(V=-V_0/2\). The line-charge expression must not be continued into the metal.

nodes.alt: Original two-line-charge construction of a cylindrical equipotential surface with distances l1 and l2.

children.text: The charge on the positive cylinder is \(\lambda l\), so \[C=\pi\epsilon_0l/\ln3.\]
The stationary potential obeys the same Laplace problem. Since \(\mathbf j=\sigma\mathbf E\), its flux is \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) times electric displacement flux. Thus \[I=\pi\sigma lV_0/\ln3.\]
Geometry cancels: \(RC=\epsilon_0/\sigma\), the dielectric relaxation time.

Translational symmetry gives an axial field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf z}\). Ampere's law yields \(\partial_yB_z=\mu_0j_x\) and \(\partial_xB_z=-\mu_0j_y\). In the central strip \(|x|<a\), with the source's symmetry \(B_z(x,0)=0\), \[B_z=\frac{\mu_0\sigma V_0}{2\ln3}\left[\arctan\frac y{4a+x}+\arctan\frac y{4a-x}\right].\] A rectangular Ampere loop symmetric about \(y=0\) gives the same result by integrating \(j_x\) across it. Away from this strip, continue the angular functions on the appropriate exterior branches rather than blindly using principal arctangents. A physical finite cylinder and its battery leads require the return-current geometry, omitted by the ideal edge-free model. The source's unqualified principal-arctangent formula is therefore used only in its valid central region here.

statement.text:
Physics of Spin
Use the classical analogue \(\dot{\mathbf L}=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B\), \(\boldsymbol\mu=-\gamma\mathbf L\), with γ>0. All frequencies in this problem are angular frequencies. A frame S′ rotates about z at +ω, with axes coincident with laboratory axes at t=0. The derivative rule is \((d\mathbf A/dt)_{lab}=(d\mathbf A/dt)_{rot}+\omega\hat z\times\mathbf A\). In part C an ensemble has Nup+Ndown=N and axial magnetization M=(Nup−Ndown)μ=Nμz. Initially all moments point along +z. The later measurement thought experiment uses its stated uncertainty estimate Δpx Δx≳ħ and its convention |μx|=|μz|=γħ.
a.1. Conserved moment and angle
Prove that |μ| is constant for any magnetic field. For stationary B show that its angle with μ is constant.
a.2. Larmor frequency
For B=B0 zhat find ω0 and its precession sense.
b.1. Effective rotating-frame field
Show that \((d\boldsymbol\mu/dt)_{rot}=-\gamma\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B_{eff}\), and find Beff.
b.2. Detuning in rotating frame
For static B=B0 zhat find the signed rotating-frame precession Δ in terms of ω0 and ω.
b.3. Co-rotating applied field
Add b(t)=b[cos(ωt)xhat+sin(ωt)yhat]. Derive the rotating-frame precession speed Ω.
b.4. Counter-rotating field
Instead add b[cos(ωt)xhat−sin(ωt)yhat]. Find Beff in S′ and its time average.
c.1. Rotating-wave approximation
Apply B=B0 zhat+2b cos(ω0t)xhat, with b≪B0 and ω=ω0=γB0. Show the approximate effective field and find Ω.
c.2. Magnetization oscillation
Find the angle α between the moment and the resonant effective field and prove M(t)=Nμ cos(Ωt).
c.3. Rabi populations
Find and plot Pup(t),Pdown(t) on the same axes.
d.1. Resolving the spin beams

A silver beam travels along −y. A first z-biased Stern-Gerlach region and screen SC1 at distance D prepare +z moments. The screen opening has width Δx. The next x-biased region exerts Fx=μx C, with μx=±γħ. If the flight time after SC1 is t, show the condition needed to distinguish the two x beams.
d.2. Loss of axial-spin information
The second region has Bx=B0+Cx. Show that resolving μx causes a large spread in precession angle and destroys the prepared μz information in this model.

children.text: \(\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=-\gamma\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B\). Therefore \(d\mu^2/dt=2\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=0\). If B is fixed, \(d(\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B)/dt=0\) also. Both magnitudes and their dot product are fixed, so the angle is fixed.
\(\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=\gamma\mathbf B\times\boldsymbol\mu\), so the angular velocity vector is +γB0 zhat and \(\omega_0=\gamma B_0\).

Subtract frame rotation from the lab derivative. Since \(-\omega\hat z\times\boldsymbol\mu=\omega\boldsymbol\mu\times\hat z\), the effective field is \(\mathbf B_{eff}=\mathbf B-(\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\).
The signed axial angular velocity is \(\Delta=\omega_0-\omega\). Its nonnegative speed is |Δ|. The sign records the direction of relative rotation.
The rotating field is constant along x′. Thus \(\mathbf B_{eff}=b\hat x^{\prime}+(B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\) and \[\Omega=\gamma\sqrt{(B_0-\omega/\gamma)^2+b^2}.\]

The field rotates at −2ω in S′: \[\mathbf B_{eff}=(B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}+b[\cos2\omega t\,\hat x^{\prime}-\sin2\omega t\,\hat y^{\prime}].\] Averaging a full rotation leaves only \((B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\).

Split the linear oscillation into equal co- and counter-rotating fields. On resonance the static axial effective field cancels. The counter-rotating piece oscillates at 2ω0, much faster than γb, so its leading average vanishes. Thus \(\mathbf B_{eff}\simeq b\hat x^{\prime}\), \(\Omega=\gamma b\).
Initially μ is along z and Beff is along x′, so α=π/2 and remains fixed. Rotation about x′ gives \(\mu_z=\mu\cos\Omega t\). Since z′=z, the measured axial magnetization is \(M=N\mu\cos\Omega t\).
Solve Pup+Pdown=1 and Pup−Pdown=M/(Nμ): \[P_{up}=\cos^2(\Omega t/2),\qquad P_{down}=\sin^2(\Omega t/2).\] They are complementary, have period 2π/Ω, and exchange populations at t=π/Ω. At t=0 Pup=1.

Uncertainty gives transverse velocity spread \(\Delta v_x\gtrsim\hbar/(m\Delta x)\), so width grows by roughly ħt/(mΔx). Opposite forces separate the beam centres by \(d_x=|\mu_x|Ct^2/m\). Resolution requires \[|\mu_x|C\Delta x\,t/\hbar\gg1.\]

Field variation is ΔB=CΔx, giving \(\Delta\omega=\gamma C\Delta x=(|\mu_x|/\hbar)C\Delta x\). The resolution condition therefore implies Δωt≫1. The ensemble acquires a broad spread of rotations around x, so its original definite z projection is lost. This gives the intended incompatibility argument under the stated semiclassical estimate.

solution.text:
Physics of Spin
a.1. Conserved moment and angle
\(\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=-\gamma\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B\). Therefore \(d\mu^2/dt=2\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=0\). If B is fixed, \(d(\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B)/dt=0\) also. Both magnitudes and their dot product are fixed, so the angle is fixed.
a.2. Larmor frequency
\(\dot{\boldsymbol\mu}=\gamma\mathbf B\times\boldsymbol\mu\), so the angular velocity vector is +γB0 zhat and \(\omega_0=\gamma B_0\).
b.1. Effective rotating-frame field
Subtract frame rotation from the lab derivative. Since \(-\omega\hat z\times\boldsymbol\mu=\omega\boldsymbol\mu\times\hat z\), the effective field is \(\mathbf B_{eff}=\mathbf B-(\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\).
b.2. Detuning in rotating frame
The signed axial angular velocity is \(\Delta=\omega_0-\omega\). Its nonnegative speed is |Δ|. The sign records the direction of relative rotation.
b.3. Co-rotating applied field
The rotating field is constant along x′. Thus \(\mathbf B_{eff}=b\hat x^{\prime}+(B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\) and \[\Omega=\gamma\sqrt{(B_0-\omega/\gamma)^2+b^2}.\]
b.4. Counter-rotating field
The field rotates at −2ω in S′: \[\mathbf B_{eff}=(B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}+b[\cos2\omega t\,\hat x^{\prime}-\sin2\omega t\,\hat y^{\prime}].\] Averaging a full rotation leaves only \((B_0-\omega/\gamma)\hat z^{\prime}\).
c.1. Rotating-wave approximation
Split the linear oscillation into equal co- and counter-rotating fields. On resonance the static axial effective field cancels. The counter-rotating piece oscillates at 2ω0, much faster than γb, so its leading average vanishes. Thus \(\mathbf B_{eff}\simeq b\hat x^{\prime}\), \(\Omega=\gamma b\).
c.2. Magnetization oscillation
Initially μ is along z and Beff is along x′, so α=π/2 and remains fixed. Rotation about x′ gives \(\mu_z=\mu\cos\Omega t\). Since z′=z, the measured axial magnetization is \(M=N\mu\cos\Omega t\).
c.3. Rabi populations
Solve Pup+Pdown=1 and Pup−Pdown=M/(Nμ): \[P_{up}=\cos^2(\Omega t/2),\qquad P_{down}=\sin^2(\Omega t/2).\] They are complementary, have period 2π/Ω, and exchange populations at t=π/Ω. At t=0 Pup=1.
d.1. Resolving the spin beams
Uncertainty gives transverse velocity spread \(\Delta v_x\gtrsim\hbar/(m\Delta x)\), so width grows by roughly ħt/(mΔx). Opposite forces separate the beam centres by \(d_x=|\mu_x|Ct^2/m\). Resolution requires \[|\mu_x|C\Delta x\,t/\hbar\gg1.\]
d.2. Loss of axial-spin information
Field variation is ΔB=CΔx, giving \(\Delta\omega=\gamma C\Delta x=(|\mu_x|/\hbar)C\Delta x\). The resolution condition therefore implies Δωt≫1. The ensemble acquires a broad spread of rotations around x, so its original definite z projection is lost. This gives the intended incompatibility argument under the stated semiclassical estimate.

statement.text:
The Drag on a Falling Magnet
A clear and detailed discussion of eddy currents was first provided by the British physicist Sir James H. Jeans (1877–1946) in The mathematical theory of electricity and magnetism (1925). The present problem is based on electricity and magnetism.


A small magnet with dipole moment of magnitude \(p\) and mass \(m\) is dropped through a very long vertically held non-magnetic metallic tube as shown in Figure 1, which is not to scale. In general the fall is governed by
\[m\ddot z=mg-k\dot z.\tag{1}\]
Here \(g\) is gravitational acceleration. The damping parameter \(k\) is due to the generation of eddy currents in the tube.
I.1 (0.5 point)

I.2 (1.0 point)

solution.text:
Detailed answer and grading scheme
I.1
The equation of motion is \(m\ddot z=mg-k\dot z\). At terminal velocity \(\ddot z=0\) (0.2 mark), giving
\[v_T=\dot z=\frac{mg}{k}.\]
Terminal velocity: 0.3 mark.
I.2
\[\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{m}v(t),\qquad v(0)=z(0)=0,\]
\[v(t)=\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-kt/m})=\frac{dz}{dt}.\]
Velocity: 0.5 mark. Integrating
\[\int_0^z dz=\int_0^t\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-kt/m})\,dt,\qquad z(t)=\frac{mg}{k}\left[t+\frac{m}{k}(e^{-kt/m}-1)\right].\]
Position: 0.5 mark.
I.3. Method I
Because of the relative speed \(v\) between the magnet and ring in the magnet's field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf k}+B_\rho\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}\), the induced emf is
\[e_i=\int(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=vB_a\,2\pi a,\]
The integral and substitution receive 0.8 and 0.4 mark, respectively, where
\[B_a=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3pa(z_0-z)}{[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\tag{2}\]
Field expression: 0.3 mark.
I.3. Method II
The magnetic flux through the ring is
\[\phi=\int_0^a B_z\,2\pi\rho\,d\rho=2\pi\int_0^a\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\rho p}{[\rho^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{3/2}}\left[\frac{3(z_0-z)^2}{\rho^2+(z_0-z)^2}-1\right]d\rho,\]
\[\phi=\frac{\mu_0pa^2}{2[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{3/2}},\qquad e_i=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}=-v\frac{d\phi}{dz},\]
\[e_i=\frac{3\mu_0pa^2v(z_0-z)}{2[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\]
The flux integral, its substitution, integrated flux, Faraday-law step, and final emf receive 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.4 mark. The source prints a signed expression while the question requests a magnitude. Magnitudes use absolute values when the magnet has passed the ring.
I.4
The \(B_z\) component causes radially outward forces on the ring, with zero net force by symmetry (0.4 mark). Only \(B_\rho\) contributes
\[d\mathbf f_{\mathrm{em}}=i(d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B),\qquad |\mathbf f_{\mathrm{em}}|=i\,2\pi aB_a,\]
where \(B_a\) is given by Eq. (2). Force: 0.6 mark.
I.5
By Newton's third law, the ring exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet. Its magnitude is \(f_{\mathrm{em}}\) (0.5 mark).
I.6
\[e_i=L\frac{di}{dt}+iR.\]
Circuit equation: 0.5 mark.
I.7
Potential energy is converted into kinetic energy \(mv^2/2\) (0.3 mark), magnetic energy \(Li^2/2\) (0.3 mark), and Joule heat \(\int_0^t i(t^{\prime})^2R\,dt^{\prime}\) accumulated up to time \(t\) (0.4 mark).
I.8
The source ticks No (0.5 mark), referring to the microscopic magnetic Lorentz force: it is perpendicular to each charge velocity. The magnet nevertheless loses mechanical energy through the macroscopic braking force. Induced electric fields transfer energy into the circuit and Joule heating, so No does not mean there is no energy transfer from the falling magnet.
I.9
\[\Delta R=\frac{2\pi a}{\sigma w\Delta z'}.\]
Ring resistance: 0.5 mark.
I.10
For one ring at \(z'\), the force is \(f_{\mathrm{em}}=(2\pi a)iB'_a\), where
\[B'_a=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3pa(z'-z)}{[a^2+(z'-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\]
Field: 0.3 mark. The induced current is
\[i=\frac{e_i}{\Delta R}=\frac{\sigma we_i}{2\pi a}\Delta z'.\]
Current: 0.5 mark. Therefore the force from the entire pipe is
\[F=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{\mathrm{em}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(B'_a)^2(2\pi a)w\sigma\,dz'\,\dot z.\]
Force integral: 0.2 mark. For the very long pipe the limits can be taken as infinite. Substitution gives
\[F=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2 18p^2a^3\pi w\sigma\dot z\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{(z'-z)^2}{[(z'-z)^2+a^2]^5}\,dz'.\]
Substitution: 0.5 mark. Let \(u=(z'-z)/a\). This is the opposite sign to the variable defined in the question, which leaves this even integral unchanged.
\[F=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2\frac{18p^2\pi\sigma w\dot z}{a^4}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^2}{(1+u^2)^5}\,du,\]
\[k=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2\frac{18p^2\pi\sigma w}{a^4}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^2}{(1+u^2)^5}\,du.\]
Damping parameter: 0.5 mark.
I.11
Given \(k=f(\mu_0,p,R_0,a)\), the dimensions are
\[[\mu_0]=I^{-2}MLT^{-2},\quad[p]=IL^2,\quad[R_0]=I^{-2}ML^2T^{-3},\quad[a]=L,\quad[k]=MT^{-1}.\]
The first three dimension statements receive 0.2, 0.1, and 0.2 mark. They give
\[k=\frac{p^2\mu_0^2}{a^4R_0}.\]
Final expression: 0.5 mark.

children.text: This problem deals with the two beam phenomena associated with light, its interference, polarization and superposition. The particular context of the problem was studied by the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam (1934-1969).

nodes.alt: Original portrait and caption of the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam, 1934-1969.

children.text: Consider the experimental set up as shown in Fig. (1). Two coherent monochromatic light beams (marked as beam 1 and 2), travelling in the \(z\) direction, are incident on two narrow slits and separated by a distance \(d\) (\(S_1S_2=d\)). After passing through the slits the two beams interfere and the pattern is observed on the screen \(S\). The distance between the slits and the screen is \(D\) and \(D\gg d\). Assume that the width of each slit \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is much smaller than the wavelength of light.

nodes.alt: Figure 1. Two coherent beams travel along z through slits S1 and S2 separated by d. Screen S is a distance D away. Theta is measured from the z direction for the outgoing rays.

children.text: III.1. Two linearly polarized beams (1.0 point)
Let the beams 1 and 2 be linearly polarized at \(z=0\). The corresponding electric field vectors are given by

where \(\hat i\) is the unit vector along the x-axis, \(\omega\) is angular frequency of light and \(E_0\) is the amplitude. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen where \(\theta\) is the angle shown in Fig. (1). Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\), where \(c\) is the speed of light. Also, note that the intensity is proportional to the time average of the square of the electric field. Here you may take the proportionality constant to be \(\beta\). You may ignore the attenuation in the magnitude of the electric fields with distance from the slits to any point on the screen.

A perfectly transparent glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) is introduced in the path of beam 1 before the slits. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c,\omega,\mu\) and \(w\).

An optical device (known as quarter wave plate (QWP)) is introduced in the path of beam 1, before the slits, replacing the glass slab. This device changes the polarization of the beam from the linear polarization state \(\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)\) to a circular polarization state which is given by
\[\vec E_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}[\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)+\hat j E_0\sin(\omega t)].\tag{2}\]

Here \(\hat j\) is the unit vector along the y-axis. Assume that the device does not introduce any additional path difference and that it is perfectly transparent. Note that the tip of the electric field vector traces a circle as time elapses and hence, the beam is said to be circularly polarized. We assume that the angle \(\theta\) is small enough so that intensity from slit one does not depend on the angle \(\theta\) even for \(\hat j\) polarization.
III.3.a. Find the expression for the intensity \(I(\theta)\) of the light that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\).
III.3.b. What is the maximum intensity \(I_{\max}\)?
III.3.c. What is the minimum intensity \(I_{\min}\)?

nodes.alt: Figure 2. Beam 1 passes a quarter wave plate at z=a, polarizer I between a and b, and polarizer II between b and c before slit S1. Beam 2 travels directly to slit S2.

children.text: Now consider the experimental setup (see Fig. (2)) in which beam 1 is subjected to the device (QWP) described in part 3 and a linear polarizer (marked as I), between \(z=a\) and \(z=b\), which allows only the component of the electric field parallel to an axis \(\hat i'\) to pass through. The unit vector \(\hat i'\) is defined as

Another linear polarizer (marked as II) between \(z=b\) and \(z=c\) polarizes the beam back to \(\hat i\) direction. Thus beam 1 is back to its original state of polarization. Assume that the polarizers do not introduce any path difference and are perfectly transparent.
III.4.a. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the first polarizer at \(z=b\), \(\vec E_1(z=b)\).
III.4.b. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the second polarizer at \(z=c\), \(\vec E_1(z=c)\).
III.4.c. What is the phase difference \(\alpha\) between the two beams at the slits?

The most general type of polarization is elliptical polarization. A convenient way of expressing elliptical polarization is to consider it as a superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized components, i.e.
\[\vec E=\hat i'E_0\cos e\cos(\omega t)+\hat j'E_0\sin e\sin(\omega t),\tag{3}\]
where \(\hat i'\) and \(\hat j'\) and this state of polarization are depicted in Fig. 3.

nodes.alt: Figure 3. The electric-field tip traces an ellipse with principal axes i-prime and j-prime. The semiaxes are E0 cos e and E0 sin e, and the principal frame is rotated relative to i and j.

children.text: The tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse as time elapses. Here \(e\) represents the ellipticity and is given by \(\tan e=\text{Semi-minor axis of the ellipse}/\text{Semi-major axis of the ellipse}\).

Linear polarization (Eqs. (1)) and circular polarization (Eq. (2)) are special cases of elliptical polarization (Eq. (3)). The two parameters \(\gamma\in[0,\pi]\) and \(e\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]\) completely describe the state of polarization.

The polarization state can also be represented by a point on a sphere of unit radius called the Poincare sphere. The polarization of the beam described in Eq. (3) is represented by a point \(P\) on the Poincare sphere (see Fig. 4), then latitude \(\angle PCD=2e\) and longitude \(\angle ACD=2\gamma\). Here \(C\) is the center.

nodes.alt: Figure 4. Unit Poincare sphere centered at C. ACD is the longitude 2 gamma and DCP is the latitude 2 e of polarization point P. D lies on the equator beneath P.

children.text: Consider a point on the equator of the Poincare sphere. III.5.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm Eq}\) corresponding to this point. III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?
Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere. III.6.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm NP}\) corresponding to this point. III.6.b. What is its state of polarization?

Now consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at \(z=0\)) be represented by a point \(A_1\) on the Poincare sphere, after the optical device let the state (at \(z=a\)) be represented by point \(A_2\), and after the first polarizer (say, at \(z=b\)) let the state be represented by point \(A_3\). At \(z=c\), the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by \(A_1\). Locate these points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\)) on the Poincare sphere.

If these three points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\) from part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere. The phase difference \(\alpha\) obtained in part 4 and the area \(S\) of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate \(S\) to \(\alpha\).
This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.

Two coherent monochromatic light beams (marked as beam 1 and 2), travelling in the \(z\) direction, are incident on two narrow slits and separated by a distance \(d\) (\(S_1S_2=d\)). After passing through the slits the two beams interfere and the pattern is observed on the screen \(S\). The distance between the slits and the screen is \(D\) and \(D\gg d\). Assume that the width of each slit \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is much smaller than the wavelength of light.

III.1. Two linearly polarized beams (1.0 point)
Let the beams 1 and 2 be linearly polarized at \(z=0\). The corresponding electric field vectors are given by
\[\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t),\tag{1a}\]
\[\vec E_2=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t),\tag{1b}\]
where \(\hat i\) is the unit vector along the x-axis, \(\omega\) is angular frequency of light and \(E_0\) is the amplitude. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen where \(\theta\) is the angle shown in Fig. (1). Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\), where \(c\) is the speed of light. Also, note that the intensity is proportional to the time average of the square of the electric field. Here you may take the proportionality constant to be \(\beta\). You may ignore the attenuation in the magnitude of the electric fields with distance from the slits to any point on the screen.
III.2. Glass slab (1.0 point)
A perfectly transparent glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) is introduced in the path of beam 1 before the slits. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c,\omega,\mu\) and \(w\).
III.3. Quarter wave plate (2.0 points)
An optical device (known as quarter wave plate (QWP)) is introduced in the path of beam 1, before the slits, replacing the glass slab. This device changes the polarization of the beam from the linear polarization state \(\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)\) to a circular polarization state which is given by
\[\vec E_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}[\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)+\hat j E_0\sin(\omega t)].\tag{2}\]
Here \(\hat j\) is the unit vector along the y-axis. Assume that the device does not introduce any additional path difference and that it is perfectly transparent. Note that the tip of the electric field vector traces a circle as time elapses and hence, the beam is said to be circularly polarized. We assume that the angle \(\theta\) is small enough so that intensity from slit one does not depend on the angle \(\theta\) even for \(\hat j\) polarization.
III.3.a. Find the expression for the intensity \(I(\theta)\) of the light that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\).
III.3.b. What is the maximum intensity \(I_{\max}\)?
III.3.c. What is the minimum intensity \(I_{\min}\)?
III.4. Two polarizers (2.0 points)

Now consider the experimental setup (see Fig. (2)) in which beam 1 is subjected to the device (QWP) described in part 3 and a linear polarizer (marked as I), between \(z=a\) and \(z=b\), which allows only the component of the electric field parallel to an axis \(\hat i'\) to pass through. The unit vector \(\hat i'\) is defined as
\[\hat i'=\hat i\cos\gamma+\hat j\sin\gamma.\]
Another linear polarizer (marked as II) between \(z=b\) and \(z=c\) polarizes the beam back to \(\hat i\) direction. Thus beam 1 is back to its original state of polarization. Assume that the polarizers do not introduce any path difference and are perfectly transparent.
III.4.a. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the first polarizer at \(z=b\), \(\vec E_1(z=b)\).
III.4.b. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the second polarizer at \(z=c\), \(\vec E_1(z=c)\).
III.4.c. What is the phase difference \(\alpha\) between the two beams at the slits?
The most general type of polarization is elliptical polarization. A convenient way of expressing elliptical polarization is to consider it as a superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized components, i.e.
\[\vec E=\hat i'E_0\cos e\cos(\omega t)+\hat j'E_0\sin e\sin(\omega t),\tag{3}\]
where \(\hat i'\) and \(\hat j'\) and this state of polarization are depicted in Fig. 3.

The tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse as time elapses. Here \(e\) represents the ellipticity and is given by \(\tan e=\text{Semi-minor axis of the ellipse}/\text{Semi-major axis of the ellipse}\).
Linear polarization (Eqs. (1)) and circular polarization (Eq. (2)) are special cases of elliptical polarization (Eq. (3)). The two parameters \(\gamma\in[0,\pi]\) and \(e\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]\) completely describe the state of polarization.
The polarization state can also be represented by a point on a sphere of unit radius called the Poincare sphere. The polarization of the beam described in Eq. (3) is represented by a point \(P\) on the Poincare sphere (see Fig. 4), then latitude \(\angle PCD=2e\) and longitude \(\angle ACD=2\gamma\). Here \(C\) is the center.

III.5. Equator (0.5 point)
Consider a point on the equator of the Poincare sphere. III.5.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm Eq}\) corresponding to this point. III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?
III.6. North pole (0.5 point)
Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere. III.6.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm NP}\) corresponding to this point. III.6.b. What is its state of polarization?
III.7. Polarization cycle (1.5 points)
Now consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at \(z=0\)) be represented by a point \(A_1\) on the Poincare sphere, after the optical device let the state (at \(z=a\)) be represented by point \(A_2\), and after the first polarizer (say, at \(z=b\)) let the state be represented by point \(A_3\). At \(z=c\), the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by \(A_1\). Locate these points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\)) on the Poincare sphere.
III.8. Geometric phase (1.5 points)
If these three points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\) from part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere. The phase difference \(\alpha\) obtained in part 4 and the area \(S\) of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate \(S\) to \(\alpha\).
This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.
